title: Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?
title_en: Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?

inline_images.caption: Global Editorial Director of WIRED Katie Drummond and Senior Correspondent at WIRED Lauren Goode.
inline_images.alt: Global Editorial Director of WIRED Katie Drummond and Senior Correspondent at WIRED Lauren Goode.

author: Wired AI
article_content:
These thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the company is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy.

WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions. She also spent last week breaking news about his downfall, despite being in Europe on vacation. (Sorry, Lauren. You can have those PTO days back.) So at the end of a very long week for WIRED’s newsroom, I called Lauren to talk about what she makes of Huang’s ouster, what it means for AI, and where this all goes next. We also made a bet about Huang’s future—one involving a meal he recently made semi-famous.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: Lauren, first of all, thank you for your tirelessness these past few days. The last time I saw you, we were both in Miami for WIRED’s big event, and you were getting on a red-eye that night to go to Europe for vacation, which didn’t exactly go as planned. When you saw that first story about Jensen’s affair on Sunday, what did you think? What went through your mind?

LAUREN GOODE: Oof. The story first started bubbling up a while ago because The New York Times, and a lot of credit is due to The New York Times here, first reported on Nvidia’s relationship, if you want to call it that, with this company Megaspeed, back in the fall of 2025.

It was a very unusual story. And for some reason it just didn’t capture the attention of people the way that more recent reporting that we and others have been doing has.

Anyone who’s sort of been paying attention to that story, or had some sources in the industry, were starting to hear things. But the fact that the affair with this person, who goes by Alice Huang, was confirmed, that’s the kind of story that always captures people’s attention in a different way.

There are few things people love to read about more than extramarital affairs, especially when they involve powerful people. The reason it wasn’t surprising to you, was it because of that previous reporting and what you had been hearing here and there? Or was there another reason that you saw that story and thought, “OK, actually some of this is not shocking to me”?

It was both. I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but in the fall of 2024 we were doing a WIRED outing, a few of us hanging out, and we started chatting about whether or not we thought a lot of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley had girlfriends or extramarital affairs or situations. Because there are some people in Silicon Valley who are actually quite open about that. I remember us talking about it at the time, and there’s part of me that always kind of assumes that there are elements of their personal lives that we’re never going to have a full window into.

Not that we were talking about Jensen that evening, but it’s always been in my mind. Then, yes, I think being on the ground in Silicon Valley, you often hear things. But a lot of times there’s a certain threshold that things have to cross in order for us as journalists to consider something reportable or something worth chasing down as reportable.

I think an important distinction is that people cheat, people have affairs all the time, Silicon Valley or otherwise.

What tips this over into newsworthiness is, A) the Chinese espionage of it all, and B) the affair with a subordinate.

You reported that Jensen’s resignation—which really, to be clear, is the board of Nvidia ousting him—probably had more to do with the alleged affair with a subordinate than this other extramarital relationship, which is tied up in espionage allegations. A source told you this. Can you explain why that affair would tip the balance for the board?

I just think it’s important to note that this doesn’t seem like it was simply a moral decision. Someone had posted on X that “I can't believe the board caved to moral pressure.” To me, this doesn’t seem like it’s a moral issue.

I think if you’re looking at the three things that could have led to serious scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s behavior, there’s: One, extramarital affairs. Two, alleged extramarital affairs with subordinates within his own company. And three, an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese operative, which puts Jensen Huang in this position where the board and the investigators who are looking into this are trying to determine what he knew and when he knew it, and basically whether he was aware of the fact that chips were making their way into China.

This isn’t just about the fact that someone had a girlfriend outside of their marriage. I think what is still to be revealed here could in fact be very, very serious in nature.

Now, you also reported on Monday, in a fantastic scoop for WIRED, that Jensen hired a crisis comms firm a year ago. In October 2025 he hired a fixer, Risa Heller, who is very well known for working with high-profile men who are facing allegations of sexual misconduct, among other things. I’m talking about Anthony Weiner, Mario Batali, writer Jeffrey Toobin. Tell us a little bit about that story and what you found out.

I really feel like with everything else going on this week, I could have gone without ever hearing about all of those stories again.

Oh, you don't want to hear about Anthony Weiner all the time?

No, it turns out. I had kind of forgotten that. I was like, “I think I blocked that from my memory.” And Jeff Toobin—what a throwback.

But this firm, it’s a really interesting firm run by this woman named Risa Heller. They have offices in New York and LA, and yes, they have this reputation for dealing with a lot of sexual misconduct cases, as well as other types of corporate and personal PR needs for high-profile people.

A source had told me a while ago, and I'm not gonna timestamp it, but a while ago that it had been rumored that Jensen Huang had hired this firm. So immediately my antenna went up, and I was like, “Wait, what?”

I thought it was curious, but I didn’t know exactly what the nature of the contract was or when they had been hired, and then eventually through more reporting, I was able to get confirmation of some of the details.

What we know is that this firm, Heller, started working with Jensen Huang sometime in 2025, and ostensibly, Huang and his family had hired Heller for their own personal PR outside of Nvidia's walls. This is because when you’re someone like Jensen Huang, you have a lot going on. You have a family office. You do a lot of work with philanthropy. You’re hosting personal events. He’s also been grooming his adult children to take over these higher profile roles within Nvidia, so some of the PR might have ostensibly been to work on creating more of a public-facing image for his kids.

We do know, though, based on more reporting, that as of October 2025, and then closer to the end of the year, Nvidia’s internal teams had been instructed to start looping this outside crisis firm, Heller, into all press inquiries, all communications related to Jensen.

That was definitely a change from the prior terms of his working relationship with Heller, and also timing-wise coincided with that first New York Times story I mentioned. I think that it was published on October 9th, 2025, and first highlighted Megaspeed and what appeared to be a very close relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang.

I can’t decide if he should get his money back for hiring this crisis comms firm, because this crisis has certainly not been contained, or if the fact that this is now coming up a year later suggests that maybe they did their job quite well for a while.

Well, first of all, I don’t think he needs the money back.

… on how his assets get divided, yes. Or if maybe they won’t divorce. You know, it’s also a very Silicon Valley thing not to necessarily do that.

I also think it’s possible that Jensen himself was not totally upfront with this firm when he hired them. Or, if they knew something was up, they may not have known all of the details. So if that is the case, hypothetically, then you can’t necessarily do everything you would typically do in terms of reputation management. TL;DR, it didn’t work out so well for him in the end.

No, things are not going well for Jensen. Now, Nvidia has named an interim CEO to replace him. Surprise, surprise, to both of us and women everywhere, she’s a woman.

What do we know about Colette Kress, who is the interim CEO of Nvidia?

Well, we know that when we emailed Jensen this summer to say, “Hey, Jensen, who do you think the most powerful women in Silicon Valley are?” He didn't mention Colette. Jensen mentioned Dina Powell from Meta and Ruth Porat from Google, both really high-ranking women, presidents of those companies.

And then [SpaceX president and COO] Gwynne Shotwell, because I prompted him. But no Colette, and that struck me as interesting at the time, too, though I didn’t press him on that. And then we did end up giving Colette a nod in our big feature that we did about high-ranking women in Silicon Valley.

Colette has been with Nvidia since 2013. Prior to that, she worked at Cisco, Microsoft. She’s CFO. She’s a financial whiz. She’s the person who appears on earnings calls with him every quarter.

She actually does a lot of the speaking, because she’s a person who has really, really deep knowledge of Nvidia’s complex financials. She’s the person who gives guidance for the next quarter. She’s CFO of arguably the world’s most important company. I think it makes sense that she would be slotted into this role.

Nvidia doesn’t really have a traditional hierarchy. They don’t have a traditional chief operating officer, for example. You know, when Steve Jobs was at the end of his tenure and he was very sick, Tim Cook, who was the operations whiz at Apple for many years prior, was basically groomed to be the CEO.

Nvidia doesn’t have someone like that. So it makes sense for now that Colette is the person who would slot in, because part of Nvidia’s goal has to be, at this point, easing the stock market. I don’t know if you've been following, but, I mean, it’s pretty bad out there.

I would say that, against my will, I am seeing a lot about Nvidia stock not doing well. I have not looked at my 401(k). I try really hard not to because I’m a control freak, and I simply cannot control how many affairs this man is having and what impact that has on my finances.

These things, though, help paint a picture of Jensen’s character and the way he ran the company. The fact that Nvidia did not do succession planning. There was no hierarchy; he had dozens of direct reports. There was no successor waiting in the wings. What do those things combined tell us about Jensen and Nvidia?

As I understand it, Katie, even you have had to do a succession plan, right?

Yes, without revealing too many details, Condé Nast, like most normal companies, has people in senior leadership roles do succession planning. They take it really seriously. It’s an annual exercise that we do, and my understanding is that that is very par for the course at most companies, at any company, and particularly a company of Nvidia’s stature and importance on a global scale. The idea that there would not be a formal succession plan is shocking to me.

It is shocking, and it’s shocking not just from the perspective that Jensen perhaps didn’t do that or didn’t have a super well-formulated one, but that the board wouldn’t demand that. I’ve heard a few different theories floated as to why this is. One theory is that Jensen may have had a lot of the insecurities that come with being a cofounder, CEO, someone who’s been living and breathing this company, his baby, since 1993, and not necessarily wanting to stuff the ranks with people who are just as capable, if not more capable in some measures, than himself, right?

Like you don’t create an environment in which someone could theoretically replace you that easily. So that’s one theory. The other theory is that—and Jensen himself has said this, both to me and other people in interviews too—he truly believed that keeping a flat org was better for the flow of information, that once you start to create a structure that’s too hierarchical, then any kind of changes that happen in the company, any kind of new information that comes out, even in some kind of white paper, fundamentally changes the direction of the way the industry is going.

I mean, think about the way people inside the AI industry probably reacted when they first saw the famous Transformer paper in 2017 and said, “Oh my gosh, this is going to change everything.” If you’re a big, fat, bloated, slow organization, you’re probably five years behind on your AI strategy. If you’re lean at the top, you can basically say, “Let’s go. We’re going in this direction now,” and you won’t encounter a lot of barriers to doing that. So that helps explain the flat org. It doesn’t necessarily explain the lack of a succession plan.

The third theory that’s been floated to me is that maybe in some, I don’t know, alternate universe, he really did think that his children, one of his two children, who are both working within Nvidia, would one day be the inevitable successors.

Again, we’re coming back to this theme of control. I’m curious to hear a little bit more about that observation, this idea of Jensen as fixated on storytelling and the stories that were told about Nvidia and about AI.

That particular interview was July of 2024, and Nvidia had invited me to interview Jensen again at the SIGGRAPH Conference in Denver, which is this whole confab of computer graphics nerds. It’s a really fun conference.

During the preparation for it, when I got on the call with some Nvidia comms executives, Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter, appeared on the call and she basically took the lead and said, “Here’s this cluster of slides that when you’re on stage, Jensen’s going to be referencing, and he’s gonna have a lot to say about each slide, and it would be great if you could tee him up at this point.”

And I said, “Well, wait a second. This is not a standard journalistic interview. Like, what’s going on here?” The whole thing felt very strange, but I made it clear I planned to ask him the questions I really felt I needed to ask him as a journalist. It was just very clear he did not want to answer a lot of my questions, and that he was going to just own the stage and reference his slides. I remember that he talked about how he made a little Jensen AI of himself, and the crowd was all, “Ha! Jensen AI,” and I was like, “What is happening?”

It was so strange. Afterwards, he did this impromptu Q&A with the crowd. A bunch of people rushed the stage. I could see someone from his PR team being like, “What just happened? What is he doing?” Not standard operating procedure. I thought, wow. It felt to me like Jensen Huang was just riding high on this wave, this AI wave and this incredible success that Nvidia was experiencing and the way the AI industry was growing.

But it occurred to me that he was really, really obsessive with controlling the narrative, and it reminded me of something that he’d said the first time we’d ever spoken, which was that he really admired the CEO of Adobe because he felt that the CEO of Adobe was a very good storyteller, and that he never had a pitch deck when he first pitched Nvidia as a company because he just thought it was better to tell a story.

Storytelling is so important in terms of establishing the culture of a company. He was very good at creating his own story, his own image of himself as this founder CEO who was utterly obsessed with his own company and really passionate about everything.

I guess we know where some of that passion led him.

We do indeed. It’s interesting that you talk about Jensen as a crowd favorite, because he did very much become that. He’s incredibly charismatic. He’s a great public speaker. He can really own a room. He can spin a great yarn. You describe in the cover story about Jensen, that you were “Jensen-pilled” after spending time with him, because he is so compelling.

That was interesting to me this week, in seeing how many leaders in Silicon Valley came out in support of him, despite these very, very troubling allegations, which to be clear, again, go beyond having an affair. This is beyond moral decision-making. Regardless of that, everyone from Elon Musk to Jason Calacanis came out guns blazing for Jensen.

Do you think that speaks to how revered he is in the industry, or do you think that that speaks to the fact that he is mission-critical for the industry’s ongoing growth? Are these defenses of Jensen essentially self-interested on the part of industry leaders?

I don't think they’re all self-interested. There are at least three layers to this, and one is that there are executives and lower-level tech workers who have worked for Jensen directly, and who came away from the experience with not a great taste in their mouths. They left feeling uninspired, and they actually saw a more egotistical side of him that they didn’t like, an obsessive side. There have been stories reported by other outlets about how he has sometimes berated some of his top lieutenants in front of other people. There’s almost a Dr. Jensen and Mr. Huang narrative here. He's got two sides to him. But he’s very smart and almost can come across as sort of mensch-y. I think people really admire him.

Then I think, yes, there are people who probably own Nvidia stock, they’re industry watchers, they’re tech enthusiasts, and they see him perhaps still as a kind of our generation’s rock star who also happens to be keeping the economy afloat with his company.

So there are varying levels of interest there in terms of people who just either wish this didn’t happen, or really wish in some alternate universe he would be reinstated, which would be shocking to me at this point.

I will say WIRED had a great scoop last week, much credit to our amazing journalists, of Nvidia employees who would like to see Jensen back. There is a great deal of reverence for him, in a way that I have to admit gave me acute flashbacks to 2023, when Sam Altman was ousted at OpenAI. Very different circumstances, but yet again, a woman was installed to clean up that mess, and employees revolted and called for Sam to come back. I mean, these allegations are much more significant and serious and consequential. That said, the jury’s still out on whether Jensen makes a comeback in two weeks.

Really? You think there’s a possibility?

Wow. OK. I would be very surprised. We should make a bet.

Oh, Lauren. I was going to say dinner the next time I’m in San Francisco.

Dinner sounds good. Let’s do it. You know what? Whoever loses the bet has to buy dinner at Proposition Chicken, which according to, was it the Daily …?

The Daily Mail reported that Proposition Chicken, which is a slightly elevated fast food chicken place in San Francisco, was being delivered to Jensen Huang’s house in Pacific Heights the other day.

OK. I’m in. Two weeks from today, we will see.

I want to ask you lastly about ripple effects. Nvidia has invested in or bought outright plenty of AI startups. It finances a lot of the build-out happening in this industry. I have been stomping around the New York office all week screaming things like, “The global economy, the global economy!” I mean, this is much bigger than just this company, right? So what are the industry effects that we should all be watching out for from here?

What I’ve heard so far from people is that in the short term—even though we’re seeing this dip right now—there’s still just such incredible demand for Nvidia chips, and they plan everything basically 18 to 24 months out in terms of producing those chips, that I don't think we’ll see any really serious softness in Nvidia in the short term.

But I think that the long tail of Nvidia is going to be interesting, because another CEO could come in with a totally different approach to how Nvidia spends its capital and how it also makes investments in outside companies.

Would a new CEO come in right now and make the kind of investment in CoreWeave or Perplexity, for example, that Jensen decided to? Quite possibly no. Would the new CEO come in and decide to spend so much on, let’s say, Nvidia’s healthcare division? We don’t really know. Would the new CEO come in and be as much of an open source booster as Jensen Huang had become? We don’t really know.

It’s just hard to say. The guys at Hugging Face are probably quite happy that they got in when they did.

Another thing that Jensen had set Nvidia on the path of in the past couple years was really investing in what they’re doing with CPUs as well as GPUs, which is an area that Intel and AMD are in, as well as Arm.

Was that the right path to set the company on, to over-index a little bit on CPUs for now because of the ways that the AI industry is shifting from training on high-powered GPUs to inference computing on slightly lower-powered CPUs? I think it was a smart move, but let’s see how that shakes out.

I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but back in 2008, shortly after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, a venture capitalist at Sequoia sent around a pitch deck to all of that firm’s portfolio companies that became very famous in the industry, and it’s called “RIP Good Times.”

In that pitch deck, this very prescient VC basically laid out all of the things that they wanted their portfolio companies to do, which meant saving a lot of cash. Like, this is a gird-your-loins moment. I think if we see something like that kind of mentality start to develop in Silicon Valley in the coming weeks and months, then I think that’s a very big indication that people are genuinely worried about what this Nvidia tumble means.

I am going to ask you to make one final prediction.

OK. I’m very bad at predictions, by the way, but please.

Two years ago, you said, “Huang is the man of the hour. The year. Maybe even the decade.” I would argue that that decade has been cut short, but I also think that someone like Jensen doesn’t just go quietly into the night. If he’s not reinstalled at Nvidia, and I’m wrong, and I’m buying your chicken in two weeks, where does someone like that go? Where do you expect we will see Jensen pop up in a year, in two years?

There’s a glib answer and it’s either Jensen goes to jail, or Jensen starts a podcast. I’m sure he’s hoping right now it’s the podcast outcome.

Realistically, let’s say that he’s not implicated in the end result of any kind of federal investigation. And let’s say he’s not reinstated. In either case, I don’t think this is the last we’re going to hear from Jensen Huang.

This leadership transition introduces immediate strategic uncertainty for NVIDIA and the global AI hardware supply chain, with the market closely monitoring subsequent corporate governance shifts.

article_content_zh:
这些想法当然是黄仁勋提出的。在完全疯狂的几天里，这位亿万富翁首席执行官兼英伟达联合创始人从一位具有全球影响力的硅谷高管变成了一个教训，告诉你如果想保住工作就不能做什么，以及随之而来的非凡力量。这真是一团糟——对于黄和他的家人来说，当然，对于英伟达来说也是如此，该公司在人工智能行业以及整个全球经济中发挥着重要作用。

《连线》杂志的高级记者 Lauren Goode 多年来一直在报道 Nvidia 和黄仁勋，包括多次采访黄仁勋本人。尽管她正在欧洲度假，但她上周还爆料了有关他倒台的消息。 （对不起，劳伦。你可以把那些 PTO 日子还回去。） 因此，在《连线》新闻编辑室漫长的一周结束时，我打电话给劳伦，谈论她对黄的罢免的看法，这对人工智能意味着什么，以及这一切的下一步发展。我们还对黄的未来打了赌——赌的是他最近半出名的一顿饭。

为了篇幅和清晰度，本次采访经过编辑。

凯蒂·德拉蒙德：劳伦，首先，感谢你过去几天的不懈努力。我上次见你的时候，我们都在迈阿密参加《连线》杂志的大型活动，那天晚上你坐红眼航班去欧洲度假，结果跟计划不太一样。当你在周日看到詹森出轨的第一篇报道时，你是怎么想的？你在想什么？

劳伦·古德： 噢。这个故事不久前就开始流传，因为《纽约时报》在 2025 年秋天首次报道了 Nvidia 与这家公司 Megaspeed 的关系（如果你想这么称呼的话），这在很大程度上要归功于《纽约时报》。

这是一个非常不寻常的故事。由于某种原因，它并没有像我们和其他人最近所做的报道那样吸引人们的注意力。

任何关注这个故事的人，或者在这个行业有一些消息来源的人，都开始听到一些事情。但随着与这个名叫Alice Huang的人的恋情被证实，这样的故事总是能以不同的方式吸引人们的注意力。

没有什么比婚外情更让人们喜欢阅读的了，尤其是当它们涉及有权势的人时。你对此并不感到惊讶，是因为之前的报道以及你到处听到的内容吗？或者是否还有其他原因让您看到这个故事并想：“好吧，实际上其中一些内容并不令我感到震惊”？

两者都是。我不知道你是否还记得，凯蒂，但在 2024 年秋天，我们正在进行一次《连线》郊游，我们几个人出去玩，我们开始讨论我们是否认为硅谷最有权势的人有女朋友或婚外情或情况。因为硅谷有些人对此持开放态度。我记得我们当时谈论过这个问题，我的一部分总是认为他们个人生活中的某些元素是我们永远无法全面了解的。

那天晚上我们并不是在谈论詹森，但它一直在我的脑海里。然后，是的，我认为在硅谷，你经常会听到一些事情。但很多时候，事情必须跨越一定的门槛，作为记者，我们才能认为某件事是值得报道的，或者是值得追究的值得报道的事情。

我认为一个重要的区别是人们会欺骗，人们总是有外遇，无论是在硅谷还是其他地方。

使这件事具有新闻价值的是，A）中国的间谍活动，以及 B）与下属的风流韵事。

你报道说，詹森的辞职——明确地说，是英伟达董事会罢免了他——可能更多地与所谓的与下属的婚外情有关，而不是与间谍指控有关的其他婚外关系。有消息人士告诉你这一点。您能解释一下为什么那件事会打破董事会的平衡吗？

我只是认为重要的是要注意这似乎不仅仅是一个道德决定。有人在 X 上发帖称“我不敢相信董事会屈服于道德压力。”对我来说，这似乎不是一个道德问题。

title: Claude now builds interactive websites inside canvas graphics, reviving the Flash era with real HTML
title_en: Claude now builds interactive websites inside canvas graphics, reviving the Flash era with real HTML
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Claude can now embed text, buttons, and other web elements into complex graphics and 3D effects. Web pages have always faced a tradeoff. Standard HTML elements are clickable, selectable, and readable by screen readers, but they're hard to warp visually. Canvas lets you draw anything you want, but the browser treats it like a flat image. You can't select text or click links inside it. HTML-in-Canvas changes that by placing real page elements inside canvas graphics while keeping them fully interactive.

Felix Rieseberg works on Claude at Anthropic. He wrote on X that Claude can now build "bizarre & beautiful sites" with the feature, adding that it reminds him of the Flash era. A demo page shows 15 examples, including websites rendered as knitting patterns, 3D cubes, or exploded layer views. The content stays as real text you can highlight and copy.

Google is developing HTML-in-Canvas as a web standard that preserves both interactivity and accessibility. The feature works in Chrome and Edge starting with version 157 and in Claude's desktop apps from version 5.11492. Safari and Firefox don't support it yet. Users need to ask Claude for HTML-in-Canvas explicitly in their prompt. Claude keeps getting more creative with visual tasks. Recently, Claude Fable 5.2 painted photorealistic artwork stroke by stroke using self-written Python code.AdAd

title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
title_en: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
author: MIT Tech Review
article_content:
In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

title: Anthropic says the key to agent memory is knowing what to forget, not how much to store
title_en: Anthropic says the key to agent memory is knowing what to forget, not how much to store

inline_images.alt: During "Dreaming," Claude processes old transcripts in idle periods and builds the upper layers of i

author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Anthropic studied how Claude retains knowledge across sessions. Its tests show that selective notes outperform exhaustive archives and that having Claude review its own memories after the fact can correct errors.

Anyone who works with an AI agent on a project over several days hits a wall fast, because every new session starts from scratch. In a research post, Anthropic describes how Claude is supposed to retain knowledge across sessions while the model stays unchanged. Claude writes notes to a folder that it can read back later.

The core problem, according to Anthropic, is selection. Before it knows what comes next, the agent has to decide in the moment what might matter later, so every note is a bet on the future.Ad

In an Anthropic test with Pokémon Red, the older Claude Sonnet 3.7 treated everything as potentially important and, across roughly 10,000 game steps, created 413 files in 225 folders, often a separate one for each battle and item it found. Because the game state keeps changing, the archive goes stale fast. At times, the model did nothing but reorganize its notes instead of playing, and it finished with just a single badge.Ad

The newer Claude Fable 5 limited its memory to a few files and earned four badges. Fable 5 didn't record information already visible on screen and instead wrote down plans, strategies, and rules it had tested. Anthropic's comparison, however, covers only a single playthrough per model.

Anthropic recommends explaining the purpose of memory to Claude and letting the model decide how to use it. In one benchmark, according to Anthropic, rigid instructions such as "only record mistakes" wiped out most of the advantage for stronger models. Older models, by contrast, benefited from clear instructions, such as being told to actually read their notes before every response.Ad

The bigger risk comes from faulty notes that the agent blindly trusts later. Dreaming, an idea that builds on research from Letta and UC Berkeley, is designed to address this. Much like the human brain processes experiences during sleep, Claude goes through transcripts of earlier sessions during a break and checks its notes against them.

In the Pokémon test, Claude had incorrectly noted which side of a mountain a landmark was on. Relying on that faulty note, Claude fell into the same trap three times, eventually wanted to give up, and missed its goal. After a Dreaming pass, Claude caught the error by checking the note against the transcript and found the right path.Ad

According to Anthropic, Dreaming can also organize larger knowledge bases. Claude built a linked wiki from about 350,000 internal documents from Stainless, a software company Anthropic acquired. Dreaming is supposed to generate new pages while fixing gaps, duplicates, and broken links. The payoff was greatest when Claude could combine the wiki with search, so the wiki worked as a complement rather than a replacement.Ad

In a separate legal test by Anthropic, a wiki helped most with questions whose answers were spread across multiple documents. Claude scored 87 percent with the wiki, compared to 73 percent with search alone. For simple lookup tasks, the wiki performed roughly on par with search, and in one case it even grew larger than the source documents.

Anthropic acknowledges that key questions remain open. Taking notes mid-task distracts the agent from its work, Dreaming costs extra compute, and its results arrive only after a delay. Wikis and notes also need regular upkeep, or errors and hallucinations pile up. Anthropic also warns against automatically loading too many memories into every session, because they eat up context and pass any bad note along to every future session.

All of these tests come from Anthropic. The overall takeaway is that a useful agent memory depends less on storing as much as possible than on keeping the right information and correcting mistakes later.

Anthropic introduced Dreaming in May as a research preview for Claude Managed Agents, the company's cloud platform for AI agents. The service reads an existing memory store and up to 100 past sessions, removes duplicate and outdated entries, and creates a reorganized store, leaving the original untouched. At launch, Dreaming supported only Claude Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6.

OpenAI also calls ChatGPT's memory, which it overhauled in June, "Dreaming." That system maintains a user profile in the background and automatically corrects outdated information. According to OpenAI, this raised temporal accuracy from 52.2 to 75.1 percent.

Researchers at Google and Google DeepMind also let AI agents dream, but they use dreaming to improve an agent's search strategy. Their agent works through alternative solutions using results it has already stored, without calling the model again. Google has also built WikiSkill, a wiki for agents. As in Anthropic's system, WikiSkill keeps raw transcripts, distilled knowledge, and specific instructions in separate layers.

title_zh: Anthropic揭示AI代理记忆优化核心：减法胜于加法
summary_zh: Anthropic通过Pokémon游戏测试发现，AI代理的长程记忆效能取决于精简信息存储，而非冗余存档，引入“睡眠复盘”机制可修正记忆偏差
article_content_zh:
Anthropic 研究了克劳德如何在不同的课程中保留知识。它的测试表明，选择性笔记胜过详尽的档案，并且让克劳德在事后回顾自己的记忆可以纠正错误。

任何在一个项目上与人工智能代理一起工作几天的人都会很快碰壁，因为每个新的会话都是从头开始的。在一篇研究文章中，Anthropic 描述了 Claude 如何在模型保持不变的情况下跨会话保留知识。克劳德将注释写入一个文件夹，以便稍后读取。

根据 Anthropic 的说法，核心问题是选择。在知道接下来会发生什么之前，智能体必须立即决定稍后可能发生的事情，因此每一个音符都是对未来的赌注。

在 Pokémon Red 的 Anthropic 测试中，较旧的 Claude Sonnet 3.7 将所有内容视为潜在重要的内容，并在大约 10,000 个游戏步骤中，在 225 个文件夹中创建了 413 个文件，通常为它发现的每一场战斗和项目创建一个单独的文件。由于游戏状态不断变化，存档很快就会过时。有时，模型除了重新组织音符而不是演奏之外什么也不做，最后只留下一个徽章。

较新的《克劳德寓言 5》将其内存限制为几个文件，并获得了四个徽章。 《神鬼寓言 5》并没有记录屏幕上已经可见的信息，而是写下了已经测试过的计划、策略和规则。然而，Anthropic 的比较仅涵盖每个模型的一次游戏。

Anthropic 建议向 Claude 解释记忆的用途，并让模型决定如何使用它。根据 Anthropic 的说法，在一项基准测试中，诸如“仅记录错误”之类的严格指令消除了更强大模型的大部分优势。相比之下，较旧的模型受益于明确的指示，例如被告知在每次回答之前实际阅读他们的笔记。

更大的风险来自于代理人后来盲目信任的错误票据。梦想是一个建立在莱塔和加州大学伯克利分校研究基础上的想法，旨在解决这个问题。就像人类大脑在睡眠期间处理经历一样，克劳德在休息期间查看早期会议的记录，并对照记录进行检查。

在神奇宝贝测试中，克劳德错误地指出了地标位于山的哪一侧。靠着那张错误的音符，克劳德三度陷入同样的​​陷阱，最终想要放弃，却未能达到目的。在梦想通过后，克劳德通过检查记录中的注释发现了错误，并找到了正确的路径。

据Anthropic介绍，Dreaming还可以组织更大的知识库。克劳德利用 Anthropic 收购的软件公司不锈钢的约 350,000 份内部文档构建了一个链接维基。梦想应该生成新页面，同时修复间隙、重复和损坏的链接。当克劳德能够将 wiki 与搜索结合起来时，回报是最大的，因此 wiki 作为补充而不是替代。

在 Anthropic 进行的一项单独的法律测试中，维基百科对答案分散在多个文档中的问题提供了最大的帮助。克劳德在 wiki 上的得分为 87%，而仅在搜索方面得分为 73%。对于简单的查找任务，wiki 的性能与搜索大致相当，在一种情况下，它甚至比源文档还要大。

Anthropic 承认关键问题仍然悬而未决。在任务中做笔记会分散代理的工作注意力，做梦会消耗额外的计算资源，而且结果只有在延迟后才会到达。维基和注释也需要定期维护，否则错误和幻觉就会堆积起来。 Anthropic 还警告不要在每个会话中自动加载太多记忆，因为它们会耗尽上下文并将任何不良记录传递给未来的每个会话。

所有这些测试都来自 Anthropic。总的结论是，有用的代理记忆更多地取决于保留正确的信息并在以后纠正错误，而不是尽可能多地存储。

Anthropic 在 5 月份推出了 Dreaming，作为该公司的 AI 代理云平台 Claude Managed Agents 的研究预览。该服务读取现有内存存储和最多 100 个过去的会话，删除重复和过时的条目，并创建重新组织的存储，使原始存储保持不变。发布时，Dreaming 仅支持 Claude Opus 4.7 和 Sonnet 4.6。

OpenAI 还将 6 月份检修的 ChatGPT 内存称为“梦想”。该系统在后台维护用户配置文件并自动更正过时的信息。据 OpenAI 称，这将时间准确度从 52.2% 提高到了 75.1%。

title: Moody's: major US life insurers like Athene held $85.2B in AI debt as of June 30, up 24% from December 31, and the figure could rise to $185B by the end of 2027 (New York Times)
title_en: Moody's: major US life insurers like Athene held $85.2B in AI debt as of June 30, up 24% from December 31, and the figure could rise to $185B by the end of 2027 (New York Times)

inline_images.caption: An xAI supercomputing facility near Memphis that is used for artificial intelligence training.Credit...Karen Pulfer Focht/Reuters
inline_images.alt: An xAI supercomputing facility near Memphis that is used for artificial intelligence training.Credit

author: New York Times
article_content:
When Elon Musk needed help financing a large purchase of artificial intelligence chips earlier this year, Wall Street offered an elegant solution.

Mr. Musk and his team of advisers created a financial entity that would borrow billions to buy the chips and then lease them back to xAI, his artificial intelligence effort. This way, xAI wasn’t technically the borrower, which helped make its official debt load look smaller to investors.

To help fund this complicated arrangement, $2.4 billion of the debt was sold to an insurance company called Athene, which manages life insurance policies and annuities for retirees, according to a Moody’s Ratings report.

The deal was part of an increasingly popular playbook: tapping insurance companies, which are historically among the most cautious investors, to make loans to tech titans like Mr. Musk and further fuel the A.I. boom.

The amount of A.I. debt being held by insurance companies has soared this year. U.S. life insurers, including some of the largest like Athene and Corebridge Financial, held $85.2 billion in A.I. debt as of June 30, up 24 percent from six months prior, according to Moody’s.

While this accounts for just 2.1 percent of life insurers’ total debt, their exposure is expected to grow quickly. Life insurers could hold up to $185 billion of A.I. investments by the end of next year, according to Moody’s.

Life insurers owned about 15 percent of A.I. data center debt as of June 30, according to a recent estimate by Barclay’s.

These debt investments carry multiple risks. For one, only a few technology companies, including Nvidia, Meta, Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI, are providing the guarantees for these deals, which concentrates the risk. There are also often ways for tech companies to walk away from these A.I. projects if their development is delayed.

“The life insurance industry is now in effect backing large swaths of the A.I. industry,” said Andrew Granato, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Law, who has studied the overlap between private equity and insurers.

“We should all be concerned about this, especially as the debt deals get more opaque,” he added.

Making possible this flood of insurance money into risky A.I. deals are credit rating agencies like Moody’s and S&P Global Ratings. They have blessed this rapidly expanding pool of debt with relatively safe credit ratings, which meet the criteria that insurance firms need to invest in a particular asset.

Much of this activity is being driven by giant Wall Street firms that are affiliated with insurance companies and sometimes help manage their investments. Athene, which bought some of the xAI debt, is a subsidiary of the Wall Street firm Apollo.

“Athene finances what we view as the safest and most defensible parts of the A.I. ecosystem,” an Apollo spokeswoman said in a statement.

SpaceX, which owns xAI, did not respond to a request for comment.

Insurers are attracted to A.I. debt because it is regarded as secure, but still offers market-beating returns. A.I. companies, in turn, have come to view the life insurance industry as crucial to supporting their data center expansions.

Last month, Brannin McBee, a co-founder and chief development officer of the data center company CoreWeave, told The Financial Times that he viewed insurers as an “unlimited” source of capital for future borrowing.

“Like, that’s all the money in the world that sits in the insurance tranche,” he said.

His comments spooked CoreWeave’s investors and lenders. Its stock dropped sharply the next day and the price of its bonds fell quickly, too. The bonds of other A.I.-related companies and data center projects have also dropped in recent weeks as investors have become more wary of debt risks.

A spokesman for CoreWeave declined to comment.

One of the lenders loudly voicing concerns is Ares Management, one of the largest private credit firms with $691 billion in assets.

Ares cites Meta’s data center in Richland Parish, La., as a prime example.

Rather than owning the project outright, Meta took only a 20 percent stake while the investment firm Blue Owl owns the rest.

Yet, S&P Global was comfortable enough to rate the project’s $27 billion in debt just one notch below Meta’s strong corporate rating because of guarantees the tech company provided. Those included a $28 billion lease guarantee over 20 years or to find a tenant if Meta walked away.

That rating helped open the door for life insurers, which, according to Moodys, funded $3.4 billion of the deal.

But Meta is not promising to repay the project’s debt investors. In a statement, a Meta spokesperson wrote that “Meta has not guaranteed repayment of the bonds.”

In a statement, a Blue Owl spokesman said: “When institutional investors and insurers buy this debt, they are not taking a hidden risk. They are buying exposure to the contractual obligations of some of the strongest corporate credits in the world.”

In another example, Meta signed a deal in March to procure A.I. computing capacity from CoreWeave in four data centers.

When CoreWeave sought a rating for an $8.5 billion loan tied to these projects, the rating agencies looked at Meta’s strong credit rating rather than CoreWeave’s, which is in junk territory, and gave the deal one of its highest ratings. Insurers were buyers of the CoreWeave projects’ debt also, according to S&P Market Intelligence.

But investors are increasingly questioning whether giant companies like Meta deserve such high ratings.

“These companies are not as safe as they once were,” Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a professor at Columbia Business School, said. “They’re sort of playing this game where they can pretend like they don’t have these liabilities.”

Meta, for example, has signed $356 billion in leases, including for data centers that it has not yet started. That amount is four times larger than the $84 billion of debt that it reported in its latest quarterly filing. Meta has committed an additional $455 billion in deals to buy chips, other infrastructure and hardware, agreements that it cannot cancel.

Last month, S&P Global announced it had revised its 2027 outlook for Meta’s credit rating to negative from stable, citing the surge in future leases and uncertainty about Meta’s ability to turn A.I. spending into revenue. For now, though, Meta’s rating remains the same.

In an interview, Naveen Sarma, an S&P Global Ratings analyst focused on Meta, said his firm did not consider a future lease commitment as existing debt because Meta does not have to start making the lease payments until it starts using the data center.

The Meta spokesperson said the company “respectfully disagrees” with S&P’s outlook. “We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile,” he said.

Moody’s acknowledged the risk of all the debt accumulating off the tech companies’ books in a recent paper. But the firm does not consider those commitments to be existing debt when rating a company’s credit, a Moody’s spokeswoman said.

As for SpaceX, the company’s auditors determined the money that it intended to borrow off its books earlier this year to buy chips should ultimately be recorded as company debt.

But Mr. Musk and Wall Street continue to find innovative ways to keep borrowing. Earlier this month, Mr. Musk raised $40 billion to finance more A.I. chips through a financial entity that will keep that debt off SpaceX’s books for now.

SpaceX could pull off the deal, Mr. Musk said in a post on X, because “we’re investment grade.”

title_zh: 险资深度介入AI融资，隐性杠杆风险攀升
summary_zh: 美国寿险业AI债持仓半年暴增24%至852亿美元，且呈现出通过SPV绕道借贷的复杂化趋势，引发金融稳定性监管担忧
article_content_zh:
今年早些时候，当埃隆·马斯克(Elon Musk)需要为大量购买人工智能芯片融资时，华尔街提供了一个优雅的解决方案。

马斯克和他的顾问团队创建了一家金融实体，该实体将借入数十亿美元购买芯片，然后将其租回给他的人工智能项目 xAI。这样一来，从技术上讲，xAI 就不是借款人，这有助于使其官方债务负担在投资者看来更小。

根据穆迪评级报告，为了为这一复杂的安排提供资金，其中 24 亿美元的债务被出售给一家名为 Athene 的保险公司，该公司为退休人员管理人寿保险单和年金。

这笔交易是一个日益流行的策略的一部分：利用历史上最谨慎的投资者之一的保险公司向马斯克等科技巨头提供贷款，并进一步推动人工智能的发展。繁荣。

A.I. 的数量今年保险公司持有的债务猛增。美国人寿保险公司，包括 Athene 和 Corebridge Financial 等一些最大的保险公司，持有 852 亿美元的 A.I.据穆迪称，截至 6 月 30 日，债务比六个月前增加了 24%。

虽然这仅占人寿保险公司总债务的 2.1%，但其风险预计将迅速增长。人寿保险公司可以持有高达 1850 亿美元的人工智能资产。据穆迪称，预计将在明年年底前完成投资。

人寿保险公司持有 A.I. 约 15% 的股份。根据巴克莱最近的估计，截至 6 月 30 日的数据中心债务。

这些债务投资带有多重风险。其一，只有 Nvidia、Meta、Alphabet、SpaceX、Anthropic 和 OpenAI 等少数科技公司为这些交易提供担保，风险集中。科技公司也有很多方法可以摆脱这些人工智能。如果项目的开发被延迟。

德克萨斯大学奥斯汀分校法学院助理教授安德鲁·格拉纳托（Andrew Granato）表示：“人寿保险行业现在实际上支持了人工智能行业的大部分。”他研究了私募股权与保险公司之间的重叠。

“我们都应该关注这一点，尤其是在债务交易变得更加不透明的情况下，”他补充道。

让大量的保险资金投入有风险的人工智能成为可能。交易者是穆迪和标准普尔全球评级等信用评级机构。他们为这个迅速扩大的债务池提供了相对安全的信用评级，这些评级符合保险公司投资特定资产所需的标准。

这些活动大部分是由隶属于保险公司的华尔街巨头公司推动的，有时还帮助管理他们的投资。购买了部分 xAI 债务的 Athene 是华尔街阿波罗公司的子公司。

“雅典娜为我们认为人工智能生态系统中最安全、最有防御能力的部分提供资金，”阿波罗发言人在一份声明中表示。

xAI 的所有者 SpaceX 没有回应置评请求。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 截至6月30日，以Athene为代表的美国主要寿险公司持有的AI相关债务总额已达852亿美元，较半年前增长24%，预计到2027年末将攀升至1850亿美元。科技巨头正通过复杂的SPV（特殊目的实体）融资模式将大额算力采购债务置于表外，此类债务高度集中于少数顶级科技厂商，引起了学界及金融界对保险资金风险敞口的广泛质疑。

author: New York Post
article_content:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said Monday he “would not mind” if Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia CEO, claiming that the tech boss had “learned a big lesson” from his romantic entanglement with a suspected Chinese spy.

“I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told reporters as he left the White House for a trip to the Philippines and China in response to a Financial Times report that Huang had put together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.

Huang stepped down Friday following revelations of a series of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at a Singapore-based Nvidia client suspected by US intelligence of being in the pay of Beijing.

“I don’t know that she’s a Chinese spy,” Trump said of Alice Huang, reflecting reported internal dissension over the intelligence community’s assessment.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: Google's TIG reports the first observed instance of attackers using an autonomous AI framework with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits (Duncan Riley/SiliconANGLE)
title_en: Google's TIG reports the first observed instance of attackers using an autonomous AI framework with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits (Duncan Riley/SiliconANGLE)

inline_images.caption: theCUBE
inline_images.alt: theCUBE

inline_images.caption: theCUBE Research
inline_images.alt: theCUBE Research

author: SiliconANGLE
article_content:
A new report out today from Google LLC’s Google Threat Intelligence Group finds that for the first time, attackers have used an artificial intelligence framework running with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits.

Called exploit_agent, the framework turned up on an exposed staging server, where it was wired into several frontier and locally hosted large language models. Its job, according to GTIG, is continuous comparison of popular web application code before and after each patch announcement. Once a likely flaw is identified, the exploit it drafts is executed automatically.

Data taken from victims was sitting on the same server, alongside scripts for brute-forcing, installing webshells and even removing webshells left by rival attackers. Victim telemetry suggests the operator was most interested in French websites tied to media, entertainment and education. Written in Russian, one comment in the framework’s configuration file tells whoever set it up to enter the keys “right here, not in the chat.”

In the previous edition of the quarterly tracker two months ago, GTIG said it had not observed fully autonomous attack pipelines deployed against targets in the wild. That changed over the past quarter, according to the new report, titled “Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold.” Because the source material for a patched flaw is finite, GTIG believes attackers may find it more efficient to point LLMs at n-day vulnerabilities than to hunt for zero-days.

How quickly the gap between disclosure and a working exploit can close shows in the case of two flaws in print management servers from PaperCut Software Pty Ltd., chained together and exploited as zero-days in late August. Security researchers and Huntress Labs Inc. used large language models to generate working exploits within a day of disclosure.

A campaign tracked by GreyNoise Intelligence Inc. four days after disclosure is believed to have relied on LLMs to build its exploits before it hit hundreds of organizations. One foothold in that campaign reached domain administrator within minutes, GreyNoise found.

Elsewhere, open-source agentic penetration testing frameworks are being used to automate discrete steps of live intrusions. During one intrusion against the U.S. aerospace sector, a threat actor was observed using the multi-agent framework CAIRN.

Another actor ran a customized platform built on PentAGI between late August and early October to scan a wide range of organizations in Asia for vulnerabilities. For now, the noisy forensic trail left by unrestricted autonomous execution is said to make the frameworks easier to detect.

According to GTIG, influence operations now use models for far more than writing posts. Using cloud phone farms, a turnkey platform that one commercial contractor was building with help from the Gemini API is designed to run more than 100,000 social media accounts. To make generated photos pass as smartphone shots, prompts behind a separate platform, which targeted political sentiment across Europe and the Middle East, are said to have called for deliberate camera flaws.

Among government-backed actors, photos on the fake recruiter profiles that a suspected North Korean group tracked as UNC6836 used to approach cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe were found to carry Google’s SynthID watermarks. By way of altered .claude/settings.json files in internal code repositories, the group later rigged each launch of Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code to download its SOMBERMEME backdoor.

Google said it disabled the accounts and assets tied to the Gemini misuse it found. Google DeepMind has also used the findings to strengthen its classifiers.

article_content_zh:
谷歌有限责任公司的谷歌威胁情报小组今天发布的一份新报告发现，攻击者首次使用无人参与的人工智能框架将安全补丁转化为漏洞。

该框架名为exploit_agent，出现在一个暴露的临时服务器上，它被连接到几个前沿和本地托管的大型语言模型中。据 GTIG 称，其工作是在每个补丁发布前后持续比较流行的 Web 应用程序代码。一旦发现可能的缺陷，它所起草的漏洞就会自动执行。

从受害者那里获取的数据与暴力破解、安装 Webshel​​l 甚至删除竞争对手留下的 Webshel​​l 的脚本一起位于同一服务器上。受害者遥测表明，该运营商对与媒体、娱乐和教育相关的法国网站最感兴趣。该框架的配置文件中的一条注释是用俄语写的，告诉设置它的人“就在这里，而不是在聊天中”输入按键。

在两个月前的上一期季度跟踪报告中，GTIG 表示，它没有观察到针对野外目标部署的完全自主的攻击管道。根据题为“代理威胁活动跨越重大阈值”的新报告，这种情况在过去一个季度发生了变化。由于修补缺陷的源材料是有限的，GTIG 认为攻击者可能会发现让法学硕士针对 n 天漏洞比寻找 0 天漏洞更有效。

PaperCut Software Pty Ltd. 的打印管理服务器中存在两个缺陷，这两个缺陷相互关联并在 8 月下旬被作为零日漏洞利用，这说明了披露与有效利用之间的差距能够以多快的速度缩小。安全研究人员和 Huntress Labs Inc. 使用大型语言模型在披露后的一天内生成了有效的漏洞。

GreyNoise Intelligence Inc. 在披露四天后跟踪的一项活动据信是依靠法学硕士来构建其漏洞，然后才袭击数百个组织。 GreyNoise 发现，该活动的一个立足点在几分钟内就到达了域管理员。

在其他地方，开源代理渗透测试框架被用来自动化实时入侵的离散步骤。在一次针对美国航空航天领域的入侵中，观察到威胁行为者使用多代理框架 CAIRN。

另一位参与者在 8 月底到 10 月初期间运行了一个基于 PentAGI 构建的定制平台，以扫描亚洲的各种组织是否存在漏洞。目前，不受限制的自主执行留下的嘈杂的取证痕迹据说使框架更容易被检测到。

GTIG 表示，影响力运营现在使用模型的用途远远超出了撰写帖子的范围。一家商业承包商在 Gemini API 的帮助下构建了一个统包平台，该平台使用云电话农场，旨在运行超过 100,000 个社交媒体帐户。为了让生成的照片像智能手机拍摄的照片一样，一个单独的平台背后的提示据称要求故意制造相机缺陷，该平台针对整个欧洲和中东的政治情绪。

在政府支持的参与者中，一个被怀疑为 UNC6836 的朝鲜组织用来接触北美和欧洲的加密货币组织的虚假招聘人员资料中的照片被发现带有谷歌的 SynthID 水印。通过更改内部代码存储库中的 .claude/settings.json 文件，该组织后来操纵了 Anthropic PBC 的 Claude Code 的每次启动，以下载其 SOMBERMEME 后门。

谷歌表示，它已禁用与发现的 Gemini 滥用行为相关的账户和资产。谷歌 DeepMind 还利用这些发现来增强其分类器。

通过与 CUBE 社区互动，支持我们保持内容开放和免费的使命。加入 theCUBE 的校友信任网络，技术领导者在此相互联系、分享智慧并创造机会。

SiliconANGLE Media 由科技梦想家 John Furrier 和 Dave Vellante 创立，建立了一个由行业领先的数字媒体品牌组成的动态生态系统，覆盖超过 1500 万精英科技专业人士。我们全新专有的 theCUBE AI 视频云在观众互动方面取得了突破性进展，利用 CUBEai.com 神经网络帮助科技公司做出数据驱动的决策并保持行业对话的前沿。

title: Tel Aviv- and SF-based Corma, which builds AI agents custom-trained for cyber defense, raised a $125M Series A led by NEA, after raising a $60M seed in August (Angus Loten/Wall Street Journal)
title_en: Tel Aviv- and SF-based Corma, which builds AI agents custom-trained for cyber defense, raised a $125M Series A led by NEA, after raising a $60M seed in August (Angus Loten/Wall Street Journal)
author: Wall Street Journal
article_content:
Corma raised $60M seed from Sequoia, Khosla, Coatue. Building first defensive cybersecurity foundation model. In simulations, AI attackers won 88%, defenders caught 12%. Already deployed at Fortune 100/500 orgs. Team from DeepMind and Unit 8200.

In hundreds of simulations modelled on Fortune 500 companies with dozens of security tools, Corma tested leading AI models including GPT and Claude. First, the models attacked the simulated organisations and planted persistent threats. Then the same models were asked to defend and find what they had planted.

The attackers succeeded in 88% of simulations. The defenders caught 12%. The same AI that is increasingly capable of sophisticated attacks is poorly equipped to stop them. Corma raised $60 million in a seed round led by Sequoia Capital, with Khosla Ventures and Coatue, to build the defensive model the industry does not have.

The company, founded in 2025 and headquartered in Tel Aviv and San Francisco, is building a foundation model from the ground up for cybersecurity defence. Rather than selling software, Corma deploys AI agents that operate across an organisation’s existing security tools and carry out tasks end to end.

“We don’t replace anyone and we are not a product,” CEO Alon Pluda told Calcalist. “We sell virtual human resources.” Each organisation determines how many it needs. In early deployments at Fortune 100 and Fortune 500 companies across healthcare, financial services, energy, and retail, Corma’s systems reduced threat response times by more than 94% and expanded security coverage 15x.

The team brings together frontier AI researchers from Google and DeepMind with cybersecurity specialists from Israel’s Unit 8200. OpenAI just paused work on its Astra model because it could not rule out that the system had reached “critical cybersecurity” capabilities, meaning it could find and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities without human help.

That is the offensive side accelerating. Corma is betting that the defensive side needs its own purpose-built model rather than hoping general-purpose AI will do both jobs.

The gap Corma identified is structural. Offensive cybersecurity leverages the same coding and reasoning capabilities that make frontier models powerful. Defensive cybersecurity requires processing enormous volumes of audit logs, identifying weak signals over long periods, and maintaining consistency across thousands of decisions, tasks that general-purpose models are not trained for.

AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have all escaped test environments and breached other organisations in recent weeks. The attackers are already autonomous. Corma’s argument is that the defenders need to be too.

article_content_zh:
Corma 从 Sequoia、Khosla、Coatue 筹集了 6000 万美元的种子资金。构建第一个防御性网络安全基础模型。在模拟中，AI 攻击者获胜 88%，防御者获胜 12%。已部署在《财富》100/500 强组织中。来自 DeepMind 和 Unit 8200 的团队。

在使用数十种安全工具以财富 500 强公司为模型进行的数百次模拟中，Corma 测试了包括 GPT 和 Claude 在内的领先人工智能模型。首先，模型攻击模拟组织并植入持续的威胁。然后，同样的模特被要求保卫并寻找他们种植的东西。

攻击者在 88% 的模拟中取得了成功。防守方抓住了12%。越来越有能力进行复杂攻击的人工智能却无力阻止它们。 Corma 在由红杉资本领投、Khosla Ventures 和 Coatue 领投的种子轮融资中筹集了 6000 万美元，以建立行业中没有的防御模式。

该公司成立于 2025 年，总部位于特拉维夫和旧金山，正在从头开始构建网络安全防御的基础模型。 Corma 不销售软件，而是部署人工智能代理，这些代理在组织现有的安全工具上运行并端到端地执行任务。

“我们不会取代任何人，我们也不是一种产品，”首席执行官 Alon Pluda 告诉 Calcalist。 “我们出售虚拟人力资源。”每个组织决定其需要的数量。在医疗保健、金融服务、能源和零售等财富 100 强和财富 500 强公司的早期部署中，Corma 的系统将威胁响应时间缩短了 94% 以上，并将安全覆盖范围扩大了 15 倍。

该团队汇集了来自谷歌和 DeepMind 的前沿人工智能研究人员以及来自以色列 Unit 8200 的网络安全专家。OpenAI 刚刚暂停了其 Astra 模型的工作，因为它不能排除该系统已经达到“关键网络安全”能力，这意味着它可以在没有人类帮助的情况下发现和利用零日漏洞。

那就是进攻方加速。 Corma 认为防守方需要自己的专用模型，而不是希望通用人工智能能够完成这两项工作。

Corma 发现的差距是结构性的。进攻性网络安全利用相同的编码和推理功能，使前沿模型变得强大。防御性网络安全需要处理大量审计日志，长期识别微弱信号，并保持数千个决策的一致性，而通用模型并未针对这些任务进行训练。

最近几周，OpenAI、Anthropic 和 Meta 的 AI 模型都逃脱了测试环境并侵入了其他组织。攻击者已经是自治的。科尔马的观点是，防守者也需要这样做。

title: Audible is trying to make it easier to find audiobooks you’ll actually like
title_en: Audible is trying to make it easier to find audiobooks you’ll actually like

inline_images.caption: Jess Weatherbed

inline_images.caption: Audible audio discovery hero

inline_images.caption: Jess Weatherbed

author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Audible is introducing an AI-assisted synopsis feature that’s designed to help users determine whether they’ll enjoy an audiobook before they jump in and start listening to it. The new audio discovery feature combines audiobook samples, AI overviews, and author commentary to give users more information before choosing their next story, in addition to recommended audiobook collections that are personalized to individual listening tastes.

Audio discovery provides a soundbite synopsis, with the aim of preventing Audible users from having to research titles on other platforms. The feature plays users a snippet of the audiobook and a brief AI-generated overview including its themes and listener reactions, drawing from reviews and other publicly available data. It can also include commentary from an author or Audible editor, which is pulled directly from past Audible interviews.

“Picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend. With audio discovery, you’ll get a quick audio take on why the title might be right for you, from our editors, fellow listeners, or even the author,” Audible chief product officer Andy Tsao said in the announcement. “Some of the best listening experiences are those rare finds or hidden gems, and we want to make those great discoveries happen more often and more easily.”

Audio discovery is rolling out on select English-language titles in the US, with plans to eventually expand to other regions.

Audible is also using AI to personalize audiobook collections around users’ listening tastes, in an effort to make titles that don’t appear on best-selling lists easier to discover. Like audio discovery, these personalized collections are rolling out to customers in the US, and also include commentary from Audible’s editors.

[Image: Audible users in the US will also start seeing AI-curated recommendation categories based on what they usually listen to. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/Audible_Collections_Newsroom_1080x608.png?quality=90&strip=all]

These are the latest AI-powered features that Audible is introducing in an effort to attract new users and fend off growing competition from rival platforms like Spotify. As part of this update, Audible is also expanding two beta features: Ask a Question, which allows users to ask AI about characters, plot points, references, and more; and Recaps, which provides spoiler-free audio summaries of what the user has already listened to. These are now available for a “select set” of additional English-language titles in the US, according to Audible, with a broader rollout planned to start in December.

Audible 推出了一项人工智能辅助概要功能，旨在帮助用户在开始收听有声读物之前确定他们是否会喜欢有声读物。新的音频发现功能结合了有声读物样本、人工智能概述和作者评论，除了根据个人聆听品味个性化推荐的有声读物合集之外，还可以在选择下一个故事之前为用户提供更多信息。

音频发现提供了原声摘要，旨在防止 Audible 用户在其他平台上研究标题。该功能向用户播放有声读物的片段以及人工智能生成的简短概述，包括其主题和听众的反应，这些概述来自评论和其他公开数据。它还可以包括作者或 Audible 编辑的评论，这些评论直接摘自过去的 Audible 采访。

Audible 首席产品官 Andy Tsao 在声明中表示：“选择你的下一首歌曲应该感觉就像从朋友那里得到提示。通过音频发现，你可以从我们的编辑、其他听众甚至作者那里快速了解为什么这个标题可能适合你。” “一些最好的聆听体验是那些罕见的发现或隐藏的宝石，我们希望让这些伟大的发现更频繁、更容易地发生。”

音频发现功能正在美国的部分英语游戏中推出，并计划最终扩展到其他地区。

Audible 还利用人工智能根据用户的聆听品味个性化有声读物收藏，努力让未出现在畅销书排行榜上的图书更容易被发现。与音频发现一样，这些个性化合集正在向美国客户推出，其中还包括 Audible 编辑的评论。

这些是 Audible 推出的最新人工智能功能，旨在吸引新用户并抵御 Spotify 等竞争对手平台日益激烈的竞争。作为本次更新的一部分，Audible 还扩展了两个测试版功能：提问，允许用户向 AI 询问角色、情节点、参考资料等； Recaps，它提供用户已经听过的内容的无剧透音频摘要。据 Audible 称，这些内容现已在美国推出“精选集”的其他英语游戏，并计划于 12 月开始更广泛的推广。

title: Google Maps can now create trip itineraries for you

author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Google is launching a new AI trip-planning feature for Maps that allows the app to create custom itineraries for you and provide real-time details about each stop. The update, which is rolling out to the Gemini-powered Ask Maps chatbot inside the app, lets you plan a one-day outing or a trip spanning several days.

As an example, Google says you can use Ask Maps to plan a day trip for holiday shopping, or have it create a schedule for a three-day road trip with stops for coastal hikes and oceanfront dining. From there, Ask Maps will generate a day-by-day schedule with a list of stops, while also showing your route and numbered pins for each location on the map. You can share the itinerary with friends or family members, as well as export it to Google Docs on desktop.

You can ask Maps to show your trip schedule before you leave, or select the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. Along with directions, Google Maps will display real-time information about traffic, a location’s hours, and more. You can also view “know before you go” details about parking, car charging, weather conditions, potential delays, and tolls during your trip.

In addition to trip planning, you can now use Ask Maps to find specific beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments, and have it call the locations for you. You can also use Ask Maps to find saved places on your list by asking something like, “Which spots on saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”

Google is expanding Ask Maps to over 30 countries in Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the UK. Trip-planning and saved list search is rolling out to the more than 200 countries where Ask Maps is available, while “know before you go” tips and appointment-finding are launching in the US to start.

title: Oakland-based Numa, which builds an AI platform to manage car dealership customer service, raised a $45M Series C, a source says at a $500M post-money valuation
title_en: Oakland-based Numa, which builds an AI platform to manage car dealership customer service, raised a $45M Series C, a source says at a $500M post-money valuation
title_zh: 汽车经销商客户服务 AI 平台 Numa 完成 4500 万美元 C 轮融资，投后估值达 5 亿美元
author: Camila Grigera Naón
article_content:
Artificial intelligence promises to untangle the messy workflows that have long plagued legacy industries. One startup is bringing that pitch to car dealerships. On Monday, Oakland-based company Numa announced a $45 million Series C round to build out an AI operating system designed to handle the daily grind of dealership customer service, from answering calls and booking appointments to keeping customers updated on their cars.

It works like this: Numa’s AI agents connect to a dealership’s software to check inventory down to a car’s trim and features, pull repair updates and log sales leads alongside conversation transcripts. The platform also handles routine warranty paperwork and flags exchanges that may signal an unhappy customer for managers to review.

“Think about things like filling out warranty paperwork. That is a drudgery of a job that nobody wants to do, and people do it poorly. You can apply an AI and do it instantly,” Numa CEO Tasso Roumeliotis told Fortune.

The latest round valued Numa at $500 million after the investment, according to a source familiar with the company.

Numa’s pitch comes as more companies put AI agents to work. In a survey of roughly 2,100 senior leaders across 20 countries and industries ranging from automotive to healthcare, accounting and consulting firm KPMG found that 34% reported widespread employee adoption of AI agents in the third quarter of 2026, up from 25% in the first quarter.

For Roumeliotis, Numa began with a familiar team and a new problem to solve.

He had previously built Location Labs, a mobile technology company that tapped into the early spread of GPS-enabled cellphones to help people track one another’s locations. After selling the business in 2015, he joined venture firm Draper Fisher Jurvetson as an entrepreneur-in-residence.

While he was there, former colleagues from Location Labs approached him with a proposition: They wanted to build another company together. The group included engineers, product specialists and executives who had taken on bigger roles under Roumeliotis.

In 2017, they launched Number AI to help small businesses receive and respond to texts through their existing landline numbers, using natural language processing to bring newer technology to businesses still relying on older tools.

But as they worked with car dealerships, they found problems that went beyond missed messages. Employees juggled calls, paperwork and manual follow-ups, leaving customers waiting. The team narrowed its focus to the automotive industry and renamed the company Numa.

Blue Cloud Ventures also saw an opportunity in dealerships still relying on older software.

“I look at the auto dealership… as a little bit like jumbo shrimp. It’s a massive niche,” Mir Arif, the venture capital firm’s managing partner, told Fortune. “All of them [are still] working off legacy software or literally pen and paper.”

Today, the company has about 160 employees across its Bay Area headquarters, a sales and marketing office in Kansas City and an AI development office in Montreal. More than 1,500 dealerships in the U.S. and Canada use its software, including Longo Toyota, Norm Reeves Honda and Gold Coast Cadillac.

title: US Moves to Curb Remote Access to Nvidia's Advanced AI Chips
title_en: US Moves to Curb Remote Access to Nvidia's Advanced AI Chips
author: Maggie Eastland and Magan Crane
article_content:
WASHINGTON — The US Commerce Department moved on Monday to limit several countries from providing Chinese companies remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips through overseas data centers, significantly expanding export controls to close a critical cloud computing loophole.

Under the interim final rule issued by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the US government is establishing mandatory export license requirements for transferring advanced semiconductors and cloud compute capacity to five intermediary nations: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil.

The new regulation directly targets data centers and neocloud operators globally that provide high aggregate Total Processing Performance (TPP) computing power to entities headquartered in China or Macau. Existing facilities catering to these clients have been granted a 90-day grace period to apply for licenses and transition operations into compliance.

The aggressive policy shift comes as Washington intensifies scrutiny over how restricted American technology reaches Chinese tech giants despite sweeping hardware export restrictions. In recent months, reports revealed that companies in China had increasingly bypassed physical chip embargos by renting computing clusters running Nvidia Corp. H100 and H200 accelerators stationed across Southeast Asia.

Enforcement concerns escalated following the sudden departure of former Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, amid congressional inquiries into transactions with Singapore-based provider Megaspeed International. Megaspeed had imported billions of dollars worth of Nvidia hardware between 2023 and 2025, leasing high-performance clusters to overseas clients including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. and ByteDance Ltd.

While renting cloud compute does not violate legacy rules restricted to physical hardware delivery, the Commerce Department determined that remote access effectively nullifies national security protections by enabling Chinese frontier labs to train advanced large language models using American supercomputing infrastructure.

Under the new framework, cloud providers must implement verified customer identity protocols and adhere to strict compute quotas. Global data center operators serving clients in designated restricted regions will be prohibited from dedicating more than 50% of aggregate cluster capacity to Chinese firms without explicit Commerce Department authorization.

The interim rule takes effect immediately with an open public comment period. Lawmakers on Capitol Hill welcomed the measure as an essential step toward hardening the semiconductor perimeter, with members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee indicating plans for oversight hearings on export control enforcement mechanisms.

The move follows concerns that Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a key Nvidia partner, may have been facilitating access to restricted computing power for Chinese tech giants through Southeast Asian data centers.
key_points_zh: 美商务部通过新规堵塞AI芯片云端租赁的监管合规漏洞
Megaspeed公司因向中国企业提供大量算力租用面临多方审查
后续监管将重点转向算力远程访问的实时监控与物理拦截
key_points_en: Commerce Department addresses cloud-based AI chip export evasion
Megaspeed International under scrutiny for providing computing power to Chinese firms
Increased focus on monitoring and intercepting remote cross-border computational access
ai_analysis.takeaway_zh: 此举标志着美国出口管制的重心从单纯的“实物硬件禁运”转向“算力使用权管控”，反映出美方对云端算力作为战略资源流动的高度警觉。此项监管可能迫使跨国云服务商重构全球数据中心架构，并提高其在东南亚及其他地区运营的合规披露成本。
ai_analysis.takeaway_en: This shift marks a strategic transition from restricting physical hardware to controlling access to computational power, reflecting intensified scrutiny over cloud-based AI resources. The regulation will likely force global cloud providers to restructure their data center presence and significantly increase compliance costs in Southeast Asia.

article_content_zh:
华盛顿——美国商务部周一采取行动，限制多个国家通过海外数据中心向中国企业提供先进人工智能芯片的远程访问权限，大幅扩展了出口管制范围，以堵塞关键的云计算监管漏洞。

根据美国工业与安全局（BIS）发布的临时最终规则，美国政府对向五个中间国家转移先进半导体及云算力设立了强制性出口许可证要求：这五个国家分别是新加坡、马来西亚、泰国、印度尼西亚和巴西。

该新规直接针对全球范围内向总部位于中国大陆或澳门的实体提供高聚合总处理性能（TPP）算力的数据中心与“新云”（neocloud）运营商。目前正为这些客户提供服务的基础设施获得了 90 天的宽限期，以便申请许可证并调整运营以符合监管要求。

这一强硬的政策转向出台之际，华盛顿正进一步强化对受限美国技术如何绕过全面硬件出口禁令流入中国科技巨头的审查。近几个月以来的多份报道显示，中国企业越来越多地通过租用部署在东南亚各地、配备英伟达 H100 和 H200 加速卡的计算集群，来规避实物芯片禁运。

随着英伟达前首席执行官黄仁勋突然离任，执法层面的担忧急剧升温，国会正对英伟达与新加坡云算力提供商 Megaspeed International 之间的交易展开调查。Megaspeed 在 2023 年至 2025 年期间进口了价值数十亿美元的英伟达硬件，并将高性能计算集群转租给包括阿里巴巴集团和字节跳动在内的海外客户。

尽管租用云算力并不违反仅限于实物硬件交付的传统出口管制规则，但商务部认定，远程访问实质上削弱了国家安全保护屏障，使中国前沿实验室得以利用美国超算基础设施训练先进的大语言模型。

在新的监管框架下，云服务提供商必须执行经核验的客户身份识别协议（KYC），并恪守严格的算力配额。为指定受限地区客户提供服务的全球数据中心运营商，在未经商务部明确批准的情况下，严禁将超过 50% 的集群总算力分配给中国企业。

该临时规则立即生效，并开启公开征求意见期。国会议员对该举措表示欢迎，称其为巩固半导体防线所迈出的关键一步，众议院外交事务委员会成员已表态计划就出口管制执法机制举行专题监督听证会。

【起因与机理】防止高性能计算能力通过云端跨境租用规避美国对华出口管制限制
【调查与监管诉求】美商务部通过新规堵塞AI芯片云端租赁的监管合规漏洞。
【涉及范围与推进】后续监管将重点转向算力远程访问的实时监控与物理拦截。

[Root Cause & Mechanism] To prevent evasion of export controls through cross-border cloud computing services

image_caption: US Moves to Restrict Remote Access to Advanced AI Chips (Bloomberg TV)
video_title: US Moves to Restrict Remote Access to Advanced AI Chips
paragraphs: WASHINGTON — The US Commerce Department moved on Monday to limit several countries from providing Chinese companies remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips through overseas data centers, significantly expanding export controls to close a critical cloud computing loophole.

Under the interim final rule issued by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the US government is establishing mandatory export license requirements for transferring advanced semiconductors and cloud compute capacity to five intermediary nations: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil.

The new regulation directly targets data centers and neocloud operators globally that provide high aggregate Total Processing Performance (TPP) computing power to entities headquartered in China or Macau. Existing facilities catering to these clients have been granted a 90-day grace period to apply for licenses and transition operations into compliance.

The aggressive policy shift comes as Washington intensifies scrutiny over how restricted American technology reaches Chinese tech giants despite sweeping hardware export restrictions. In recent months, reports revealed that companies in China had increasingly bypassed physical chip embargos by renting computing clusters running Nvidia Corp. H100 and H200 accelerators stationed across Southeast Asia.

Enforcement concerns escalated following the sudden departure of former Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, amid congressional inquiries into transactions with Singapore-based provider Megaspeed International. Megaspeed had imported billions of dollars worth of Nvidia hardware between 2023 and 2025, leasing high-performance clusters to overseas clients including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. and ByteDance Ltd.

While renting cloud compute does not violate legacy rules restricted to physical hardware delivery, the Commerce Department determined that remote access effectively nullifies national security protections by enabling Chinese frontier labs to train advanced large language models using American supercomputing infrastructure.

Under the new framework, cloud providers must implement verified customer identity protocols and adhere to strict compute quotas. Global data center operators serving clients in designated restricted regions will be prohibited from dedicating more than 50% of aggregate cluster capacity to Chinese firms without explicit Commerce Department authorization.

The interim rule takes effect immediately with an open public comment period. Lawmakers on Capitol Hill welcomed the measure as an essential step toward hardening the semiconductor perimeter, with members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee indicating plans for oversight hearings on export control enforcement mechanisms.

title: Arion Kurtaj, a 21-year-old Lapsus$ member, pleads guilty in UK court to hacking Rockstar, Uber, BT, and others, after being released from a secure hospital (Joe Tidy/BBC)
title_en: Arion Kurtaj, a 21-year-old Lapsus$ member, pleads guilty in UK court to hacking Rockstar, Uber, BT, and others, after being released from a secure hospital (Joe Tidy/BBC)

inline_images.caption: BBC Arion Kurtaj on a fishing trip, holding a fish.
inline_images.alt: BBC Arion Kurtaj on a fishing trip, holding a fish.

author: BBC
article_content:
A hacker has pleaded guilty to a string of online crimes, including trying to extort the makers of Grand Theft Auto 6 after stealing dozens of unfinished clips of the game.

21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, carried out the hack in 2022, and was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.

But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.

On Monday, Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.

Kurtaj breached Rockstar Games in 2022 whilst he was on bail for multiple other hacking offences and under police protection.

He was being housed in a Travelodge in Bicester to protect him from rival hackers who threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.

With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.

He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."

The company refused to cooperate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.

Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.79m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.

The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.

At the time, doctors deemed Kurtaj unfit to stand in a traditional trial due to the severity of his autism, so instead he was given what is known as a trial of the facts.

The jury was asked to determine whether or not he committed the alleged acts - not if he did so with criminal intent.

In December 2023 the court ruled that he would remain at a secure hospital for life unless doctors deem him no longer a danger.

A routine assessment late last year deemed that he was now fit to stand a criminal trial which was scheduled to take place at Woolwhich Crown Court.

But Kurtaj pleaded guilty to all offences.

He sat in the dock with short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt but no tie.

The now 21-year-old blinked frequently during the hearing and stood to confirm his name, and pled guilty to all counts with no visible emotion.

Those included hacks on BT/EE, Revolut and Uber where he used social engineering techniques to gain access to internal systems.

The court heard that during his hack on Uber he posted a picture of a penis as part of his attempts to force the company to pay a ransom.

His hacks on the companies are estimated to have caused around £10m of damage.

Using the data stolen from the firms, he and other members of the gang targeted cryptocurrency investors.

The prosecution argued that the gang stole at least $300,000 from individual victims.

Kurtaj also pleaded guilty to physical assaults on workers whilst in custody including multiple biting incidents.

Whilst in prison he was caught with a mobile phone after sending a taunting text message to police and posting updates on Snapchat.

Kurtaj will be sentenced at a later date.

In the 2023 original trial, another Lapsus$ member, who was 17, was found guilty at Southwark Crown Court.

The 17-year-old, who could not be named at the time due to his age, was sentenced to an 18-month Youth Rehabilitation Order, including intense supervision and a ban on using VPNs online.

Earlier this year that same hacker, now named as Thalha Jubair, was jailed for five years and six months after continuing his cyber crime offences with another group known as Scattered Spider.

Amongst victims was Transport for London which was subjected to a disruptive cyber attack that caused around £39m of damage and caused chaos inside the firm.

article_content_zh:
一名黑客承认了一系列网络犯罪行为，包括在窃取了《侠盗猎车手 6》游戏的数十个未完成的剪辑后试图勒索该游戏的制作者。

来自牛津的 21 岁的 Arion Kurtaj 于 2022 年实施了黑客攻击，最初由于他患有严重的自闭症，他被判处在安全医院无限期住院。

但不同寻常的是，他随后被认为适合接受审判，并于一月份被释放到普通监狱。

周一，Kurtaj 在伍尔维奇刑事法庭承认了他在 16 岁和 17 岁时与黑客团伙 Lapsus$ 一起实施的 Rockstar Games 黑客事件以及其他几起黑客事件。

Kurtaj 于 2022 年入侵了 Rockstar Games，当时他因多次其他黑客犯罪而被保释并受到警方保护。

他被安置在比斯特的一家 Travelodge 旅馆中，以保护他免受竞争对手黑客的威胁，这些黑客威胁要攻击他，因为他被盗的比特币藏匿处。

电脑被没收后，Kurtaj 使用插入酒店房间电视的 Amazon Fire Stick 以及蓝牙键盘和鼠标对 Rockstar 进行了攻击。

他窃取了公司内部数据，包括 90 个剪辑，显示了未完成且备受期待的《侠盗猎车手 6》的近 60 分钟的游戏过程。

然后他闯入公司内部的 Slack 消息系统宣称：“如果 Rockstar 在 24 小时内没有通过 Telegram 联系我，我将开始发布源代码。”

该公司拒绝合作，因此他以 TeaPotUberHacker 用户名将剪辑和源代码发布到论坛上。

Rockstar Games 表示，该公司花费了 500 万美元（379 万英镑）来从黑客攻击中恢复过来，此外还花费了数千小时的员工时间。

该公司还表示，这次泄露首次揭露了游戏中的一个可玩角色是女性——出于营销目的，该公司正在严密保守这一秘密。

当时，由于库尔塔吉患有严重的自闭症，医生认为他不适合参加传统的审判，因此他接受了所谓的事实审判。

陪审团被要求确定他是否实施了所指控的行为，而不是确定他是否具有犯罪意图。

author: MIT Tech Review
article_content:
How do you measure progress towards the future? In the Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, our series “Are we there yet?” examines how far six potentially transformative technologies have come after years of promises.

We spoke to experts, researchers and engineers to find out what’s holding them back, then scored each on a progress meter from zero to ten.  Find out how we rated each of these technologies—and how close they are to delivering on their promise.Nuclear-powered spaceshipsExercise in a pillInterspecies communicationSolid-state batteriesCleaning up PFASEliminating traffic deaths

Could technology keep your brain going beyond death? Far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to make it happen, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores these ideas and how close they might be to reality.
