article_content:
With OpenAI models and Codex, Revolut is giving its teams more room to solve complex problems—from software engineering to financial crime.

Revolut⁠(opens in a new window) was built to challenge the way people interact with money. That ambition now stretches across more than 40 markets, 800,000 businesses and a consumer base that’s grown by 23% in the last 12 months.

Add to that a company culture that expects small, lean teams to move quickly and it’s no surprise that ChatGPT and Codex have proven a natural fit.

“The perfect description for a high-caliber Revolut person is someone who can identify a problem really quickly, deduce the solution, design four scenarios, identify the best one of those four then take it to market,” says Kim Maniovich, Revolut’s Global Head of Business Marketing.

“Partnering with OpenAI enables us to build a lot of these solutions in a way that’s incredibly lean, cost-efficient and really tailored to the unique way that we work.”

But moving faster is only part of the opportunity. For Revolut, the bigger question is what becomes possible when talented people spend less time on the mechanics of getting things done—and more time tackling problems that could fundamentally change financial services.

As Revolut grows, so does the complexity of protecting its customers. According to one report⁠(opens in a new window), over half of adults worldwide reported a scam encounter in 2025.

For Revolut, every transaction creates another opportunity to identify suspicious activity, investigate potential risks and implement robust and tailored protections for its customers. But the sheer volume of those transactions far outstrips the human resources available to any bank.

“The biggest problem we can tackle with AI today is the scaling of humans versus the demand that we get,” says AI Lead David Abitbol. That’s why one of Revolut’s largest AI applications is a FinCrime agent powered by OpenAI models.

Rather than requiring investigators to work through every eligible case manually, the agent can examine information, apply Revolut’s rules and complete the defined process automatically.

The release of GPT‑5.5 was a turning point. It was then, says Abitbol, that the models had become capable and cost-effective enough for Revolut to delegate screening and investigation workflows entirely to the agent. The result is greater capacity to monitor transactions without increasing investigator headcount at the same rate as demand.

That, adds Information Security Engineer Mo Amiri, “translates directly into stronger protection and a more resilient system our customers can trust.”

‘Move fast but build trust’ could easily be Revolut’s internal engineering slogan. While Abitbol points out that Codex has delivered a 30-60% reduction in coding time, he’s also clear that certain guardrails are non-negotiable.

“We have a systematic framework where anyone in the company who’s building anything with AI has the same set of standards across development, A/B testing, and business metric prediction,” he says. “So every engineer is held to the same standard of quality across the company. We started to get enough intelligence for reasonable costs where we could increasingly delegate initial investigations and screenings to the agent.”

For Senior Platform Engineer Dmitry Pitik, that 30-60% reduction in coding time became tangible while he was building an internal code-review service. He designed the system, broke it into features and initially assumed he’d need a development team to implement it.

“I realised I don’t need a whole team of developers to implement this,” he recalls. “I can just launch different agents and assign each of them a particular task.” Codex became his implementation team, while Dmitry spent more time designing the system, planning the work and reviewing what came back.

This is a pattern that Abitbol has seen across Revolut. As Codex returns capacity to engineers they’re using that reclaimed time “to spend more time discussing design and the best solution. So we spend more time designing instead of implementing.”

That doesn’t remove the need for engineering expertise, it just changes where that expertise is applied. “Every developer is responsible for the code they produce, and we don’t blindly trust AI,” Pitik says. The result is a different division of work: AI can help with implementation, while engineers devote more attention to the decisions that determine whether the software is useful, reliable and worth building.

That overhead is worth it. As Codex works on one task, Pitik can work in parallel on another. That kind of multitasking is essential in a company where, as Kim Maniovich explains, the average employee has “three different jobs.” Using Codex creates a virtuous (if challenging) flywheel where “month on month the targets we’re setting get more aggressive, but also more attainable. And so the bar keeps moving up. AI is making that possible.”

Examples of what Revolut has been able to do with this new-found capacity include developing a tool to build web UIs for internal apps and external-facing products.

Or turning seven years of design documentation into AI-readable context in a single day, creating a foundation for tools intended to help designers work more effectively. The exercise illustrates how AI can make accumulated organisational knowledge more accessible, reducing the effort required to work with complex systems. “We can shift focus from the things which are important but hard to do without AI to the things which matter for customers,” says Senior Designer Dmytro Pavlov.

Mo Amiri’s job is to make sure all of this speed is matched by security—not just for customers but for Revolut’s own employees. That gives him two views of AI at once: how it can help Revolut investigate a problem, and what teams need before they can deploy it safely.

In a phishing investigation, for example, an analyst once had to gather an email, inspect its links and attachments, trace the sender and assemble the evidence manually. “With stronger AI tools, we can uncover those connections instantly, and dig deeper into the questions that really matter,” he says.

While AI does the legwork and presents an investigator with a structured case, it’s still down to the individual to review the original records, decide whether the explanation makes sense and approve any action.

Amiri applies the same thinking when teams bring new AI applications into Revolut. He follows the complete chain: what information the system sees, where that information goes, which tools it can reach, what it can do with that access and what happens when something fails. He also tests whether apparently convincing conclusions are actually supported by the evidence.

“The most critical decision is always about accountability,” he says. “If an AI tool suggests a code change, a human engineer needs to understand that change well enough to stand by it. That directly drives how we design the review process, giving developers the context they need without cluttering their everyday workflow.”

For Revolut, safeguards aren’t separate from innovation. They help establish the conditions under which teams can confidently adopt more capable technology. “That’s how you earn real confidence in AI,” he explains, “by making thoughtful decisions upfront and testing as you go.”

Start with a problem worth solving. Revolut has put AI to work where demand is growing fastest and the stakes for customers are highest.

Use speed to raise ambition, not lower standards. Time saved on coding and investigation creates room for better design, harder questions and more consequential work.

Keep people on the hook. AI can gather evidence, write code and recommend action. A person still needs to understand the work well enough to stand behind it.

Build trust before you scale. Be clear about what a system can see, what it can do and what happens when it fails—then test those decisions as you go.

Make your knowledge usable. AI works better when it can reach clear, well-organised context. The same exercise often shows where the organisation itself needs to be clearer.

Kim Maniovich connects that future to the culture driving the work. “I hope that we can take the values that we operate by every day—this unapologetic ambition, the desire to never settle—and enable people to apply that to their own lives through the products that we build for them.”

As AI makes it easier to build, the differentiator becomes knowing what to build—and maintaining the judgment, standards and customer understanding to do it well. For Revolut, that’s the bigger promise of intelligence at work: less time spent on the mechanics of getting things done, and more capacity to make financial services safer, simpler and more useful for everyone.

article_content_zh:
借助 OpenAI 模型和 Codex，Revolut 为其团队提供了更多空间来解决从软件工程到金融犯罪的复杂问题。

Revolut⁠（在新窗口中打开）旨在挑战人们与金钱互动的方式。这一雄心现已覆盖 40 多个市场、80 万家企业以及过去 12 个月增长了 23% 的消费者群。

再加上公司文化要求小型、精干的团队能够快速行动，因此事实证明 ChatGPT 和 Codex 是天生的搭档也就不足为奇了。

Revolut 全球业务营销主管 Kim Maniovich 表示：“对高素质 Revolut 人员的完美描述是能够快速识别问题、推断解决方案、设计四种方案、确定这四种方案中最好的一种，然后将其推向市场。”

“与 OpenAI 合作使我们能够以极其精简、经济高效且真正适合我们独特工作方式的方式构建许多此类解决方案。”

但更快的行动只是机遇的一部分。对于 Revolut 来说，更大的问题是，当有才华的人花更少的时间在完成工作的机制上，而花更多的时间来解决可能从根本上改变金融服务的问题时，会发生什么。

随着 Revolut 的发展，保护客户的复杂性也随之增加。根据一份报告（在新窗口中打开），全球超过一半的成年人报告称在 2025 年遭遇过诈骗。

对于 Revolut 来说，每笔交易都会创造另一个机会来识别可疑活动、调查潜在风险并为其客户实施强大且量身定制的保护。但这些交易的绝对数量远远超出了任何银行可用的人力资源。

人工智能负责人戴维·阿比特博尔 (David Abitbol) 表示：“当今人工智能可以解决的最大问题是人类的规模与我们所获得的需求之间的关系。”这就是为什么 Revolut 最大的人工智能应用程序之一是由 OpenAI 模型支持的 FinCrime 代理。

代理可以检查信息、应用 Revolut 规则并自动完成定义的流程，而不是要求调查人员手动处理每个符合条件的案件。

GPT-5.5 的发布是一个转折点。 Abitbol 表示，就在那时，这些模型已经变得足够强大且具有成本效益，Revolut 可以将筛选和调查工作流程完全委托给代理。其结果是，在不按需求增加调查员人数的情况下，监控交易的能力得到提高。

信息安全工程师 Mo Amiri 补充道，“这直接转化为我们的客户可以信赖的更强大的保护和更具弹性的系统。”

“快速行动，但建立信任”很容易成为 Revolut 的内部工程口号。虽然 Abitbol 指出 Codex 已将编码时间缩短了 30-60%，但他也明确指出某些护栏是不容协商的。

“我们有一个系统框架，公司中使用人工智能构建任何东西的任何人在开发、A/B 测试和业务指标预测方面都拥有相同的一套标准，”他说。 “因此，整个公司的每位工程师都必须遵守相同的质量标准。我们开始以合理的成本获得足够的情报，从而可以将初步调查和筛查越来越多地委托给代理。”

title: Analysis: global manufacturing, utility, and mining companies have shed $4.2T in market value since June as the AI "picks and shovels" trade swings into reverse (Clara Murray/Financial Times)
title_en: Analysis: global manufacturing, utility, and mining companies have shed $4.2T in market value since June as the AI "picks and shovels" trade swings into reverse (Clara Murray/Financial Times)
author: Financial Times
article_content:
Global manufacturing, utility and mining companies have shed $4.2tn in value since June as the AI “picks and shovels” trade swings into reverse.

Companies more frequently linked by media coverage to data centre construction have been hit hardest by the sell-off, an FT analysis found, as investors’ confidence in the AI boom wobbles.

The losses wiped out almost half of the $9.4tn in value that the same companies gained in the previous 12 months as investors piled into the manufacturers of everything from jet engines adapted to power hyperscale data centres to the advanced fibre optics needed to connect AI server racks.

Caterpillar, a leading supplier of gas generators to data centres, has seen its market capitalisation slashed by $214bn, or 44 per cent, since its shares hit an all-time high on June 30, according to FactSet data.

Nuclear power company Oklo plunged 49 per cent despite signing a contract with Meta in January. Comfort Systems, which makes HVAC systems, and Corning, a fibre optics manufacturer, both lost around half of their value over the same period.

Paul Kedrosky, a venture capitalist and fellow at the MIT Institute, said investors had been wrong to start treating old-school industrial firms like semiconductor stocks. “It had become endless in discussions with hedge funds and family offices, this idea that everything was now a growth stock — which is ludicrous, of course.”

The sell-off comes amid wider market turmoil for AI-related shares, as investors question whether escalating debt-financed capital expenditures at hyperscalers and mounting political opposition to data centres in the US could lead to a bust.

That has hit industrial groups whose fortunes are increasingly bound to the build-out. The sector has been the second-worst-performing in the S&P 500 since the summer, after technology.

“There has been a lot of institutional investment piling blindly into these trades that probably fuelled an overly enthusiastic valuation on some of these [companies],” said Brett Ryan, senior US economist at Deutsche Bank.

The stock market was “finally benchmarking to what credit was already telling you” about the growth in risky financing for data centre construction, he added.

However, others argue that the companies supplying the boom were on solid foundations, with demand still vastly outstripping supply. Spending on data centre construction — excluding IT equipment and chips — hit $96bn in the US in the 12 months to September, the latest government data showed.

“In terms of the fundamentals of revenues and the potential earnings for these companies, we are still looking at a very strong prospect,” said Alex Cordovil, an analyst at Dell’Oro Group.

Wider trends such as electrification and supply chain restructuring continued to support many industrial firms’ core businesses. “The build-out is not decelerating as of yet . . . backlogs are at record highs, meaning that until 2027 . . . revenue growth is already baked in,” he added.

Richard S Warzala, chief executive of Allient, an industrial controls maker, said demand for AI was not going to decline. “They can have a moratorium on new data centre installation, but those that are already started need to be completed,” he said in an earnings call on November 5.

Third-quarter results showed strong demand. Many gas turbine manufacturers said they were taking billions of dollars in orders in the first nine months of 2026. article_content_en:
Global manufacturing, utility and mining companies have shed $4.2tn in value since June as the AI “picks and shovels” trade swings into reverse.

Companies more frequently linked by media coverage to data centre construction have been hit hardest by the sell-off, an FT analysis found, as investors’ confidence in the AI boom wobbles.

The losses wiped out almost half of the $9.4tn in value that the same companies gained in the previous 12 months as investors piled into the manufacturers of everything from jet engines adapted to power hyperscale data centres to the advanced fibre optics needed to connect AI server racks.

Caterpillar, a leading supplier of gas generators to data centres, has seen its market capitalisation slashed by $214bn, or 44 per cent, since its shares hit an all-time high on June 30, according to FactSet data.

Nuclear power company Oklo plunged 49 per cent despite signing a contract with Meta in January. Comfort Systems, which makes HVAC systems, and Corning, a fibre optics manufacturer, both lost around half of their value over the same period.

Paul Kedrosky, a venture capitalist and fellow at the MIT Institute, said investors had been wrong to start treating old-school industrial firms like semiconductor stocks. “It had become endless in discussions with hedge funds and family offices, this idea that everything was now a growth stock — which is ludicrous, of course.”

The sell-off comes amid wider market turmoil for AI-related shares, as investors question whether escalating debt-financed capital expenditures at hyperscalers and mounting political opposition to data centres in the US could lead to a bust.

That has hit industrial groups whose fortunes are increasingly bound to the build-out. The sector has been the second-worst-performing in the S&P 500 since the summer, after technology.

“There has been a lot of institutional investment piling blindly into these trades that probably fuelled an overly enthusiastic valuation on some of these [companies],” said Brett Ryan, senior US economist at Deutsche Bank.

The stock market was “finally benchmarking to what credit was already telling you” about the growth in risky financing for data centre construction, he added.

However, others argue that the companies supplying the boom were on solid foundations, with demand still vastly outstripping supply. Spending on data centre construction — excluding IT equipment and chips — hit $96bn in the US in the 12 months to September, the latest government data showed.

“In terms of the fundamentals of revenues and the potential earnings for these companies, we are still looking at a very strong prospect,” said Alex Cordovil, an analyst at Dell’Oro Group.

Wider trends such as electrification and supply chain restructuring continued to support many industrial firms’ core businesses. “The build-out is not decelerating as of yet . . . backlogs are at record highs, meaning that until 2027 . . . revenue growth is already baked in,” he added.

Richard S Warzala, chief executive of Allient, an industrial controls maker, said demand for AI was not going to decline. “They can have a moratorium on new data centre installation, but those that are already started need to be completed,” he said in an earnings call on November 5.

Third-quarter results showed strong demand. Many gas turbine manufacturers said they were taking billions of dollars in orders in the first nine months of 2026. Caterpillar reported a record $78bn backlog and said its power generation sales grew 75 per cent year-on-year, driven by data centre demand.

Kedrosky cautioned that backlogs and orders were trailing indicators reflecting expectations, with people “double and triple ordering to protect their position in the queue given perceived scarcity”.

The impact of the data centre moratoriums and restrictions widely backed by US voters in this month’s midterm elections is still unclear.

Citi researchers said in a note published after the elections that while they expected tighter regulations to bring more volatility to the data centre industry, widespread restrictions on construction remained unlikely.

Joseph Dominguez of Constellation Energy told investors that the market movement following the election had been an “overreaction” and Democrats “care very deeply” about protecting blue-collar jobs at data centres.

Others say any bans would just shift construction to more friendly jurisdictions.

“At the end of the day, if there is demand for these things, they will get built somewhere,” said Deutsche Bank’s Ryan.
article_content_zh:
自 6 月份以来，随着人工智能“镐和铲”贸易的逆转，全球制造、公用事业和采矿公司的价值已减少 4.2 兆美元。

英国《金融时报》分析发现，随着投资者对人工智能热潮的信心动摇，那些经常被媒体报道与数据中心建设联系在一起的公司受到抛售的打击最为严重。

这些损失几乎抹去了这些公司在过去 12 个月中获得的 9.4 万亿美元价值的一半，因为投资者纷纷涌入这些制造商，从适合为超大规模数据中心供电的喷气发动机到连接人工智能服务器机架所需的先进光纤。

根据 FactSet 数据，卡特彼勒是数据中心燃气发电机的领先供应商，自 6 月 30 日股价创下历史新高以来，其市值已缩水 2140 亿美元，即 44%。

尽管核电公司 Oklo 一月份与 Meta 签署了合同，但股价仍暴跌 49%。制造暖通空调系统的舒适系统公司和光纤制造商康宁公司的价值同期都损失了大约一半。

风险投资家、麻省理工学院研究员保罗·凯德罗斯基 (Paul Kedrosky) 表示，投资者开始将传统工业公司视为半导体股票，这是错误的。 “与对冲基金和家族办公室的讨论变得无休无止，这种认为现在一切都是成长型股票的想法——当然，这是荒谬的。”

此次抛售正值人工智能相关股票出现更广泛的市场动荡，因为投资者质疑超大规模企业债务融资资本支出的不断增加以及对美国数据中心的政治反对是否会导致破产。

这对工业集团造成了打击，它们的命运越来越依赖于扩建。自夏季以来，该行业一直是标准普尔 500 指数中表现第二差的行业，仅次于科技行业。

德意志银行高级美国经济学家布雷特·瑞安（Brett Ryan）表示：“大量机构投资盲目涌入这些交易，可能导致对其中一些公司的估值过于热情。”

他补充说，股市“最终以信贷已经告诉你的信息为基准”关于数据中心建设风险融资的增长。

然而，其他人则认为，为繁荣提供服务的公司基础稳固，需求仍然大大超过供应。最新的政府数据显示，截至 9 月份的 12 个月内，美国数据中心建设支出（不包括 IT 设备和芯片）达到 960 亿美元。

Dell'Oro Group 分析师 Alex Cordovil 表示：“就这些公司的收入基本面和潜在收益而言，我们仍然看到非常强劲的前景。”

电气化和供应链重组等更广泛的趋势继续支持许多工业企业的核心业务。 “到目前为止，扩建尚未放缓……积压订单创历史新高，这意味着到 2027 年……收入增长已经开始显现，”他补充道。

工业控制制造商 Allient 的首席执行官理查德·S·瓦尔扎拉 (Richard S Warzala) 表示，对人工智能的需求不会下降。他在 11 月 5 日的财报电话会议上表示：“他们可以暂停新数据中心的安装，但那些已经开始的数据中心需要完成。”

title: Startups unveil plans to develop floating offshore data centers to bypass land and power constraints, while experts warn of challenges like saltwater corrosion (Jackie Snow/Wall Street Journal)
title_en: Startups unveil plans to develop floating offshore data centers to bypass land and power constraints, while experts warn of challenges like saltwater corrosion (Jackie Snow/Wall Street Journal)
author: Wall Street Journal
article_content:
Floating data centers? A Dallas startup bets on a new approach for a controversial industry Trevor Bach September 26, 2026 8 min read Dallas startup Mousterian is planning to put its data centers on water to help with cooling and water usage. (Photo

But those data centers, which sometimes occupy hundreds of acres and use the resource equivalent of small cities, are located on land, often near people's homes. A Dallas startup, called Mousterian, is taking a different approach: Developing data centers that float on water.

The unique design, said Min Suh, Mousterian's CEO and cofounder, allows the floating data centers avoid municipal water supplies entirely, because they use the surrounding body of water as part of a closed-loop cooling system. The floating data centers also don't make noise and are ideally located near power plants, so they can access energy easily and avoid bothering residents, because people generally aren't living in such heavy industrial zones anyway.

"We like to think, 'If we are going to build a data center, we're trying to do it in the most sustainable way possible,' " said Suh.

Now several years into an AI-driven construction boom, the United States is home to over 4,000 data centers, including more than 1,000 hyperscalers, the largest facilities. Many of the biggest are in Texas, including Stargate, a potentially $500 billion joint venture in Abilene led by OpenAI, and Frontier, an incoming 1,200-acre project in Shackelford County. Numerous projects are also underway in data center-heavy D-FW, which was recently ranked by Cushman and Wakefield as the top primary data center market in the Americas.

The boom has created a rush of Texas construction jobs and been welcomed by many political and business leaders. "I think of [data centers] almost like the highways and the airports that are the fundamental infrastructure of the future," Dallas Regional Chamber executive Mike Rosa told The News last year.

But the computing centers' vast energy and water consumption — the biggest culprit is their cooling systems — has emerged as a persistent flashpoint, prompting community outrage and various local and state moratoriums.

In Texas, Abbott's new moratorium mandates an audit of pending data center projects that includes details on their cooling systems and impact on local water supplies, and politicians including Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico, the state's Democratic gubernatorial and U.S. Senate candidates, are also loudly calling for tighter water regulations.

One controversial project — a planned data center about 60 miles southeast of Dallas that was expected to pull millions of gallons of water per day from Cedar Creek Lake, which also supplies drinking water for Fort Worth — was already scrapped.

"We're killing ourselves letting the data centers in," said Ashley Cook, a lawyer who led the fight against the project. "You're basically turning a rural residential peaceful community into an industrial corridor."

Some industry leaders have pushed back against the water-guzzling stigma, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who has called the water issue "totally fake" even while pushing for more renewable energy use. Experts say the consumption issues are in fact relatively nuanced and localized. Each facility's design and technology is also important.

Yet as the world's seemingly insatiable demand for computing power keeps rising, developers have also been exploring more novel solutions. Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, among others, have unveiled plans for data centers in space. Earlier this year, a wind-powered, underwater data center began operating several miles off the coast of Shanghai. In Norway, a data center complex was built into an abandoned mine, with seawater-based cooling from an adjacent fjord.

Several years ago, a California-based company called Nautilus Data Technologies developed the world's first floating data center, which it built atop a refurbished, 700-ton barge in the San Joaquin River at the industrial Port of Stockton. The two-story operation, which resembles a white shipping container, began operating in 2021 with a cooling system that cycles around 4,500 gallons of river water per minute, with screens that serve as filters to keep fish and plants out of the intake system.

The site proved more ecologically sustainable, with far lower electricity and operating costs than typical land-based operations, according to Nautilus. It was also well received by local officials, and attracted San Joaquin County as an anchor tenant.

For some of its developers, it also served as a launching pad: "Taking those lessons of building the first floating data center," said Suh, "we kind of took all the best components of different technologies available and basically created this new company."

Suh, who has extensive data center experience but was not involved with the California floating data center project, cofounded Mousterian — the name refers to the Middle Paleolithic era, when humans first started using complex tools — with Chase Ott-Wick, a former senior engineer on the California project, and Gabe Andrews, another data center veteran and former Nautilus executive.

The 10-person company, which is self-funded and quietly launched last year, is based in downtown Dallas and handles data center design, engineering and development. In addition to floating data centers, it also develops land-based and water-adjacent facilities — Suh said it's best to characterize the company as "a high-performance data center developer with unique facility offerings versus a purely floating data center company" — but is broadly focused on delivering projects that require far less energy and don't use municipal groundwater.

"A lot of the tech companies and hyperscalers were still maybe 10 to 15 years behind on how they were developing and delivering data centers," said Suh, who also pointed to conspicuous examples of companies building water-guzzling facilities in dry areas like the American West. "And so we're trying to push the envelope the opposite way, by being kind of very water sensitive."

The startup has already landed major institutional partners: Earlier this year, in its highest-profile move yet, Mousterian signed an agreement with Samsung Heavy Industries, one of the world's largest shipbuilders, which last month led to an engineering contract to jointly develop a fleet of floating data centers.

Under the terms of the deal, Mousterian and the Korean manufacturing giant are co-designing the vessels, which will be manufactured by Samsung in South Korea and then shipped and finished by Mousterian likely in Texas or Louisiana. Mousterian is also designing the facilities' internal equipment.

The floating data centers will have about a one-acre footprint and a capacity of about 50 megawatts, which roughly qualifies them as large data centers. (Stargate, the massive Abilene project, is designed for a capacity of up to 1,200 megawatts.)

The plan is for the new floating fleet to be deployed in different locations around the U.S. Mousterian currently has a half dozen different project sites — featuring a mix of floating and land-based designs — in various stages, including a hybrid floating and land-based campus next to a power plant in Houston and what it's calling "a large-scale floating campus" in the San Jose, Calif. area.

Suh declined to provide more details about the other projects' locations, but the floating data centers are typically located in sites like deep river harbors or shipping channels, where they're moored close enough to land so that employees can easily walk back and forth between the floating facility and complementary land-based facilities.

"Within 30 seconds, you know, you're in a regular air-conditioned office, with a bathroom and kitchen," Suh said.

The data centers will also source energy that's not connected to the public grid, while their pass-through water cooling systems will help give them a Power Usage Effectiveness, or PUE, score of 1.15 or 1.2, Suh said, which would rank among the industry's best. Traditional data centers' PUE scores, where 1.0 indicates perfect energy efficiency, are typically 1.5 or higher.

The floating data center concept has its complications, said Ed Hirs, an energy economist at the University of Houston, including a potentially high development cost, the access to large power sources and even environmental issues, if the warmer water discharging back into the water source disrupts marine life.

"It's all a matter of how much money they want to spend," Hirs said.

Another major challenge is identifying the right locations, because of the very specific requirements needed to make the projects work. But being an industry innovator also has its benefits.

"It's just that we're the only company looking for these sites right now," Suh said, "so we've kind of had our pick."

Suh, who has extensive data center experience but was not involved with the California floating data center project, cofounded Mousterian — the name refers to the Middle Paleolithic era, when humans first started using complex tools — with Chase Ott-Wick, a former senior engineer on the California project, and Gabe Andrews, another data center veteran and former Nautilus executive.

The 10-person company, which is self-funded and quietly launched last year, is based in downtown Dallas and handles data center design, engineering and development. In addition to floating data centers, it also develops land-based and water-adjacent facilities — Suh said it's best to characterize the company as "a high-performance data center developer with unique facility offerings versus a purely floating data center company" — but is broadly focused on delivering projects that require far less energy and don't use municipal groundwater.

"A lot of the tech companies and hyperscalers were still maybe 10 to 15 years behind on how they were developing and delivering data centers," said Suh, who also pointed to conspicuous examples of companies building water-guzzling facilities in dry areas like the American West. "And so we're trying to push the envelope the opposite way, by being kind of very water sensitive."

The startup has already landed major institutional partners: Earlier this year, in its highest-profile move yet, Mousterian signed an agreement with Samsung Heavy Industries, one of the world's largest shipbuilders, which last month led to an engineering contract to jointly develop a fleet of floating data centers.

Under the terms of the deal, Mousterian and the Korean manufacturing giant are co-designing the vessels, which will be manufactured by Samsung in South Korea and then shipped and finished by Mousterian likely in Texas or Louisiana. Mousterian is also designing the facilities' internal equipment.

The floating data centers will have about a one-acre footprint and a capacity of about 50 megawatts, which roughly qualifies them as large data centers. (Stargate, the massive Abilene project, is designed for a capacity of up to 1,200 megawatts.)

The plan is for the new floating fleet to be deployed in different locations around the U.S. Mousterian currently has a half dozen different project sites — featuring a mix of floating and land-based designs — in various stages, including a hybrid floating and land-based campus next to a power plant in Houston and what it's calling "a large-scale floating campus" in the San Jose, Calif. area.

Suh declined to provide more details about the other projects' locations, but the floating data centers are typically located in sites like deep river harbors or shipping channels, where they're moored close enough to land so that employees can easily walk back and forth between the floating facility and complementary land-based facilities.

"Within 30 seconds, you know, you're in a regular air-conditioned office, with a bathroom and kitchen," Suh said.

The data centers will also source energy that's not connected to the public grid, while their pass-through water cooling systems will help give them a Power Usage Effectiveness, or PUE, score of 1.15 or 1.2, Suh said, which would rank among the industry's best. Traditional data centers' PUE scores, where 1.0 indicates perfect energy efficiency, are typically 1.5 or higher.

The floating data center concept has its complications, said Ed Hirs, an energy economist at the University of Houston, including a potentially high development cost, the access to large power sources and even environmental issues, if the warmer water discharging back into the water source disrupts marine life.

"It's all a matter of how much money they want to spend," Hirs said.

Another major challenge is identifying the right locations, because of the very specific requirements needed to make the projects work. But being an industry innovator also has its benefits.

"It's just that we're the only company looking for these sites right now," Suh said, "so we've kind of had our pick."

This article originally published at Floating data centers? A Dallas startup bets on a new approach for a controversial industry.
title_zh: 初创公司Mousterian布局海上浮动数据中心
summary_zh: 达拉斯初创公司Mousterian拟利用闭环水冷系统研发浮动式数据中心，以规避陆地设施的能耗压力与社区争议
article_content_zh:
浮动数据中心？达拉斯一家初创公司押注于有争议行业的新方法 Trevor Bach 2026 年 9 月 26 日 8 分钟阅读 达拉斯初创公司 Mousterian 计划将其数据中心置于水上，以帮助冷却和用水。 （迈克尔·霍格 (Michael Hogue) 提供的照片）数据中心因噪音大、丑陋且消耗大量电力和水而受到指责。它们最近还变得具有政治毒性，导致在红橡树和凯勒等达拉斯-沃斯堡社区举行有争议的公开会议，并导致州长格雷格·阿博特出人意料地暂停。

但这些数据中心有时占地数百英亩，使用的资源相当于小城市，它们位于陆地上，通常靠近人们的家。达拉斯的一家名为 Mousterian 的初创公司正在采取不同的方法：开发漂浮在水面上的数据中心。

Mousterian 首席执行官兼联合创始人 Min Suh 表示，这种独特的设计使浮动数据中心完全避免了市政供水，因为它们使用周围的水体作为闭环冷却系统的一部分。浮动数据中心也不会产生噪音，而且位置理想，靠近发电厂，因此可以轻松获取能源，避免打扰居民，因为人们通常不会住在这样的重工业区。

他说：“我们喜欢这样想，‘如果我们要建一个数据中心，我们就要尽可能以最可持续的方式来做。’”

如今，人工智能驱动的建设热潮已持续数年，美国已拥有 4,000 多个数据中心，其中包括 1,000 多个超大规模数据中心（最大的设施）。其中许多最大的项目都在德克萨斯州，包括 Stargate（由 OpenAI 领导的位于阿比林的一家可能价值 5000 亿美元的合资企业）和 Frontier（即将在沙克尔福德县占地 1,200 英亩的项目）。以数据中心为主的 D-FW 也正在进行许多项目，该地区最近被 Cushman 和 Wakefield 评为美洲最大的主要数据中心市场。

这种繁荣创造了德克萨斯州建筑业就业岗位的热潮，并受到许多政界和商界领袖的欢迎。 “我认为[数据中心]几乎就像高速公路和机场一样，是未来的基础设施，”达拉斯地区商会执行官迈克罗莎去年告诉新闻。

但计算中心巨大的能源和水消耗——最大的罪魁祸首是它们的冷却系统——已经成为一个持续的导火索，引发了社区的愤怒和各种地方和州的暂停。

在得克萨斯州，雅培新的暂停令要求对悬而未决的数据中心项目进行审计，其中包括其冷却系统的详细信息以及对当地供水的影响，该州民主党州长和美国参议院候选人吉娜·伊诺霍萨和詹姆斯·塔拉里科等政界人士也大声呼吁加强水监管。

一个有争议的项目——位于达拉斯东南约 60 英里处的一个计划中的数据中心，预计每天从雪松溪湖抽取数百万加仑的水，该湖也为沃斯堡提供饮用水——已经被废弃。

领导反对该项目的律师阿什利·库克 (Ashley Cook) 表示：“让数据中心进入我们正在自杀。” “你基本上是在把一个宁静的农村住宅社区变成一个工业走廊。”

一些行业领袖对耗水的耻辱进行了反击，其中包括 OpenAI 首席执行官萨姆·奥尔特曼 (Sam Altman)，他称水问题“完全是假的”，尽管他在推动更多可再生能源的使用。专家表示，消费问题实际上是相对微妙和局部的。每个设施的设计和技术也很重要。

然而，随着世界对计算能力看似永无止境的需求不断增长，开发人员也一直在探索更多新颖的解决方案。埃隆·马斯克和杰夫·贝佐斯等人公布了太空数据中心计划。今年早些时候，一个风力水下数据中心开始在距离上海海岸几英里的地方运营。在挪威，一个数据中心综合体建在一个废弃的矿井中，利用邻近峡湾的海水进行冷却。

几年前，一家名为 Nautilus Data Technologies 的加州公司开发了世界上第一个浮动数据中心，该中心建在斯托克顿工业港圣华金河上一艘翻新的 700 吨驳船上。这个两层楼的工厂类似于白色集装箱，于 2021 年开始运营，其冷却系统每分钟循环约 4,500 加仑河水，并配有滤网作为过滤器，以防止鱼类和植物进入进水系统。

鹦鹉螺公司表示，事实证明，该地点更具生态可持续性，电力和运营成本比典型的陆上运营低得多。它还受到当地官员的好评，并吸引了圣华金县作为主要租户。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 达拉斯初创公司Mousterian正开发海上浮动式数据中心架构，利用周边水体构建闭环冷却系统，旨在彻底摆脱对市政供水的依赖并缓解工业噪声对陆地社区的干扰。该方案选址优先靠近电力设施，意在通过物理空间隔离解决当前AI算力扩张引发的土地合规性与公共资源争夺压力。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Dallas-based startup Mousterian is developing floating data center architectures that utilize surrounding water bodies for closed-loop cooling systems to eliminate reliance on municipal water and mitigate noise pollution. The design prioritizes proximity to power plants to address land-use compliance issues and resource competition challenges stemming from the current AI compute expansion.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 海上数据中心将AI算力基础设施向公海或工业水域转移，实质上是对电力与资源管辖权的一场博弈，旨在绕过日益严苛的陆地环保准入机制。尽管该模式解决了冷却效率与土地溢价问题，但必须克服盐雾腐蚀带来的硬件运维成本激增，以及海上能源输送链路的高额资产折旧风险。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Relocating AI infrastructure to maritime or industrial water bodies serves as a strategic maneuver to circumvent increasingly stringent terrestrial environmental regulations. While this architecture improves cooling efficiency and optimizes land costs, it faces significant technical hurdles, including high hardware maintenance costs from saltwater corrosion and the capital-intensive nature of maritime power transmission infrastructure.

article_content:
This news was originally shared by LVMH’s Media Division and can be read here⁠(opens in a new window).

Paris, 16 November 2026—LVMH Group’s Media Division and OpenAI announce the signing of a strategic agreement to support new uses of artificial intelligence across all the division’s publications and make their journalism more accessible through ChatGPT. The agreement includes the deployment of OpenAI tools and ChatGPT Enterprise to teams across the media division, enabling them to develop AI applications tailored to their day-to-day work.

Their shared ambition is to empower teams across the media division to experiment with and develop practical uses of AI that support journalism and high-quality reporting.

Artificial intelligence is a powerful tool that, when put to work in newsrooms, enables journalists to focus on the core of their profession: investigating, analysing and writing. Teams will be able to explore applications such as document research, document comparison and preliminary translation. The goal is to enable them to devote more time to investigative reporting, analysis and reporting in the field.

In addition, in an increasingly crowded information landscape, personalisation has become a major priority. Artificial intelligence is an essential tool for developing and delivering products and services that meet the needs of customers, readers and advertisers alike, helping to attract and retain them and grow revenue across the publications.

This partnership is a company-wide initiative that also enhances the presence of content from LVMH Group’s Media Division in ChatGPT, providing summaries and excerpts in response to relevant user questions, identifying their sources and including direct links to the original articles. The partnership will extend across all the division’s publications and support the evolution of roles throughout the organisation: streamlining operations, improving efficiency, and encouraging innovation and creativity to prepare today’s publications for tomorrow. The rollout will be supported by training tailored to everyone’s use cases.

LVMH Group’s media division, Groupe Les Echos-Le Parisien, brings together 17 media brands covering news, finance, culture, heritage, arts and music. With 1,800 employees, including nearly 700 journalists, it reaches more than 27 million people in France every month.

The Group’s media brands: Boursier.com⁠(opens in a new window), Capital Finance, Challenges, Connaissance des Arts, Historia, Investir, La Lettre de l’Expansion, L’Agefi, Le Parisien, Aujourd’hui en France, Les Echos, L’Opinion, medici.tv⁠(opens in a new window), Mezzo, Mieux Vivre Votre Argent, Paris Match, Radio Classique.

The Group’s exhibitions and publishing houses: Citadelles & Mazenod, Fine Arts Paris, In Fine, Salon du Dessin.

title_zh: LVMH媒体部与OpenAI达成人工智能战略合作
summary_zh: LVMH集团旗下媒体部门宣布与OpenAI达成战略合作，通过部署ChatGPT企业版优化新闻生产流程并实现内容检索优化
article_content_zh:
此消息最初由 LVMH 媒体部门分享，可在此处阅读（在新窗口中打开）。

巴黎，2026 年 11 月 16 日——LVMH 集团媒体部门和 OpenAI 宣布签署战略协议，支持该部门所有出版物中人工智能的新用途，并通过 ChatGPT 让他们的新闻报道更容易获取。该协议包括向媒体部门的团队部署 OpenAI 工具和 ChatGPT Enterprise，使他们能够开发适合其日常工作的 AI 应用程序。

他们的共同目标是让整个媒体部门的团队能够试验和开发人工智能的实际用途，以支持新闻业和高质量的报道。

人工智能是一种强大的工具，当在新闻编辑室中使用时，记者能够专注于其职业的核心：调查、分析和写作。团队将能够探索文档研究、文档比较和初步翻译等应用。目标是让他们能够投入更多时间进行实地调查报告、分析和报告。

此外，在日益拥挤的信息环境中，个性化已成为首要任务。人工智能是开发和提供满足客户、读者和广告商需求的产品和服务的重要工具，有助于吸引和留住他们并增加出版物的收入。

这一合作伙伴关系是一项全公司范围内的举措，还增强了 LVMH 集团媒体部门内容在 ChatGPT 中的展示，提供摘要和摘录以回答相关用户问题，识别其来源并包括原始文章的直接链接。该合作伙伴关系将扩展到该部门的所有出版物，并支持整个组织的角色演变：简化运营、提高效率、鼓励创新和创造力，为明天的出版物做好准备。此次推出将得到针对每个人的用例量身定制的培训的支持。

LVMH集团的媒体部门Groupe Les Echos-Le Parisien汇集了17个媒体品牌，涵盖新闻、财经、文化、遗产、艺术和音乐。该公司拥有 1,800 名员工，其中包括近 700 名记者，每月覆盖法国超过 2,700 万人。

集团旗下媒体品牌：Boursier.com⁠（在新窗口中打开）、Capital Finance、Challenges、Connaissance des Arts、Historia、Investir、La Lettre de l’Expansion、L’Agefi、Le Parisien、Aujourd’hui en France、Les Echos、L’Opinion、medici.tv⁠（在新窗口中打开）、Mezzo、Mieux Vivre Votre Argent、Paris比赛，经典广播电台。

集团旗下展览和出版社：Citadelles & Mazenod、Fine Arts Paris、In Fine、Salon du Dessin。

title: Delhi-based Bharat Semi, which is developing programmable image sensors combining capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, raised a $24M seed (Jagmeet Singh/TechCrunch)
title_en: Delhi-based Bharat Semi, which is developing programmable image sensors combining capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, raised a $24M seed (Jagmeet Singh/TechCrunch)

inline_images.caption: Image Credits:Bharat Semi
inline_images.alt: Image Credits:Bharat Semi

author: TechCrunch
article_content:
Bharat Semi, an Indian semiconductor startup, has raised $24 million in seed funding to develop AI-enabled image sensors, as it seeks to win customers in the United States and elsewhere.

The investment comes as the nearly five-year-old, pre-revenue startup says it has secured design wins with U.S. defense technology company General Atomics and India’s Kaynes Semicon. Its image sensors, however, remain under development, with the startup targeting its initial commercial production in 2027.

India has committed billions of dollars to build up a domestic semiconductor industry, with a hope to become an alternative manufacturing hub as U.S. companies look to diversify supply chains beyond China. The country, however, has yet to establish itself as a major chip manufacturing hub. Meanwhile, the AI boom is also giving Indian startups such as Bharat Semi an opportunity to develop specialized chips for global markets.

The New Delhi-based startup is developing programmable image sensors that combine image capture, processing, and AI capabilities on a single chip, reducing the need to send visual data to separate processors. The move could cut system costs by at least 70% compared with conventional setups that use a separate image sensor, image signal processor, and a system-on-chip, co-founder Vrinda Kapoor (pictured above, right) said in an interview.

“Our aim here is to move from sensors to sense-making solutions,” Kapoor told TechCrunch.

Kapoor, a South Park Commons fellow who earlier worked in healthcare technology, co-founded Bharat Semi in late 2021 with Vinayak Dalmia (pictured above, left), the startup’s managing director, who previously worked at McKinsey and in private equity. Its chief technology officer, Boyd Fowler, previously held the same role at image-sensor maker OmniVision.

Bharat Semi is targeting smart homes, industrial automation, surveillance, and aerospace. Without disclosing specifics, Kapoor pointed to air conditioners that could detect when a room is empty and adjust automatically and drones that could process visual information — even with the absence of more expensive computing hardware elsewhere in the system.

The startup’s first-generation sensors are already in prototyping, while its second-generation sensors, which will incorporate more advanced AI capabilities, are expected to reach the prototype stage by mid-2027, Kapoor said. Moreover, the startup plans to get those newer sensors into customers’ hands by the end of 2027.

The all-equity seed round was led by Info Edge Group, South Park Commons, and Indus Bridge Ventures, with participation from Valour Capital, Micromax, Gaingels, and individual investors. Bharat Semi, Kapoor said, plans to use the funding to expand its engineering team, complete product development, and bring its sensors to market.

Bharat Semi has about 75 employees across India and the U.S., including 10 to 12 in its American operations, which span engineering and business development in Santa Clara. The startup plans to increase its U.S. headcount to around 20 by mid-2027, Kapoor said. It has also begun hiring engineers in Europe.

“It’s a story of can we build a global technology company out of India,” Kapoor said.

In 2024, Bharat Semi announced plans for a semiconductor fabrication project in India involving a technology partnership with the U.S. Space Force. The initiative, Kapoor said, remains in development and the startup is working to identify domestic partners that would build and operate the facility.

The project is separate from Bharat Semi’s image-sensor business, Kapoor added. The startup plans to remain fabless, outsourcing chip manufacturing while focusing on semiconductor design and software. The new funding will not be used to finance the proposed fabrication facility.

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

Jagmeet covers startups, tech policy-related updates, and all other major tech-centric developments from India for TechCrunch. He previously worked as a principal correspondent at NDTV.

article_content_zh:
印度半导体初创公司 Bharat Semi 已筹集 2400 万美元种子资金，用于开发支持人工智能的图像传感器，以赢得美国和其他地方的客户。

这项投资是在这家成立近五年、尚未实现营收的初创公司表示，它已获得美国国防技术公司通用原子公司和印度凯恩斯半导体公司的设计胜利之际进行的。然而，其图像传感器仍在开发中，该初创公司的目标是在 2027 年进行首次商业生产。

印度已投入数十亿美元建设国内半导体产业，希望在美国公司寻求中国以外的供应链多元化之际成为替代制造中心。然而，该国尚未将自己打造为主要的芯片制造中心。与此同时，人工智能的繁荣也为 Bharat Semi 等印度初创公司提供了为全球市场开发专用芯片的机会。

这家总部位于新德里的初创公司正在开发可编程图像传感器，将图像捕获、处理和人工智能功能结合在单个芯片上，从而减少将视觉数据发送到单独处理器的需要。联合创始人 Vrinda Kapoor（上图右）在接受采访时表示，与使用独立图像传感器、图像信号处理器和片上系统的传统设置相比，此举可以将系统成本降低至少 70%。

“我们的目标是从传感器转向感知解决方案，”卡普尔告诉 TechCrunch。

卡普尔是南方公园下议院研究员，此前曾在医疗保健技术领域工作过，他于 2021 年底与该初创公司董事总经理 Vinayak Dalmia（上图左）共同创立了 Bharat Semi，后者曾在麦肯锡和私募股权部门工作过。其首席技术官博伊德·福勒 (Boyd Fowler) 此前曾在图像传感器制造商 OmniVision 担任过相同职务。

Bharat Semi 的目标市场是智能家居、工业自动化、监控和航空航天。卡普尔没有透露具体细节，他指出空调可以检测房间何时空并自动调整，无人机也可以处理视觉信息——即使系统中其他地方没有更昂贵的计算硬件。

Kapoor 表示，该初创公司的第一代传感器已经进入原型设计阶段，而其第二代传感器将融入更先进的人工智能功能，预计将于 2027 年中期进入原型阶段。此外，该初创公司计划在 2027 年底前将这些更新的传感器交付给客户。

全股权种子轮融资由 Info Edge Group、South Park Commons 和 Indus Bridge Ventures 领投，Valor Capital、Micromax、Gaingels 和个人投资者跟投。卡普尔表示，Bharat Semi 计划利用这笔资金扩大其工程团队、完成产品开发并将其传感器推向市场。

Bharat Semi 在印度和美国拥有约 75 名员工，其中 10 至 12 名员工在其美国业务部门，负责圣克拉拉的工程和业务开发。 Kapoor 表示，该初创公司计划到 2027 年中期将其美国员工人数增加到 20 人左右。它还开始在欧洲招聘工程师。

卡普尔说：“这是一个关于我们能否在印度建立一家全球科技公司的故事。”

2024 年，Bharat Semi 宣布计划在印度开展半导体制造项目，涉及与美国太空军的技术合作。卡普尔表示，该计划仍在开发中，该初创公司正在努力寻找建造和运营该设施的国内合作伙伴。

卡普尔补充说，该项目与 Bharat Semi 的图像传感器业务是分开的。该初创公司计划保持无晶圆厂，外包芯片制造，同时专注于半导体设计和软件。新资金将不会用于资助拟议的制造设施。

当您通过我们文章中的链接购买时，我们可能会赚取少量佣金。这并不影响我们的编辑独立性。

author: OpenAI 官方动态
article_content:
We have signed agreements with four independent assessors—Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire—for our first phase of embedded assessments. As AI capabilities advance rapidly and the potential risks grow, public reporting from independent assessments can give people a clearer view of how labs are evaluating and managing those risks.

Embedded assessments give independent experts deep access to a lab’s internal models and systems to assess model alignment and the effectiveness of safeguards over an extended period of time, especially where relevant to our safety cases. Based on what each evaluation needs, assessors receive access to some of the same internal resources our researchers use, including model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems, technical documentation, and discussions with the researchers and engineers responsible for the work. This access gives assessors the evidence and context to pursue independent evaluations and uncover failures we may not have anticipated.

Our initial assessments focus on alignment and safeguards for models during training and internal use, complementing our safety cases. They build on our priorities and principles for third party assessments and years of work with third party evaluators, including a recent pilot assessment of our internal monitoring systems⁠(opens in a new window) with deep internal access and an investigation of the Hugging Face incident⁠(opens in a new window). We’ll use what we learn to deepen our work with independent experts in the coming months. These efforts also support our commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where we agreed to independent assessments of our safety controls. These collaborations can contribute to stronger shared standards for independent assessment and public transparency across the industry.

In this pilot assessment, Apollo Research⁠(opens in a new window) will assess whether models could covertly work against their developers’ intentions and whether our safeguards would detect such behavior. Drawing on evidence from training, safety testing, and internal use. Apollo will assess four claims in two stages:

Training did not incentivize subversion.

Strong evaluations and red teaming do not elicit subversion.

Models have not attempted subversion during internal use.

Reasoning behind subversion would be detectable.

For the first stage of Apollo’s assessment, we’ll provide access to selected public and unreleased models and training checkpoints, relevant training data and evaluation results, training intervention records, monitoring systems and flagged behaviors, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

Goodfire⁠(opens in a new window) will embed interpretability researchers and use the Goodfire platform to analyze model internals. The main objective of their assessment is training run monitoring, debugging, and alignment. The primary audience for their assessments are internal OpenAI researchers, who will use their findings to make safety improvements. Goodfire will also publish learnings and findings as the collaboration progresses.

Alignment assessment: For the first phase, METR will assess misaligned behavior in our largest reinforcement learning run to date, including failures that our existing tests and monitors may have missed. Within the selected run and agreed access, resources, and safety arrangements, METR would independently set assessment priorities and iterate on searches, analyses, and elicitation experiments. Access will include sampling relevant checkpoints, training and eval rollouts, and misalignment monitoring records for this run. For this first phase, the assessment will focus on our largest frontier RL run.1

Monitor assessment: We recently worked with METR to conduct a monitor stress testing exercise2. We have preliminarily agreed to conduct another monitor assessment⁠(opens in a new window) which we intend to be broader, but this is pending mutual agreement on the assessment scope.

Transluce⁠(opens in a new window) will conduct an initial assessment of our post-training alignment evaluations, examining their quality and coverage. For the initial assessment, we will provide Transluce with access to selected public and unreleased models, our post-training alignment evaluations and relevant results, supporting model behavior data and safety case documentation, and researchers who can provide context, alongside the tools and compute needed to conduct independent testing.

OpenAI and Transluce also share the intent to conduct a follow-on assessment of approximately eight weeks in early 2027, with broader access to additional models, deeper access to our alignment evaluations, and information on how evaluation results inform model release decisions.

We’ve developed protocols and processes with input from the assessors to balance deep access with security, confidentiality, oversight, and the independence and integrity of assessments. We are sharing them to shed light on how we will work with embedded assessors, and to advance discussion about norms for embedded assessments, which have yet to be standardized. We expect that these will need to evolve as we learn more about how to best conduct these assessments. Especially in the early stages of embedded assessments, we expect technical access challenges, space constraints, evolving security protocols, and other unexpected issues to arise. We hope to work through these challenges collaboratively with our embedded assessors and share lessons learned.

Each engagement begins with an agreed scope and the access, resources, and safety arrangements needed to conduct a rigorous assessment. Some assessments test specific safety claims; others give assessors room to discover unexpected failure modes within a defined system or training run. In both cases, assessors need the freedom to follow evidence, refine their methods, and propose further assessments when findings warrant it. We also have a process for addressing additional access needs as assessments develop. When direct access could expose our most sensitive IP, such as model weights or architecture, we will consider alternatives, including pairing assessors with OpenAI researchers to run analyses.

Assessors who need access to sensitive confidential information will work on site at OpenAI offices and be provided OpenAI devices to conduct their work. The primary purpose is to protect the security of the information they access. Working onsite also gives assessors the opportunity to engage with dedicated staff who can help them navigate their access and provide context for their assessments. We also expect our embedded assessors to follow at minimum3 the same security standards as OpenAI employees when running experiments and evaluations.

Our Safety and Security Committee (SSC), an independent oversight committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board, will have visibility into the embedded assessment and the ability to exercise their oversight responsibilities before, during, and at their conclusion. They will receive unredacted reports, and both the assessors and the SSC will be able to speak with each other during the assessment, including privately. Disagreements among OpenAI and any evaluator will be escalated to the Safety Advisory Group and OpenAI executives, who will have a specified time period to resolve them, and the SSC will be notified of any such disagreements promptly when escalated. If a disagreement remains, the matter will be referred to the SSC for resolution.

Discussions with employees help assessors understand internal information and the context behind the work. OpenAI will authorize and provide guidance to staff members who can speak to assessors, and assessors may request additional staff to speak with as needed. To encourage open, candid conversations and protect the privacy of our staff, these discussions are off the record, meaning that they can inform the assessments but cannot be published or attributed to employees. Through a separate attestation pathway, assessors can request OpenAI-attested statements verifying, correcting, or clarifying something they learned in conversation with employees. These statements are not attributed to individuals or intended to characterize individual views. Assessors may publish statements that OpenAI attests to, or disclose that OpenAI declined to attest to a statement.

Managing conflicts of interest clearly and transparently—including those involving personal relationships, financial interests4, and other issues—is important to the integrity and independence of evaluations. Cool-off periods5 also need to be designed carefully, so assessors can work responsibly across labs while handling competitive information sensitively. We are working with our assessors to develop clear processes for both conflicts and cool-off periods, including allowing for flexibility in mitigations and transparency in decisions to request recusal.

Assessors maintain independence in publishing their assessments, but we will retain the right to redact confidential information, consistent with our previous third-party engagements. We may also request responsible disclosure delays to allow time to act on findings that could pose security or safety risks and remediate issues that remain.

Public reporting will help people understand the findings and their limitations, while more detailed confidential reports give oversight bodies the evidence they need to act. We want these assessments to improve how we identify and address risks, and give the public a clearer basis for judging our safety work.

These assessments bring an independent perspective to our ongoing alignment and safety work. Public reporting on their findings will make that work more transparent and provide greater assurance about how risks are being identified and addressed. We expect this first phase of assessments to lead to longer-term, consistent embedded engagements over time that can continuously provide third party safety signals and recommended improvements on our most load bearing safety claims and safety cases.

We’ll continue working with multiple independent third parties to help build a healthy assessment ecosystem with diverse expertise and approaches. Some investigations need sustained, on-site work with sensitive systems; others primarily evaluate deployed or soon to be deployed models or review public documentation.

In the coming months, we’ll support external assessments across a broader range of safety questions. We are also exploring future embedded assessments that would examine compliance with our safety frameworks, as well as our organizational culture and processes. We are committed to expanding this work and helping build the capacity and shared standards needed to sustain it.

This scope is less expansive than what METR outlines in their alignment assessment proposal⁠(opens in a new window), which envisions a broad survey of misalignment.

We recently conducted a 3 week long monitor red teaming exercise with METR, which granted them access to our codebase, monitors, relevant trajectories, and discussions with OpenAI research staff for the purpose of better understanding our monitors. https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-22-red-teaming-openai-agent-monitoring/⁠(opens in a new window)

In some cases, there will be more stringent standards applied depending on the conditions of the experiment to allow for careful security vetting.

but we believe it is important to disclose this.

We ask staff at third party organizations who participate in an embedded assessment to observe a brief cool-off period before embedding with another AI developer, to reduce the risk of inadvertent disclosure of confidential information.

article_content_zh:
我们已与四家独立评估机构（Apollo Research、METR、Transluce 和 Goodfire）签署了嵌入式评估第一阶段的协议。随着人工智能能力的快速发展和潜在风险的增加，独立评估的公开报告可以让人们更清楚地了解实验室如何评估和管理这些风险。

嵌入式评估使独立专家能够深入访问实验室的内部模型和系统，以评估模型的一致性和保护措施在较长时间内的有效性，特别是与我们的安全案例相关的情况。根据每次评估的需求，评估人员可以访问我们的研究人员使用的一些相同的内部资源，包括模型检查点、源代码、培训和评估数据、监控系统、技术文档以及与负责工作的研究人员和工程师的讨论。这种访问为评估人员提供了证据和背景，以进行独立评估并发现我们可能未预料到的失败。

我们的初步评估重点是培训和内部使用期间模型的一致性和保障措施，以补充我们的安全案例。它们建立在我们第三方评估的优先事项和原则以及与第三方评估人员多年的合作基础上，包括最近对我们的内部监控系统进行的试点评估⁠（在新窗口中打开）以及深入的内部访问以及对拥抱脸事件的调查⁠（在新窗口中打开）。在接下来的几个月里，我们将利用我们所学到的知识来深化与独立专家的合作。这些努力也支持我们根据《白宫超级情报协议》做出的承诺，我们同意对我们的安全控制进行独立评估。这些合作有助于为整个行业的独立评估和公共透明度制定更强有力的共享标准。

在这次试点评估中，Apollo Research⁠（在新窗口中打开）将评估模型是否可以秘密地违背开发人员的意图，以及我们的防护措施是否会检测到此类行为。借鉴培训、安全测试和内部使用的证据。 Apollo 将分两个阶段评估四项索赔：

培训并没有激励颠覆。

强烈的评价和红队不会引发颠覆。

模型在内部使用过程中并没有尝试颠覆。

颠覆背后的推理是可以察觉的。

在阿波罗评估的第一阶段，我们将提供对选定的公开和未发布的模型和训练检查点、相关训练数据和评估结果、训练干预记录、监控系统和标记行为的访问权限，以及可以提供背景信息的研究人员以及进行独立测试所需的工具和计算。

Goodfire⁠（在新窗口中打开）将嵌入可解释性研究人员并使用 Goodfire 平台来分析模型内部结构。他们评估的主要目标是训练运行监控、调试和对齐。他们评估的主要受众是 OpenAI 内部研究人员，他们将利用他们的发现来改进安全性。随着合作的进展，Goodfire 还将发布经验教训和发现。

一致性评估：在第一阶段，METR 将评估我们迄今为止最大的强化学习运行中的不一致行为，包括我们现有的测试和监视器可能遗漏的失败。在选定的运行和商定的访问、资源和安全安排内，METR 将独立设置评估优先级并迭代搜索、分析和启发实验。访问权限将包括对相关检查点进行采样、培训和评估部署以及本次运行的偏差监控记录。对于第一阶段，评估将重点关注我们最大的前沿强化学习运行。1

监控评估：我们最近与 METR 合作进行了监控压力测试2。我们初步同意进行另一次监测评估⁠（在新窗口中打开），我们打算扩大范围，但这有待双方就评估范围达成一致。

Transluce⁠（在新窗口中打开）将对我们的培训后对齐评估进行初步评估，检查其质量和覆盖范围。对于初步评估，我们将为 Transluce 提供对选定的公开和未发布模型的访问权限、我们的训练后一致性评估和相关结果、支持模型行为数据和安全案例文档，以及可以提供背景信息以及进行独立测试所需的工具和计算的研究人员。

OpenAI 和 Transluce 还同意在 2027 年初进行大约八周的后续评估，更广泛地访问其他模型，更深入地访问我们的一致性评估，以及有关评估结果如何为模型发布决策提供信息的信息。

article_content:
Zus Health, a Fierce 15 of 2025 honoree, wants to use its nationwide data network and longitudinal patient record as the infrastructure on which AI-powered clinical applications can run. (BlackJack3D/GettyImages) As healthcare companies race to build AI copilots and agents, startup Zus Health is betting that the bigger opportunity is creating the connected patient data layer those applications need to work reliably.

Zus Health, Jonathan Bush's health tech company, picked up $33 million in series B funding to build out the data foundation for healthcare AI. Drive Capital led the series B round. Sanofi Ventures, HealthX Ventures and Alumni Ventures, as well as existing investors Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), F-Prime, Maverick Ventures and JAZZ Venture Partners also backed the round.

The financing brings Zus's total capital raised to more than $100 million, and the fresh funding will support the company's continued investment in its intelligent patient record platform, national healthcare data network and AI-powered clinical workflows.

Zus has built its platform in three layers, according to Bush. The company first focused on building a nationwide patient record, a data network that pulls information into that record, and increasingly, AI-enabled workflows that automate care tasks using a more complete view of the patient.

Electronic health record systems (EHRs) succeeded at digitizing healthcare but failed to make patient information portable across organizations, Bush, founder and CEO of Zus Health, told Fierce Healthcare. Clinicians and care teams still spend valuable time searching for records and reconciling incomplete information. For patients, that can mean repeating their medical history at every appointment or relying on memory to recall past treatments. Advances in artificial intelligence now offer an opportunity to make healthcare information not just accessible, but actionable, according to Zus Health executives.

Launched in 2021, Zus Health developed what Bush calls an "always-on, FHIR-native, API-first medical record." It offers a shared health data platform designed to accelerate healthcare data interoperability by providing easy-to-use patient data at the point of care via a standalone app, API (application programming interface), embedded components and direct EHR integration. At the center of its approach is an intelligent, continuously updated patient record that serves as a shared foundation for healthcare applications.

The company's Zus Aggregated Profile (ZAP) brings fragmented clinical information together into a unified, longitudinal patient record, supported by AI-powered clinical intelligence that makes the information easier to use across applications and workflows, according to the company. The platform also has nationwide connectivity across EHR networks, pharmacy data, care event notifications, labs and other clinical data sources that continuously updates the patient record without requiring customers to build their own connectivity infrastructure.

"We're finally on to the last and critical piece of what I think the future of medical records looks like, which is standing up workflows that automate all of the tasks of patient care in a very bespoke way," Bush told Fierce Healthcare. "[Zus Health] developed the first data-rich networked medical record platform in the industry's history. Whether Zus wins or somebody else beats Zus at it, all electronic medical records in the future will be national."

He added, "And now, with AI, we have an extraordinary opportunity to build workflows that actually make delivering care easier, faster and more effective."

The company is betting that the next competitive player in healthcare AI will be the data infrastructure underneath the applications.

Zus Health, a Fierce 15 of 2025 honoree, wants to use its nationwide data network and longitudinal patient record as the infrastructure on which AI-powered clinical applications can run. The company's platform enables EHRs and other applications to work from a more complete, cross-provider view of the patient. Zus Health built AI solutions and flexible integration capabilities to put connected information to work across clinical and operational use cases, while enabling healthcare organizations to build applications tailored to their needs.

Zus works with value-based care organizations, digital health companies, provider organizations, as well as diagnostics and precision medicine companies. The company claims that in August alone its nationwide network supported more than 110 million networked transactions, while its AI-native clinical platform generated 39 million evidence citations year-to-date across its solutions—demonstrating both the scale of its connectivity and how patient information is being put to work across healthcare.

Zus supports solutions spanning pre-visit preparation, transitions of care, risk adjustment, quality gap closure and population health management. Its clinical intelligence capabilities, including AI-powered generated patient summaries (GPS), turn fragmented patient records into information care teams can use more efficiently and confidently.

The company plans to use the series B funding to build out its AI-powered clinical intelligence and capabilities and broaden its healthcare data network connectivity. Zus plans to expand its solutions to automate population health and care management workflows, while enabling customers and developers to create AI-powered workflows across value-based care, specialty care and other high-value use cases.

The company is seeing rapid growth in specialty care, particularly oncology, where complex patient records are spread across multiple providers. Zus' continuously updated, aggregated patient data enables more comprehensive and efficient reviews of treatment eligibility, clinical trial criteria and genetic testing—tasks that traditionally required extensive manual work by nurses and analysts using fragmented legacy EHR systems, Bush noted.

"We believe healthcare is entering a new era in which AI can fundamentally change how care is delivered, but that transformation depends on having reliable, connected patient information," said Molly Bonakdarpour, general partner at Drive Capital, in a statement. "Zus has built the foundation to address that challenge at scale. Its combination of technology, market opportunity and leadership gives us conviction in the company's ability to help shape the next generation of healthcare."

title_zh: 医疗数据平台Zus Health完成3300万美元B轮融资
summary_zh: Zus Health获Drive Capital领投3300万美元，旨在构建医疗AI应用所需的底层数据互联架构
article_content_zh:
Zus Health 是 2025 年 Fierce 15 获奖者，希望利用其全国数据网络和纵向患者记录作为人工智能驱动的临床应用程序可以运行的基础设施。 (BlackJack3D/GettyImages) 随着医疗保健公司竞相打造人工智能副驾驶员和代理，初创公司 Zus Health 认为更大的机会是创建这些应用程序可靠运行所需的互联患者数据层。

乔纳森·布什 (Jonathan Bush) 的健康科技公司 Zus Health 获得了 3300 万美元的 B 轮融资，用于构建医疗保健人工智能的数据基础。 Drive Capital领投了B轮融资。赛诺菲风险投资公司 (Sanofi Ventures)、HealthX Ventures 和 Alumni Ventures 以及现有投资者 Andreessen Horowitz (a16z)、F-Prime、Maverick Ventures 和 JAZZ Venture Partners 也支持了此轮融资。

此次融资使 Zus 筹集的总资金超过 1 亿美元，新的资金将支持该公司对其智能病历平台、国家医疗数据网络和人工智能驱动的临床工作流程的持续投资。

布什表示，Zus 将其平台分为三层。该公司首先专注于建立全国范围的患者记录、将信息提取到该记录中的数据网络，以及越来越多的人工智能支持的工作流程，利用更完整的患者视图自动执行护理任务。

Zus Health 创始人兼首席执行官 Bush 告诉 Fierce Healthcare，电子健康记录系统 (EHR) 成功实现了医疗保健数字化，但未能使患者信息在组织之间可移植。临床医生和护理团队仍然花费宝贵的时间搜索记录并核对不完整的信息。对于患者来说，这可能意味着在每次预约时重复他们的病史或依靠记忆来回忆过去的治疗。 Zus Health 高管表示，人工智能的进步现在提供了一个机会，使医疗信息不仅可访问，而且可操作。

Zus Health 于 2021 年推出，开发了 Bush 所说的“始终在线、FHIR 原生、API 优先的医疗记录”。它提供了一个共享健康数据平台，旨在通过独立应用程序、API（应用程序编程接口）、嵌入式组件和直接 EHR 集成在护理点提供易于使用的患者数据，从而加速医疗保健数据的互操作性。其方法的核心是智能、持续更新的患者记录，作为医疗保健应用程序的共享基础。

该公司表示，该公司的 Zus 聚合档案 (ZAP) 将碎片化的临床信息整合到统一的纵向患者记录中，并由人工智能驱动的临床智能支持，使信息更容易在应用程序和工作流程中使用。该平台还具有跨 EHR 网络、药房数据、护理事件通知、实验室和其他临床数据源的全国连接性，可以持续更新患者记录，而无需客户构建自己的连接基础设施。

布什对 Fierce Healthcare 表示：“我们终于看到了我认为医疗记录未来的最后一个关键部分，即建立工作流程，以一种非常定制的方式自动化所有患者护理任务。” “[Zus Health] 开发了行业历史上第一个数据丰富的网络医疗记录平台。无论 Zus 获胜还是其他人击败 Zus，未来所有电子医疗记录都将是全国性的。”

他补充道，“现在，有了人工智能，我们就有了一个绝佳的机会来构建工作流程，使护理服务变得更容易、更快、更有效。”

该公司押注医疗保健人工智能领域的下一个竞争者将是应用程序底层的数据基础设施。

Zus Health 是 2025 年 Fierce 15 获奖者，希望利用其全国数据网络和纵向患者记录作为人工智能驱动的临床应用程序可以运行的基础设施。该公司的平台使电子病历和其他应用程序能够从更完整的、跨提供商的患者角度进行工作。 Zus Health 构建了人工智能解决方案和灵活的集成功能，将互联信息应用于临床和运营用例，同时使医疗保健组织能够构建适合其需求的应用程序。

Zus 与基于价值的护理组织、数字健康公司、提供商组织以及诊断和精准医疗公司合作。该公司声称，仅 8 月份，其全国网络就支持了超过 1.1 亿笔网络交易，而其 AI 原生临床平台今年迄今在其解决方案中产生了 3900 万次证据引用，这既展示了其连接规模，也展示了患者信息如何在整个医疗保健领域发挥作用。

Zus 支持涵盖就诊前准备、护理过渡、风险调整、质量差距缩小和人口健康管理的解决方案。其临床智能功能，包括人工智能生成的患者摘要 (GPS)，将碎片化的患者记录转化为护理团队可以更有效、更自信地使用的信息。

该公司计划利用 B 系列资金构建其人工智能驱动的临床智能和能力，并扩大其医疗数据网络连接。 Zus 计划扩展其解决方案，以实现人口健康和护理管理工作流程的自动化，同时使客户和开发人员能够跨基于价值的护理、专业护理和其他高价值用例创建人工智能驱动的工作流程。

title: Copenhagen-based AI accounting software maker Sumary raised a $25M seed led by Singular, bringing total funding to $29.2M after a $4.2M pre-seed in Nov. 2025 (Sofia Chesnokova/Tech Funding News)
title_en: Copenhagen-based AI accounting software maker Sumary raised a $25M seed led by Singular, bringing total funding to $29.2M after a $4.2M pre-seed in Nov. 2025 (Sofia Chesnokova/Tech Funding News)
author: Tech Funding News
article_content:
Copenhagen-based Sumary, which develops AI software for accounting firms amid a battle with AI-native firms, just closed a $25 million seed round, led by Singular.

Existing investors byFounders, Partech and Tenity also joining in. The angel investor list included Steve Anavi (Qonto), Tuomas Artman (Linear), Stanislas Polu (Dust), Steffen Tjerrild (Synthesia), Jannick Malling (Public.com), Ben Freeman (Omnea), and several others.

This round is nearly six times the $4.2 million pre-seed raised in November 2025, led by byFounders, bringing Sumary’s total funding to date to $29.2 million. Sumary claims it’s the largest seed round ever for accounting software in Europe.

Pascar Sivam, co-founder and CEO of Sumary, said, “Accounting firms are being asked to do more with fewer people. Software has to take on the preparation properly, so accountants can give their time to the people who depend on them: their clients and their own teams. That is what we have built. This round lets us bring that to firms across the UK and Europe much faster.”

London is Sumary’s commercial hub, while Denmark remains the centre of its technology and AI research. Sivam and COO Frederik Skov Wacher are both moving to lead UK growth. The company is expanding into Europe, with the Benelux being the first market.

Sivam started Sumary with Bastian Schneider, Lucas Rantzau, Frederik Hvilshøj, and Skov Wacher. Sivam and Schneider are both former McKinsey consultants, and Hvilshøj was a lead ML engineer at Encord and has a PhD in explainable deep learning and generative models from Aarhus.

In a nutshell, Sumary is an AI operating system for accounting that automates workflows, checks transactions and provides insights. It handles the key tasks of the monthly close, VAT returns, and year-end for all clients and ledgers. Every step is set up for the accountant to review and approve. For example, a VAT return would be delivered as a draft for review and sign-off.

Sumary’s Copenhagen research team has created a benchmark based on actual accounting work, and they run all the top AI models against it before using them with clients. The company reports that after three months on the platform, firms are spending 50% less time on their monthly close and 75% less time on their VAT returns.

The startup says it has arrangements with most of the 20 largest accounting firms across the Nordics and contracts with several leading UK firms. Customers include Deloitte, Grant Thornton and Baker Tilly.

Since July, the AI accounting space has split. Some startups are selling AI to established firms. Basis landed $100 million at $1.15 billion in February, while Kabilio in Barcelona raised €10 million on 5th November and serves over 500 accounting firms. Ravical in Belgium secured a $17 million seed round on 29th October.

Other startups are operating as accounting firms in their own right. Skalar raised €12 million in July, Integral raised an €18 million Series A in September, Dougs raised €50 million in October, and Gradient came out of stealth with $4 million that same month. Each of them is an AI accounting firm.

Sivam has picked a side: “Dozens, and probably soon hundreds, of AI accounting firms are being built as we speak. We want to offer existing accounting firms the chance to deliver customer value that is as good as, if not better than, these new entrants, by adopting AI quickly across their operations. With the right technology, they can lead this transformation rather than be disrupted by it.”

Sumary says it will work with any ledger the accountant is currently using and aims to be the firm’s operational partner. The end game is for accountants to spend less time on drudgery and more time on advisory.

Grand View Research valued the European accounting software market at $5.4 billion in 2024 and forecasts it will reach $8.4 billion by 2030.

Jeremy Uzan, a general partner at Singular, added, “Sumary has one of the strongest founding teams we have seen in Europe at this stage and their commercial momentum is exceptional. They have combined deep AI research capabilities with an understanding of how accounting firms operate and are already winning the trust of some of the industry’s largest players. We believe Sumary has what it takes to become the defining AI platform for accounting in Europe.”

The big question is: will the profession trust tools that assist existing firms, or tools used to build entirely new firms around AI? Sumary has opted to support existing firms and now has $25M to demonstrate what it can do.

title_zh: 会计AI平台Sumary获2500万美元种子轮融资
summary_zh: 哥本哈根AI会计软件开发商Sumary完成2500万美元种子轮融资，由Singular领投，累计融资金额达2920万美元
article_content_zh:
总部位于哥本哈根的 Sumary 为会计师事务所开发人工智能软件，正在与人工智能本土公司展开竞争，该公司刚刚完成了由 Singular 领投的 2500 万美元种子轮融资。

Founders、Partech 和 Tenity 等现有投资者也加入其中。天使投资人名单包括 Steve Anavi (Qonto)、Tuomas Artman (Linear)、Stanislas Polu (Dust)、Steffen Tjerrild (Synthesia)、Jannick Malling (Public.com)、Ben Freeman (Omnea) 等。

此轮融资几乎是 2025 年 11 月由 byFounders 领投的 420 万美元种子前融资的六倍，使 Sumary 迄今为止的融资总额达到 2920 万美元。 Sumary 声称这是欧洲会计软件领域有史以来最大的种子轮融资。

Sumary 联合创始人兼首席执行官帕斯卡·西瓦姆 (Pascar Sivam) 表示：“会计师事务所被要求用更少的人员做更多的事情。软件必须做好适当的准备，这样会计师就可以把时间留给依赖它们的人：他们的客户和他们自己的团队。这就是我们所建立的。这一轮让我们能够更快地将这一点带到英国和欧洲的公司。”

伦敦是 Sumary 的商业中心，而丹麦仍然是其技术和人工智能研究的中心。 Sivam 和首席运营官 Frederik Skov Wacher 都将领导英国的增长。该公司正在向欧洲扩张，比荷卢经济联盟是第一个市场。

Sivam 与 Bastian Schneider、Lucas Rantzau、Frederik Hvilshøj 和 Skov Wacher 一起创立了 Sumary。 Sivam 和 Schneider 都是前麦肯锡顾问，Hvilshøj 是 Encord 的首席机器学习工程师，并拥有奥尔胡斯的可解释深度学习和生成模型博士学位。

简而言之，Sumary 是一个用于会计的人工智能操作系统，可以自动化工作流程、检查交易并提供见解。它为所有客户和分类账处理月结、增值税申报和年终的关键任务。每一步都经过会计师的审查和批准。例如，增值税申报表将作为草稿交付以供审核和签署。

Sumary 的哥本哈根研究团队根据实际会计工作创建了一个基准，他们在与客户一起使用之前，针对该基准运行所有顶级人工智能模型。该公司报告称，使用该平台三个月后，公司花在月结账上的时间减少了 50%，花在增值税申报表上的时间减少了 75%。

该初创公司表示，它与北欧 20 家最大的会计师事务所中的大多数都有安排，并与几家领先的英国公司签订了合同。客户包括德勤、均富会计师事务所和天职会计师事务所。

自 7 月以来，人工智能会计领域已经分裂。一些初创公司正在向老牌公司出售人工智能。 Basis 在 2 月份筹集了 1 亿美元，达到 11.5 亿美元，而巴塞罗那的 Kabilio 则在 11 月 5 日筹集了 1000 万欧元，为 500 多家会计师事务所提供服务。比利时的 Ravical 于 10 月 29 日获得了 1700 万美元的种子轮融资。

其他初创公司本身也以会计师事务所的形式运营。 Skalar 在 7 月份筹集了 1200 万欧元，Integral 在 9 月份筹集了 1800 万欧元的 A 轮融资，Dougs 在 10 月份筹集了 5000 万欧元，Gradient 同月则筹集了 400 万美元。他们都是一家人工智能会计师事务所。

Sivam 已经选择了一边：“就在我们说话的时候，数十家甚至可能很快数百家人工智能会计师事务所正在建立。我们希望为现有会计师事务所提供机会，通过在其业务中快速采用人工智能，提供与这些新进入者一样好的客户价值，甚至更好。有了正确的技术，他们可以引领这一转型，而不是被它打乱。”

Sumary 表示，它将与该会计师目前使用的任何分类账配合使用，并致力于成为该公司的运营合作伙伴。最终的目标是让会计师花更少的时间在苦差事上，花更多的时间在咨询上。

Grand View Research 对 2024 年欧洲会计软件市场的估值为 54 亿美元，并预测到 2030 年将达到 84 亿美元。

author: Financial Times
article_content:
US lawmakers are accelerating efforts to crack down on advanced AI chips reaching China in the wake of revelations that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Democrats and Republicans have both thrown support behind a raft of bills curbing sales of sensitive chips overseas and giving Congress the ability to review and potentially block sales already approved by the Trump administration.

“There’s absolutely increased momentum for this legislation in light of the recent scandal,” said Owen Tedford, a senior research analyst at Beacon Policy Advisers, a Washington consultancy that monitors congressional action.

Huang, who had battled to ease export rules, resigned earlier this week following revelations that he had extramarital affairs, including with a woman who was an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed.

The US has been investigating for more than a year whether Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China, while the woman, Alice Huang, is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence.

“Nvidia may feel like they’re done or trying to move on, but Washington is not ready to move on,” Tedford said.

Nvidia chips are used to train the most advanced AI models from labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic, and restricting their export is seen by proponents as essential to keeping America’s technical edge.

While the proposals have already been making headway on Capitol Hill, the political furore over the Trump administration’s failure to stop Nvidia’s chips being exported to Megaspeed has supercharged efforts.

One bill, the Remote Access Security Act, would stop Chinese companies from remotely accessing chips overseas through cloud services, even when they are barred from buying the physical chips.

Three senior Republican lawmakers on Friday urged their colleagues to immediately pass several of the bills clamping down on AI chip exports.

Republicans John Moolenaar, Brian Mast and Rick Crawford, who chair committees on China, foreign affairs and intelligence in the House of Representatives, wrote to Huang, Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter and the commerce official overseeing export controls, Jeffrey Kessler, requesting their appearance in front of Congress.

“We need to know the full extent to which our national security has been put at risk,” they wrote, adding that “this situation is a prime example of why Congress must immediately pass” four bills aimed at boosting oversight.

Many of the proposals have also this week attracted the support of the outgoing Speaker of the House, Republican Mike Johnson, and his likely successor, Hakeem Jeffries. The measures are likely to be attached to the final version of the annual US defence spending legislation, as legislators work to hammer out the final text.

The National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) broadly funds the US Department of Defense and is considered a “must-pass” bill, meaning the president is highly unlikely to use his veto power to reject the measures sent to his desk.

The NDAA will be considered by the current Republican-majority Congress before the lawmakers elected in November’s midterm elections take their seats in January.

“The momentum has just totally swung,” said Emily Kilcrease, a former US trade official now at the Center for a New American Security think-tank.

“It’s because of the Nvidia scandal. It’s because of the midterm results. You know, it’s because we actually do have a vehicle with the NDAA coming up as a must-pass in the lame duck.”

Still, one Senate GOP aide cautioned that legislators might run out of time this year. “The list of things to accomplish is long, and time is short,” they said.

The renewed energy behind efforts to rein in the sale of chips to China comes as furious lawmakers demand Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick explain how he allowed Nvidia to sell chips to Megaspeed.

The FT has reported Lutnick’s commerce department delayed efforts to add Megaspeed to Washington’s blacklist of companies the US considers a risk to national security. American companies require licences from the commerce department to export goods to companies on the so-called entity list.

Treasury secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department had been “in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months”.
