author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are. The company is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine. Participants will use a new iOS app to ask medical questions and then rate the responses based on criteria including accuracy, detail, and relevance.

The app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, with Apple looking for up to 200,000 people to contribute. Participants 21 and older must be based in the US, and although the app doesn’t use Apple Intelligence, it does require an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 26 or later.

Study participants can use the app to ask health-related questions and receive easily understandable responses with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources. The app relies on text-based prompts, and while dictation is an option using the iOS keyboard, the app isn’t integrated with Siri or Apple Intelligence.

[Image: Participants in the study will be given the opportunity to rate responses to health questions from the app. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/applestudy2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

During enrolment, participants are given the option to share Apple HealthKit data, like their activity, sleep, or clinical lab results, so responses will include more context about their own personal health. But privacy is a priority, and Apple says it has taken measures to ensure users’ information remains confidential and the data collected won’t be used to train AI models. The aim is to improve the design and functionality of AI-powered health tools so they can deliver relevant health information that’s easier for users to understand and act on.

“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life. Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” said Sumbul Desai, MD, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness.

title_zh: 苹果启动健康AI应用效能研究计划
summary_zh: 苹果联手临床AI平台OpenEvidence启动大规模健康AI交互研究，招募20万名美国用户评估医疗问答工具准确性
article_content_zh:
苹果今天宣布了一项新研究，旨在更好地了解人们如何与对话式人工智能健康工具互动以及他们的反应实际上有多有用。该公司正在与 OpenEvidence 合作开展 Apple Health AI 使用研究，OpenEvidence 是医疗保健专业人员使用的临床 AI 平台，可根据《新英格兰医学杂志》等来源的医疗信息生成答案。参与者将使用新的 iOS 应用程序提出医疗问题，然后根据准确性、细节和相关性等标准对回答进行评分。

该应用程序现已可供下载，并于今日开始注册，Apple 正在寻找最多 20 万人参与贡献。 21 岁及以上的参与者必须居住在美国，尽管该应用程序不使用 Apple Intelligence，但它确实需要运行 iOS 26 或更高版本的 iPhone 15 Pro。

研究参与者可以使用该应用程序提出与健康相关的问题，并收到易于理解的答复，其中包含同行评审的临床资源的链接。该应用程序依赖于基于文本的提示，虽然可以使用 iOS 键盘进行听写，但该应用程序未与 Siri 或 Apple Intelligence 集成。

在注册过程中，参与者可以选择共享 Apple HealthKit 数据，例如他们的活动、睡眠或临床实验室结果，因此回复将包括更多有关他们个人健康状况的背景信息。但隐私是重中之重，苹果表示已采取措施确保用户信息保密，并且收集的数据不会用于训练人工智能模型。目的是改进人工智能健康工具的设计和功能，以便它们能够提供更容易让用户理解和采取行动的相关健康信息。

“在 Apple，我们相信负责任的创新始于科学严谨性和临床基础。健康是非常个性化的，进行专门的研究是了解人们如何在日常生活中参与、理解和评估健康 AI 的最深思熟虑的方式。这项研究的见解将有助于推进更广泛的科学对话，并确保随着技术的发展，我们继续构建值得信赖的工具，真正为人们的健康之旅提供支持，无论他们身在何处。”Apple 健康与健身副总裁 Sumbul Desai 医学博士说道。

title: How Samsung aims to be a one-stop shop that builds, runs, and powers data centers; sources: its IT arm is in early talks to sign Anthropic and OpenAI as tenants (Financial Times)
title_en: How Samsung aims to be a one-stop shop that builds, runs, and powers data centers; sources: its IT arm is in early talks to sign Anthropic and OpenAI as tenants (Financial Times)
author: Financial Times
article_content:
After conquering memory chips, Samsung wants to turn other parts of its sprawling business into AI supply chain champions, but analysts question whether it can replicate its success with semiconductors across the group.

In the past year, the South Korean conglomerate has taken steps to try to become a one-stop provider of AI infrastructure. It has invested $1bn in a KKR- and Nvidia-backed data centre operator, acquired a European cooling systems maker and signed a partnership with OpenAI to develop AI infrastructure.

The group’s hope is to be able to offer a service in which it can build data centres through its construction arm, operate them through its IT services unit and provide energy storage systems through its battery maker, in addition to supplying memory chips.

“Moving forward, Samsung is poised to expand its role from a traditional hardware component supplier to an active architect of the global AI infrastructure ecosystem,” it said following its $1bn investment in Helix Digital Infrastructure in September.

Samsung is betting that its future in the AI boom lies beyond semiconductors, a highly lucrative but also highly cyclical industry.

While best known for Samsung Electronics — the manufacturing juggernaut that makes chips, Galaxy smartphones and household appliances — Samsung Group is a vast conglomerate with businesses as wide-ranging as insurance and security services.

Many of them started as internal units to serve the conglomerate and still count Samsung as their primary customer, but the group hopes some of the subsidiaries can expand to external clients as AI demand takes hold.

Samsung SDS, which began as an in-house IT services provider and operates data centres mostly to support the group, is in early-stage talks with Anthropic and OpenAI to potentially sign them on as tenants. Analysts expect the company to generate annual data centre revenue of Won6.6tn ($4.9bn) by 2031, roughly six times current levels.

Last year, Samsung signed a partnership with OpenAI to supply advanced memory chips to the company’s Stargate data centre initiative.

The agreement included Samsung SDS collaborating with OpenAI on designing, developing and operating data centres. Construction arm Samsung C&T and shipbuilder Samsung Heavy Industries also said they would work with the US tech company on developing floating data centres.

Morgan Stanley said in a recent report that Samsung SDS was well positioned to benefit from a surge in data centre construction, a trend reinforced by governments around the world passing laws requiring information to be stored domestically.

McKinsey estimates global data centre capacity demand could almost triple by 2030, with AI workloads accounting for about 70 per cent of the total. Meeting AI computing needs alone could require $5.2tn in capital expenditure.

“Samsung has an opportunity to provide a total solution,” said Joungho Kim, a professor of electrical engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology. “US Big Tech companies are strong in AI and software, but they rely heavily on external suppliers for hardware.”

However, recent tech earnings have sparked investor concerns about the astronomical sums being spent on AI infrastructure and whether future demand will justify the cost.

Electoral victories of Democratic candidates in the US who pledged to halt data centre construction in their states have added to worries of regulatory pushback.

But Sanjeev Rana, head of Korea research at CLSA, said that while there would be “ups and downs” in the market, the spending was “structural”.

“In several years [and] decades, we are going to see huge investments in AI data centre-related products,” he said.

For Samsung, the challenge is bringing together disparate parts of its business empire.

Until 2017, the conglomerate had a Future Strategy Office responsible for group-wide decisions, but it was dismantled following a political corruption scandal involving its leadership.

Since then, Samsung has relied on so-called co-ordination bodies that are more lightly staffed, have fewer resources and are split based on business lines.

Analysts said the lack of a central decision-making body could complicate efforts to pursue more ambitious AI infrastructure projects that require close co-operation.

“Samsung has a broad range of capabilities, but it has been relatively weak at bringing them together [into an integrated offering],” said Peter Lee, an analyst at Citi.

There are also questions about experience serving external customers at scale as several subsidiaries remain heavily dependent on Samsung for work.

Rana said the group’s more immediate opportunity was in designing the systems inside data centres rather than operating the facilities themselves.

Samsung already supplies a range of components used in AI infrastructure including high-bandwidth memory chips, advanced packaging substrates for semiconductors and backup battery units for servers.

“Improving and extending the advantages in components will serve it better. And these are high-margin businesses,” said Rana. “Owning or operating data centres, I am not sure actually that will play to their strengths.”

article_content_en:
After conquering memory chips, Samsung wants to turn other parts of its sprawling business into AI supply chain champions, but analysts question whether it can replicate its success with semiconductors across the group.

In the past year, the South Korean conglomerate has taken steps to try to become a one-stop provider of AI infrastructure. It has invested $1bn in a KKR- and Nvidia-backed data centre operator, acquired a European cooling systems maker and signed a partnership with OpenAI to develop AI infrastructure.

The group’s hope is to be able to offer a service in which it can build data centres through its construction arm, operate them through its IT services unit and provide energy storage systems through its battery maker, in addition to supplying memory chips.

“Moving forward, Samsung is poised to expand its role from a traditional hardware component supplier to an active architect of the global AI infrastructure ecosystem,” it said following its $1bn investment in Helix Digital Infrastructure in September.

Samsung is betting that its future in the AI boom lies beyond semiconductors, a highly lucrative but also highly cyclical industry.

While best known for Samsung Electronics — the manufacturing juggernaut that makes chips, Galaxy smartphones and household appliances — Samsung Group is a vast conglomerate with businesses as wide-ranging as insurance and security services.

Many of them started as internal units to serve the conglomerate and still count Samsung as their primary customer, but the group hopes some of the subsidiaries can expand to external clients as AI demand takes hold.

Samsung SDS, which began as an in-house IT services provider and operates data centres mostly to support the group, is in early-stage talks with Anthropic and OpenAI to potentially sign them on as tenants. Analysts expect the company to generate annual data centre revenue of Won6.6tn ($4.9bn) by 2031, roughly six times current levels.

Last year, Samsung signed a partnership with OpenAI to supply advanced memory chips to the company’s Stargate data centre initiative.

The agreement included Samsung SDS collaborating with OpenAI on designing, developing and operating data centres. Construction arm Samsung C&T and shipbuilder Samsung Heavy Industries also said they would work with the US tech company on developing floating data centres.

Morgan Stanley said in a recent report that Samsung SDS was well positioned to benefit from a surge in data centre construction, a trend reinforced by governments around the world passing laws requiring information to be stored domestically.

McKinsey estimates global data centre capacity demand could almost triple by 2030, with AI workloads accounting for about 70 per cent of the total. Meeting AI computing needs alone could require $5.2tn in capital expenditure.

“Samsung has an opportunity to provide a total solution,” said Joungho Kim, a professor of electrical engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology. “US Big Tech companies are strong in AI and software, but they rely heavily on external suppliers for hardware.”

However, recent tech earnings have sparked investor concerns about the astronomical sums being spent on AI infrastructure and whether future demand will justify the cost.

Electoral victories of Democratic candidates in the US who pledged to halt data centre construction in their states have added to worries of regulatory pushback.

But Sanjeev Rana, head of Korea research at CLSA, said that while there would be “ups and downs” in the market, the spending was “structural”.

“In several years [and] decades, we are going to see huge investments in AI data centre-related products,” he said.

For Samsung, the challenge is bringing together disparate parts of its business empire.

Until 2017, the conglomerate had a Future Strategy Office responsible for group-wide decisions, but it was dismantled following a political corruption scandal involving its leadership.

Since then, Samsung has relied on so-called co-ordination bodies that are more lightly staffed, have fewer resources and are split based on business lines.

Analysts said the lack of a central decision-making body could complicate efforts to pursue more ambitious AI infrastructure projects that require close co-operation.

“Samsung has a broad range of capabilities, but it has been relatively weak at bringing them together [into an integrated offering],” said Peter Lee, an analyst at Citi.

There are also questions about experience serving external customers at scale as several subsidiaries remain heavily dependent on Samsung for work.

Rana said the group’s more immediate opportunity was in designing the systems inside data centres rather than operating the facilities themselves.

Samsung already supplies a range of components used in AI infrastructure including high-bandwidth memory chips, advanced packaging substrates for semiconductors and backup battery units for servers.

“Improving and extending the advantages in components will serve it better. And these are high-margin businesses,” said Rana. “Owning or operating data centres, I am not sure actually that will play to their strengths.”
article_content_zh:
在征服存储芯片之后，三星希望将其庞大业务的其他部分转变为人工智能供应链冠军，但分析师质疑它是否可以在整个集团的半导体领域复制其成功。

去年，这家韩国企业集团已采取措施，试图成为人工智能基础设施的一站式提供商。它已向 KKR 和 Nvidia 支持的数据中心运营商投资 10 亿美元，收购了欧洲冷却系统制造商，并与 OpenAI 签署了合作伙伴关系以开发人工智能基础设施。

该集团希望能够提供一项服务，除了提供存储芯片外，还可以通过其建筑部门建造数据中心，通过 IT 服务部门运营数据中心，并通过电池制造商提供能源存储系统。

“展望未来，三星准备将其角色从传统的硬件组件供应商扩大为全球人工智能基础设施生态系统的积极架构师，”该公司在 9 月份向 Helix Digital Infrastructure 投资 10 亿美元后表示。

三星认为，其在人工智能热潮中的未来不仅仅局限于半导体，这是一个利润丰厚但周期性很强的行业。

三星集团以生产芯片、Galaxy 智能手机和家用电器的制造巨头三星电子而闻名，但它也是一家庞大的企业集团，业务范围广泛，包括保险和安全服务。

其中许多子公司最初是为该集团服务的内部部门，并且仍然将三星视为其主要客户，但该集团希望随着人工智能需求的增长，一些子公司能够扩展到外部客户。

三星 SDS 最初是一家内部 IT 服务提供商，运营数据中心主要是为了支持该集团，目前正在与 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 进行早期谈判，有可能签约它们作为租户。分析师预计，到 2031 年，该公司数据中心的年收入将达到 6.6 万亿韩元（49 亿美元），大约是当前水平的六倍。

去年，三星与 OpenAI 签署了合作伙伴关系，为其 Stargate 数据中心计划提供先进的存储芯片。

该协议包括三星 SDS 与 OpenAI 合作设计、开发和运营数据中心。建筑公司三星物产和造船商三星重工也表示，他们将与这家美国科技公司合作开发浮动数据中心。

摩根士丹利在最近的一份报告中表示，三星 SDS 处于有利地位，可以从数据中心建设的激增中受益，世界各国政府通过要求在国内存储信息的法律强化了这一趋势。

麦肯锡估计，到 2030 年，全球数据中心容量需求可能几乎增加两倍，其中人工智能工作负载约占总量的 70%。仅满足人工智能计算需求就可能需要 5.2 万亿美元的资本支出。

“三星有机会提供整体解决方案，”韩国科学技术院电气工程教授 Joungho Kim 表示。 “美国大型科技公司在人工智能和软件方面实力雄厚，但他们在硬件方面严重依赖外部供应商。”

然而，最近的科技收益引发了投资者对人工智能基础设施花费的天文数字以及未来需求是否足以证明成本的担忧。

article_content:
The new partnership will help young people build AI skills for the future workforce, prioritizing those not in education or employment.

The King’s Trust⁠(opens in a new window) has announced a major partnership with OpenAI designed to help up to 25,000 young people build AI skills for work, prioritizing those not in education, employment or training.

OpenAI is making a £1m donation to the youth charity to support this work.

This is part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications that The Trust will launch in the coming months, designed to help young people stay ahead of a changing labor market.

The announcement comes as The King’s Trust marks its 50th year and looks to the future, helping ensure young people are supported to succeed in an increasingly AI-enabled world.

The King’s Trust and OpenAI have launched a £1 million partnership to help young people across the UK build AI skills for work, prioritizing those who are not in education, employment or training (NEET). The program aims to support up to 25,000 young people over the next 18 months, helping them develop practical skills and confidence to move toward education and employment in an AI-enabled economy.

The program will help address a gap in young people’s experience of AI while responding to their appetite to learn. The Open University’s Business Barometer 2026⁠(opens in a new window) found that 68% of 16–24-year-olds surveyed who were not in education, employment or training would be willing to train or upskill to improve their job prospects.

The partnership will help prepare young people for the opportunities and challenges of a rapidly changing world of work by combining opportunities to learn AI skills with recognized qualifications and practical experience. It forms part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications being developed by The King’s Trust, designed to equip young people with the skills employers need as AI transforms the world of work.

Working with employers, AI specialists and young people, The King’s Trust is exploring the skills young people will need in a world of work where AI is becoming part of everyday life, and how these can complement the employability skills already embedded across its programs.

Building on a 50-year legacy of supporting more than 1.3 million young people, The King’s Trust wants to ensure the next generation gains the skills and confidence needed to thrive in an AI-enabled economy.

Ahead of the final report of the independent Young People and Work review, the Rt Hon Alan Milburn welcomed the partnership, reflecting on the shared ambition to improve young people’s opportunities to learn and earn.

For OpenAI, the partnership forms part of a broader commitment to helping young people develop the skills and confidence to benefit from AI. It builds on wider efforts to make practical AI learning more accessible, including through OpenAI Academy, which provides free learning resources for students, job-seekers and other learners.

新的合作伙伴关系将帮助年轻人为未来的劳动力培养人工智能技能，优先考虑那些没有接受过教育或就业的人。

国王信托基金会（在新窗口中打开）宣布与 OpenAI 建立重要合作伙伴关系，旨在帮助多达 25,000 名年轻人培养工作所需的人工智能技能，优先考虑那些没有接受教育、就业或培训的年轻人。

OpenAI 正在向青年慈善机构捐赠 100 万英镑来支持这项工作。

这是该信托基金将在未来几个月推出的更广泛的国家认可人工智能资格计划的一部分，旨在帮助年轻人在不断变化的劳动力市场中保持领先地位。

这一消息发布之际，国王信托基金会正值成立 50 周年，并着眼于未来，帮助确保年轻人在人工智能日益普及的世界中获得成功。

国王信托基金会和 OpenAI 启动了一项 100 万英镑的合作伙伴关系，帮助英国各地的年轻人培养工作所需的人工智能技能，优先考虑那些没有接受教育、就业或培训的人 (NEET)。该计划旨在在未来 18 个月内为多达 25,000 名年轻人提供支持，帮助他们培养实用技能和信心，以在人工智能经济中接受教育和就业。

该计划将有助于弥补年轻人在人工智能体验方面的差距，同时满足他们的学习欲望。开放大学的 2026 年商业晴雨表（在新窗口中打开）发现，在接受调查的 16 至 24 岁未接受教育、就业或培训的人中，68% 愿意接受培训或提升技能以改善其就业前景。

该合作伙伴关系将通过将学习人工智能技能的机会与公认的资格和实践经验相结合，帮助年轻人为快速变化的工作世界的机遇和挑战做好准备。它是国王信托基金正在开发的更广泛的国家认可人工智能资格计划的一部分，旨在为年轻人提供雇主在人工智能改变工作世界时所需的技能。

国王信托基金与雇主、人工智能专家和年轻人合作​​，正在探索年轻人在人工智能正在成为日常生活一部分的工作世界中所需的技能，以及这些技能如何补充其项目中已经嵌入的就业技能。

国王信托基金会以 50 年来支持超过 130 万年轻人的传统为基础，希望确保下一代获得在人工智能经济中蓬勃发展所需的技能和信心。

在独立的年轻人与工作审查最终报告发布之前，艾伦·米尔本 (Alan Milburn) 阁下对此次合作表示欢迎，并反思了改善年轻人学习和赚钱机会的共同目标。

对于 OpenAI 来说，此次合作是其更广泛承诺的一部分，旨在帮助年轻人培养从人工智能中受益的技能和信心。它建立在更广泛的努力基础上，使实用的人工智能学习变得更加容易，包括通过 OpenAI Academy 为学生、求职者和其他学习者提供免费的学习资源。

title: Anthropic Is About to Become the World’s Most Important AI Stock
title_en: Anthropic Is About to Become the World’s Most Important AI Stock
author: Bloomberg
article_content:
Anthropic IPO Reportedly Oversubscribed as Company Targets $90.4 Billion in Combined Offerings Fiona Craig Wed, November 11, 2026 at 6:33 AM PST 5 min read ANTH.PVT Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) has reportedly received investor orders exceeding the number of shares available in its planned initial public offering (IPO) by several times, according to a Bloomberg News report published Wednesday, as the artificial intelligence company prepares for a potential stock market listing.

The reported demand has been supported by substantial indications of interest from prospective institutional investors, including large orders typically associated with anchor investors, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Anthropic is seeking to raise as much as $90.4 billion through its IPO and a concurrent private placement, according to regulatory filings cited in the report.

The company is targeting a fully diluted valuation of approximately $1.4 trillion, although the final offering price, valuation and number of shares allocated remain subject to change.

Bloomberg reported that demand for Anthropic's planned IPO has exceeded the available share allocation multiple times.

Large institutional orders, sometimes described as anchor-size orders, have reportedly contributed to the level of demand.

Such orders can provide underwriters with an indication of institutional participation before the final offering price and share allocations are determined.

However, preliminary indications of interest do not necessarily represent completed purchases, and final allocations may differ from initial requests.

The details of Anthropic's offering remain subject to revision as the company and its underwriting banks continue the marketing process.

Anthropic is preparing to raise up to $90.4 billion through a combination of its initial public offering and a concurrent private placement.

According to the reported filing details, the combined fundraising would exceed the size of SpaceX's planned IPO.

The two transactions would provide investors with different routes to participate in Anthropic's equity offering.

The public offering would make shares available through the stock market listing, while the private placement would involve a separate allocation to eligible investors.

The company has not finalised the offering terms, and the eventual proceeds will depend on the number of shares sold and their final pricing.

The reported fundraising target would place Anthropic's proposed transaction among the largest equity offerings announced to date.

Anthropic is reportedly seeking a fully diluted valuation of approximately $1.4 trillion.

A fully diluted valuation takes into account the company's equity on the assumption that relevant convertible securities, options and other potential share issuances are reflected in the share count.

The valuation target was previously reported by Bloomberg and remains dependent on the final terms of the offering.

According to the report, the initial pricing approach could provide flexibility for adjustments during the IPO marketing process.

If investor demand continues to exceed the available allocation, Anthropic and its underwriters could consider revising the proposed offering price.

article_content_zh:
Anthropic 的 IPO 超额认购，公司目标是 904 亿美元的联合发行 Fiona Craig 太平洋标准时间 2026 年 11 月 11 日星期三上午 6:33 阅读 5 分钟 ANTH.PVT 据彭博新闻社周三发布的报道，Anthropic （纳斯达克股票代码：ANT）收到的投资者订单数倍于其计划的首次公开募股 (IPO) 中可用的股票数量，该人工智能公司正在为潜在股票做准备市场上市。

彭博社援引知情人士的话报道称，潜在机构投资者的大量兴趣表明了所报告的需求，其中包括通常与锚定投资者相关的大额订单。

报告中引用的监管文件显示，Anthropic 正寻求通过 IPO 和同时进行的私募筹集高达 904 亿美元的资金。

该公司的目标是完全摊薄后估值约为 1.4 万亿美元，但最终发行价、估值和分配的股票数量仍可能发生变化。

彭博社报道称，Anthropic 计划 IPO 的需求已超过可用股票分配数倍。

大型机构订单（有时被称为锚定规模订单）对需求水平做出了贡献。

此类订单可以在确定最终发行价和股票分配之前向承销商提供机构参与的指示。

然而，初步的兴趣并不一定代表已完成的购买，最终的分配可能与最初的请求不同。

随着公司及其承销银行继续进行营销流程，Anthropic 发行的细节仍有待修改。

Anthropic 正准备通过首次公开募股和同步私募相结合的方式筹集高达 904 亿美元的资金。

根据报道的备案细节，此次融资总额将超过 SpaceX 计划的 IPO 规模。

这两笔交易将为投资者提供参与 Anthropic 股票发行的不同途径。

公开发行将通过股票市场上市提供股票，而私募将涉及向合格投资者单独分配。

该公司尚未最终确定发行条款，最终收益将取决于出售的股票数量及其最终定价。

所报告的融资目标将使 Anthropic 拟议的交易成为迄今为止宣布的最大的股票发行交易之一。

Anthropic 正在寻求约 1.4 万亿美元的完全摊薄估值。

完全稀释估值考虑了公司的股权，假设相关可转换证券、期权和其他潜在股票发行已反映在股票数量中。

彭博社此前曾报道过这一估值目标，但仍取决于此次发行的最终条款。

报告称，初始定价方式可以为IPO营销过程中的调整提供灵活性。

如果投资者需求继续超过可用分配，Anthropic 及其承销商可以考虑修改拟议发行价。

然而，所提供的报告中尚未披露最终定价决定。

最终估值将取决于股票价格以及公司上市时完全稀释后的股数。

在拟议的上市之前，Anthropic 还在扩大其机构投资者的范围。

该公司计划于周五举办一场直播活动，首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 和摩根大通首席执行官杰米·戴蒙 (Jamie Dimon) 出席。

该活动是 Anthropic 在发行过程中与潜在投资者沟通的努力的一部分。

投资者演示和管理层讨论可以提供有关公司运营、财务状况、业务战略和发行收益计划的信息。

所提供的报告没有提供该活动的详细议程，也没有具体说明预计将讨论的财务信息。

计划中的演示文稿发布之际，该公司正在继续评估机构对其拟议股票出售的兴趣。

彭博社的报告还描述了涉及现有 Anthropic 投资者寻求将风险转移给其他潜在买家的活动。

一些投资者正在推销其预期 IPO 分配的部分资金，而 IPO 前股权的持有者则通过特殊目的工具提供投资敞口。

这些安排可以在公司公开市场首次亮相之前或前后提供间接购买公司股票的机会。

特殊目的工具是可以代表参与投资者持有资产的投资结构。

根据其条款，此类结构可能允许现有投资者减少风险敞口，同时收取与交易相关的费用。

这一活动还引发了有关现有投资者在上市期间可能寻求出售的股票数量的问题。

然而，该报告没有量化这些安排所涉及的股票数量，也没有确定公开交易开始后可能发生的抛售量。

根据报告中引用的文件，高盛和摩根士丹利担任 Anthropic 计划 IPO 的牵头银行。

另外 20 家银行参与了此次交易。

承销小组负责与发行过程相关的活动，包括投资者营销、订单收集和股票分配。

Anthropic 计划在纳斯达克全球精选市场上市，股票代码为 ANT。

最终发行价、股份分配和交易开始日期尚未在所提供的信息中得到确认。

随着交易的进展，该公司及其银行集团将继续评估投资者的需求。

Anthropic 计划在股票市场首次亮相，吸引了比现有股票数量多几倍的初步投资者订单。

该公司正在通过首次公开募股（IPO）和同时进行的私募融资寻求高达 904 亿美元的融资，据报道，完全摊薄后的估值目标约为 1.4 万亿美元。

此次发行由高盛和摩根士丹利牵头，另有 20 家银行参与。

Anthropic 还正在准备一场由首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 和摩根大通首席执行官杰米·戴蒙 (Jamie Dimon) 参加的投资者活动，作为其机构营销活动的一部分。

与此同时，有关现有股东营销分配和通过特殊目的载体发行敞口的报告表明，二次投资安排正在与计划上市同时发展。

IPO 的最终规模、定价和分配仍可能发生变化，报告的需求水平并不能保证交易的最终结果。

title: Rocket from Boeing-Lockheed firm fails mid-flight, destroys payload of Amazon satellites
title_en: Rocket from Boeing-Lockheed firm fails mid-flight, destroys payload of Amazon satellites

inline_images.caption: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket lifts off before suffering mid-flight failure. (Photo: REUTERS)
inline_images.caption_en: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket lifts off before suffering mid-flight failure. (Photo: REUTERS)
inline_images.caption_zh: 联合发射联盟（ULA）Vulcan 火箭点火升空，随后在飞行中途出现严重故障。(摄影：路透社)
inline_images.alt: Rocket from Boeing-Lockheed firm fails mid-flight, destroys payload of Amazon satellites

author: Reuters
article_content:
Nov 15 (Reuters) - A Vulcan rocket owned by United Launch Alliance, the joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed on Sunday shortly after liftoff from Florida, destroying its payload of 40 satellites from Amazon's Leo internet network in the launch company's first mission failure.

The rocket failed roughly 10 minutes after liftoff from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, and the cause was not immediately clear. It represented a major setback for the two-decade-old company's new flagship rocket as ULA sought to begin a regular cadence of launches for Amazon's burgeoning satellite internet constellation.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in a statement.

"Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don't have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today," ULA said.

The failure is expected to lead to a lengthy technical investigation that would keep the rocket off the market for months. This could deepen a US launch bottleneck brought on by other rocket mishaps and challenges across the industry as well as the looming retirement of SpaceX's Falcon 9, the world's most active rocket. SpaceX is no longer accepting bookings for the Falcon 9.

"There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon said in a statement, referring to the name of Sunday's mission. "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."

The Sunday flight was Vulcan's fifth since its 2024 debut and first in nine months, following a launch hiatus drawn out by separate technical investigations into its solid rocket side boosters and its core BE-4 engines, which are supplied by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin space company.

Blue Origin is working with ULA in the investigation into Sunday's failure, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The boosters were being scrutinized for issues encountered on Vulcan's last two flights, including a mission in February for the US Space Force. Both missions successfully delivered their payloads to orbit, but the Pentagon had not yet approved the rocket to resume flying national security payloads, pending its performance with the Amazon mission on Sunday.

Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket with the BE-4 engine had a launchpad explosion in May, and its investigation determined the engine was the cause. That led the company to modify those delivered to ULA for Vulcan, ULA spokesperson Jessica Rye told Reuters in August.

It was unclear if the BE-4 engines played a role in Sunday's mission failure. It appeared to occur after the separation of Vulcan's second stage, the portion carrying the Amazon satellites, from the first-stage booster powered by the BE-4 engines.

ULA was formed in 2006 in a merger of Boeing's Delta rocket program and Lockheed Martin's Atlas rocket program. The company had embraced what was a 100% mission success record ever since. Its Delta and Atlas rockets had only suffered a handful of failures in the decades before the merger.

AMAZON'S ELUSIVE ACCESS TO SPACE

The failure is another setback for Amazon as it races to deploy satellites using third-party launch providers, many of which have had groundings and failures. The New Glenn explosion in May happened days before it was due to launch Amazon Leo satellites.

The rocket failures have persistently held up Amazon's bid to rival SpaceX's vast Starlink internet network, which has more than 11,000 satellites and millions of customers worldwide.

SpaceX's wide lead over its satellite rivals is due in part to the advantage of having its own rocket to launch its satellites, while other companies spend billions of dollars on external launches.

Since 2025, 398 Leo satellites have been deployed across 14 launches, about 12% of the 3,236 satellites Amazon needs for global service coverage. The company has hoped to start initial internet service this year.

summary_zh: 波音与洛克希德马丁合资组建的联合发射联盟（ULA）旗下的 Vulcan 火箭在佛罗里达升空约 10 分钟后发生严重异常导致任务失败，火箭搭载的亚马逊 Leo 星座首批 40 颗互联网卫星全部损毁
article_content_zh:
11月15日（路透社）- 由波音与洛克希德·马丁合资组建的联合发射联盟（ULA）旗下的 Vulcan 火箭，周日从佛罗里达州升空后不久发生严重故障，导致其运载的亚马逊 Leo 互联网星座首批 40 颗卫星全部损毁。这也是该发射服务商成立以来的首次任务失利。

该火箭在从佛罗里达州卡纳维拉尔角太空军基地发射升空约 10 分钟后发生故障，具体故障原因尚无法立即确定。这对于拥有二十年历史的 ULA 公司而言是一次重大打击，该公司此前正全力推动其全新旗舰火箭进入高频常态化发射，以支持亚马逊加速构建低轨卫星互联网星座。

ULA 在声明中表示：“根据发射主管接收到的遥测数据，我们确认从 41 号航天发射复合体升空的 Vulcan 火箭在飞行进行到 10 分钟时遭遇异常，未能将亚马逊的任务载荷送入预定轨道。”

ULA 补充道：“每次飞行都会产生宝贵数据，每次飞行也都会让我们汲取经验。鉴于异常刚刚发生，我们目前尚未掌握确切数据来完全判定今日发生的具体故障细节。”

预计此次事故将引发为期数月的漫长技术调查，使 Vulcan 火箭被迫暂停发射。这也将加剧美国商业运载市场的运力瓶颈，由于此前全行业发生的多次火箭事故以及全球现役最活跃的 SpaceX 猎鹰 9 号（Falcon 9）面临退役（SpaceX 已不再接受猎鹰 9 号新预订），全行业可用运力已高度吃紧。

亚马逊在声明中谈及周日代号为 LV-01 的任务时表示：“任何航天发射都伴随着固有风险，对于初次执行关键任务的火箭而言尤其如此。ULA 一直是亚马逊值得信赖的合作伙伴，我们相信他们能从这次任务中吸取教训，并顺利实现 Vulcan 火箭的长期发展蓝图。”

周日的发射是 Vulcan 火箭自 2024 年首飞以来的第五次任务，也是历经 9 个月停飞后的首次亮相。此前该公司曾因对其固体助推器以及由亚马逊创始人杰夫·贝索斯旗下的蓝色起源（Blue Origin）提供的核心 BE-4 发动机展开独立技术调查而推迟了发射计划。

据一位不愿透露姓名的知情人士称，蓝色起源目前正与 ULA 紧密配合，全力投入对周日故障原因的联合排查。

此前 Vulcan 在最后两次飞行中（包括今年 2 月为美国太空军执行的一次任务）暴露出固体助推器缺陷，因而受到严格审查。尽管这两次任务最终均成功将有效载荷送入轨道，但五角大楼仍在等待周日亚马逊任务的表现，尚未批准恢复使用该火箭发射高优先级国家安全载荷。

蓝色起源配备 BE-4 发动机的 New Glenn 火箭曾于今年 5 月发生发射台爆炸事故，后续调查确定发动机本身即为事故起因。ULA 发言人杰西卡·莱伊（Jessica Rye）8 月曾对路透社表示，这促使蓝色起源对交付给 ULA 用于 Vulcan 火箭的发动机进行了针对性设计修改。

目前尚不清楚 BE-4 发动机是否在周日的任务故障中起到了直接作用。初步迹象表明，异常似乎发生在搭载亚马逊卫星的 Vulcan 第二级与由 BE-4 发动机驱动的第一级助推器分离之后。

ULA 成立于 2006 年，由波音的 Delta 火箭项目与洛克希德·马丁的 Atlas 火箭项目合并而成。合并以来该公司一直保持着 100% 的发射成功纪录，其 Delta 和 Atlas 火箭在合并前的数十年间也仅遭遇过极少数失败。

亚马逊坎坷的太空入轨之路

这次失败是亚马逊在太空竞赛中的又一次挫折。由于高度依赖第三方商业发射服务商，亚马逊的卫星部署进程屡遭推迟，而其中许多服务商的火箭均曾遭遇停飞或事故。今年 5 月 New Glenn 的爆炸事故正是发生在原定发射亚马逊 Leo 卫星的前几天。

火箭事故的频发持续阻碍了亚马逊对抗 SpaceX 庞大“星链”（Starlink）网络的宏伟计划。目前星链已在轨运营超过 11,000 颗卫星，并在全球范围内拥有数百万付费用户。

SpaceX 相比其卫星竞争对手建立起的巨大领先优势，很大程度上得益于其拥有自主火箭发射卫星的绝对掌控力，而其他科技企业则不得不耗资数十亿美元采购外部商业发射名额。

自 2025 年以来，亚马逊已通过 14 次发射部署了 398 颗 Leo 卫星，约占其全球网络覆盖所需 3,236 颗卫星的 12%。该公司此前一直希望在今年启动初期互联网服务。

paragraphs: Nov 15 (Reuters) - A Vulcan rocket owned by United Launch Alliance, the joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed on Sunday shortly after liftoff from Florida, destroying its payload of 40 satellites from Amazon's Leo internet network in the launch company's first mission failure.

The rocket failed roughly 10 minutes after liftoff from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, and the cause was not immediately clear. It represented a major setback for the two-decade-old company's new flagship rocket as ULA sought to begin a regular cadence of launches for Amazon's burgeoning satellite internet constellation.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in a statement.
"Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don't have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today," ULA said.

The failure is expected to lead to a lengthy technical investigation that would keep the rocket off the market for months. This could deepen a US launch bottleneck brought on by other rocket mishaps and challenges across the industry as well as the looming retirement of SpaceX's Falcon 9, the world's most active rocket. SpaceX is no longer accepting bookings for the Falcon 9.

"There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon said in a statement, referring to the name of Sunday's mission. "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."

The Sunday flight was Vulcan's fifth since its 2024 debut and first in nine months, following a launch hiatus drawn out by separate technical investigations into its solid rocket side boosters and its core BE-4 engines, which are supplied by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin space company.
Blue Origin is working with ULA in the investigation into Sunday's failure, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The boosters were being scrutinized for issues encountered on Vulcan's last two flights, including a mission in February for the US Space Force. Both missions successfully delivered their payloads to orbit, but the Pentagon had not yet approved the rocket to resume flying national security payloads, pending its performance with the Amazon mission on Sunday.

Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket with the BE-4 engine had a launchpad explosion in May, and its investigation determined the engine was the cause. That led the company to modify those delivered to ULA for Vulcan, ULA spokesperson Jessica Rye told Reuters in August.

It was unclear if the BE-4 engines played a role in Sunday's mission failure. It appeared to occur after the separation of Vulcan's second stage, the portion carrying the Amazon satellites, from the first-stage booster powered by the BE-4 engines.

ULA was formed in 2006 in a merger of Boeing's Delta rocket program and Lockheed Martin's Atlas rocket program. The company had embraced what was a 100% mission success record ever since. Its Delta and Atlas rockets had only suffered a handful of failures in the decades before the merger.
AMAZON'S ELUSIVE ACCESS TO SPACE

The failure is another setback for Amazon as it races to deploy satellites using third-party launch providers, many of which have had groundings and failures. The New Glenn explosion in May happened days before it was due to launch Amazon Leo satellites.
The rocket failures have persistently held up Amazon's bid to rival SpaceX's vast Starlink internet network, which has more than 11,000 satellites and millions of customers worldwide.
SpaceX's wide lead over its satellite rivals is due in part to the advantage of having its own rocket to launch its satellites, while other companies spend billions of dollars on external launches.

Since 2025, 398 Leo satellites have been deployed across 14 launches, about 12% of the 3,236 satellites Amazon needs for global service coverage. The company has hoped to start initial internet service this year.

"There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon said in a statement, referring to the name of Sunday's mission. "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."

The Sunday flight was Vulcan's fifth since its 2024 debut and first in nine months, following a launch hiatus drawn out by separate technical investigations into its solid rocket side boosters and its core BE-4 engines, which are supplied by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin space company.

Blue Origin is working with ULA in the investigation into Sunday's failure, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The boosters were being scrutinized for issues encountered on Vulcan's last two flights, including a mission in February for the US Space Force. Both missions successfully delivered their payloads to orbit, but the Pentagon had not yet approved the rocket to resume flying national security payloads, pending its performance with the Amazon mission on Sunday.

Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket with the BE-4 engine had a launchpad explosion in May, and its investigation determined the engine was the cause. That led the company to modify those delivered to ULA for Vulcan, ULA spokesperson Jessica Rye told Reuters in August.

It was unclear if the BE-4 engines played a role in Sunday's mission failure. It appeared to occur after the separation of Vulcan's second stage, the portion carrying the Amazon satellites, from the first-stage booster powered by the BE-4 engines.

ULA was formed in 2006 in a merger of Boeing's Delta rocket program and Lockheed Martin's Atlas rocket program. The company had embraced what was a 100% mission success record ever since. Its Delta and Atlas rockets had only suffered a handful of failures in the decades before the merger.

AMAZON'S ELUSIVE ACCESS TO SPACE

The failure is another setback for Amazon as it races to deploy satellites using third-party launch providers, many of which have had groundings and failures. The New Glenn explosion in May happened days before it was due to launch Amazon Leo satellites.

The rocket failures have persistently held up Amazon's bid to rival SpaceX's vast Starlink internet network, which has more than 11,000 satellites and millions of customers worldwide.

SpaceX's wide lead over its satellite rivals is due in part to the advantage of having its own rocket to launch its satellites, while other companies spend billions of dollars on external launches.

Since 2025, 398 Leo satellites have been deployed across 14 launches, about 12% of the 3,236 satellites Amazon needs for global service coverage. The company has hoped to start initial internet service this year.

author: Epoch AI
content_snippet: This is a condensed version of a longer report on our website — Huawei, China's biggest AI chip developer, is drawing on China's abundant energy to build data centers.
summary_en: Epoch AI analysis reveals that Huawei's Horinger AI data center cluster holds approximately 7% of the total compute capacity of SpaceX's Colossus 2. Driven by constraints in advanced process node chip procurement and manufacturing capacity, this infrastructure is unlikely to bridge the scale gap with global leading clusters before 2028.
title_zh: 华为和林格尔数据中心AI算力规模深度解析
summary_zh: 研究显示华为和林格尔数据中心算力仅为SpaceX Colossus 2的7%，预计2028年前难现量级超越
article_content_zh:
Epoch AI的研究报告通过量化基准测试与基础设施建模，对比了华为和林格尔数据中心与SpaceX Colossus 2集群的规模。评估结果指出，华为受限于当前的制程工艺，虽然在集群部署规模上有序扩张，但若要达到当前顶级集群（如Colossus 2）的算力水平，在芯片流片与先进封装产能未发生结构性变革前，短期内无法填平差距。

分析师强调，中国在算力构建上的策略已从单纯追求制程领先，转向强化高性能互联架构（如基于昇腾系列的集群方案）。然而，在单体算力卡性能受制于禁令的前提下，通过堆叠数量构建大规模集群的成本与能效挑战将成为未来四年行业部署的主要考验。

article_content:
In the first guest post on our science blog, physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, describes how he worked with GPT‑6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. Craig leads the particle theory group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics.

The Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen’s 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. And yet for all of its successes over the more than fifty years of its existence, a foundational problem remains: how to give the full theory a nonperturbative definition, one that does not rely on treating its interactions as small corrections. In an October preprint⁠(opens in a new window) prepared with the aid of GPT‑6 Astra, I proposed a candidate definition on a lattice—a grid representing spacetime.

I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. To explain what we did, it helps to start with what is missing from our existing description of the Standard Model.

What does it mean to say that we lack a definition of the Standard Model? Quantum mechanics and special relativity tell us how the particles and forces of the Standard Model interact. Unfortunately, we don’t yet know how to make complete predictions based directly on these interactions. Instead, we often start by imagining that the interactions are turned off, so that electrons would no longer repel each other. We can solve that problem exactly, then put the interactions back in as a series of small corrections. When the corrections get progressively smaller, a few terms can give a remarkably precise answer—for example, it has allowed physicists to predict the strength of the electron’s magnetism to within a few parts in a trillion. This approach is known as perturbation theory.

However, much of the richness of the Standard Model lies outside the realm of perturbation theory. Take the mass of the proton: the proton is made up of three quarks, but its mass comes primarily from the motion and interactions of the quarks and the strong force-carrying gluons inside it. If you turn off the strong force, the proton falls apart entirely, so perturbation theory is not a useful guide to understanding the size of the proton’s mass. More powerful methods are needed to access information about the theory nonperturbatively, where the interactions are present from the start and not treated as small corrections.

For the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, we don’t have a nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined. A promising alternative is to discretize spacetime into a grid of points, known as a lattice. The spacing of the grid defines the shortest distance our theory can resolve, and studying a finite grid allows us to give a rigorous nonperturbative definition of the theory at a given spacing. It also enables us to put the theory on a computer, where we can calculate its predictions directly without resorting to perturbation theory. This approach, known as lattice field theory, has led to remarkable progress in our understanding of the strong force over the last few decades, including a quantitative understanding of the mass of the proton from first principles.

If lattice field theory has been so successful for the strong force, why haven’t we extended it to a nonperturbative lattice definition of the entire Standard Model? Here a crucial difference stands in the way: the Standard Model is an example of what is known as a chiral theory.

A chiral theory is one that looks different under reflection in space. Think of gloves in a mirror: the mirror image of a left-handed glove is a right-handed glove. If you have one of each kind, the mirror image does as well, so your collection of gloves looks the same under reflection in space. But if you only have a left-handed glove, the right-handed glove in the mirror is different.

This notion of handedness extends to many of the fundamental particles in the Standard Model, known as fermions, including quarks and electrons. Most forces in the Standard Model are not chiral: the strong force and electromagnetism, for example, treat left-handed and right-handed fermions in the same way. Such theories can be put on a lattice more readily.

But the third fundamental force of the Standard Model, the weak force, lacks this reflection symmetry. It treats left- and right-handed fermions differently, and so does not look the same under mirror reflections that exchange left and right. This treating of different-handed particles differently is what makes the Standard Model a chiral theory. And it turns out that putting chiral theories on a lattice is profoundly challenging. If we try to put a left-handed fermion on the lattice, the most natural rules give you a right-handed partner you never asked for. This is a surprising outcome, which we’ll unpack momentarily. Whatever the reason, this means a straightforward lattice formulation of the Standard Model gives the wrong particle content for the weak force. Doubling is one reason a complete nonperturbative definition of the Standard Model has been missing since the theory took shape.

To understand doubling, consider an analogy with light. Light has two polarizations, which describe the orientation of the electric field as the light moves through space. (This is familiar if you wear polarized sunglasses, which block the horizontally-polarized light that reflects off water or roads while letting through vertically-polarized light.) Although polarized sunglasses pick out a basis of horizontal and vertical polarizations, for our analogy it will be more useful to pick a basis where these two polarizations are left-circular and right-circular, meaning that the electric field is rotating either clockwise or counterclockwise around the direction of motion. As we’ve said, electromagnetism is reflection-symmetric, so its actual laws are the same for both left-circular and right-circular polarizations. (For the technically inclined, left and right refer to chirality when we talk about fermions. In our analogy with light, they refer to the photon’s helicity, which tells us whether its spin points along or against its direction of travel.)

But imagine you wanted to emulate a world with only left-circular light, akin to the way the weak interactions single out left-handed fermions. To study this in the lab, you could put a laser producing left-circular light into a box with a mirror at either end. The light could build up as it bounced back and forth, allowing you to study it carefully—kind of like putting the Standard Model on a lattice. In each case you are bounding the accessible length scales of the theory to gain control—the lattice bounds the shortest accessible distances, while the box bounds the longest distances.

If you built the box using ordinary mirrors (like putting a chiral theory on the lattice in the most straightforward way), you’d be in for a surprise: the left-circular light coming out of the laser becomes right-circular when it bounces off the mirror at the other end, so now the box contains both polarizations of light. This occurs because the mirror reverses the direction of the light without changing how the electric field is rotating (as seen from the same end of the box), which flips the polarization. This is a bit like the appearance of doublers when you put a left-handed fermion on the lattice. You supplied only left-handed light, and the box supplied the other hand.

There is a clever fix. You can make a chiral mirror using special films whose molecules line up in layers. The alignment turns a little from one layer to the next, tracing a spiral down into the film. For light whose wavelength and handedness match the spiral, the small reflections from different layers reinforce one another, flipping the rotation of the electric field in the light that bounces back. The film sends left-handed light back left-handed and lets right-handed light pass through. Such chiral mirrors have been around for more than a decade, and the phenomenon even occurs in nature: some scarab beetles have a similar spiral in their shiny shells. If you constructed your box using chiral mirrors, then the light traveling in both directions would be left-circular.

A similar trick works on the lattice: decades ago, Paul Ginsparg and Nobel laureate Ken Wilson1 worked out the lattice rules analogous to the requirement that chiral mirrors reverse the rotation of the electric field upon reflection. Rajamani Narayanan and Herbert Neuberger2 built the analog of the chiral mirrors by finding the necessary definition of fundamental particles on the lattice, known as overlap fermions. Finally, Martin Lüscher3 showed how to tell the difference between left-handed and right-handed overlap fermions on the lattice, while Yoshio Kikukawa4 and collaborators explored how this might be used to describe weak interactions in the Standard Model. However, one piece was still missing.

To identify that piece, let’s come back to our box with chiral mirrors. The circular polarization of light tells us which way the electric field turns as light propagates, but there’s another important property of the light in our experiment: the optical phase. Imagine water waves rolling past the pilings of a dock, and watch the water rise and fall at one piling. The wave’s phase is the stage of that rise and fall you catch it in when you look, perhaps just past its highest point and on its way down. For our circularly polarized light, the optical phase tracks the same kind of cycle at a fixed spot in the beam, with the electric field pointing up at the “crest” and down at the “trough.”

The relative phase of two waves determines how much they add or cancel at the same point. At one piling of a dock, two waves arriving in phase lift the water higher as their crests meet, while a crest arriving with a trough can leave the water close to its usual level. Similarly, light with the same phase in the same place builds up, while light with different phases can cancel out. In our box with chiral mirrors, left-circular light is now bouncing back and forth inside the box. After a lap, the returning light meets fresh light from the laser going in the same direction. If their electric fields are in step, they reinforce and the light builds up inside the box. If the fields are half a cycle apart, they point in opposite directions and the returning light cancels some of the fresh light. To build up a strong beam, we want the phase of each return to arrive in step with the source.

To get the phase right, we can rotate one chiral mirror relative to the other. Imagine a mark at twelve o’clock on the rim, and spin the mirror about the beam as though the beam were its axle. Moving the mark to three o’clock turns every layer of the film by a quarter turn and shifts the phase of the reflected light by half a cycle. We can set the angle to make up for the phase accumulated on the rest of the trip. Once the returning light arrives in step with the laser, we have a splendid laboratory for studying purely left-handed light.

Imagine changing the force fields until they return to where they started. The orange arcs show the phase the left-handed fermions pick up on that round trip, first on the original grid and then on finer ones. Each bracket pairs two neighboring grids. Adding up the differences between their arcs recovers the phase shift on the original grid. The teal arrow undoes that shift, bringing the fermion measure back to its starting phase.

On the lattice, overlap fermions give us a way of keeping only the left-handed fermions that we want, and getting rid of the doublers. But this doesn’t tell us how to set the phase. (The phase in question is quite different from the one we’ve encountered in our chiral mirror thought experiment, but the analogy is good.) On the lattice, this becomes tricky because the phase depends on what the forces of the Standard Model are doing at every grid point. Lüscher worked out the phase prescription for a simpler class of theories such as a chiral version of electromagnetism, but the alignment for the full Standard Model remained open for more than 25 years.

We can try to assign a phase by starting with one configuration of forces on the lattice and following the allowed left-handed fermions as we change the force fields in small steps. Now take a series of steps that bring the force fields back to where they started. The same states are allowed at the end, yet the way we carried them around the loop can leave us with a different phase. In the box, we adjusted the mirror to compensate for the phase the light picked up on a lap. On the lattice we have to work out how to compensate for the phase picked up around every loop.

My idea was to take the force fields on the grid where we want to define the theory and represent those same fields on a succession of finer grids. Comparing the allowed fermion states on two successive grids tells us one part of the phase correction for a small change in the forces. Adding up those parts gives us the phase rule on the original grid. The proof shows that it gives the right correction around every allowed loop. The correction for a change at one spot depends mainly on the fields nearby, and different mathematical descriptions of the same fields give the same answer. This supplies the measure for the Standard Model at finite lattice spacing, under a bound on field strengths at the scale of the grid.

Developing this refinement strategy into a proof required several rounds of work with Astra and discussions with outside experts. GPT‑6 Astra was essential to turning the refinement idea into a working construction. It suggested the right way to carry a given set of force fields onto finer grids, showed that the comparisons on finer grids would converge to a definite answer, and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. Human experts also played a key role; lattice field theorists Maarten Golterman, Andreas Kronfeld, and Yigal Shamir graciously spent time looking over Astra’s proof and asking probing questions that helped me to build confidence in the result. Their experience with the problem and the questions they asked were invaluable as the construction took shape.

The result is a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition for the Standard Model, potentially answering a question that had been open for more than fifty years. As with all scientific progress, however, this construction is much more a beginning than an end. Scientific dialogue among experts is required to decide if this prescription has all the properties we desire. The method that Astra and I proposed is far more an answer in principle than an answer in practice; much work lies ahead to make it useful for realistic lattice simulations. Right now I’m thinking a lot about whether this construction satisfies reflection positivity at finite lattice spacing, a condition that helps connect calculations in this lattice model to a quantum theory in which probabilities are conserved.

The construction also leaves open the question of defining the interacting theory in continuous spacetime. OpenAI’s recent proof of the existence of Yang-Mills theory (of which the strong and weak forces of the Standard Model are examples) provides the missing puzzle piece. This enabled them to prove the existence of the simplest unified Yang-Mills theory that includes the gauge fields and fermions of the Standard Model by starting with overlap fermions on the lattice and taking the continuum limit. I’m optimistic these developments will lead to new progress in our understanding of the Standard Model.

P. H. Ginsparg and K. G. Wilson, “A remnant of chiral symmetry on the lattice⁠(opens in a new window)”, Phys. Rev. D 25, 2649 (1982)

R. Narayanan and H. Neuberger, “Chiral determinant as an overlap of two vacua⁠(opens in a new window)”, Nucl. Phys. B 412, 574–606 (1994)

M. Lüscher, “Abelian chiral gauge theories on the lattice with exact gauge invariance⁠(opens in a new window),” §2.4, Nucl. Phys. B 549, 295–334 (1999)

D. Kadoh and Y. Kikukawa, “A construction of the Glashow–Weinberg–Salam model on the lattice with exact gauge invariance⁠(opens in a new window)”, JHEP 05 (2008) 095

article_content_zh:
在我们科学博客的第一篇客座文章中，OpenAI 的访问科学家、物理学家 Nathaniel Craig 描述了他如何与 GPT-6 Astra 合作研究标准模型的候选晶格定义。克雷格领导着加州大学圣塔芭芭拉分校的粒子理论小组，并且是卡夫里理论物理研究所的永久成员。

粒子物理学的标准模型是一个非常成功的自然理论，描述了已知的基本粒子和四种基本力中的三种——强力、弱力和电磁力。该理论的成功取决于理论计算和实验之间在十八个数量级上的出色一致性，从氢21厘米无线电发射的低能量到大型强子对撞机碰撞的高能量。然而，尽管它在五十多年的存在中取得了所有的成功，但一个基本问题仍然存在：如何给整个理论一个非微扰的定义，一个不依赖于将其相互作用视为小修正的定义。在 10 月份借助 GPT-6 Astra 准备的预印本（在新窗口中打开）中，我提出了关于晶格（代表时空的网格）的候选定义。

我有一个解决这个问题的策略，但无法证明它在它需要涵盖的所有情况下都有效。阿斯特拉帮助将该策略转化为结构，并率先开发了详细的证明。为了解释我们所做的事情，从我们现有的标准模型描述中缺少的内容开始会有所帮助。

我们缺乏标准模型的定义是什么意思？量子力学和狭义相对论告诉我们标准模型中的粒子和力如何相互作用。不幸的是，我们还不知道如何直接根据这些相互作用做出完整的预测。相反，我们通常首先想象相互作用被关闭，这样电子就不再相互排斥。我们可以准确地解决这个问题，然后将交互作为一系列小的修正重新放回原处。当修正值逐渐变小时，一些项就可以给出非常精确的答案——例如，它使物理学家能够将电子磁性的强度预测到万亿分之一以内。这种方法称为微扰理论。

然而，标准模型的大部分丰富性超出了微扰理论的范围。以质子的质量为例：质子由三个夸克组成，但其质量主要来自夸克及其内部强载力胶子的运动和相互作用。如果关闭强力，质子就会完全分解，因此微扰理论对于理解质子质量的大小并无帮助。需要更强大的方法来非扰动地获取有关理论的信息，其中相互作用从一开始就存在，并且不被视为小修正。

对于连续时空中的完整标准模型，我们没有非微扰定义，甚至没有理解相互作用的理论在数学上是否得到了很好的定义。一个有前途的替代方案是将时空离散化为点网格，称为晶格。网格的间距定义了我们的理论可以解析的最短距离，研究有限网格使我们能够在给定的间距下给出理论的严格非微扰定义。它还使我们能够将理论放在计算机上，我们可以直接计算其预测，而无需诉诸微扰理论。这种被称为晶格场理论的方法在过去几十年中使我们对强力的理解取得了显着进展，包括从第一原理对质子质量的定量理解。

如果晶格场理论在强力方面如此成功，为什么我们没有将其扩展到整个标准模型的非微扰晶格定义呢？这里有一个关键的区别：标准模型是所谓的手性理论的一个例子。

手性理论是一种在空间反射下看起来不同的理论。想象一下镜子中的手套：左手手套的镜像是右手手套。如果您每种都有一个，镜像也会起作用，因此您收集的手套在空间反射下看起来是一样的。但如果你只有左手手套，镜子里的右手手套就不一样了。

这种旋性的概念延伸到标准模型中的许多基本粒子，即费米子，包括夸克和电子。标准模型中的大多数力都不是手性的：例如，强力和电磁力以相同的方式处理左手费米子和右手费米子。这样的理论可以更容易地放在一个格子上。

但标准模型的第三种基本力，即弱力，缺乏这种反射对称性。它以不同的方式对待左手费米子和右手费米子，因此在左右交换的镜面反射下看起来并不相同。这种对不同手性粒子的不同处理使得标准模型成为手性理论。事实证明，将手性理论置于晶格上是极具挑战性的。如果我们尝试在晶格上放置一个左手费米子，最自然的规则会给你一个你从未要求过的右手伙伴。这是一个令人惊讶的结果，我们将立即解开。不管是什么原因，这意味着标准模型的简单晶格公式给出了弱力的错误粒子含量。自该理论形成以来，加倍是标准模型完整的非微扰定义缺失的原因之一。

要理解倍增，请考虑与光的类比。光有两种偏振，这描述了光在空间中移动时电场的方向。 （如果您佩戴偏光太阳镜，这种情况很常见，偏光太阳镜会阻挡从水或道路反射的水平偏振光，同时让垂直偏振光透过。）虽然偏光太阳镜选择了水平和垂直偏振的基础，但对于我们的类比，选择这两种偏振为左圆和右圆的基础会更有用，这意味着电场围绕运动方向顺时针或逆时针旋转。正如我们所说，电磁学是反射对称的，因此其实际定律对于左圆偏振和右圆偏振都是相同的。 （对于技术性的人来说，当我们谈论费米子时，左和右指的是手性。在我们与光的类比中，它们指的是光子的螺旋性，它告诉我们它的自旋点是沿着还是反对它的行进方向。）

但想象一下，您想要模拟一个只有左旋光的世界，类似于弱相互作用挑选出左手费米子的方式。为了在实验室中研究这一点，您可以将产生左圆形光的激光器放入两端都有镜子的盒子中。当光线来回反射时，光线会逐渐增强，让你可以仔细研究它——有点像把标准模型放在格子上。在每种情况下，你都在限制理论的可访问长度尺度以获得控制——格子限制了最短的可访问距离，而盒子限制了最长的距离。

如果您使用普通镜子构建盒子（就像以最直接的方式将手性理论放在晶格上），您会感到惊讶：从激光器发出的左圆形光在从另一端的镜子反射时变成右圆形光，因此现在盒子包含两种偏振光。发生这种情况是因为镜子反转了光的方向，但没有改变电场的旋转方式（从盒子的同一端看到），从而翻转了偏振。这有点像将左手费米子放在晶格上时倍增器的外观。你只提供左手光，盒子提供另一只手光。

有一个巧妙的解决办法。您可以使用分子分层排列的特殊薄膜来制作手性镜。排列从一层到下一层稍微转动，沿着螺旋线向下进入薄膜。对于波长和旋向与螺旋相匹配的光，来自不同层的微小反射会相互增强，从而翻转反射回来的光中电场的旋转。薄膜将左手光发送回左手，并让右手光通过。这种手性镜子已经存在了十多年，这种现象甚至在自然界中也发生过：一些圣甲虫的闪亮外壳上有类似的螺旋。如果您使用手性镜构建盒子，那么沿两个方向传播的光将是左圆形。

author: OpenAI 官方动态
article_content:
We’re starting the OpenAI science blog to give scientists and academic researchers a place to share what they’re discovering with AI and how they’re doing the work. Our mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and accelerating scientific discovery is one of the most impactful ways we can work toward that goal.

Research and discoveries: New scientific results and updates on ongoing research from OpenAI, our collaborators, and the broader scientific community.

Methods and practical guidance: Examples of how scientists use our models for tasks such as scientific computing, data analysis, exploring literature, and planning experiments. We’ll share approaches others can adapt, including how to check the work and where a method falls short.

Perspectives from the scientific community: Firsthand accounts from researchers using AI, what they are learning, and how these capabilities are affecting their disciplines. We’ll also discuss open questions about scientific practice and how to make these tools useful to more people.

Science expands our understanding of the world and makes advances possible, from better medicines to new sources of energy. Many of those advances begin with fundamental questions whose practical significance becomes clear only years later.

In recent months, we’ve seen an expanding range of scientific problems our models can address. In September, an internal OpenAI system produced a proof addressing the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem⁠, a longstanding question about the equations describing fluid motion. In early October, we released a broad range of mathematical results⁠. Among them was a result on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis⁠(opens in a new window), with a result that sharpens estimates of how many prime numbers lie below a given number. Later that month, we shared results across mathematics, computer science, and physics⁠ concerning how waves concentrate, the limits of efficient computation, and the mathematical foundations of interlacing quantum field theory.

In biology, researchers are using AI to analyze complex datasets, connect findings across fields, and develop new hypotheses to test in the lab. Working with PerturbAI and Scripps Research⁠, thousands of agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind analyzed existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes. By connecting the effects of gene disruptions with scientific literature, they identified possible biological mechanisms for scientists to test. Researchers are also developing their own approaches: César de la Fuente’s team uses ChatGPT and Codex⁠ to build algorithms that identify potential antibiotic molecules, which they then make and test in the lab.

These capabilities bring new possibilities and changes to scientific practice. In mathematics, systems that generate proofs raise questions about how new arguments are checked, explained, and incorporated into the field. In experimental sciences, exploring more hypotheses creates opportunities — and challenges — in deciding which experiments to pursue. Across disciplines, researchers are considering what these tools mean for training, attribution, and the skills their work requires. The implications will differ by field, and scientific communities should help shape how these tools are used.

We hope this blog helps more people understand how AI is changing science and how they can use it to explore new questions and make discoveries of their own.

article_content_zh:
我们正在开设 OpenAI 科学博客，为科学家和学术研究人员提供一个分享他们在人工智能方面的发现以及他们如何开展工作的地方。我们的使命是确保通用人工智能造福全人类，而加速科学发现是我们实现这一目标的最有影响力的方式之一。

研究和发现：OpenAI、我们的合作者以及更广泛的科学界正在进行的研究的新科学成果和更新。

方法和实践指导：科学家如何使用我们的模型执行科学计算、数据分析、文献探索和规划实验等任务的示例。我们将分享其他人可以采用的方法，包括如何检查工作以及方法的不足之处。

科学界的观点：使用人工智能的研究人员的第一手资料，他们正在学习什么，以及这些能力如何影响他们的学科。我们还将讨论有关科学实践以及如何使这些工具对更多人有用的开放性问题。

科学扩大了我们对世界的了解，并使从更好的药物到新能源的进步成为可能。其中许多进展都是从基本问题开始的，其实际意义在几年后才变得清晰。

近几个月来，我们发现我们的模型可以解决越来越多的科学问题。 9 月，内部 OpenAI 系统提出了解决纳维-斯托克斯存在性和平滑性问题的证明，这是一个关于描述流体运动方程的长期存在的问题。十月初，我们发布了广泛的数学结果⁠。其中包括拟黎曼假设的结果⁠（在新窗口中打开），该结果使对有多少素数低于给定数字的估计更加清晰。当月晚些时候，我们分享了数学、计算机科学和物理学的成果，涉及波如何集中、有效计算的极限以及交错量子场论的数学基础。

在生物学领域，研究人员正在使用人工智能来分析复杂的数据集，连接跨领域的发现，并开发新的假设以在实验室中进行测试。与 PerturbAI 和 Scripps Research 合作，数千名由 GPT‑Rosalind 提供支持的代理在 32 分钟内分析了来自数百万小鼠脑细胞的现有实验数据。通过将基因破坏的影响与科学文献联系起来，他们确定了可能的生物学机制供科学家测试。研究人员也在开发自己的方法：César de la Fuente 的团队使用 ChatGPT 和 Codex⁠ 构建识别潜在抗生素分子的算法，然后在实验室中进行制造和测试。

这些能力给科学实践带来了新的可能性和变化。在数学中，生成证明的系统提出了如何检查、解释新论点并将其纳入该领域的问题。在实验科学中，探索更多的假设为决定进行哪些实验创造了机遇和挑战。跨学科的研究人员正在考虑这些工具对于培训、归因以及工作所需技能意味着什么。不同领域的影响会有所不同，科学界应该帮助塑造这些工具的使用方式。

我们希望这个博客可以帮助更多的人了解人工智能如何改变科学，以及如何利用它来探索新问题并做出自己的发现。

article_content:
1 of 2 | Foto tomada de video de TVBS que muestra a Alice Huang en una cena organizada por Jensen Huang, CEO de Nvidia, en un restaurante en Taipéi, Taiwán, el 22 de mayo del 2025. (TVBS via AP)

Foto tomada de video de TVBS que muestra a Alice Huang en una cena organizada por Jensen Huang, CEO de Nvidia, en un restaurante en Taipéi, Taiwán, el 22 de mayo del 2025. (TVBS via AP)

Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.

Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.

“The company has retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation,” it said in an emailed statement.

Alice Huang “left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company,” the statement said. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters.”

A customer and cloud partner of Nvidia, Megaspeed has faced scrutiny in recent months, including from U.S. authorities, over allegations that it circumvented U.S. export restrictions to route large quantities of advanced chips to Chinese companies. Last December, it said there was “no evidence” of illicit chip transfers.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that “it doesn’t matter to me” whether Alice Huang is a spy. He said his concern is “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the U.S. export restrictions” or not.

“Jensen’s foibles are his foibles. Obviously, it’s a problem if in fact he was having relationships with subordinates,” Bessent said in an appearance on Fox News Channel’s “Sunday Morning Futures.” “I want to keep coming back to: ‘What was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?’”

Bessent blames Lutnick’s Commerce Department for not restricting Nvidia chip exports 4 MIN READ 161 Bessent moves to a military base over safety concerns, an AP source says 1 MIN READ 352 Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calls for more balanced US-China trade ties ahead of Trump-Xi talks 1 MIN READ 18 Bessent said the Nvidia board of directors should look outside the company for a new CEO because “they need a dramatic shake-up.”

Singapore’s government said Thursday that it initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in February 2025, including possible “false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers.”

Authorities also investigated Alice Huang, whom the government identified as Megaspeed’s then-CEO, chairperson and one of its key controllers.

Singapore authorities questioned her and withheld her passport last year. They later concluded there was insufficient evidence that she had committed a crime, despite suspecting she had provided “inaccurate” information to downplay her role at the company.

An earlier New York Times report suggested U.S. officials believed Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its advanced chips more available to China.

As scrutiny intensified and reports of her romantic relationship with Jensen Huang gained attention, Nvidia announced Thursday that he was stepping down as CEO.

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday, however, that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, President Donald Trump said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”

Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated.

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.

By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.

Despite those public records, short seller Culper Research cited a Megaspeed employee in a report released this May as saying Alice Huang was “actually still our boss” and remained involved in daily operations.

The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3 billion.

In a separate statement Thursday issued under James Tan’s name, Megaspeed said it takes its obligations under U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously.”

The company said it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security and was ready to cooperate fully with other relevant U.S. authorities.

总部位于新加坡的云计算公司 Megaspeed International 周日表示，中国女商人爱丽丝·黄 (Alice Huang) 去年离开了该公司，她与英伟达前首席执行官黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 的关系引发了美国国家安全担忧。

Megaspeed 因涉嫌向中国公司转让先进的 Nvidia 芯片而受到审查，该公司还宣布了一项由外部律师牵头的内部调查。

该公司在一份电子邮件声明中表示：“该公司已聘请外部法律顾问进行彻底的内部调查。”

声明称，Alice Huang“自 2025 年 8 月 30 日起离开 Megaspeed，目前在该公司没有任何职位”。 “Megaspeed不对黄女士的个人和私人事务发表评论。”

作为 Nvidia 的客户和云合作伙伴，Megaspeed 近几个月受到包括美国当局在内的审查，原因是该公司被指控规避美国出口限制，向中国公司输送大量先进芯片。去年 12 月，该公司表示“没有证据”表明存在非法芯片转移。

美国财政部长斯科特·贝森特周日表示，爱丽丝·黄是否是间谍“对我来说并不重要”。他表示，他担心的是“英伟达是否有遵守美国出口限制的文化”。

“詹森的缺点就是他的缺点。显然，如果他实际上与下属有关系，那就是一个问题，”贝森特在福克斯新闻频道的“周日早间期货”节目中说道。 “我想继续回想：‘英伟达的文化是什么，他们是否通过这些看似非法的销售来增加收入和收益？’”

Bessent 指责 Lutnick 的商务部不限制 Nvidia 芯片出口 4 MIN READ 161 美联社消息人士称，Bessent 出于安全考虑而迁往军事基地 1 MIN READ 352 财政部长斯科特·贝森特 (Scott Bessent) 呼吁在特朗普与习近平会谈之前建立更加平衡的美中贸易关系 1 MIN READ 18 Bessent 表示 Nvidia 董事会应该在公司外部寻找新首席执行官，因为“他们需要一场戏剧性的变革。”

新加坡政府周四表示，已于 2025 年 2 月启动了对 Megaspeed 的调查，其中包括可能存在“与购买服务器有关的虚假声明”。

当局还调查了 Alice Huang，政府认定她是 Megaspeed 时任首席执行官、董事长兼关键控制人之一。

新加坡当局去年对她进行了讯问并扣押了她的护照。他们后来得出结论，没有足够的证据表明她犯罪，尽管怀疑她提供了“不准确”的信息来淡化她在公司的角色。

《纽约时报》早些时候的一篇报道暗示，美国官员认为爱丽丝·黄是一名中国间谍，被招募来可能影响英伟达，使其更容易为中国提供其先进芯片。

title: Sources: Jensen Huang has discussed a comeback as Nvidia CEO with confidants, as allies form a "war room" to lobby for his return and seek White House support (Financial Times)
title_en: Sources: Jensen Huang has discussed a comeback as Nvidia CEO with confidants, as allies form a "war room" to lobby for his return and seek White House support (Financial Times)
author: Financial Times
article_content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the chipmaker "absolutely must" work with Chinese AI companies on monitoring risks around the "potentially dangerous" technology.

"We absolutely should work with each other so that we advance the technology safely," he told CNBC during a media briefing on Wednesday evening in London.

Discussions around AI safety have intensified in recent months, after researchers from AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic called for a slowdown in developing the tech and warned of existential risks to humanity.

While OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei have called for greater regulation, Huang has emerged as a prominent voice in opposition to that view.

Huang said that "dialogue" was the way to work with Chinese AI companies, adding that he has "dialogues with many of the researchers in China."

"We ought to enhance the dialogue," he added. "The United States should do it... I advocated that the U.K. do the same thing."

AI safety has become a key topic between the U.S. and Chinese governments, with both countries weighing how to address the risks posed by the rapidly advancing tech.

Prior to U.S. President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed the prospect of a "U.S.-China AI dialogue" with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, in September, including a channel for incidents "up to a national security level."

A Chinese readout of the meeting said President Xi pointed out that China and the U.S. "may have competition, but they may cooperate even more" in AI. "The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI," Xi said, per the readout.

Huang said that the U.K. is in a position "in the world to be able to be a convener of many of these dialogues" related to AI, because of the country's "intellectual capital."

Discussions around AI safety have intensified in recent months, after researchers from AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic called for a slowdown in developing the tech and warned of existential risks to humanity.

While OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei have called for greater regulation, Huang has emerged as a prominent voice in opposition to that view.

Huang said that "dialogue" was the way to work with Chinese AI companies, adding that he has "dialogues with many of the researchers in China."

"We ought to enhance the dialogue," he added. "The United States should do it... I advocated that the U.K. do the same thing."

AI safety has become a key topic between the U.S. and Chinese governments, with both countries weighing how to address the risks posed by the rapidly advancing tech.

Prior to U.S. President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed the prospect of a "U.S.-China AI dialogue" with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, in September, including a channel for incidents "up to a national security level."

A Chinese readout of the meeting said President Xi pointed out that China and the U.S. "may have competition, but they may cooperate even more" in AI. "The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI," Xi said, per the readout.

Huang said that the U.K. is in a position "in the world to be able to be a convener of many of these dialogues" related to AI, because of the country's "intellectual capital."

article_content_zh:
英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋表示，该芯片制造商“绝对必须”与中国人工智能公司合作，监控“潜在危险”技术的风险。

周三晚上在伦敦举行的媒体吹风会上，他对 CNBC 表示：“我们绝对应该相互合作，以便安全地推进技术。”

近几个月来，在 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 等人工智能实验室的研究人员呼吁放慢技术开发速度并警告人类面临生存风险之后，围绕人工智能安全的讨论愈演愈烈。

尽管 OpenAI 的 Sam Altman 和 Anthropic 的 Dario Amodei 呼吁加强监管，但黄仁勋已成为反对这一观点的重要声音。

黄说，“对话”是与中国人工智能公司合作的方式，并补充说他“与中国的许多研究人员进行了对话”。

“我们应该加强对话，”他补充道。 “美国应该这样做……我主张英国也这样做。”

人工智能安全已成为美国和中国政府之间的一个关键话题，两国都在权衡如何应对快速发展的技术带来的风险。

在美国总统唐纳德·特朗普与中国国家主席习近平会晤之前，美国财政部长斯科特·贝森特 (Scott Bessent) 于 9 月与中国财政部长何立峰讨论了“美中人工智能对话”的前景，其中包括“国家安全级别”事件的沟通渠道。

会议的中方宣读称，习近平主席指出，中美在人工智能领域“可能存在竞争，但可能有更多合作”。习近平表示，“双方可以继续就人工智能问题开展对话，就人工智能的风险和收益交换意见，共同防止人工智能的误用和滥用。”

黄说，由于英国拥有“智力资本”，英国在“世界上能够成为与人工智能相关的许多此类对话的召集者”。
