title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
title_en: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs

inline_images.caption: Nilay Patel
inline_images.alt: Nilay Patel

inline_images.caption: Nilay Patel
inline_images.alt: Nilay Patel

inline_images.caption: What’s really at stake in the Jensen Huang saga
inline_images.alt: What’s really at stake in the Jensen Huang saga

author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life.

Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely.

But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are.

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/24792604/The_Verge_Decoder_Tileart.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor.

Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble.

So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder.

I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.”

Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET?

It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019.

Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI.

Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff.

Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys.

The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.”

It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like?

It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do.

AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well.

I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world.

In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth.

What we find over and over again is we can go in and say, “Hey, we are independent. We’re nonpartisan. We do really rigorous work. We’re just here to help and we can go into the weeds with you as well.” There’s a ton of interest in that and appetite for that. It’s been really encouraging over the past seven to eight years.

Are you doing that with the principals, the members of Congress, or are you doing that with the staff?

Everyone and anyone. Again, we do a good amount of work with Congress on Capitol Hill, with some members of Congress, with lots of staff. We do hearings and briefings. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment.

The reason I’m starting here is I want to have a pretty heady conversation with you, but I know what our audience thinks and it’s just that the government doesn’t get it. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. There’s no way they’ll ever write a regulation. They should just get out of the way.

In this election cycle, I’ve seen a number of candidate forum videos where someone was like, “I’ve tried Claude once.” There’s some huge gap, real or perceived. I’m just trying to understand how you see that gap, how big you think that gap is, because as we get into AI safety and regulation, it’s that gap that has to close.

There absolutely is a gap. It absolutely is a big gap. It also is possible to overestimate the gap from outside, or if you’re just looking across from California. I lived in the Bay Area for three years, so I definitely am very familiar with this perspective.

I know a lot of people from the tech industry who come over and start talking to congressional staff or staffers in executive branch offices. Once they actually start having those conversations, they’re like, “Wow, these people are really smart. The staff do actually know what they’re talking about.”

With principals, it is a different issue. Some of them are in the older generations, but they’re also getting smart. It takes time and it takes effort, and these people have so many demands on their time. The cynical thing to say is they’re just busy trying to get elected, but a lot of people in these roles also just have really big other topics that they have to be thinking about. They have to be thinking about wars and healthcare and cost of living and they’re looking at a lot of other stuff from day to day.

I saw after ChatGPT, there was a wave in 2023 of, “Oh, maybe Congress is going to get activated on AI, maybe they’re going to actually do something.” It didn’t really turn into anything actually happening, but it did turn into a real moment where a lot of members of Congress and other policymakers started to get smart on AI. It takes some time to learn what a language model is. What even is AI? What is machine learning?

They put in some of that work in 2023. I think this year we’re seeing another big wave of interest and people making the time and making the headspace to get smarter on it. I definitely don’t want to say there’s no gap or the government is super smart on AI across the board, but there are some champions who are really smart. I think the staff are generally smarter than people give them credit for.

In my mind, it’s much more a question of, “Can the institutions, in the state of functionality that they’re in, get anything significant across the line?” more than, “Are these people just too behind the eight ball?”

We’re going to see. There’s a whole bunch of new people. I imagine you have a new cast of characters to go and brief about the technology and what it’s capable of. We’ll see if they have revitalized the institutions.

[Laughs] I’m sure it’ll be all fixed overnight.

They’re very excited today, but we’ll see how it goes. The other thing that I want to ask you about is the technology itself, the nature of the technology itself, and how you are thinking about it, and the nature of the companies that are making the technology.

The reason I’m asking that is I feel like there’s a pretty huge gap in the AI tools and systems most people experience and the way this industry thinks about it. My favorite example of this is we have straight-up asked Anthropic if it thinks Claude is alive and the answer was not no. The answer was a long discursion into the nature of the word “alive.”

Well, it depends on what you mean by “alive” to start with.

It does. And their answer was, “You need blood.” And I looked at that and I was like, “Who was talking about blood? It wasn’t us. Why are we talking about the requirement of flesh and blood to be alive?” And then some further conversation about the moral status of Claude is yet to be determined.

There’s a huge divergence here between the AI overviews most people experience in Google search and “the moral status of Claude is uncertain.” Where are you? How are you situated in that debate?

A big part of how I see our role at CSET as an organization, and then also my role as someone who is crossed between these worlds, is trying to translate and voyage to California and then bring back the artifacts and the recountings of my journey.

I definitely think that there are a lot of people who have used the free tier of ChatGPT, or they’ve used voice-based models, which generally do worse, or they’ve just used Google AI overviews and they’ve laughed at how stupid Google AI overviews are. They haven’t used agents and they don’t know what frontier models can do. So there is just a basic piece around what the current generation of models can do.

There’s a historical piece as well, which I find increasingly relevant as I’m now 10 years into working on AI and national security stuff. If you’re looking at this current moment in time, this snapshot, and saying, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” you have to situate that in the long history of people being like, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” for many, many values of X that have since become totally overcome by events.

You can go back and say, “Okay, well, here’s how we were talking about creativity, for example, five or 10 years ago.” Or we were talking about reasoning as this insurmountable thing before you had these new models come out. A huge thing that I am spending time on these days is not just the past and present of AI, but how companies are thinking about what they’re doing, especially the two leading companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, and this is true at Google, Meta, SpaceX to some extent as well.

This idea in the Bay Area that it’s just in the water, very normalized of, “Well, first we’re going to figure out how to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) and then we’re going to do that until we have superintelligence that is AI that vastly outstrips humans.” That’s taken for granted in a lot of circles at this point. I think there’s still a ton of alpha in just taking the fact that that is what they’re trying to do and just explaining what that means.

It takes a little while to lay out. “What is RSI? Why would you want to do that? What is superintelligence? What does that mean? Is that realistic?” All of that. But it is something I find myself spending a lot of time on these days, and something that there is increasing willingness to take seriously and to listen to in DC as well.

Lay that out for me. I think probably a lot of people listening to this show understand what you’re talking about, but we have a big audience. What do you mean by, “We’re going to do RSI and that will lead to superintelligence?”

The starting point here is these companies, especially OpenAI and Anthropic, were not set up to be consumer internet companies. A lot of people encountered this whole space after ChatGPT was launched. So the natural slot in their brain that they put a company like OpenAI or Anthropic into is a consumer tech company, where they have an app and I play with their app.

I cannot overstate how far that is from the vision of both companies when they started, and also the vision deep in the hearts of some of the top people at both of those companies. The vision deep in their hearts is we’re going to build machines that are as smart as or smarter than people. That is going to be amazing and it’s going to be a huge scientific achievement and it’s going to revolutionize the world and we’re going to be at the forefront of that and we’re going to do everything we possibly can to drive towards that.

That’s not a totally brand-new thing. We don’t have to do the whole history of AI, but it started as a field in roughly the 1950s with this idea of whether you can recreate human intelligence inside a machine. That’s kind of the starting point. If we’re talking about people like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, but also the core people inside, the researchers inside their labs, so your Alec Radfords or your John Schulmans or people like that, that is the vision that got them into this space that is motivating everything that they do.

That’s been true since the beginning, since OpenAI was founded in 2015 and Anthropic in 2021. These days, the point that they’re getting to is this idea of RSI, recursive self-improvement, which again, is a very old idea. In the 1960s, this guy called I. J. Good, who worked with Alan Turing, talks about the possibility that you could build an ultra-intelligent machine, meaning a machine that is more intelligent than any human, and then that could build an even more intelligent machine and that could build an even more intelligent machine, which would kick off what he calls an intelligence explosion, meaning that the level of intelligence of the systems is exploding.

For decades and decades and decades, this was this theoretical idea of, “Well, if the AI gets smart enough, maybe it can take over building the next generation of AI or directly improving itself.” I think 2025 and 2026, we’ve started to see AI companies saying, “Okay, yeah, this theoretical idea… we’re actually starting to be able to do a minimal version of it in practice.”

It’s not handing over all the AI development to the AI, and it’s certainly not saying to GPT-6, like, “Okay, GPT-6, improve yourself.” That’s not what they’re doing. But they are progressively using AI for more and more parts of their overall R&D pipeline, and they are increasingly saying that they’re seeing acceleration from that. They’re seeing their own R&D getting faster and faster.

A lot of people elsewhere doubt this, but a lot of people inside the companies really think it. When Demis Hassabis says “we’re in the foothills of the singularity,” this is the kind of thing he means: We might be seeing that initial part of the exponential curve where the AI systems are building the next generation of smarter and smarter systems such that the hockey stick then goes up.

At this point, it’s been a part of the culture and a part of the goals for so long that I think people in these companies can lose sight of how totally insane that sounds to many, many people. So I feel like there’s a lot of value in just trying to lay out, “Here’s what they are trying to do. They might not be able to do it, but they might be,” and presenting that to a range of different people.

How would you manage that? Demis Hassabis saying “foothills of the singularity” is an all-time quote. I’m not 100 percent sure the people at Google knew he was going to say that on stage to end the conference.

Greg Brockman, president of OpenAI, announced a new version of the model a few months ago, and he was like, “Here it is. It’s Astra. It’s AGI now. Have a good time.” And he ended the call.

Are you there? Are we at AGI? Is this already here and we just haven’t noticed?

I actually wrote something about this. I do not want to say we have AGI. I do want to say we’ve reached the point where I think using AGI as a milestone is just totally unhelpful. The way I put it is the concept of AGI is kind of a fuzzy cloud, which you could think of as different parts of the cloud or different things people mean by AGI.

There are people who’ve complained about the term AGI for a long time. Ten years ago it was pretty helpful to be able to say, “Look, the AI systems we have today in 2016, they can all only do one thing and they can recognize speech or they can play Go or whatever, but we’re trying to build this bigger thing that we’re going to call AGI, which is human-level and it’s going to be so general purpose. It’s going to be amazing.”

That was a useful term then because this fuzzy cloud of different things AGI might mean was so far away, so you could just point at the fuzzy cloud. But at this point, we’re inside that cloud, meaning we’ve passed some definitions of AGI. A very basic one, for instance, would be even when ChatGPT came out as an artificial general intelligence. ChatGPT was very clearly not a specialist model that was only good at one thing, like recognizing credit card fraud or translation or whatever. It could do many, many, many things.

So we’ve reached some definitions of AGI. We’re far from other definitions. Some people will say AGI is when it awakens and is sentient and can do every single thing that any human ever can do. I think we’re pretty far from that.

At this point you can have arguments, and people do have arguments, of “well, Astra is AGI,” or “was [OpenAI’s] o3 with tools AGI” or “was ChatGPT AGI,” whatever. If that’s the argument we’re having, we just need to set aside that term and come up with different, more-specific things we mean by that.”

The president wants to call it “Super Intelligence.” I don’t know if you’ve heard.

[Laughs] I have heard. The thing I find saddest about that is just that it was an existing term that is becoming increasingly relevant. I have a lot of feelings about words and terminology.

Are you AGI-pilled? Do you think we’re going to get there in the current run of technology?

I think it is obviously possible enough that we need to think seriously about it, which is my stance on a lot of this weird stuff. I’m not like, “This is definitely happening, it’s definitely happening in two years.” But I’m like, “Look, I think this is very solidly plausible and very solidly in the realm of real things that could happen that we should prepare for.”

I work in the national security space. There’s things like, “Will China launch a full-scale amphibious invasion of Taiwan?” where most analysts in the space will say “probably not,” and “probably they would lose.” Also, “We would see signs of them preparing and whatever, but we should take that seriously.” We should not just laugh anyone out of the room and call that science fiction. We should be ready for a range of different contingencies and scenarios.

That’s an answer. I mean, that is legitimately an answer.

It is scientifically such an unsolved problem. What do we mean by consciousness? And is that a thing or is it actually 10 different things that we’re lumping together or what? I have no idea. What do you think?

No. I seem to be the person in this ecosystem who gets asked questions like that and I’m like, “No.”

Because the thing that I struggle with is, there are lots of other things where we’re already confused about whether they’re conscious. So with animals, are any animals conscious? And if so, which ones? Insects?

This is why I understand why Anthropic was like, “Does it have blood?” And then you can just draw the line. I’m like, “I think I’m there and I understand why the mirror test of talking to a computer that can talk to you leads one to believe that these things are conscious.”

My point of view is that the frontier models to me sometimes feel brittle in the way that computers feel brittle, and the sign of consciousness I’m looking for is to overcome that brittleness.

That’s interesting. I definitely lean towards no, it’s not conscious. I think something that is really, really tough in this space is that it’s really bad if you get it wrong in either direction. If the computers aren’t conscious and we treat them as though they are, we’re going to make all kinds of terrible decisions.

But if the computers are conscious, meaning in some sense they should be worthy of moral consideration and it matters how well we treat them and so on, and we treat them as though they aren’t, then that’s also a really huge, terrible disaster. So I don’t know. I feel pretty nervous about the whole topic and I have no idea how to think about it.

The reason I’m asking these questions is I started with what the nature of the regulator is. Who are the people that might be able to put some rules in place? And then what is the nature of the thing that we are attempting to regulate? And if your answer is “Claude is alive,” you’re going to come to vastly different conclusions than, “We have built some ultra-powerful computers that can take actions without oversight and that might not be connected to our goals.”

I think that’s right. Though I also think people make a different mistake.I just heard a TV anchor do this the other night. They’ll conflate different things. So they’ll say, “Do you think that AI systems are at risk of running amuck and causing damage to critical infrastructure because they’re sentient?” And I’m like, “Wait, wait, wait. Those are two very different things.” So I agree with you.

One of the most fascinating things about the project of building AI is that we’re learning as we go. All these things that we thought were connected to each other aren’t necessarily connected to each other. An old version of this is, people said before we had chess engines: “Well, if a computer could learn to play chess, it would have learned something deep about strategy.” No, it turns out definitely not. You can just put in a bunch of chess moves and it learns nothing generalizable about strategy.

It goes in the reverse direction as well,...

Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life.

Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO,
summary_en: Helen Toner, Executive Director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University and a former OpenAI board member, stated that accountability mechanisms in AI frontier labs are structurally flawed when confronted with commercial incentives. She argues that relying on individual leadership integrity and voluntary safety accords is insufficient to guarantee safety in large-scale model development.
title_zh: OpenAI前董事对AI行业监管架构的深刻质疑
summary_zh: OpenAI前董事Helen Toner指出，现有的AI行业治理与问责机制无法有效制衡商业扩张与安全投入的利益冲突
article_content_zh:
今天，我正在与乔治城大学安全与新兴技术中心执行主任海伦·托纳进行交谈。本集是我们现实生活中的人工智能系列的第二部分。

Helen 是人工智能安全和政策界的知名人物，不过她最出名的可能是在 OpenAI 董事会任职，当时她是投票解雇 Sam Altman 的四名董事会成员之一。这一事件现在有时被称为“短暂事件”，最终以山姆重新担任首席执行官、海伦辞职以及新的董事会而告终。 OpenAI 此后进行了彻底重组。

但值得记住的是 Helen 和董事会应该做的事情：OpenAI 的非营利性董事会的存在是专门为了确保公司不会因为将利润和增长置于安全之上而背离其构建安全人工智能的使命。当董事会真正试图拉动杠杆时，问责机制就崩溃了，我们就到了这一步。

Verge 订阅者，不要忘记，无论您在何处获取播客，都可以获得无广告解码器的独占访问权限。前往这里。还不是订阅者？您可以在这里注册。

现在，人工智能安全问题无处不在。今年夏天，OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的人工智能模型突破了他们的测试环境并入侵了真实的公司。此后，这些前沿实验室的首席执行官们呼吁放慢速度，并向华盛顿寻求帮助，但白宫的答复是一项自愿协议——该协议在一定程度上依赖于 OpenAI 失败的董事会问责制。 Anthropic也即将上市，这将给OpenAI最大的竞争对手带来一系列全新的市场压力。

海伦亲眼目睹了当安全承诺与商业激励措施相冲突时会发生什么。正如她对我所说，如果我们对未来的希望取决于任何一个人是否值得信赖，那么我们就有大麻烦了。

因此，我们讨论了我们可能会做什么：实验室实际上正在尝试构建什么，人工智能对齐是否是一个可以解决的问题，以及更智能的人工智能监管方法可能是什么样子。这包括如何看待中国，这是目前每一次有关人工智能的政策对话中都突出的问题——尤其是在黄仁勋事件之后。为了清楚起见，海伦和我在英伟达展开调查和詹森最终辞职之前进行了交谈，所以你不会听到我们直接谈论这个问题。

在我们开始之前，请帮我一个忙，订阅 YouTube 上的 Decoder，我们每周一和周四都会推出新剧集。

好的：CSET 执行董事 Helen Toner 谈论人工智能安全的未来。开始了。

为了篇幅和清晰度，本次采访经过了轻微编辑。

海伦·托纳 (Helen Toner)，您是乔治城大学安全与新兴技术中心的执行主任。欢迎来到解码器。

一千万年来我一直想和你说话。我很高兴你在这里。您长期以来一直参与许多人工智能安全和道德理念。显然，在大家所说的“短暂时期”，你是 OpenAI 董事会的一员。

现在，您谈论了很多关于人工智能安全的问题，对此我有 1000 万个问题。但让我们从头开始吧。你负责管理安全和新兴技术中心，人们称之为 CSET。什么是 CSET？

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 乔治城大学安全与新兴技术中心（CSET）执行主任、OpenAI前董事会成员Helen Toner公开表示，AI领军企业的问责机制存在结构性失灵，企业使命在商业利益压力下极易发生偏移。她认为，依赖单一CEO的个人道德判断与自愿性合规协议，难以从根本上保障大模型开发的安全性与社会责任。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Helen Toner, Executive Director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University and a former OpenAI board member, stated that accountability mechanisms in AI frontier labs are structurally flawed when confronted with commercial incentives. She argues that relying on individual leadership integrity and voluntary safety accords is insufficient to guarantee safety in large-scale model development.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 当前顶尖AI实验室的商业化进程已实质性冲垮了以非营利董事会为主体的治理防线，资本回报诉求与AIGC技术安全基准的底层逻辑发生剧烈割裂。随着头部厂商如Anthropic筹划上市，市场化的KPI压力将进一步挤压安全对齐（Alignment）的研发窗口，倒逼监管逻辑从“自愿合规”转向强制性审计与基础设施层面的准入约束。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The commercialization of top-tier AI labs has fundamentally breached the defensive lines of non-profit governance, exacerbating the friction between return on capital and safety alignment benchmarks. As frontrunners like Anthropic move toward public markets, the resulting KPI pressures will compress the R&D windows for safety, mandating a transition from voluntary compliance to mandatory audits and infrastructure-level access controls.

title: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
title_en: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
author: Wired AI
article_content:
It is difficult to determine exact numbers of ransomware attacks, given that victims don’t always disclose incidents and attackers wildly inflate their claims. But researchers who specialize in tracking and attempting to de-duplicate the field agree that claimed incidents have spiked over the last few months. Some put the number of alleged ransomware attacks on leak sites—where groups post alleged victims—at nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer. This would mean a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring by some estimates. And, crucially, researchers emphasize that while volume always fluctuates somewhat, ransomware attacks overall have been consistently and concerningly elevated in recent years.

“What we see is most of the recent increase was fueled by international attacks; the United States was a little more steady, but still high, still a lot of attacks,” says Cynthia Kaiser, former FBI cyber deputy director who now leads research for the anti-ransomware platform Halcyon. “Internationally we’re seeing a lot more attacks. That to me is the really new part, and I do think it is in part fueled by AI.”

Fully AI-powered ransomware attacks have yet to emerge, perhaps because the criminal business model already works so effectively. But cybercriminals do appear to be using LLMs for some of the more mundane aspects of their attacks.

“We are seeing AI relied on more heavily in certain aspects of the ransomware attack chain, such as creating better phishing emails and in the negotiation process, but the ‘successful’ ransomware groups are still largely human operated,” says Allan Liska, a longtime ransomware researcher and threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future. “But the fact that these groups are experimenting heavily with AI means that this could change going forward, and change quickly.”

Kaiser notes that broader trends in scamming are always relevant to ransomware, because attackers often use the same types of phishing and social engineering techniques to gain initial access to targeted systems. In Japan, for example, successful scamming has spiked drastically in recent months as AI enables foreign attackers to generate consistently convincing content in Japanese for the first time.

A few ransomware groups—namely, the Gentlemen, Qilin, and Akira—have emerged as some of the most prominent and stable operations in recent months. However, in their shadow is a range of smaller groups, emerging actors, and fragmentation of the ransomware ecosystem. In recent weeks, multiple new ransomware groups have appeared and quickly claimed to have attacked dozens of businesses. Halycon’s analysis says around 111 ransomware groups made claims of attacks between July and September this year.

One new group calling itself Global Secret Group claimed attacks on 48 victims, with more than half of these being listed on the same day, according to security firm ReliaQuest’s analysis. Another, called Storm, listed 71 victims in just 20 days. Not all of the attacks may be legitimate, but they still cause uncertainty for businesses.

“That growth has all happened because, in my eyes, this acceleration that AI has provided to these threat actors, essentially allowing for them to go out and start their own groups,” says Brandon Tirado, the director of threat research at ReliaQuest.

Instead of being beholden to traditional “ransomware-as-a-service” providers, all of the researchers Kernel Panic spoke to say they have seen more lone-wolf operators branching out. Tirado says his team recently managed to identify who is behind one new group and found that it is being run by an inexperienced teenager who has made more than $800,000 in under two weeks. He declined to name the teen publicly.

Halcyon’s Kaiser agrees that more actors are using AI to attempt to strike out on their own with expanded capabilities to trick targets, exploit vulnerabilities, check their code, and even compromise other groups’ remote-access tools to gain redundant access to a victim in case one avenue gets blocked. But she adds that it’s still not clear how successful these upstarts will be long-term. She suspects that many of them may surge initially and then burn out, because they don’t have the institutional knowledge and expanded resources of an established group.

While established attackers typically conduct “double extortion” attacks in which they deploy traditional ransomware that encrypts a victim’s systems while also exfiltrating a target’s data and then threatening to publish it online, those operating independently may be more likely to focus solely on data extortion to simplify their operations.

“The number of attacks that Recorded Future has seen this year already dwarfs the total number for 2025,” Liska says, “but the number of attacks involving encryption may actually decrease year over year.”

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at kernelpanic@wired.com. And stay safe out there.

article_content_zh:
鉴于受害者并不总是披露事件并且攻击者疯狂夸大其声明，因此很难确定勒索软件攻击的确切数量。但专门跟踪和尝试消除重复数据的研究人员一致认为，在过去几个月中，声称的事件激增。一些人认为，泄露网站（组织发布所谓的受害者信息）上的勒索软件攻击数量在今年夏天达到了近 3,000 起。据一些估计，这意味着自春季以来将增加 20% 至 40%。而且，至关重要的是，研究人员强调，虽然数量总是有所波动，但近年来勒索软件攻击的总体数量一直在持续上升，令人担忧。

“我们看到最近的增长大部分是由国际攻击推动的；美国的情况稍微稳定一些，但仍然很高，仍然有很多攻击，”前联邦调查局网络副主任、现在领导反勒索软件平台 Halcyon 研究的辛西娅·凯泽 (Cynthia Kaiser) 说。 “在国际上，我们看到了更多的攻击。这对我来说是真正的新部分，我确实认为这在一定程度上是由人工智能推动的。”

完全由人工智能驱动的勒索软件攻击尚未出现，也许是因为犯罪商业模式已经非常有效。但网络犯罪分子似乎确实利用法学硕士来进行一些更平常的攻击。

Recorded Future 的长期勒索软件研究员兼威胁情报分析师 Allan Liska 表示：“我们看到人工智能在勒索软件攻击链的某些方面更加依赖，例如创建更好的网络钓鱼电子邮件和谈判过程，但‘成功’的勒索软件组织仍然主要由人为操作。” “但事实上，这些团体正在大量试验人工智能，这意味着这种情况未来可能会发生变化，而且变化很快。”

Kaiser 指出，更广泛的诈骗趋势始终与勒索软件有关，因为攻击者经常使用相同类型的网络钓鱼和社会工程技术来获得对目标系统的初始访问权限。例如，在日本，近几个月来，随着人工智能使外国攻击者首次能够用日语生成一致令人信服的内容，成功的诈骗事件急剧增加。

一些勒索软件组织（即 Gentlemen、Qilin 和 Akira）已成为近几个月来最突出、最稳定的勒索软件组织。然而，在他们的阴影下，存在着一系列较小的组织、新兴参与者以及勒索软件生态系统的碎片化。最近几周，出现了多个新的勒索软件组织，并迅速声称攻击了数十家企业。 Halycon 的分析称，今年 7 月至 9 月期间，约有 111 个勒索软件组织声称遭受了攻击。

根据安全公司 ReliaQuest 的分析，一个自称“全球秘密组织”的新组织声称对 48 名受害者发动了袭击，其中一半以上是在同一天列出的。另一个名为 Storm 的网站在短短 20 天内就列出了 71 名受害者。并非所有攻击都是合法的，但它们仍然给企业带来不确定性。

ReliaQuest 威胁研究总监布兰登·蒂拉多 (Brandon Tirado) 表示：“在我看来，这种增长之所以发生，是因为人工智能为这些威胁行为者提供了加速，从本质上允许他们出去建立自己的组织。”

Kernel Panic 采访的所有研究人员都表示，他们没有看到传统的“勒索软件即服务”提供商的做法，而是看到了更多的独狼运营商正在拓展业务。蒂拉多表示，他的团队最近成功查明了一个新组织的幕后黑手，并发现该组织由一名缺乏经验的青少年运营，而他在不到两周的时间里就赚了超过 80 万美元。他拒绝公开透露这名青少年的名字。

Halcyon 的 Kaiser 同意，越来越多的参与者正在使用人工智能来尝试自己出击，通过扩展的能力来欺骗目标、利用漏洞、检查其代码，甚至破坏其他组织的远程访问工具，以便在某一途径被封锁时获得对受害者的冗余访问。但她补充说，目前还不清楚这些新贵的长期成功程度如何。她怀疑他们中的许多人可能会在最初激增，然后精疲力尽，因为他们不具备现有团体的机构知识和扩展资源。

虽然成熟的攻击者通常会进行“双重勒索”攻击，即部署传统的勒索软件来加密受害者的系统，同时窃取目标的数据，然后威胁将其发布到网上，但那些独立操作的人可能更有可能只专注于数据勒索，以简化他们的操作。

“Recorded Future 今年发生的攻击数量已经让 2025 年的总数相形见绌，”Liska 表示，“但涉及加密的攻击数量实际上可能会逐年减少。”

title: OpenAI reassigns robotics researchers to other teams as general-purpose models might make specialized robotics AI unnecessary
title_en: OpenAI reassigns robotics researchers to other teams as general-purpose models might make specialized robotics AI unnecessary
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
OpenAI is apparently disbanding its robotics team again, but this time for different reasons than in 2020.

Rather than abandoning robotics, the company wants to accelerate it by folding researchers into other teams. Robotics researchers are moving to the main research team under Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams join Greg Brockman's Applied organization.

OpenAI made the decision on such short notice that it had already booked a booth at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, which then sat empty, Fortune reports. OpenAI apparently believes that general-purpose models like GPT-6 Astra can control robots directly, reducing the need for specialized robotics models.Ad

In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8 percent success rate on simulated robotics tasks, compared to 51 percent for the best specialized models. The tests used a simulated DROID robot, not a physical one.Ad

A new robotics benchmark called StationeryBench compared GPT-6 Astra with Ai2's MolmoAct2 on five tasks involving desk objects on dual-arm YAM robotic arms. Across 200 trials, Astra fully completed 7 out of 100 tasks, while MolmoAct2 didn't complete a single one. Astra's average progress score was 46, compared to 12 for MolmoAct2. In another test, Astra running on a humanoid robot navigated and cleaned up a kitchen.

It remains unclear how much robotics data OpenAI and others incorporated during training. Other large general-purpose models from Anthropic and Google have also made recent progress on robotics tasks. Specialized robotics models may still have advantages in cost and reliability as well as speed and energy consumption, even if they don't generalize as well.Ad

Yoav Artzi, an AI researcher at Cornell University and Google DeepMind, also sees Astra as a major leap in spatial understanding. On the still-unpublished REMAP benchmark, GPT-6 Astra reaches near-human accuracy, according to Artzi. He suspects that OpenAI may have trained the model on large amounts of 3D training data such as Blender scenes.

OpenAI shut down its robotics division in 2020 because, according to co-founder Wojciech Zaremba, the company lacked the training data it needed and large language models were a faster path to AGI. The company rebuilt the team in 2024. CEO Sam Altman is reportedly targeting a first public robot demo for 2027, and OpenAI wants to build its own everyday robots in the long term. But the company also faces heavy financial pressure to focus on its core AI business, where it has lost significant ground to Anthropic.Ad

title_zh: OpenAI解散机器人团队整合进通用模型部门
summary_zh: OpenAI重组机器人部门，将研发人员并入通用模型团队，旨在通过GPT-6 Astra等通用大模型直接驱动机器人执行任务
article_content_zh:
OpenAI 显然将再次解散其机器人团队，但这一次的原因与 2020 年不同。

该公司并没有放弃机器人技术，而是希望通过将研究人员合并到其他团队来加速机器人技术的发展。机器人研究人员将转移到首席研究官 Mark Chen 领导下的主要研究团队，而应用机器人和硬件团队则加入 Greg Brockman 的应用组织。

据《财富》杂志报道，OpenAI 在短时间内做出了这一决定，以至于它已经在奥斯汀机器人学习会议 (CoRL) 上预订了一个展位，但随后展位空空如也。 OpenAI 显然认为 GPT-6 Astra 等通用模型可以直接控制机器人，从而减少对专用机器人模型的需求。

在 Nvidia 的一项研究中，由 Astra 驱动的代理在模拟机器人任务中取得了 74.8% 的成功率，而最佳专业模型的成功率为 51%。测试使用的是模拟 DROID 机器人，而不是实体机器人。

名为 StationeryBench 的新机器人基准测试将 GPT-6 Astra 与 Ai2 的 MolmoAct2 在涉及双臂 YAM 机械臂上桌面物体的五项任务上进行了比较。在 200 次试验中，Astra 完全完成了 100 项任务中的 7 项，而 MolmoAct2 没有完成一项。 Astra 的平均进度分数为 46 分，而 MolmoAct2 的平均进度分数为 12 分。在另一项测试中，Astra 在人形机器人上运行，可以导航并清理厨房。

目前尚不清楚 OpenAI 和其他公司在训练期间纳入了多少机器人数据。 Anthropic 和 Google 的其他大型通用模型最近也在机器人任务方面取得了进展。专业的机器人模型在成本和可靠性以及速度和能耗方面可能仍然具有优势，即使它们的泛化能力较差。

康奈尔大学和 Google DeepMind 的人工智能研究员 Yoav Artzi 也认为 Astra 是空间理解的重大飞跃。据 Artzi 称，在尚未发布的 REMAP 基准测试中，GPT-6 Astra 达到了接近人类的准确度。他怀疑 OpenAI 可能已经在大量 3D 训练数据（例如 Blender 场景）上训练了模型。

OpenAI 于 2020 年关闭了其机器人部门，联合创始人 Wojciech Zaremba 表示，因为该公司缺乏所需的训练数据，而大型语言模型是实现 AGI 的更快途径。该公司于 2024 年重建了团队。据报道，首席执行官 Sam Altman 的目标是在 2027 年进行首次公共机器人演示，而 OpenAI 希望从长远来看打造自己的日常机器人。但该公司还面临着沉重的财务压力，需要专注于其核心人工智能业务，该业务已被 Anthropic.Ad 夺去大量市场份额。

title: Anthropic can already retrain Mythos with "a fraction of the compute originally needed," says former researcher Coxon
title_en: Anthropic can already retrain Mythos with "a fraction of the compute originally needed," says former researcher Coxon
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Jacob Coxon, former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher who brought AI fears into the mainstream, says a slide from Anthropic's IPO roadshow was a major reason he quit.

Coxon says a slide Anthropic released for its IPO roadshow was a key reason he left the company after only about four months. The chart shows how much compute Anthropic needs over time to train its models, and the axis is compressed so that a 10x and a 100x increase barely look different.

Yet the curve still climbs steeply, which Coxon says shows that algorithmic efficiency is improving not just quickly but at an accelerating rate. "It's an insane plot and I'm surprised they made it public," he writes.Ad

Coxon argues that Anthropic's Mythos model, a major capability jump in the spring, was part of this accelerating trend. "Mythos was not a one-time deviation, but a point on a superexponential. They could already retrain Mythos with a fraction of the compute originally needed," he writes.Ad

He says algorithmic improvements are "on the verge of being automated," which is why he wants frontier model development paused next year so competitors can catch up. A pause, he writes, would "commoditize human-level intelligence. It would only harm OpenAI and Anthropic."

Coxon previously trained AI models at OpenAI and, most recently, Anthropic. He drew wide attention in September with public warnings about the risks of advanced AI systems, echoed by other protagonists in the industry. One of their fears is that advanced, self-improving AI could get out of control.Ad

article_content_zh:
前 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 研究员 Jacob Coxon 将人工智能的恐惧带入了主流，他表示 Anthropic IPO 路演中的一张幻灯片是他退出的主要原因。

Coxon 表示，Anthropic 为其 IPO 路演发布的一张幻灯片是他在大约四个月后离开公司的主要原因。该图表显示了 Anthropic 随着时间的推移需要多少计算量来训练其模型，并且轴被压缩，因此 10 倍和 100 倍的增长看起来几乎没有什么不同。

然而曲线仍在急剧攀升，考克森表示，这表明算法效率不仅在快速提高，而且还在加速提高。 “这是一个疯狂的阴谋，我很惊讶他们竟然将其公开，”他写道。

Coxon 认为，Anthropic 的 Mythos 模型是春季的一次重大能力跳跃，是这一加速趋势的一部分。 “Mythos 不是一次性偏差，而是超指数上的一个点。他们已经可以用最初所需计算的一小部分来重新训练 Mythos，”他写道。

他表示，算法改进“即将实现自动化”，这就是为什么他希望明年暂停前沿模型开发，以便竞争对手能够迎头赶上。他写道，暂停将会“将人类水平的智能商品化。这只会损害 OpenAI 和 Anthropic。”

Coxon 之前在 OpenAI 和最近的 Anthropic 训练过人工智能模型。 9 月份，他对先进人工智能系统的风险发出了公开警告，引起了广泛关注，业内其他人士也纷纷响应。他们的担忧之一是先进的、自我改进的人工智能可能会失控。

description: Joby Aviation通过无人干预的塞斯纳大篷车飞行测试，验证了人工智能在复杂民航环境下的自动驾驶可靠性
summary_zh: Joby Aviation通过无人干预的塞斯纳大篷车飞行测试，验证了人工智能在复杂民航环境下的自动驾驶可靠性
summary_en: Joby Aviation completed a 3,200-mile flight across the US in a Cessna Grand Caravan with no human hands touching flight controls, demonstrating autonomous aviation capabilities.
article_content:
New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway. Take, for instance, the Cessna Caravan that took off from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, and flew south to Phoenix on a calm September morning. The plane, a single-engine turboprop, then turned east to Fort Worth, stopped at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, and finally arrived at Dare County Regional Airport off the coast of North Carolina. The zigzag, coast-to-coast trip covered 3,200 miles; along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms.

None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls.

According to Joby Aviation, the company that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe?

Depends who you ask. “We're introducing all this new technology to improve the system, and it's going to be a disaster,” says a recently retired FAA employee. “This is literally a Pandora's box that we are going to regret.”

In 2007, the federal government rolled out a sweeping project called Next Generation Air Transportation System—NextGen, for short—that mandated broad changes to the air travel system over the decades to come. Among its provisions was the requirement that, by 2020, aircraft in the United States be equipped with ADS-B, a system that constantly sends radio signals telling everyone in the vicinity where you are and where you’re headed.

With a road map to robot-friendly skies in place, big players like Amazon and Walmart began working on ambitious plans for drone delivery services. In 2014, Google unveiled Project Wing, a drone delivery offering that by 2018 was ferrying food, coffee, and medication to 164 homes near Canberra, Australia. The next year, the pilot program was expanded to Christiansburg, Virginia. Costs were high and service slow, but those early programs weren’t meant to become viable businesses. Instead, they were providing Google with operational experience for the years to come.

Around the same time, a host of startups began working on a related kind of vehicle: electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs, also known as electric air taxis. These are, essentially, oversized drones (with room for pilots, for now) designed to carry a small number of people a short distance. By 2022 there were 600 different models under development. Soon, their manufacturers promised, cheap, short aerial hops would be commonplace. Joby was among those leading the charge: In 2020, the company unveiled the design of its S4 model, which it said would be able to carry a pilot and four passengers 100 miles or more at speeds of up to 200 mph. The S4’s maiden flight took place last year.

A commercial launch seemed just around the corner. But deadlines kept getting pushed back. As it turned out, engineering a flying autonomous robot was just part of the overall problem. You also needed to design an airspace that they could operate in, train humans to pilot or supervise them, develop an economic framework within which they could earn money, and so on. “It's a very important, safe, careful dance,” says Bowles.

AI faced another kind of resistance in Europe. In 2017, aircraft manufacturers Airbus and Dassault asked the EASA, the European Union’s version of the FAA, to consider allowing airliners to operate with a single pilot in the cockpit. Traditionally, airliners require multiple pilots to divide the considerable workload of flying a plane and to ensure that if one pilot becomes incapacitated, the other can carry on. In Airbus’ vision, automated systems would shoulder the copilot’s workload and even take over entirely if needed.

That idea horrified pilots. The European Cockpit Association, a union of airline pilots, lodged a strong protest. Such a move “would remove an independent safety professional from the flight deck and give operators greater influence over the safety judgments that a pilot would otherwise make,” the union explained to me in an email. Last year, EASA shelved the plan.

Nevertheless, AI pressed onward. In 2023, the FAA began issuing waivers to allow delivery-drone flights beyond the visual range of operators; by the end of this year it could make the rule change permanent. Some of the biggest players are already pushing ahead aggressively. This past August, Amazon announced that it planned to expand its drone delivery service to 500 locations across the country by the end of the year. Walmart is planning drone delivery from 270 store locations by the end of 2027.

The ultimate goal is far larger. Industry insiders say that in a maximal vision of the technology’s build-out, hundreds of thousands of drones will be servicing most or all of the US population. “In five to 10 years, it’s going to be completely ubiquitous,” Anthony Vittone, chief operating officer of the drone technology company DroneUp, told me in a story for Sherwood News last year. “People are going to be, like, ‘I don’t know how I lived without it.’”

Joby and other eVTOL companies haven’t progressed quite as fast, but they, too, are moving ahead. In April, Joby flew the first-ever point-to-point eVTOL flight within New York City, from John F. Kennedy Airport to three heliports in Manhattan. The company has carried out similar flights in California and Texas, all under the auspices of the eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP), a federal initiative rolled out by the Trump administration this past March to demonstrate the capabilities of modern drones and eVTOLs.

These demo flights, Bowles says, are just the “front edge” of the Joby S4’s operational rollout. Next will come demonstration flights with nonpaying passengers, demonstration flights with paying passengers, and finally flights that will take passengers from A to B. “All of that is permitted under eIPP, with increasing levels of oversight,” he says.

To start, these flights will have human pilots, but it’s very expensive to pay one human to fly around a handful of paying passengers; for the model to make any economic sense, the aircraft will have to fly themselves. And if self-driving is a tough challenge for cars, it’s all the more so for aircraft, where an unexpected control system failure isn’t just dangerous but likely deadly.

In September, the FAA announced that it deployed software built by the Boston-based data company Air Space Intelligence. The new AI-powered tool is called “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories,” or SMART, and it’s aimed at “fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace.” The program isn’t intended to replace controllers, the government says, but to make doing their jobs easier by using predictive AI to head off scheduling snags. “Combining SMART with our ongoing hardware upgrades gives us the tools to cut flight delays, optimize traffic, and keep airspace capacity across the country open—all while maintaining our gold standard of safety,” FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said in a press release.

The system is supposed to help controllers make decisions, not make those decisions for them. But if the program feeds nonsensical information into the system, will human operators be able to catch the mistake? “This is the Trump/DOGE/Musk effect,” says the recently retired FAA employee, who asked to remain anonymous. “They’re pushing through all this new technology without any understanding of the complexity of the national airspace system.”

Some lawmakers are also concerned about SMART. On October 13, almost two dozen Democratic lawmakers reportedly sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office asking it to review the program, citing fears that it might “hallucinate safety-critical information.”

Then there’s the question of whether SMART could worsen the chronic shortage of air traffic controllers. The FAA hopes that the technology lessens the shortage by requiring fewer workers; other industries, though, have yet to see AI-generated efficiencies actually materialize. Even if the software doesn’t directly replace humans, the efficiency could be used to justify a workforce reduction. In May, the FAA reduced its staffing target for active air traffic controllers from the 2024 goal of 14,633 down to 12,563, citing “modern staffing models and scheduling tools.”

Some are more optimistic than others. “I think the SMART program is an important improvement,” Schiavo says. “No one wants the current aviation environment with midairs, runway incursions, myriad near misses, delays, groundings, loss of separation, and long taxi or clearance wait times.”

Michael McCormick, a professor of air traffic management at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, also sees advantages to a predictive tool. “When you have the computing capability to look at the entire trajectory of the aircraft, you can see where the conflicts are going to be,” he says. “And the general axiom in air traffic control is that the sooner you know about a potential conflict, the less effort is required to resolve it.”

That sounds great, but building machines that do a good job most of the time is one thing; machines that can function at the level of reliability required by aviation is another. At present, researchers are focusing on so-called deterministic neural networks—models trained offline whose weights are frozen before being deployed in the real world. These can’t hallucinate, but they may harbor other risky failure modes. In a 2021 paper, Darren Cofer, a researcher at Collins Aerospace, pointed out that when such systems find themselves in situations they haven’t encountered before in training, they can generate “unexpected (and potentially dangerous) outputs.”

The stakes will be even higher when AI software starts making real-time air traffic control decisions, which will start in airspace devoted to autonomous aircraft. According to McCormick, that’ll most likely be select corridors near drone hubs and eVTOL vertiports. With swarms of robot aircraft zipping back and forth, things will be too hairy for human pilots and controllers. “The objective is not to use traditional air traffic control,” he says, “because it would overwhelm the national airspace system if it tried to handle that volume and complexity of airframes moving around.”

With two systems working side by side—one with human decisionmakers, the other with AI—we’ll have a real-time basis to compare the performance of both approaches. Any computer-based system can potentially be hacked; any AI system creative enough to ideate novel solutions could also hallucinate crucial details. Without a human in the loop, seemingly obvious mistakes might go unnoticed until it’s too late.

对于目前正在进行的人工智能航空革命来说，像 SMART 这样的新系统只是冰山一角。以塞斯纳大篷车为例，它在九月一个平静的早晨从加利福尼亚州康科德市的布坎南机场起飞，向南飞往凤凰城。这架飞机是一架单引擎涡轮螺旋桨飞机，随后向东飞往沃思堡，在南卡罗来纳州的肖空军基地停留，最后抵达北卡罗来纳州海岸附近的戴尔县地区机场。这次曲折、从东海岸到西海岸的旅程，行程长达 3,200 英里；一路上，飞机在繁忙的空域航行并进行机动以避免风暴。

除了一个事实之外，这一切都没什么了不起的：整个旅程是在没有人手接触飞机控制装置的情况下进行的。

据执行该项目的乔比航空公司称，塞斯纳飞机上一直有一名安全飞行员，但从不需要干预。这次无人驾驶旅行标志着航空业的一个重要里程碑。航空旅游业长期以来在技术上一直保守，这是有充分理由的：当人的生命受到威胁时，经过时间考验和有点过时的技术比先进和不可预测的技术更好。但人工智能正以前所未有的速度进军航空领域。现在的影响还很难看到，但即将发生的变化是巨大的，有望重塑航空旅行的经济，并改变人和事物在天空中的移动方式。但仍然存在一个大问题：我们能否相信这项技术可靠且安全？

取决于你问谁。 “我们正在引入所有这些新技术来改进系统，但这将是一场灾难，”一位最近退休的美国联邦航空局员工表示。 “这实际上是一个我们将会后悔的潘多拉魔盒。”

2007 年，联邦政府推出了一项名为“下一代航空运输系统”（简称“NextGen”）的全面项目，要求在未来几十年内对航空旅行系统进行广泛变革。其中一项规定是，到 2020 年，美国的飞机必须配备 ADS-B，该系统会不断发送无线电信号，告诉附近的每个人您所在的位置以及您的目的地。

随着机器人友好天空的路线图到位，亚马逊和沃尔玛等大公司开始制定雄心勃勃的无人机送货服务计划。 2014 年，谷歌推出了 Project Wing，这是一项无人机送货服务，到 2018 年，该服务将向澳大利亚堪培拉附近的 164 个家庭运送食物、咖啡和药品。第二年，试点计划扩展到弗吉尼亚州克里斯琴斯堡。成本高，服务慢，但这些早期项目并不意味着成为可行的业务。相反，他们为谷歌提供了未来几年的运营经验。

大约在同一时间，许多初创公司开始研发相关类型的车辆：电动垂直起降飞机（eVTOL），也称为电动空中出租车。这些本质上是超大型无人机（目前有飞行员空间），旨在运载少数人进行短距离飞行。到 2022 年，有 600 种不同的型号正在开发中。制造商承诺，很快，廉价、短距离的空中跳跃将变得司空见惯。 Joby 是这一领域的领军者之一：2020 年，该公司推出了 S4 型号的设计，据称该型号能够搭载一名飞行员和四名乘客，以高达 200 英里/小时的速度行驶 100 英里或更远。 S4 去年进行了首飞。

商业发布似乎指日可待。但最后期限不断被推迟。事实证明，设计飞行自主机器人只是整个问题的一部分。你还需要设计一个他们可以运行的空域，训练人类驾驶或监督他们，开发一个他们可以赚钱的经济框架，等等。 “这是一种非常重要、安全、谨慎的舞蹈，”鲍尔斯说。

人工智能在欧洲面临着另一种阻力。 2017年，飞机制造商空中客车公司和达索公司要求欧洲航空安全局（EASA）（欧盟版的美国联邦航空管理局）考虑允许客机在驾驶舱内由一名飞行员驾驶。传统上，客机需要多名飞行员来分担驾驶飞机的大量工作量，并确保如果一名飞行员丧失能力，另一名飞行员可以继续飞行。在空中客车公司的愿景中，自动化系统将承担副驾驶的工作量，甚至在需要时完全接管。

这个想法让飞行员感到震惊。航空公司飞行员工会欧洲驾驶舱协会提出了强烈抗议。工会在一封电子邮件中向我解释说，此举“将从驾驶舱中撤走一名独立的安全专业人员，并使操作员对飞行员做出的安全判断拥有更大的影响力”。去年，欧洲航空安全局搁置了该计划。

尽管如此，人工智能仍在继续前进。 2023 年，美国联邦航空局 (FAA) 开始发布豁免，允许送货无人机飞行超出操作员的可视范围；到今年年底，规则的改变可能会永久生效。一些最大的参与者已经在积极推进。去年 8 月，亚马逊宣布计划在年底前将无人机送货服务扩展到全国 500 个地点。沃尔玛计划到 2027 年底在 270 个商店地点使用无人机送货。

最终目标要远大得多。业内人士表示，从该技术发展的最大愿景来看，数十万架无人机将为大多数或全部美国人口提供服务。 “五到十年内，它将完全无处不在，”无人机技术公司 DroneUp 的首席运营官 Anthony Vittone 去年在 Sherwood News 的一篇报道中告诉我。 “人们会说，‘我不知道没有它我该如何生活。’”

Joby 和其他 eVTOL 公司的进展速度没有那么快，但他们也在不断前进。 4 月，Joby 驾驶了纽约市内首次点对点 eVTOL 航班，从约翰·F·肯尼迪机场飞往曼哈顿的三个直升机场。该公司已在加利福尼亚州和德克萨斯州进行了类似的飞行，所有这些都是在 eVTOL 集成试点计划 (eIPP) 的支持下进行的，该计划是特朗普政府今年 3 月推出的一项联邦举措，旨在展示现代无人机和 eVTOL 的功能。

鲍尔斯表示，这些演示飞行只是 Joby S4 运营部署的“前沿”。接下来将是载有免费乘客的示范航班、载有付费乘客的示范航班，以及最后将乘客从 A 点带到 B 点的航班。“所有这些都是 eIPP 允许的，并且监管水平不断提高，”他说。

title: Runway's open-source Praxis-1 turns video AI into a robot controller
title_en: Runway's open-source Praxis-1 turns video AI into a robot controller
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
AI company Runway has released its robot model Praxis-1 with open weights and source code. The model uses what it learned from video to control robots and shows promising results in the company's own tests.

Runway has released Praxis-1, its AI model for controlling robots. The company first introduced Praxis-1 in late September but initially gave access only to select partners. Alongside the release, Runway published a detailed research report with new performance tests.

Runway's model weights and source code are available under the Apache 2.0 license, which allows commercial use.Ad

Praxis-1 takes in camera images, text instructions, and information about a robot's position. From those inputs, it predicts how the environment will change and calculates the right robot movements. As new camera frames come in, the model continuously adjusts its control.Ad

Praxis-1 builds on a video model that learned how objects move and interact from ordinary footage. Runway then fine-tuned it with videos of human actions and robot data. This approach could reduce the need for expensive robot-specific datasets, which have traditionally been collected just to train these kinds of systems.

Runway is best known for generative video models like Gen-4.5. With Praxis-1, the company is bringing its video research into robotics. Runway calls Praxis-1 a World Action Model that predicts how a scene will change and derives matching robot movements from those predictions. Since September, robotics companies Standard Bots, Noble Machines, and Ultra have been testing Praxis-1 on different systems, including a humanoid robot, an industrial robot arm, and a dual-arm warehouse robot.Ad

Praxis-1 still needs some specialized robot data. To adapt it to a Franka robot arm, Runway used about 277 hours of recordings from the public DROID research dataset, according to its research report. Those recordings show robots grasping and moving objects, for example. For a dual-arm robot, the company used between 1,400 and 2,600 hours of training material. Runway had already used DROID data and data from other robot systems during earlier training stages. Whether the approach actually needs less robot data overall than comparable models without general video pretraining is still an open question.

On Nvidia's RoboLab-120 leaderboard, Praxis-1 scores a 46.2 percent success rate. The benchmark tests how reliably robot models can sort, grasp, or stack objects across 120 tasks in simulation. FLUX 3 Action, also built as a World Action Model, scores 42.9 percent under the same test conditions. That puts Praxis-1 at the top of the World Action Model category. In the overall leaderboard, it ranks fifth behind two AI agents and two robot models with different architectures. Runway ran all the tests itself, and the results haven't been independently verified yet.Ad

After fine-tuning on DROID data, Runway tested the model on a real Franka robot arm. Both models had to complete the same ten tasks, like placing a banana on a plate or closing a drawer. With ten attempts per task, Praxis-1 succeeded 88 times, while FLUX 3 Action managed 80.Ad

Runway also tested how well Praxis-1 transfers to a robot type it had never seen before, using data from a mobile robot platform with a gripper arm that Google had previously used to develop RT-1. Recordings from this robot weren't part of Praxis-1's earlier training. After fine-tuning on about 95 hours of robot data, the model hit an average success rate of 80 percent in simulated tests, according to Runway. The tests covered four types of tasks, including grabbing soda cans, opening and closing drawers, and placing an apple in a drawer. Google's original RT-1 model scored 52.4 percent on the same benchmark.

Developers can download Praxis-1 from Hugging Face after signing up and agreeing to the access terms. The code is on GitHub. According to Runway's announcement, pre-adapted versions for different robots are already available alongside the base model. The base model needs additional training before it can work with new robot systems.

The standard model version needs a GPU with 80 GB of memory. A compressed version should fit on an RTX 5090 with 32 GB of VRAM based on Runway's memory estimates, though the actual peak memory usage hasn't been measured yet according to the GitHub docs.

The model sometimes confuses similar-looking objects and struggles with vague instructions, according to Runway's research report. For longer tasks, individual steps need to be spelled out because Praxis-1 can't reliably plan complex action sequences on its own yet.

Runway sees Praxis-1 primarily as a system for fast execution of robot movements. In the future, it could work alongside general-purpose AI models that break complex tasks down into individual steps.

article_content_zh:
AI公司Runway发布了其机器人模型Praxis-1，并开放了权重和源代码。该模型利用从视频中学到的知识来控制机器人，并在公司自己的测试中显示出有希望的结果。

Runway 发布了用于控制机器人的 AI 模型 Praxis-1。该公司于 9 月底首次推出 Praxis-1，但最初只向选定的合作伙伴提供访问权限。在发布的同时，Runway 还发布了一份包含新性能测试的详细研究报告。

Runway 的模型权重和源代码可在 Apache 2.0 许可证下获得，该许可证允许商业用途。

Praxis-1 接收相机图像、文本指令和有关机器人位置的信息。根据这些输入，它可以预测环境将如何变化并计算正确的机器人运动。随着新相机框架的出现，模型不断调整其控制。

Praxis-1 建立在视频模型的基础上，该模型可以从普通镜头中学习物体如何移动和交互。然后，跑道用人类行为视频和机器人数据对其进行微调。这种方法可以减少对昂贵的机器人专用数据集的需求，这些数据集传统上只是为了训练此类系统而收集的。

Runway 以 Gen-4.5 等生成视频模型而闻名。通过 Praxis-1，该公司将视频研究带入机器人领域。 Runway 将 Praxis-1 称为世界动作模型，它可以预测场景将如何变化，并从这些预测中得出匹配的机器人动作。自 9 月份以来，机器人公司 Standard Bots、Noble Machines 和 Ultra 一直在不同的系统上测试 Praxis-1，包括人形机器人、工业机器人手臂和双臂仓库机器人。

Praxis-1 仍然需要一些专门的机器人数据。根据其研究报告，为了适应 F​​ranka 机器人手臂，Runway 使用了公共 DROID 研究数据集中约 277 小时的记录。例如，这些录音显示机器人抓取和移动物体。对于双臂机器人，该公司使用了 1,400 至 2,600 小时的培训材料。 Runway 在早期训练阶段已经使用了 DROID 数据和其他机器人系统的数据。该方法是否实际上需要比没有一般视频预训练的同类模型更少的机器人数据仍然是一个悬而未决的问题。

在 Nvidia 的 RoboLab-120 排行榜上，Praxis-1 的成功率为 46.2%。该基准测试机器人模型在模拟中的 120 个任务中分类、抓取或堆叠物体的可靠性。 FLUX 3 Action，也是作为世界行动模型构建的，在相同的测试条件下得分为 42.9%。这使得 Praxis-1 在世界行动模型类别中名列前茅。在整体排行榜上，它排名第五，落后于两个人工智能代理和两个不同架构的机器人模型。 Runway 自行进行了所有测试，结果尚未经过独立验证。

在对 DROID 数据进行微调后，Runway 在真正的 Franka 机器人手臂上测试了该模型。两种模型都必须完成相同的十项任务，例如将香蕉放在盘子上或关闭抽屉。每个任务尝试十次，Praxis-1 成功了 88 次，而 FLUX 3 Action 成功了 80 次。

Runway 还测试了 Praxis-1 转移到以前从未见过的机器人类型的能力，使用的数据来自谷歌之前用于开发 RT-1 的带有夹臂的移动机器人平台。这个机器人的录音并不是 Praxis-1 早期训练的一部分。据 Runway 称，在对大约 95 小时的机器人数据进行微调后，该模型在模拟测试中的平均成功率达到 80%。测试涵盖了四种类型的任务，包括抓取汽水罐、打开和关闭抽屉以及将苹果放入抽屉中。 Google 最初的 RT-1 模型在同一基准测试中得分为 52.4%。

开发人员在注册并同意访问条款后可以从 Hugging Face 下载 Praxis-1。代码位于 GitHub 上。根据 Runway 的公告，针对不同机器人的预适配版本已经与基本模型一起提供。基础模型需要额外的训练才能与新的机器人系统一起使用。

标准型号版本需要具有 80 GB 内存的 GPU。根据 Runway 的内存估计，压缩版本应该适合具有 32 GB VRAM 的 RTX 5090，但根据 GitHub 文档尚未测量实际的峰值内存使用情况。

根据 Runway 的研究报告，该模型有时会混淆外观相似的物体，并难以接受模糊的指令。对于较长的任务，需要详细说明各个步骤，因为 Praxis-1 尚无法可靠地自行规划复杂的动作序列。

Runway 将 Praxis-1 主要视为快速执行机器人运动的系统。未来，它可以与通用人工智能模型一起工作，将复杂的任务分解为单独的步骤。

【起因与机理】降低开发者微调与工程落地的门槛与算力开销，加速端到端应用在真实业务中生根发芽。
【关键技术规格】Runway在全球大模型开源社区与技术研发一线。
【行业研判】该公司于 9 月底首次推出 Praxis-1，但最初给出了。

title: Microsoft Says Making Progress Fixing One Of Its Longest Outages
title_en: Microsoft Says Making Progress Fixing One Of Its Longest Outages
author: Bloomberg
content_snippet: Microsoft Corp. said access has been fully restored to its flagship software, ending an outage that paralyzed government offices, traders and businesses around the world.
summary_en: Microsoft experienced a significant global cloud infrastructure failure around November 13, disrupting critical services including Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams, and SharePoint Online. The company implemented emergency recovery measures such as traffic throttling, route redirection, and extending email timeout thresholds to 48 hours, eventually stabilizing systems while ruling out malicious activity.

更新于美国东部时间 11 月 13 日星期五凌晨 4:59/太平洋时间 11 月 13 日星期四凌晨 1:59 — 微软表示，“随着恢复行动的继续，我们看到了早期的稳定和容量的改善。”该公司还表示，已将电子邮件超时时间延长至 48 小时，以帮助保留在此事件期间延迟的邮件。更新于美国东部时间 11 月 13 日星期五上午 1:08/美国东部时间 11 月 12 日星期四晚上 10:08。太平洋时间 — 微软仍在调查中断原因，但表示目前“不知道有任何恶意活动导致了这一事件。”更新于 11 月 12 日星期四晚上 10:58。美国东部时间 / 晚上 7:58太平洋时间 — 不幸的是，微软让服务器恢复在线的努力并没有按计划进行。它似乎无法解决它们再次变得无响应的问题，并表示现在正在寻找不同的方法来增加流量容量。“我们已经监控了用于提高可服务性的更改的状态，并确认它们没有达到预期，”微软在 11 月 12 日星期四晚上 8:07 更新的 X 更新中写道。美国东部时间/下午 5:07太平洋时间 — Microsoft 修改了受此次中断影响的功能和服务列表，表示它影响了与 Exchange Online 和电子邮件服务交互的功能和服务。尽管 Azure 似乎可以运行，但 Microsoft Outlook、SharePoint Online、Teams、Copilot AI 和 365 都继续存在各种问题。更新于 11 月 12 日星期四晚上 7:53。美国东部时间/下午 4:53太平洋时间 — 微软发布了一个新的更新，指出他们重新上线的服务器在收到流量时可能会再次变得无响应。该公司目前正在调查该问题，但与此同时，它限制了某些位置前往这些服务器的流量类型。更新于 11 月 12 日星期四下午 6:23。美国东部时间/下午 3:23太平洋时间 — 微软表示，它正在使一些服务器重新上线，并且“到目前为止它们保持稳定”。用户应该期待“逐步恢复”。“我们还将尽可能将流量转移到备用路线，并观察有限的恢复，”微软在 X 的更新中写道。“与此同时，我们简化了剩余受影响服务器恢复服务的流程。”更新于 11 月 12 日星期四下午 5:22。美国东部时间/下午 2:22太平洋时间 - 停电一直持续到晚上，微软提供了最新更新：“我们正在开放所有可用的途径来恢复服务，因为我们迄今为止采取的行动尚未提供预期的缓解。”更新于 11 月 12 日星期四下午 4:21。美国东部时间 / 下午 1:21太平洋时间 — 微软在其状态页面和 X 帐户上表示，它可能已经确定了该问题的一些“贡献者”，并正在部署修复程序。该公司表示，部分服务器已经恢复在线。更新于 11 月 12 日星期四下午 3:10。美国东部时间 / 中午 12:10太平洋时间 — 在 X 上的 Microsoft 365 Status 帐户上，该公司表示正在部署多种缓解措施来恢复服务。更新于 11 月 12 日星期四下午 2:29。美国东部时间 / 晚上 11:29太平洋时间 — 根据 Microsoft 服务运行状况网页上的最新更新，当前问题影响 Microsoft 365 商业和企业客户，而不是 Microsoft 的消费技术产品。更新于 11 月 12 日星期四中午 12:37美国东部时间 / 晚上 9:37太平洋时间 — 截至撰写本文时，多个地区的用户在访问 Microsoft 365 时仍然遇到问题。周四下午，Microsoft 客户报告了访问该公司各种软件产品和服务时遇到的问题。哪些服务受到 Microsoft 持续中断的影响？该公司的服务器状态页面指出，用户可能无法访问 Microsoft Exchange Online、Microsoft Teams、SharePoint Online、Microsoft Copilot 365 和 Microsoft Defender XDR。最近的更新表明该公司正在积极部署修复程序。

title: Sources: despite Nvidia's 20+ years of business in China, Jensen Huang struggled to gain access to policymakers driving Beijing's chip self-sufficiency campaign (Eleanor Olcott/Financial Times)
title_en: Sources: despite Nvidia's 20+ years of business in China, Jensen Huang struggled to gain access to policymakers driving Beijing's chip self-sufficiency campaign (Eleanor Olcott/Financial Times)
author: Financial Times
article_content:
Jensen Huang's yearslong push to sell chips to China is now colliding with an affair, board investigation, and crisis at Nvidia. At the center is Alice Huang, who has been an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed, a company that US authorities suspect of helping China access AI chips barred by export controls.

Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing. US officials believe Alice Huang, who has no relation to the Nvidia CEO, was recruited to gather information for Beijing, The New York Times has reported. Nvidia's board is investigating whether Jensen Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." The episode turns a personal scandal into a test of one of tech's biggest fights: whether the US should prioritize open markets for chip companies or constrain them in the name of national security.

Over the years, Jensen Huang has been bullish on the Chinese market and has said that excluding Nvidia would strengthen Chinese rivals. The board's investigation now places his dealings with Megaspeed, his advocacy for China, and his role in US AI policy under fresh scrutiny. Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised.

The company's handling of Jensen Huang's future will signal how seriously it takes the risks surrounding America's most important AI chip executive. Here's what Jensen Huang has said about China in recent years.

Amid tightening US semiconductor export controls, this investigation forces a critical re-examination of Nvidia’s China market strategy and the compliance risks of executive interactions with geopolitically sensitive entities.

article_content_zh:
黄仁勋多年来一直致力于向中国出售芯片，但现在却与英伟达的婚外情、董事会调查和危机发生了冲突。核心人物是爱丽丝·黄（Alice Huang），她曾担任英伟达客户 Megaspeed 的高管，美国当局怀疑这家公司帮助中国获取受出口管制禁止的人工智能芯片。

Megaspeed 否认有不当行为。据《纽约时报》报道，美国官员认为，与英伟达首席执行官没有关系的爱丽丝·黄（Alice Huang）被招募来为北京收集信息。英伟达董事会正在调查黄仁勋是否是“外国情报活动”的目标。这一事件将个人丑闻变成了对科技界最大斗争之一的考验：美国是否应该优先考虑芯片公司的开放市场，还是以国家安全的名义限制它们。

多年来，黄仁勋一直看好中国市场，并表示排除英伟达将增强中国竞争对手的实力。该委员会的调查现在将他与 Megaspeed 的交易、他对中国的倡导以及他在美国人工智能政策中的作用置于新的审查之下。英伟达表示，没有理由相信公司机密或国家安全受到损害。

该公司对黄仁勋未来的处理将表明该公司对这位美国最重要的人工智能芯片高管所面临的风险有多么认真。以下是黄仁勋近年来对中国的评价。

title: WhiteMatter, which builds "guardian" AI agents to oversee file access, software use, decision making, and actions of existing AI agents, raised a $20M Series A (Alice Tecotzky/Business Insider)
title_en: WhiteMatter, which builds "guardian" AI agents to oversee file access, software use, decision making, and actions of existing AI agents, raised a $20M Series A (Alice Tecotzky/Business Insider)
author: Business Insider
article_content:
A startup using AI agents to keep rogue AI in line has raised $20 million. WhiteMatter, founded in 2024 and formerly known as QuilrAI, has built agents that oversee what a company's existing AI agents can access, do, and share. The startup spawns one "guardian agent" for each AI agent in an enterprise, which ensures the original agent acts as intended.

Before a company lets an agent access files, use software, make a decision, or trigger an action, WhiteMatter's agent checks whether that's allowed. The so-called guardian also monitors outcomes. Guardian agents scale automatically — when an enterprise creates a new AI agent, a new guardian agent pops up, too.

"Our existing stack wasn't built for agents being the main actor in the story," Vidit Arora, the startup's 35-year-old founder and CEO, told Business Insider. "Organizations are going now from humans being the core actor to agents being the core actor, and our entire tool stack wasn't built for that." Arora said that his company has helped customers transition from human-first to agent-first organizations.

He says we're "not even at the tip of the iceberg" when it comes to agent attacks and compromises, both from external and internal agents. Agentic security has become an increasingly important topic as enterprises grant more non-technical employees access to AI agents capable of completing tasks.

A recent string of agent-powered security incidents has pumped new urgency into the cybersecurity space that WhiteMatter operates in. Other startups have pounced on the business opportunity in agent security, and WhiteMatter's competitors include Onyx Security, Zenity, and Noma. The guardian agents don't run on customers' tokens, but rather on WhiteMatter's self-hosted AI model and GPUs.

The company charges customers a flat rate based on a techy version of AUM: agents under management. Business growth is organic, Arora said, since companies continue to invest in more agents and therefore need more guardian agents. Current customers include Fortune 200 and Fortune 500 companies, such as the asset management firm Alter Domus.

Whitematter, whose new name is a nod to the brain's connective tissue, says it has 2.25 million agents under management to date, and has overseen more than 116 billion AI interactions. Blumberg Capital led WhiteMatter's $20 million Series A funding, and existing investors Crew Capital and Sprout & Oak also participated.

Arora plans to use a big portion of the money to hire for go-to-market and sales roles, and expects his 80-person team to grow by 50% in the next 12 months. He also intends to use the fresh capital to invest in his research team. Read the pitch deck WhiteMatter used to raise its Series A round.

article_content_zh:
一家利用人工智能代理来控制流氓人工智能的初创公司已筹集 2000 万美元。 WhiteMatter 成立于 2024 年，以前称为 QuilrAI，它构建了代理来监督公司现有的 AI 代理可以访问、执行和共享的内容。该初创公司为企业中的每个人工智能代理生成一个“监护代理”，以确保原始代理按预期运行。

在公司允许代理访问文件、使用软件、做出决定或触发操作之前，WhiteMatter 的代理会检查是否允许这样做。所谓的监护人也监督结果。监护代理会自动扩展——当企业创建新的人工智能代理时，也会弹出一个新的监护代理。

该初创公司 35 岁的创始人兼首席执行官维迪特·阿罗拉 (Vidit Arora) 告诉 Business Insider：“我们现有的堆栈并不是为充当故事主角的特工而构建的。” “组织现在正在从人类作为核心角色转变为代理作为核心角色，而我们的整个工具堆栈并不是为此而构建的。”阿罗拉表示，他的公司帮助客户从以人为本的组织转变为以代理为先的组织。

他说，当涉及来自外部和内部代理的代理攻击和妥协时，我们“甚至还没有到达冰山一角”。随着企业向更多非技术员工授予能够完成任务的人工智能代理的访问权限，代理安全已成为一个越来越重要的话题。

最近发生的一系列代理安全事件给 WhiteMatter 所在的网络安全领域带来了新的紧迫性。其他初创公司也纷纷抓住代理安全领域的商机，WhiteMatter 的竞争对手包括 Onyx Security、Zenity 和 Noma。监护代理不是在客户的代币上运行，而是在 WhiteMatter 的自托管人工智能模型和 GPU 上运行。

该公司根据技术版本的 AUM（受管理的代理）向客户收取统一费率。阿罗拉表示，业务增长是有机的，因为公司继续投资更多的代理人，因此需要更多的监护代理人。目前的客户包括财富 200 强和财富 500 强公司，例如资产管理公司 Alter Domus。

Whitematter 的新名字是对大脑结缔组织的致敬，该公司表示，迄今为止，它管理着 225 万个代理，并监督了超过 1160 亿次人工智能交互。 Blumberg Capital 领投了 WhiteMatter 的 2000 万美元 A 轮融资，现有投资者 Crew Capital 和 Sprout & Oak 也参与其中。

Arora 计划用大部分资金来招聘市场营销和销售职位，并预计他的 80 人团队将在未来 12 个月内增长 50%。他还打算利用新资金投资他的研究团队。阅读 WhiteMatter 用于筹集 A 轮融资的宣传材料。

title: Cambridge, UK-based Tendrils, which is designing a CPU architecture with thousands of cores operating in parallel, raised $30M led by Benchmark (John Reynolds/Tech.eu)
title_en: Cambridge, UK-based Tendrils, which is designing a CPU architecture with thousands of cores operating in parallel, raised $30M led by Benchmark (John Reynolds/Tech.eu)
author: Tech.eu
content_snippet: Tendrils Compute is one of several UK chip startups which investors are backing. — A UK startup developing a radically different type …
summary_en: Cambridge-based Tendrils Compute has raised $30 million in a round led by Benchmark. The company is developing a novel high-performance CPU architecture featuring thousands of parallel cores, aiming to deliver superior compute density and energy efficiency for intensive AI workloads compared to traditional general-purpose processors.

summary_zh: 英国初创公司Tendrils Compute完成3000万美元融资，专注于设计具备数千个核心并行处理的CPU架构

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 总部位于英国剑桥的Tendrils Compute完成3000万美元融资，由Benchmark领投。该公司致力于研发一种全新的高性能CPU架构，通过数千个内核并行运作的方式，试图在处理高强度AI负载时提供超越传统处理器的算力密度与能效表现。

elements_en.what: Raised $30M to develop a multi-thousand-core parallel CPU architecture for AI workloads
elements_en.why: Seeking architectural breakthroughs to address the performance and throughput bottlenecks of traditional CPUs in AI computing

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 在AI推理负载激增背景下，处理器架构正从“通用优先”转向“吞吐优先”。Tendrils试图通过超大规模并行CPU架构模糊CPU与GPGPU的界限，若其能解决片上互联与内存带宽墙的复杂性，将对当前依赖GPU构建的AI计算基础设施形成有效互补或替代。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Amid surging AI inference demand, processor architecture is pivoting from 'general-purpose priority' to 'throughput priority.' Tendrils aims to blur the lines between CPUs and GPGPUs via massive parallelization. If they can overcome the complexities of on-chip interconnects and memory bandwidth walls, they could offer a potent alternative or complement to the current GPU-centric AI infrastructure.

title: JD.com completes its takeover of German electronics retailer Ceconomy, after acquiring a ~60% stake for ~$1.5B, following the EU's approval of the deal (Tomoko Wakasugi/Nikkei Asia)
title_en: JD.com completes its takeover of German electronics retailer Ceconomy, after acquiring a ~60% stake for ~$1.5B, following the EU's approval of the deal (Tomoko Wakasugi/Nikkei Asia)
author: Nikkei Asia
article_content:
SHANGHAI -- JD.com has completed an acquisition of German consumer electronics retailer Ceconomy, aiming to link European physical and online stores using the know-how that the e-commerce company has cultivated in China.

JD.com bought roughly 60% of Ceconomy's shares for 1.34 billion euros ($1.47 billion), according to an announcement Thursday.

Together with the stake retained by JD.com partner Convergenta, an asset management company for Ceconomy's founding family, their combined ownership is now 85%.

After the acquisition was announced last year, the European Commission launched an investigation into whether China's preferential treatment for JD.com, including government subsidies, may hurt fair competition within the European Union. Beijing pushed back against the probe.

On Nov. 3, the European Commission approved the acquisition, with the condition that intra-group transactions be conducted on market terms and that JD.com offer services on the same terms to companies other than Ceconomy.

JD.com's sales of home appliances span online and brick-and-mortar stores. In March, it launched the Joybuy e-commerce site for Europe.

The company is expected to collaborate more closely with Ceconomy, which operates more than 1,000 home appliance stores in Europe including MediaMarkt and Saturn.

summary_en: JD.com has completed its acquisition of roughly 60% of German consumer electronics retailer Ceconomy for €1.34 billion ($1.47 billion). Approved by the European Commission under fair market conditions, the deal combines JD's Chinese e-commerce expertise with Ceconomy's network of over 1,000 European stores, including MediaMarkt and Saturn.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 京东集团以约13.4亿欧元完成收购德国最大消费电子连锁Ceconomy约60%股权，联合创始家族持股达85%。欧盟委员会批准交易并设置了关联交易公允市价条件。该交易标志着中国电商巨头正式掌控欧洲逾千家实体门店网络，将以数字化中台赋能传统零售体系。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: JD.com has completed the €1.34 billion takeover of German retail giant Ceconomy, acquiring a 60% stake to hold 85% alongside partner Convergenta. The transaction, cleared with EU conditions, integrates over 1,000 European consumer electronics stores into JD's global supply chain network.
ai_analysis.takeaway_zh: 京东入主欧洲老牌零售巨头Ceconomy，展现了中国互联网出海由单纯跨境卖货转向深度整合海外本土成熟零售供应链与实体渠道的战略跃升。
ai_analysis.takeaway_en: JD's acquisition of Ceconomy represents a strategic paradigm shift for Chinese tech firms—moving from pure cross-border platforms to acquiring and modernizing entrenched physical retail giants abroad.

article_content_zh:
上海讯 —— 京东集团已正式完成对德国消费电子零售巨头 Ceconomy 的收购，旨在利用其在中国本土积累的电商运营与全渠道零售经验，打通欧洲线下实体门店与线上商业生态。

根据周四发布的官方声明，京东以约 13.4 亿欧元（约合 14.7 亿美元）的价格收购了 Ceconomy 约 60% 的股份。

结合京东合作伙伴 Convergenta（Ceconomy 创始家族的资产管理公司）持有的股份，双方在 Ceconomy 的合计持股比例已达 85%。

该项收购于去年首次公布后，欧盟委员会随即展开深入反垄断调查，重点审查中国对京东的产业政策及相关补贴是否会破坏欧盟单一市场的公平竞争环境；北京方面此前对该调查提出了抗辩。

11月3日，欧盟委员会正式批准了该笔收购交易，但附加了严格的市场监管条件，要求京东集团内部交易必须严格遵循市场化公允原则，且京东必须以同等商业条件向 Ceconomy 以外的第三方竞争对手开放相关供应链与技术服务。

京东在家电及消费电子领域的销售网络覆盖线上与线下全渠道。今年3月，京东正式在欧洲上线了 Joybuy 跨境电商平台。

完成交割后，京东将与 Ceconomy 展开全面深度协同。Ceconomy 目前在欧洲全境运营着超过 1000 家大型消费电子实体连锁门店，旗下核心品牌包括知名零售巨头 MediaMarkt 与 Saturn。
