title: Free speech group FIRE says DOJ and DHS will end efforts to curb "ICE Sightings - Chicagoland" Facebook group and Eyes Up iOS app, which report on ICE activity (Kanishka Singh/Reuters)
title_en: Free speech group FIRE says DOJ and DHS will end efforts to curb "ICE Sightings - Chicagoland" Facebook group and Eyes Up iOS app, which report on ICE activity (Kanishka Singh/Reuters)
author: Reuters
article_content:
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Free speech group FIRE said on Friday the US government agreed to end efforts to press Apple (AAPL.O) and Facebook (META.O) to restrict platforms created by two Americans reporting Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity.

FIRE sued the federal departments of Justice and Homeland Security in February.

It alleged that Facebook's disabling of plaintiff Kae Rosado's group, "ICE Sightings – Chicagoland," in response to demands by federal officials had violated Rosado's free speech rights.

The suit alleged the same violation over Apple's removal of Eyes Up, an app created by plaintiff Mark Hodges for sharing videos of ICE operations, under government pressure.

The DOJ and DHS, whose top officials were the defendants in the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

As part of an agreement with FIRE to resolve the case, the free speech group said the government agreed to make permanent the preliminary injunction the court previously entered in favor of the plaintiffs.

An order by US District Judge Jorge Alonso said the federal government "shall take no actions, formal or informal, to demand or pressure" Facebook and Apple to suppress the "ICE Sightings – Chicagoland" Facebook group and the Eyes Up app.

ICE, which is part of DHS, has been the face of Republican President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown and deportation drive that rights groups say has violated free speech and due process rights.

Human rights groups also say the crackdown has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

Trump says his actions aim to improve domestic security. Democrats, who won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the US midterm elections, say they aim to hold the Trump administration accountable for its immigration policies.

title_zh: 美政府停止限制ICE追踪应用及群组
summary_zh: 美国政府与言论自由组织FIRE达成和解，承诺终止向Facebook和Apple等科技巨头施压，撤回对追踪ICE移民执法活动社群群组与App的审查与封锁干预

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 美国联邦司法部与国土安全部已正式与言论自由组织FIRE签署和解协议，永久停止游说并施压Apple与Meta下架追踪ICE联邦移民执法的数字工具。联邦法院法官裁定政府不得以任何形式干涉此类公民监督平台，确立了数字时代公共执法监督受第一修正案保护的重要判例。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: The U.S. DOJ and DHS settled a First Amendment lawsuit with free speech group FIRE, agreeing to permanently halt efforts coercing Apple and Meta to censor tools tracking ICE activity. The court ruling protects citizen documentation of federal law enforcement under constitutional free speech guarantees.
ai_analysis.takeaway_zh: 该案确立了关键的数字言论自由红线：政府不得通过对应用商店和社交平台进行幕后施压来变相审查民间对联邦执法行为的监督与记录。
ai_analysis.takeaway_en: This resolution establishes a vital free speech guardrail against backdoor government censorship, affirming that administrative pressure on tech platforms cannot be used to suppress public oversight of law enforcement.

article_content_zh:
华盛顿11月13日电（路透社）—— 言论自由倡导组织 FIRE 周五表示，美国政府已达成和解协议，同意终止向苹果公司（AAPL.O）和 Meta 旗下的 Facebook 施压，不再要求其限制由两名美国公民创建的用于追踪和报告美国移民与海关执法局（ICE）执法活动的数字平台。

今年2月，FIRE 代表原告向联邦司法部（DOJ）及国土安全部（DHS）提起了宪法诉讼。

诉讼指控称，Facebook 此前封锁原告 Kae Rosado 创立的“ICE Sightings – Chicagoland”（芝加哥地区 ICE 动向目击）群组并下架相关帖文，系因遵从联邦官员提出的不当审查要求，此举严重侵犯了公民受宪法保护的言论自由权利。

诉状同时指出，苹果公司在面临联邦政府施压后，强行下架了原告 Mark Hodges 开发的用于共享 ICE 执法行动现场视频的“Eyes Up”移动应用，同样构成了同类违宪侵权行为。

诉讼被告方的联邦司法部与国土安全部高级官员未立即回应路透社的置评请求。

作为与 FIRE 达成和解协议的一部分，该言论自由组织透露，美国政府已正式同意将此前法院作出的保护原告权益的初步禁令转为永久性禁令。

美国联邦地区法官豪尔赫·阿隆索（Jorge Alonso）签发的司法禁令明确指出，联邦政府“不得采取任何正式或非正式行动，直接或通过第三方机构，对‘ICE Sightings – Chicagoland’Facebook 群组以及‘Eyes Up’应用施加压迫、要求下架或进行其他形式的干涉”。

隶属于国土安全部的 ICE 一直是特朗普政府推进强硬移民执法与遣返行动的前沿机构；人权组织批评该专项行动侵犯了公民的言论自由与正当法律程序权利。

多家人权倡导组织进一步指出，移民执法严打行动在社区内造成了严重的不安全氛围，尤其是针对少数族裔，引发了公众对执法过程中系统性种族偏见与身份盘查的强烈担忧。

特朗普此前辩称其执法政策旨在加强美国本土国家安全；而在本周二中期选举中赢得国会参众两院多数席位的民主党人则强调，将严加审查并追究特朗普政府强硬移民执法政策的行政合规责任。
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】美国联邦司法部与国土安全部已正式与言论自由组织FIRE签署和解协议，永久停止游说并施压Apple与Meta下架追踪ICE联邦移民执法的数字工具。
【核心事实细节】联邦法院法官裁定政府不得以任何形式干涉此类公民监督平台，确立了数字时代公共执法监督受第一修正案保护的重要判例。
【各方立场与态度】该案确立了关键的数字言论自由红线：政府不得通过对应用商店和社交平台进行幕后施压来变相审查民间对联邦执法行为的监督与记录。

title: US officials say Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving Jensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Xi (Dan Mangan/CNBC)
title_en: US officials say Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving Jensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Xi (Dan Mangan/CNBC)
author: CNBC
article_content:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.

Officials also said that Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.

"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.

"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls.. and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."

Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."

"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.

Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."

China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.

Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed, a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.

The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.

During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.

"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.

"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

article_content_zh:
美国高级官员周五表示，预计唐纳德·特朗普总统在即将与中国国家主席习近平会面时不会提出涉及英伟达前首席执行官黄仁勋的中国情报行动的指控。

官员们还表示，特斯拉和SpaceX首席执行官埃隆·马斯克(Elon Musk)将陪同特朗普前往中国深圳，参加11月18日至19日举行的亚太经合组织峰会。

白宫周五早些时候表示，特朗普计划在那里与习近平和俄罗斯总统普京举行三方峰会。

黄仁勋与涉嫌间谍的爱丽丝黄（与他没有亲属关系）的关系引发了人们的担忧，她曾担任高管的一家新加坡公司将受限制的英伟达芯片转移到中国。

一位官员在新闻发布会上表示，“英伟达的情况应该不会对这次旅行产生任何影响”，但要求不具名。

“在我们与中国人的所有讨论和谈判中，我们不会就美国的出口管制进行谈判……而且我们也不希望它出现在我们在那里与中国人的任何对话中。”

当被问及特朗普是否会向中国领导人习近平提出对黄爱丽的指控时，该官员表示，“与习近平主席会面的重点，至少在经济方面，将是关于贸易协定的实施。”

这位官员表示：“当涉及到美国正在进行的一些国家安全问题以及检查和调查时，我们目前可能不会向中国人了解这些内容。”

另一位官员表示，“我不认为总统会提出爱丽丝黄问题。”

中国称针对黄爱丽的指控毫无根据。

本周，黄仁勋辞去了英伟达首席执行官的职务，此前有报道称，黄仁勋与云计算公司 Megaspeed 的高管爱丽丝·黄 (Alice Huang) 有染，该公司正被视为可能违反美国对这些芯片的限制，协助发送价值数十亿美元的英伟达芯片。

这一丑闻震惊了英伟达，并引发了人们对霍华德·卢特尼克领导的商务部在阻止先进芯片进入中国方面是否足够积极的质疑。

在周五的电话会议中，一名记者询问马斯克为什么要与特朗普一起旅行。

一位官员表示：“我不想代表总统解释埃隆离职的具体原因。”

title: Tesla Says It’s Starting to Sell Cybercabs for Personal Use
title_en: Tesla Says It’s Starting to Sell Cybercabs for Personal Use
author: Kara Carlson
article_content:
And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, and it works anywhere, no geofence required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. And with lease and PPA options, you can do it with zero upfront cost and start saving immediately. If you want to find the best deal, check out EnergySage. It’s a free service with hundreds of pre-vetted installers competing for your business, so you save 20 to 30% compared to going it alone. No sales calls until you pick an installer. article_content_zh:
而且它只能在特斯拉位于德克萨斯州和佛罗里达州的 Robotaxi 服务区内工作，这些地理围栏实际上比特斯拉宣传的要小得多。

特斯拉官方 Robotaxi 账户周五在 X 上公布了邀请函，并附有订单页面截图和邀请邮件。

订单页面列出的 Cyber​​cab 税前售价为 29,990 美元，预计将于 2026 年 12 月在德克萨斯州奥斯汀交付。您需要支付 1,000 美元的不可退还押金才能订购。

剩下的就是我们已经知道的了。两个座位、21 英寸中央触摸屏、20.1 立方英尺的货物空间，没有方向盘或踏板。特斯拉称其为“完全自主”，并表示您将“在应用程序中管理您的骑行”。

马斯克在 2024 年推出 Cyber​​cab 时曾承诺其售价“低于 30,000 美元”。从技术上讲，他做到了。他只是没有提到使用它每年需要花费 3,588 美元。五年内，一辆两座车的费用约为 47,600 美元（不含保险、维护、税费和收费）。

特斯拉在八个城市提供 Robotaxi 服务：德克萨斯州的奥斯汀、达拉斯、休斯顿、沃斯堡和圣安东尼奥，以及佛罗里达州的迈阿密、奥兰多和坦帕。这就是 Cyber​​cab 可以操作的地方。在其他地方，它就是你车道上的一个价值 30,000 美元的雕塑。

这些服务区域并不像特斯拉所说的那样。独立追踪者 Koby Pierce 在 Robotaxi 应用程序中测试了数千个地址，结果发现，在他检查的 6 个城市中，特斯拉实际接受接送的区域仅为广告地理围栏的 59% 至 78%。在特斯拉交付这些汽车的城市奥斯汀，这一比例约为 59%。

铁路道口是一个重要原因。在休斯顿，Robotaxi Tracker 的创建者发现该应用程序显示，行驶两个街区需要大约 40 分钟，因为该车辆似乎绕着铁路道口行驶。特斯拉还将圣安东尼奥机场列入其多边形内，但不为其提供服务。

然后是监管云。美国国家公路交通安全管理局 (NHTSA) 已命令特斯拉宣誓证明没有制动踏板的汽车符合要求制动踏板的联邦安全标准。特斯拉于 10 月 30 日做出回应，并要求对整个回应保密。 NHTSA 尚未做出裁决。无论如何，特斯拉现在正在向消费者出售汽车。

我认为这将是一团糟。看起来特斯拉只是受邀请才这样做，并在奥斯汀交付，以证明他们可以在 2026 年交付“无人监管”的车辆。

特斯拉将把这些卖给那些对拥有一辆自动驾驶汽车感到兴奋的粉丝，他们中的许多人会发现，除了一辆价值 30,000 美元的汽车之外，这些限制并不值每月 299 美元。

当然，如果你每月的 Uber 账单远远超过 300 美元，并且你在地理围栏深处生活和工作，也许纸上的数学是成立的。直到您意识到到达目的地后必须将其停放在某个地方。或者它不能带你去两个街区外的朋友家。或者因为汽车不会穿过火车轨道，15 分钟的车程变成了一个小时。对于 Uber 或 Waymo，那是别人的问题。使用 Cyber​​cab，您需要为这种特权付费。

尝试计算 X 年内的成本是没有意义的。特斯拉无论如何都可以随意改变月费（考虑到他们的整体定价历史，应该会这样做）。

这是对我来说毫无意义的部分。 Cyber​​cab 与当前的 Model Y 运行在同一台 AI4 计算机上。特斯拉已经在这些相同的地理围栏中运行无人监管的 Model Y Robotaxis。那么，为什么已经支付“全自动驾驶”费用的 Model Y 车主不能在这些区域进行无人监管的操作呢？将其应用到这些已经积累了更多数据的车辆上不是更容易吗？特斯拉不断将这一目标推迟到“明年”，目前大约是 2027 年第二季度，同时要求人们购买一款除此之外别无他用的新双座汽车。

【起因与机理】旨在验证无人驾驶车型市场化交付能力并锁定Robotaxi生态用户
【关键数据与实测】Cybercab订购价约3万美元，需配合每月299美元订阅。
【涉及范围与推进】NHTSA关于车辆安全标准合规性的调查尚无定论。

title: AI's impact on math is a preview of what AI will do to AI research, with AI matching top human researchers potentially just a couple of years away (Dwarkesh Patel/Dwarkesh Podcast)
title_en: AI's impact on math is a preview of what AI will do to AI research, with AI matching top human researchers potentially just a couple of years away (Dwarkesh Patel/Dwarkesh Podcast)
author: Dwarkesh Podcast
article_content:
00-44:26 Audio playback is not supported on your browser. Please upgrade.Many thanks to Max Farrens, Gabe Fried, and Thomas Larsen for pairing with me through significant parts of writing and researching this essay.

You can watch or listen to me narrate this essay on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts.

If you asked me earlier this year how far away we are from superintelligence, I’d probably have said at least the better part of a decade. But over the last three months, I’ve updated my views a ton. I’ve been debating people about this question, both on and off the podcast. And I’ve been watching the progress of AI on verifiable domains and thinking about what that implies for AI research itself.

I’ve now come to the view that we’re only a couple of years away, and possibly only a couple of months away, from AIs that are as good as the best humans at AI research. I’ve also come to believe that automating AI research will compress so much progress into a single year that, soon thereafter (so by 2030, but plausibly as early as next year), we’ll have AIs that are at least as good as the best human experts in every field. I know this is a wild claim, and it’s one that I myself didn’t believe even a couple of months ago. Let me walk you through how my thinking has changed.

Before we get into more speculative arguments, I want to point out that we have a lot of evidence that AI is already dramatically speeding up further AI progress at the frontier.

For example, METR, which is an independent evaluation organization, concluded after three months embedded inside Anthropic that Anthropic’s overall rate of progress on well-scoped tasks is 2x what it was a year ago, and that a “majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D.”

OpenAI published a blog post about this in September, where they showed that the heaviest 10% of AI users among OpenAI’s researchers went from using around $1,000 a day of internal coding agents at the beginning of the summer to over $7,000 a day by the end of August.

In September, Anthropic put out a similar post on its own AI uplift. They reported that, as of August, Claude “leads” more than 26% of Anthropic’s AI R&D work—up from under 1% as recently as February.1

Math is a preview of what will happen to AI research When I think about how big a deal it could be if AIs automate AI research, and how soon that could happen, a really important update for me has been just seeing how quickly AI capabilities in mathematics have exploded. Current AIs are slicing through well-scoped problems in mathematics like a hot knife through butter. It was only two years ago that I asked Dario why LLMs aren’t able to use their vast knowledge across so many different fields in order to connect different ideas and make new discoveries. And lo and behold, here we are: In a wholly verifiable domain like mathematics, AIs are doing this search-and-match discovery to such a great extent that hundreds of important results (which the top mathematicians and computer scientists in the world had spent decades trying to resolve) are being churned out as side quests to hype up future model releases.

It’s crazy how fast we went from, in 2023, “This model can’t reliably add four-digit numbers,” to, in 2024, “This model can barely solve any problems in a high school math competition,” to, in 2025, “Oh, it can win a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad,” to, earlier this year, “Wow, it’s solving open Erdős problems, but maybe just because no human has attempted to solve these particular problems, and a similar solution was already in the literature,” to, about a month ago, “Okay, it fucking solved a Millennium Prize problem in 88 hours.”

There’s a line in the novel East of Eden: “And there is one sure thing about the fall of gods: they do not fall a little; they crash and shatter.”

It’s true that progress has skewed disproportionately towards the verification-laden parts of math, like finding counterexamples (rather than coming up with new theories, say). Toby Ord posted a great essay about this recently. He writes, “While current AI systems are starting to automate mathematical proof, there is currently very little evidence that they can ask powerful questions or find profound new fields of mathematical enquiry.”

But another way to say the same point would be: Current AI systems have solved a Millennium Prize problem, all without the ability to ask powerful questions or find profound new fields of mathematical inquiry.

And this ability to solve well-scoped problems is going to be an even bigger deal for machine learning research than for mathematics, broadly construed. That’s because the goal of mathematics research is not just to prove or disprove long lists of conjectures, but to extend human understanding of mathematical concepts. Coming up with the idea of topology, group theory, or the Cartesian grid matters far more than knowing exactly how many one-unit-apart pairs you can make from n dots. We mainly care about such abstruse questions insofar as they might elicit new mathematical theories.

But in AI research, the priorities are exactly reversed. AI labs mainly care about how any new algorithmic recipe empirically makes training more efficient or elicits smarter models. They don’t care about theory for its own sake, and all the progress we’ve made in deep learning over the last decade and a half has not required much new theory anyway. The equivalent of grinding through random conjectures would be enormously valuable in machine learning in a way that it just isn’t in mathematics.

AI research is actually surprisingly similar to the type of mathematical progress that current AIs are disproportionately good at: unlocking a ton of low-hanging fruit by applying a combination of incredible persistence and a superhuman capacity to connect ideas from lots of adjacent domains.

For example, let’s talk about the transformer architecture. My friend Sholto Douglas, who is an AI researcher, has a perennially half-finished blog post where he explains how you could have invented the transformer two years earlier than people actually did. Maybe this essay will get him to quit stalling and complete it, but in the meantime, I’ll summarize a bit of the discussion I had with him about the contents of that essay.

Before the transformer paper was published in 2017, many researchers had already identified attention as a way to better parallelize training and communicate information across longer sequences. Chris Olah, who was an active researcher then, has said: “At the time, my sense is that the transformer architecture was a natural combination of many ideas (attention, residual networks) which had independently been effective, taken to quite aggressive lengths.” In other words, none of the core pieces were a surprise to researchers working in the field.

So then why didn’t people invent the transformer sooner? One reason was that this new architecture was only obviously better than the state of the art once you connected half a dozen additional tweaks and innovations. And though all of these had been in the literature for years,2 no one knew how to combine the puzzle pieces. Doing so required research taste, of course, but also tons and tons of small experiments.

But what I’ve just described above—persistently and intelligently matching dozens of different combinations of ideas—is exactly the kind of capability that AIs have shown themselves disproportionately skilled at in their contributions to mathematics.

This is all to say, even the transformer, which is arguably the biggest breakthrough in ML since AlexNet kicked off the deep learning revolution in 2012, is the kind of thing that Claude 7 could invent if Chris Olah asked it to try hard to get this attention thing to work better.

I want to clarify that some parts of AI research are, in fact, less verifiable than math. That’s why OpenAI hasn’t fired all of its researchers, despite having a model that can autonomously solve Millennium Prize problems. But I think AI research is verifiable enough that AIs will soon be as good at it as the best humans. Explaining why requires getting into the nitty-gritty of how AI research actually works, and because those details are interesting but technical, I’ve saved them for the Appendix—if you’re curious, just keep reading after the conclusion. But in the meantime, I’ll give you my estimate of when we get there.

If I had to pick my median year for when automated researchers will be as good as the very best human AI researchers (and assuming the labs don’t intentionally slow down), I’d guess 2028.

Why do I think AIs could get this good within two years? In every domain where we can check answers and give AIs thousands of rounds of practice—for example, competitive programming contests, or well-scoped open math problems—they’ve gone from worse than most humans to better than the best humans within a few years. And as I detail in the Appendix, AI research has those same verifiable properties.

Of course, a big part of what makes a top AI researcher like Ilya Sutskever so good can’t be directly verified—for example, his ability to bet, years in advance, on the right research direction. But as we’ve seen in math, models generalize far beyond what they were directly trained on. OpenAI’s model was obviously not trained by solving other Millennium Prize problems. It was trained on lots of less ambitious, more tractable math problems, and from those it generalized all the way to solving a problem no human had ever cracked. I’d expect the same in AI research, where the combination of thousands of rounds of practice on verifiable research tasks, plus the fact that each new generation of models is broadly smarter than the last, will make models excellent even at the parts of AI research we can’t directly check.

I want to be clear that there’s a pretty decent chance that hitting this milestone takes longer because some important part of AI research remains hard to automate. I’d guess there’s a 25% chance that it doesn’t happen until after 2032.3 But I also think things could move much faster, and that we could hit this milestone in 2027. Some of the most well-informed researchers I know, people who have had a very good track record of prediction over the last few years, expect AI to beat the best humans at AI research as early as next year. And 2027 is also the straightforward implication of plugging METR’s finding—that Anthropic’s rate of AI progress has doubled in a year—into a takeoff model.

If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year.

The reason my median is not that soon is that I’m uncertain about how accurate this straightforward modeling is. But we should not be surprised if we get to this milestone next year, and we should be prepared for such a world.

Once AI is as good as the best humans at AI research, algorithmic progress will get radically faster. There are three important reasons why: The automated researchers will be much faster, each of them will be very smart, and there’ll be a lot more of them.

Today’s AIs already do work at about 10 times human speed.4 And automated researchers would also be working around the clock, nights and weekends included. As a result, each individual automated researcher will be cramming in roughly 50x more work every calendar week than a human researcher can do.

Of course, that doesn’t mean AI progress will immediately accelerate 50x. Those automated researchers would still be bottlenecked by compute for experiments, which aren’t running any faster. So there would be diminishing returns. But even with extremely steep diminishing returns, this alone would make algorithmic progress proceed many times faster than it currently does.5

And this is before we account for the fact that, in this scenario, every automated researcher will be at least as good at AI R&D as the very best humans.

My sense is that around 80% of the algorithmic progress at a given frontier lab is driven by its top 50 researchers. It’s not for nothing that Zuckerberg was willing to pay hundreds of millions of dollars to acquire the best talent in the industry. And so you get another big speedup in algorithmic progress from the fact that every single engineer and researcher in this automated company will be at the level of the very best humans in today’s frontier AI labs.

Throwing more workers at a problem isn’t always helpful. For example, a swarm of agents probably couldn’t write a great novel much faster than a single agent could. But other tasks lend themselves to parallelization: For example, look at the animation below, showing a bunch of different Claudes working together to formalize Fermat’s Last Theorem. This feat had thousands of modular subtasks, each of which could be completed independently and where each agent could locally check whether its work had succeeded.

AI research is closer to formalizing a theorem than to writing a novel, because there is a lot of independent modular work to do, and there are verifiable proxies for progress. That means a swarm of agents can try a thousand different approaches and see which performs best, and they can do this independently for each different part of the pipeline. AI companies are already made up of dozens of teams working independently on different parts of model development: one team improves how the pretraining data is filtered, another helps design a particular kind of synthetic RL environment, another writes a better attention kernel, and so on. In domains like this, where different streams of work can be done and checked independently, dumping in lots of persistent hill-climbing agents tends to speed up progress a lot.

Again, there will be steeply diminishing returns just from adding more parallel researchers. Anyone who has worked on a team before knows that having 100,000 collaborators doesn’t mean you go 100,000 times faster—probably not even 100 times faster. But it’s implausible that you wouldn’t be going at least a couple of times faster from having orders of magnitude more automated labor.

So the combination of faster, smarter, and more numerous automated researchers will speed up AI progress a lot. But will this pace continue, will it get even faster, or will it slow down? That question is even more important than what the initial pace actually is.

Two competing trends are relevant here. And the subsequent pace of progress will come down to which ends up being more powerful. On the one hand, because of RSI, automated researchers will continue getting faster, smarter, and more plentiful. On the other hand, AI research will be getting harder and harder, as all the easy ideas get eaten away by the swarm.

By the way, “ideas getting harder to find” is a thing that already happens. AI companies have to quadruple their R&D compute and double their workforce every single year just to maintain the same rate of progress.

If the rate at which AIs get smarter is faster than the rate at which ideas get harder to find, then we’d get something called the “software-only singularity.” In this scenario, even without increasing compute, the AI swarm rapidly makes smarter and smarter versions of itself until, within a matter of months, we end up with a superintelligence that scrapes against the physical limits of our current chips.

But if ideas get harder to find faster than RSI makes AIs better at research, we’ll end up with what I’d call a “spark.” We’d get something like three to six years of AI progress in a single year.6 And then things would simmer down until we build more compute, because even the super-genius automated researchers need to run bigger experiments before they can make further breakthroughs.

If pressed, I’d give a 50% chance to the “spark” scenario and a 50% chance to the “software-only singularity.”

To be clear, though, even the “spark” scenario, where we make about four years of progress in the first year after automating AI research, would feel insane. That’s a jump as big as GPT-3.5 to GPT-6 Astra in just 12 months. To remind you of the scale of progress that this leap would compress, GPT-3.5 was able to write a passable limerick and autocomplete a trivial Python function, but was mostly a useless toy, whereas Astra can build whole video games from scratch and churn out Fields Medal–worthy mathematical contributions to such a great extent that we’re already desensitized.

In the last four years, we’ve gone from a preschooler to a savant intern. If you made another jump that big, but starting in 2027 or 2028, you’d probably get a mind that would be vastly superhuman in domains that are even slightly verifiable. For example, it’d be better than Nvidia at coming up with the next generation of AI accelerators. It would make more money than the current human versions of Citadel and Jane Street (if it had equal access to the market). If you gave it remote access to a materials science experiment lab, it’d be better than the rest of humanity at finding a room-temperature superconductor.

Now, at this point, you might ask: How will even a superintelligence trained within a datacenter beat human experts in domains where the basis of that human expertise is years and years of real-world experience?

The way we’re currently making AIs smarter is by RLing them on tasks that are easy to automatically grade from within a datacenter: Do the million new lines of code the AI wrote pass the unit tests? Did the AI solve more open math problems? But of course, most of the world is not like this. I made this point in a recent essay:

How would we train an AI to build a business? How would you make an AI that’s really good at winning court cases? Or having a profitable day trading in the markets? Or helping a candidate win an election? The rollout requires interacting with the world and cannot be recreated simply within the datacenter.

So how will superintelligence get good at this kind of stuff? Let me be clear: I don’t think we can just bake the answer to every real-world problem into the weights. Rather, my claim is that scaling up RL training will give AIs the abilities necessary to ramp quickly in new contexts, even in hard-to-verify domains like the ones mentioned above.

Getting really good at any complex task takes two things. One is domain-specific knowledge. The other is a more general set of skills—the kind that capable humans have—like being able to seek out relevant information, make a plan, push forward on it through mistakes and obstacles, keep track of what you’ve learned, and collaborate with other people.

During the intelligence explosion, automated engineers will build tens of thousands of times more RL training environments than we have currently. These will be far longer-running, higher-quality, and more open-ended, and will cover a much wider range, than today’s environments.

The AIs will learn to make their way in an unfathomable number of virtual worlds that are each to today’s video games what a Bugatti is to a horse and buggy. These games will be far more difficult, messy, sprawling, and realistic than anything ever made for human entertainment. They will require AIs to cooperate or compete with teams of other AIs over long periods of time. For example, an AI will be dropped into a thriving simulated digital economy full of millions of other AIs and told to cofound a successful company. And it’s not like this AI will be stuck just thinking about the ideal corporate structure… it’ll go through an evolutionary process that involves centuries of corporate competition to figure out the optimal organizational techniques.

The AIs will also train themselves on endless backtests of everything in the history of science and tech and politics and culture—they’ll have to predict every discovery, invention, war, election, and quarterly earnings report that has ever happened. Here’s one prediction training task: Can an AI figure out general relativity given a training corpus that includes no information beyond 1700, which is far earlier than any human was on track to discover GR? Another example: Given every single newspaper article until 1962, can the AI predict how the Cuban Missile Crisis is going to unfold?7

And it’s not just the training data that these automated researchers will be improving. They will also radically improve the basic learning algorithms themselves, through breakthroughs in online learning and sample efficiency (both of which have verifiable proxies, as I discuss in the Appendix). In the same way that humans are much more efficient and effective at learning from data than current LLMs are, future AIs could be far beyond humans in learning efficiency.

Why do I think we’ll see lots of transfer from verifiable tasks to these more general skills? One reason is that even at one ten-thousandth of the scale of RL training that will be happening during the intelligence explosion, we’re already seeing lots of generalization. If you point Claude Code or Codex at a project it has never seen before, it knows how to orient itself, figure out how everything fits together, and then tackle an ambitious assignment.

Of course, it’s hard to measure how much models have improved at tasks that are not easily verifiable, because if we could… those tasks would be verifiable. But you can go talk to a new model and compare it to an old one. In my experience, AIs have gotten much better at things that have very little to do with code or math—for example, helping me research the abstract questions I needed to answer to write this essay.8

The other big piece of evidence for transfer is human evolution. Our general-purpose mental architecture was developed by evolution, which is an optimization process with a really crude verifier: Did you pass your genes on or not? In the ancestral environment, the tasks which influenced that outcome were things like hunting, fending off predators, and keeping your standing in a tribe.

These are a tiny subset of the kinds of tasks humans are able to tackle today. Evolution did not specifically optimize us to be able to write a Pulitzer Prize–winning biography, or make advanced semiconductors, or lead nations of millions of people, or come up with a new branch of mathematics. But, in optimizing us for survival on the savanna, evolution built a general-purpose learner.

In training these AIs, we’re running a similar process, except we’re doing so deliberately, with tasks more closely related to those needed for success in today’s world. And unlike evolution, AI companies are trying to improve transfer during training (for example, by making sure that performance improves on difficult tasks that were held out of training). If even dumb, blind evolution can get this much transfer out of building a mind that is effective at propagating itself on the savanna, then the deliberate effort that AI companies are putting into building a flexible and general intelligence that can ramp up rapidly in any new context should advance much further.

Now, even a superintelligent learner can’t figure out everything from inside a datacenter. So even these AIs will need some real-world experience. But I think they’ll be able to get that experience much faster than people expect, and that they’ll beat top human experts within months of being deployed.

Honestly, one thing that’s guiding my intuition with all this stuff is that I have a lot of 20-something-year-old friends whom I’ve watched accomplish incredible things and build world-leading companies and ventures in domains they entered into with no previous experience.

History is full of super-competent young people who ran circles around the world they were dropped into. By the age of 27, Napoleon had stacked victory after victory against far larger armies from the other great powers of Europe. By 25, just two years after he got into the oil business, Rockefeller was running one of the world’s largest refineries.

Rockefeller and Napoleon needed experience, yes, but only a couple of years’ worth, not decades. Whatever was going on inside those guys’ brains, AIs should be able to replicate (or even exceed: There’s no reason to think humans are the ceiling on learning quickly from experience).

Furthermore, unlike Napoleon or Rockefeller, AIs can accumulate years of deployed context in just weeks of calendar time. For example, imagine that you wanted one of these future AIs to run a Fortune 500 company better than its current CEO. How quickly could it ramp up? Well, if you let it shadow that CEO, on its first morning, it could read every email, Slack message, and document that the company has ever produced. By the end of the first day, parallel copie...

00-44:26 您的浏览器不支持音频播放。请升级。非常感谢 Max Farrens、Gabe Fried 和 Thomas Larsen 与我一起完成本文的写作和研究的重要部分。

您可以在 YouTube、Spotify 和 Apple 播客上观看或听我讲述这篇文章。

如果你今年早些时候问我我们离超级智能还有多远，我可能会说至少是十年内的大部分时间。但在过去的三个月里，我更新了很多观点。我一直在播客内外与人们讨论这个问题。我一直在关注人工智能在可验证领域的进展，并思考这对人工智能研究本身意味着什么。

我现在认为，我们距离人工智能研究与人工智能研究中最优秀的人类一样优秀，只需要几年，甚至可能只有几个月的时间。我还开始相信，自动化人工智能研究将在一年内取得如此多的进展，以至于不久之后（到 2030 年，但似乎最早是明年），我们将拥有至少与各个领域最优秀的人类专家一样优秀的人工智能。我知道这是一个疯狂的说法，就连几个月前我自己也不相信。让我向您介绍一下我的想法是如何改变的。

在我们进行更多推测性争论之前，我想指出，我们有大量证据表明人工智能已经极大地加速了人工智能在前沿领域的进一步进步。

例如，独立评估组织 METR 在嵌入 Anthropic 三个月后得出结论，Anthropic 在范围广泛的任务上的总体进度是一年前的 2 倍，并且“今天这种加速的大部分可能归因于 Anthropic 广泛使用人工智能进行研发”。

OpenAI 在 9 月份发表了一篇有关此问题的博客文章，其中显示 OpenAI 研究人员中最重的 10% 的 AI 用户从夏初每天使用内部编码代理的费用约为 1,000 美元，到 8 月底每天使用的内部编码代理的费用超过 7,000 美元。

九月份，Anthropic 就其自己的人工智能提升发表了类似的帖子。他们报告称，截至 8 月，Claude“领导”了 Anthropic 超过 26% 的人工智能研发工作，而 2 月份这一比例还不到 1%。1

数学是人工智能研究将会发生的事情的预览当我想到如果人工智能自动化人工智能研究将会有多大的影响，以及这会发生多久，对我来说一个真正重要的更新就是看到人工智能在数学中的能力爆炸的速度有多快。当前的人工智能正在解决范围广泛的数学问题，就像热刀切黄油一样。就在两年前，我问达里奥，为什么法学硕士无法利用他们在如此多不同领域的丰富知识来连接不同的想法并做出新的发现。你瞧，我们在这里：在数学这样一个完全可验证的领域，人工智能正在很大程度上进行这种搜索和匹配发现，以至于数百个重要结果（世界上顶尖的数学家和计算机科学家花了几十年的时间试图解决这些问题）正在被大量生产出来，作为炒作未来模型发布的支线任务。

我们从 2023 年的“这个模型无法可靠地添加四位数字”到 2024 年的“这个模型几乎无法解决高中数学竞赛中的任何问题”，到 2025 年的“哦，它可以在国际数学奥林匹克竞赛中赢得金牌”，再到今年早些时候的“哇，它正在解决开放式 Erdős 问题，但也许只是因为没有人尝试过”，速度之快真是太疯狂了。来解决这些特定问题，类似的解决方案已经出现在文献中，”大约一个月前，“好吧，它他妈的在 88 小时内解决了千禧年奖问题。”

小说《伊甸园之东》中有一句话：“关于诸神的陨落，有一点是肯定的：他们不会堕落一点；他们会崩溃、粉碎。”

确实，进步不成比例地偏向于数学中充满验证的部分，比如寻找反例（而不是提出新理论）。托比·奥德 (Toby Ord) 最近发表了一篇关于此的精彩文章。他写道，“虽然当前的人工智能系统开始自动化数学证明，但目前几乎没有证据表明它们可以提出强有力的问题或找到深刻的数学探究新领域。”

但同样的观点的另一种说法是：当前的人工智能系统已经解决了千年奖问题，但都没有能力提出强有力的问题或找到深刻的数学探究新领域。

从广义上讲，这种解决范围广泛的问题的能力对于机器学习研究来说比数学更重要。这是因为数学研究的目标不仅仅是证明或反驳一长串猜想，而是扩展人类对数学概念的理解。提出拓扑、群论或笛卡尔网格的概念远比确切地知道可以从 n 个点组成多少个单位对更重要。我们主要关心这些深奥的问题，因为它们可能会引发新的数学理论。

title: Doc: Amazon, wary of AI agents favoring sites with better data, plans to gather data on nearly every product sold anywhere, including by crawling rivals' sites (Greg Bensinger/Reuters)
title_en: Doc: Amazon, wary of AI agents favoring sites with better data, plans to gather data on nearly every product sold anywhere, including by crawling rivals' sites (Greg Bensinger/Reuters)
author: Reuters
article_content:
SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Amazon (AMZN.O) has a secret plan to ensure shoppers never need to leave its site: own the world’s product information.

Called World Product Graph, the initiative seeks to hoover up data on virtually every item for sale on Earth, whether Amazon stocks it or not, according to an internal document reviewed by Reuters, and to people familiar with the matter.

In so doing, Amazon could truly become the everything store, offering deep data on a vast array of goods and cutting in to Google's (GOOGL.O) dominance in online search, while also fending off rival Walmart's (WMT.O) growing e-commerce business.

It also serves to address the continued rise of AI agents, software that can complete shopping tasks autonomously for users. According to the document, Amazon's own AI-driven search agent was providing inaccurate information.

And if fully implemented, World Product Graph could draw shoppers away from rival e-commerce sites that have far less data.

“Amazon cannot be the go-destination for every shopping mission if customers must leave to research product relationships on Google, brand websites, and review sites,” according to the document. “These answers exist, but the only way to find them has been to leave Amazon for painstaking research on brand websites, third party review sites and tech forums.”

Reuters could not determine if or when this plan may be implemented, though the document, written like a press release, has an aspirational future release date of October 1, 2027.

"Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn't necessarily reflect our current plans," said Amazon, in a statement. "We're constantly working on new ideas and technologies to make Amazon's product catalog comprehensive, accurate, and helpful for customers."

Already, many consumers begin researching products on Amazon. But according to a 2025 Morgan Stanley research report, the 16% of online shoppers who do so on Amazon is dwarfed by Google’s 57%. However, when customers know exactly what product they plan to buy, Amazon has the advantage, with 41% of searches starting there, compared with 23% for Google and 18% for Walmart.

World Product Graph “depends on discovering how brands organize their products on their own websites,” the document says. That will entail some brands and retailers contributing product data continuously to Amazon, but also Amazon independently crawling other retailers’ websites.

Reuters could not determine how Amazon planned to crawl the sites or whether it would need to seek permission in all cases.

Amazon has already signed up Coca-Cola (KO.N) and Bayer (BAYGn.DE), among others, to contribute product data, the document says. And the company held a “CEO-level P&G/Amazon summit” for a trial with Procter & Gamble (PG.N). The companies didn't respond to requests for comment.

Amazon is shuffling staff internally to get the project off the ground, according to one of the people, though Reuters could not determine if the October 1 date is a realistic deadline for making the plan public.

The document laying out the plan is what is known internally as a PR/FAQ — press release and frequently asked questions — which is typically a six-page narrative memo laying out the rationale and business case for a new product or service. Not all PR/FAQs lead to a service being introduced and, the people said, World Product Graph could be modified or aborted due to financial or other concerns.

The initiative is part of Amazon’s Selection & Catalog Systems unit, according to the document, and is being organized under Robert Tekiela, a vice president in the division. He did not respond to a request for comment.

With the more complete data, Amazon can help users determine with more certainty which is the most recent model or colorway of a vacuum cleaner or tablet computer while also guiding them toward more subjective criteria like which is best for them based on their shopping history or other data, the document shows.

The project would also tackle what it said had been problems with Amazon’s AI-powered search engine known as Rufus — which the company began calling “Alexa for Shopping” in May. “Many Rufus answers are factually wrong or incomplete, but customers lack expertise to detect these errors,” the document states.

Further, users conduct about 83 million searches weekly using Rufus, and running them is “expensive,” according to the document. More data would allow Amazon to use less expensive models, more efficiently.

“I used to spend an hour on Reddit figuring this stuff out,” says a fake customer in an imagined quote in the document. “It’s like the store finally knows what it’s selling.”

In its statement to Reuters, Amazon, referring to the PR/FAQ, said "the usage figures are significantly outdated" and that its data shows that Alexa for Shopping is roughly 97% accurate globally.

World Product Graph would help serve at least one other important function — staving off the growing threat of alternative AI shopping agents, the people said. CEO Andy Jassy sought during the company's third-quarter earnings call to downplay agents' impact, saying “few customers are doing much shopping this way yet” and that Amazon’s advertising business has been minimally impacted.

Yet Amazon executives have grown wary of AI shopping agents that may send customer traffic to other sites that have greater or more complete data, according to people familiar with the matter.

Meta’s Muse agent, for instance, has proven popular with customers already, garnering more than 10 million users in the US and Canada since launching in September. Amazon in the same month blocked Muse from its retail site and last year sued AI firm Perplexity to prevent similar access, a case that is ongoing.

Jassy said Alexa for Shopping has been used by over 400 million people in the past year.

Muse, however, "has the potential to become the most widely used consumer AI application since ChatGPT,” JPMorgan said in a research note. Responding to a post saying xAI's Grok agent was blocked on Amazon, Elon Musk wrote on X last month: “Maybe we should start a competitor to Amazon."

By creating the world's most extensive storehouse of product data, Amazon could ensure AI agents working on behalf of shoppers will be compelled to seek products out on Amazon.com and not other retailers’ sites, the people said. That would also help protect Amazon’s growing advertising business.

Shares of the Seattle retailer were down just over 1% at $264.12 at midday on Friday, part of a broader selloff following the resignation this week of Nvidia NVDA.O CEO Jensen Huang.

Employees have described World Product Graph as the beginnings of an effort to make the site a one-stop shop for buying anything imaginable, an expansion of existing services known as “Buy for Me” and “Shop Direct,” which list on Amazon products sold on other sites, allowing customers to buy them with Amazon as an intermediary.

“Customers have always been able to find products on Amazon,” Tekiela said in the document. “What’s been missing is understanding – how do these products relate to each other, which one is right for me, and what else should I consider?”

article_content_zh:
路透旧金山 11 月 13 日 - 亚马逊 (AMZN.O) 有一项秘密计划，旨在确保购物者永远不需要离开其网站：拥有全球产品信息。

据路透社和知情人士透露，该计划名为“世界产品图”，旨在收集地球上几乎所有待售商品的数据，无论亚马逊是否有库存。

通过这样做，亚马逊可以真正成为万能商店，提供大量商品的深度数据，并削弱谷歌 (GOOGL.O) 在在线搜索领域的主导地位，同时还能抵御竞争对手沃尔玛 (WMT.O) 不断增长的电子商务业务。

它还有助于解决人工智能代理的持续增长问题，这些软件可以为用户自主完成购物任务。根据该文件，亚马逊自己的人工智能驱动的搜索代理提供了不准确的信息。

如果完全实施，世界产品图可能会吸引购物者远离数据少得多的竞争对手电子商务网站。

该文件称：“如果顾客必须离开去谷歌、品牌网站和评论网站上研究产品关系，那么亚马逊就不可能成为每次购物任务的首选目的地。” “这些答案是存在的，但找到它们的唯一方法是离开亚马逊，在品牌网站、第三方评论网站和技术论坛上进行艰苦的研究。”

路透社无法确定该计划是否或何时实施，尽管该文件的编写方式类似于新闻稿，预计未来发布日期为 2027 年 10 月 1 日。

亚马逊在一份声明中表示：“过时的草稿文件常常描绘出不完整的画面，像这样的集思广益文件的存在并不一定反映我们当前的计划。” “我们不断致力于新的想法和技术，以使亚马逊的产品目录全面、准确，并为客户提供帮助。”

许多消费者已经开始在亚马逊上研究产品。但根据摩根士丹利 2025 年的一份研究报告，在亚马逊上购物的 16% 的消费者与谷歌的 57% 相比相形见绌。然而，当顾客确切知道他们计划购买什么产品时，亚马逊具有优势，41% 的搜索都是从那里开始的，而谷歌为 23%，沃尔玛为 18%。

文件称，世界产品图谱“取决于发现品牌如何在自己的网站上组织产品”。这将需要一些品牌和零售商不断向亚马逊提供产品数据，但亚马逊也需要独立抓取其他零售商的网站。

路透社无法确定亚马逊计划如何抓取这些网站，或者是否在所有情况下都需要寻求许可。

文件称，亚马逊已经与可口可乐 (KO.N) 和拜耳 (BAYGn.DE) 等公司签约，以提供产品数据。并与宝洁公司（PG.N）一起举办了“CEO级宝洁/亚马逊峰会”。这些公司没有回应置评请求。

据其中一名知情人士透露，亚马逊正在内部调整员工，以启动该项目，但路透社无法确定10月1日是否是公布该计划的现实截止日期。

列出该计划的文件在内部被称为 PR/FAQ（新闻稿和常见问题），通常是一份六页的叙述性备忘录，列出新产品或服务的基本原理和业务案例。知情人士表示，并非所有 PR/FAQ 都会导致推出服务，而且由于财务或其他问题，世界产品图谱可能会被修改或中止。

该文件称，该计划是亚马逊选择和目录系统部门的一部分，由该部门副总裁罗伯特·特基拉 (Robert Tekiela) 负责组织。他没有回应置评请求。

文件显示，有了更完整的数据，亚马逊可以帮助用户更确定地确定吸尘器或平板电脑的最新型号或配色，同时引导他们采用更主观的标准，例如根据他们的购物历史或其他数据选择最适合他们的标准。

该项目还将解决据称亚马逊 AI 驱动的搜索引擎 Rufus 存在的问题——该公司从 5 月份开始将其称为“Alexa for Shopping”。文件指出：“Rufus 的许多答案实际上是错误的或不完整的，但客户缺乏检测这些错误的专业知识。”

此外，根据该文件，用户每周使用 Rufus 进行约 8300 万次搜索，并且运行它们的成本“昂贵”。更多数据将使亚马逊能够更高效地使用更便宜的模型。

“我曾经在Reddit上花了一个小时来弄清楚这些东西，”一名假客户在文件中虚构的引文中说。“就好像这家商店终于知道自己在卖什么了。”

亚马逊在给路透社的声明中提到 PR/FAQ 时表示，“使用数据明显过时”，其数据显示 Alexa for Shopping 在全球范围内的准确率约为 97%。

知情人士表示，世界产品图谱将有助于提供至少一项重要功能——抵御替代人工智能购物代理日益增长的威胁。首席执行官安迪·贾西(Andy Jassy)在公司第三季度财报电话会议上寻求淡化代理商的影响，他表示“目前还很少有顾客以这种方式进行大量购物”，而且亚马逊的广告业务受到的影响微乎其微。

然而，据知情人士透露，亚马逊高管对人工智能购物代理越来越警惕，因为它们可能会将客户流量发送到拥有更多或更完整数据的其他网站。

例如，Meta 的 Muse 代理已被证明很受客户欢迎，自 9 月份推出以来在美国和加拿大拥有超过 1000 万用户。同月，亚马逊屏蔽了 Muse 的零售网站，并于去年起诉人工智能公司 Perplexity，以阻止类似的访问，该案目前仍在审理中。

Jassy 表示，去年有超过 4 亿人使用 Alexa for Shopping。

然而，摩根大通在一份研究报告中表示，Muse“有潜力成为自 ChatGPT 以来使用最广泛的消费者人工智能应用程序”。埃隆·马斯克上个月在 X 上回应称 xAI 的 Grok 代理在亚马逊上被屏蔽的帖子时写道：“也许我们应该创建一个亚马逊的竞争对手。”

知情人士表示，通过创建世界上最广泛的产品数据仓库，亚马逊可以确保代表购物者工作的人工智能代理将被迫在亚马逊网站上而不是其他零售商的网站上寻找产品。这也将有助于保护亚马逊不断增长的广告业务。

周五中午，这家西雅图零售商的股价下跌略高于 1%，至 264.12 美元，这是 Nvidia NVDA.O 首席执行官黄仁勋本周辞职后更广泛抛售的一部分。

员工们将 World Product Graph 描述为使该网站成为购买任何可以想象到的东西的一站式商店的努力的开始，是对现有服务“Buy for Me”和“Shop Direct”的扩展，这些服务列出了在其他网站上销售的亚马逊产品，允许客户通过亚马逊作为中介进行购买。

Further, users conduct about 83 million searches weekly using Rufus, and running them is “expensive,” according to the document. More data would allow Amazon to use less expensive models, more efficiently.

“I used to spend an hour on Reddit figuring this stuff out,” says a fake customer in an imagined quote in the document. “It’s like the store finally knows what it’s selling.”

In its statement to Reuters, Amazon, referring to the PR/FAQ, said "the usage figures are significantly outdated" and that its data shows that Alexa for Shopping is roughly 97% accurate globally.

World Product Graph would help serve at least one other important function — staving off the growing threat of alternative AI shopping agents, the people said. CEO Andy Jassy sought during the company's third-quarter earnings call to downplay agents' impact, saying “few customers are doing much shopping this way yet” and that Amazon’s advertising business has been minimally impacted.

Yet Amazon executives have grown wary of AI shopping agents that may send customer traffic to other sites that have greater or more complete data, according to people familiar with the matter.

Meta’s Muse agent, for instance, has proven popular with customers already, garnering more than 10 million users in the US and Canada since launching in September. Amazon in the same month blocked Muse from its retail site and last year sued AI firm Perplexity to prevent similar access, a case that is ongoing.

Jassy said Alexa for Shopping has been used by over 400 million people in the past year.

Muse, however, "has the potential to become the most widely used consumer AI application since ChatGPT,” JPMorgan said in a research note. Responding to a post saying xAI's Grok agent was blocked on Amazon, Elon Musk wrote on X last month: “Maybe we should start a competitor to Amazon."

By creating the world's most extensive storehouse of product data, Amazon could ensure AI agents working on behalf of shoppers will be compelled to seek products out on Amazon.com and not other retailers’ sites, the people said. That would also help protect Amazon’s growing advertising business.

Shares of the Seattle retailer were down just over 1% at $264.12 at midday on Friday, part of a broader selloff following the resignation this week of Nvidia NVDA.O CEO Jensen Huang.

Employees have described World Product Graph as the beginnings of an effort to make the site a one-stop shop for buying anything imaginable, an expansion of existing services known as “Buy for Me” and “Shop Direct,” which list on Amazon products sold on other sites, allowing customers to buy them with Amazon as an intermediary.

“Customers have always been able to find products on Amazon,” Tekiela said in the document. “What’s been missing is understanding – how do these products relate to each other, which one is right for me, and what else should I consider?”

title: Sources and messages: Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, including general counsel Tim Teter, about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang (Reuters)
title_en: Sources and messages: Jensen Huang misled several Nvidia leaders, including general counsel Tim Teter, about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang (Reuters)
author: Reuters
article_content:
SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang misled several of the company's leaders, including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld, about the nature of his relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, with whom he had an affair, according to two people familiar with the matter and internal correspondence reviewed by Reuters.

Reuters reviewed several exchanges from October on condition of not quoting verbatim from the messages. The news agency is the first to report on this correspondence.

On Thursday, Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, a spectacular fall from the chip industry's heights where he was a pioneer of technology central to the recent boom in artificial intelligence.

He apologized in a statement on Sunday for being unfaithful to his wife and for disappointing the company. His statement did not specifically name Alice Huang, a former top executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed International, whom the US was investigating for potentially spying for China. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang share a last name but are not related.

The New York Times earlier this week reported Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia employee, and Reuters reported on Thursday that Huang had another intimate relationship with a different Nvidia employee.

Teter did not respond to a request for comment. Wagonfeld did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A representative for ex-CEO Huang and an Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment. A phone call and email to contact information listed on a business card for Alice Huang went unanswered.

During the autumn of 2025 and in October 2026, in response to press queries that drew some Nvidia leaders' attention to his relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang, Huang at both times described their interactions as appropriate, the people said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Reuters only reviewed messages from the exchanges in October, not the ones from 2025.

In two separate messages in October, Huang told Nvidia leaders, including Teter and Wagonfeld, that the interactions reflected standard business dealings with customers. In other messages, Huang affirmed the routine nature of his interactions with Megaspeed.

Nvidia's Huang also discussed taking legal action against the New York Times after it published an article in October of last year that drew attention to his meetings in public with Alice Huang, the people said.

That article had prompted Jensen Huang to communicate with some Nvidia leaders in 2025 about their interactions, which he did not describe as an affair, the people said. Ultimately, neither Nvidia nor Huang filed a lawsuit against the paper. A spokesperson for the New York Times said the paper received no legal demand.

It is unclear when his relationship with Alice Huang became intimate. Photos posted online and verified by Reuters show them together in the US, China and elsewhere, dating as far back as December 2023.

On November 10, the independent members of Nvidia's board said they hired Wall Street law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation after the New York Times and Wall Street Journal reported on Huang's relations with Alice Huang, as well as US authorities' suspicions that she was spying for China. Beijing has denied she is a spy.

Reuters has not independently verified whether Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government.

Jensen Huang said in an interview with Bloomberg published on October 29 that the US government had not informed him about its suspicions regarding Alice Huang.

Nvidia's stock has fallen more than 30% since its October 6 closing high, erasing more than $1.8 trillion from its market capitalization.

article_content_zh:
路透在没有逐字引述的条件下，回顾了10月份的几次对话。该通讯社首先报道了这一通信。

周四，黄仁勋辞去了英伟达首席执行官的职务，这是从芯片行业巅峰的一次惊人的跌落，他是最近人工智能繁荣的核心技术先驱。

知情人士匿名表示，在2025年秋季和2026年10月，针对媒体的提问（这些提问引起了英伟达一些高层对黄仁勋与Megaspeed和黄仁慧之间关系问题的关注），黄仁勋在两次回应中均将他们之间的互动描述为恰当。路透社仅查阅了10月份的往来消息，并未查阅2025年的消息。

在10月份的两条独立消息中，黄仁勋告诉包括Teter和Wagonfeld在内的英伟达高管，这些互动反映了与客户的标准商业往来。在其他消息中，黄仁勋确认了他与Megaspeed之间互动的例行性质。

知情人士称，去年 10 月《纽约时报》发表了一篇文章，引起人们对他与爱丽丝·黄 (Alice Huang) 的公开会面的关注，之后 Nvidia 的黄还讨论了对《纽约时报》采取法律行动。

知情人士称，那篇文章促使黄仁勋在 2025 年与 Nvidia 的一些领导人就他们的互动进行了沟通，但他并未将其描述为外遇。最终，英伟达和黄仁勋都没有对该论文提起诉讼。 《纽约时报》发言人表示，该报没有收到任何法律要求。

目前尚不清楚他与黄爱丽的关系何时变得亲密。网上发布并经路透社核实的照片显示，他们在美国、中国和其他地方在一起，时间可以追溯到 2023 年 12 月。

11月10日，在《纽约时报》和《华尔街日报》报道黄与爱丽丝黄的关系以及美国当局怀疑她为中国从事间谍活动后，英伟达董事会独立成员表示，他们聘请了华尔街律师事务所Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz进行独立调查。北京否认她是间谍。

路透社尚未独立核实黄爱丽是否代表中国政府工作。

黄仁勋在 10 月 29 日接受彭博社采访时表示，美国政府尚未将其对 Alice Huang 的怀疑告知他。

自 10 月 6 日收盘高点以来，英伟达股价已下跌超过 30%，市值蒸发逾 1.8 万亿美元。

title: Sources: the FAA outage occurred after an update to the private communications network that connects the ATC system caused the system to reboot and crash (Kierra Frazier/CBS News)
title_en: Sources: the FAA outage occurred after an update to the private communications network that connects the ATC system caused the system to reboot and crash (Kierra Frazier/CBS News)
author: CBS News
article_content:
A rare nationwide ground stop on all departing U.S. flights that lasted several hours Friday has been lifted, and flights are resuming, the Federal Aviation Administration said. Officials said the issue stemmed from a "telecommunication outage."

"At 8:15 tonight, Eastern time, we've opened up the airspace," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said during a news briefing Friday night. "Now does that mean every flight is going to fly right now? It's going to be slow. So if you're watching, you're at an airport, check with your airline."

In a social media post following the briefing, the FAA said that "before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable."

The FAA had issued the ground stop on all departing flights due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." The ground stop lasted about five hours.

Duffy attributed the ground stop to outdated air traffic control technology and routers overloaded by data.

"What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," Duffy said during the news conference. ".. Our routers actually got overloaded with data and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down."

"The FAA lifted the ground stop and some flight departures are resuming," the FAA confirmed in a social media post following the briefing. "Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable."

An update to the private communications network that connects America's air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage, multiple sources told CBS News earlier Friday. The system is operated by L3Harris, which did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in Friday's briefing that new security patches introduced into the older system appeared to "overwhelm" its routers.

Duffy said the FAA would try to move as many flights as possible Friday night depending on crew capacity.

"If not, we're going to start tomorrow [Saturday] morning with our airline partners moving those aircraft. But it's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.

There were more than 10,000 delays and over 4,000 cancellations listed Friday, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.

Duffy said he thinks flights will be "back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel" during the Thanksgiving holiday later this month.

Mullin told reporters in an earlier briefing outside the White House Friday that "there was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious act against us. It was just a telecommunication outage, as of right now."

"There is no indication, we had no reason to believe, that as of right now, that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin said. "This was a telecommunication outage throughout FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights. And all the flights are accounted for."

Mullin reiterated Friday night that there was no cyberattack and the ground stop was not related to the massive global Microsoft outage.

"I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft," Mullin said during the news briefing with Duffy. "I know a lot of people are making that jump. This is so far what we've seen. There is actually no cyberattack. We're still working through that process."

He also said flights will be able to land safely.

"We are assured that everybody is safe. Everybody that's going to be in the air, that's currently on the plane, the loved ones, as I said, we're going to get you on the ground and we're doing it in a safe manner," Mullin said.

Federal agencies are all working together on the situation, Mullin added.

"I don't want to say that this is a crisis, but it is because we're.. we had to do a nationwide ground stoppage," he said.

According to the flight tracking site Flightradar24, there were about 3,100 airborne aircraft bound for U.S. airports when the ground stop began.

Delays began piling up at major airports across the country in Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York City, Los Angeles and Baltimore.

"This is absolutely unprecedented," said Robert Sumwalt, a former chair of the National Transportation Safety Board and a CBS News transportation safety expert. "I was an airline pilot for 24 years. I was in the air on 9/11. That was the last major ground stop. There was one back in 2023 for just a few hours. This is absolutely unbelievable that this could happen in this day and age."

On Friday night, Duffy renewed his call for Congress to approve emergency funding to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.

"But you will have more of these," Duffy said during the news conference. "You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build."

Mullin argued that the incident demonstrated why he believed piecemeal modernization was insufficient and said the Trump administration wants a complete replacement of the air traffic control system, at an estimated cost of $50 billion.

The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, known as FTI, is the communications backbone that connects air traffic control centers and other FAA facilities. It supports the transmission of essential voice communications and operational data used to manage air traffic.

The FAA awarded Harris Corp., the predecessor to L3Harris, a contract to modernize, operate and manage the network in July 2002, more than 24 years ago.

A November 2023 FAA-commissioned safety review described the FTI network as obsolete and said it depended on an older communications technology known as TDM.

The review also warned that the technology was no longer supported by the telecommunications infrastructure on which it relied and that an unexpected failure could leave individual FAA facilities, or even an entire regional air traffic control center, disconnected from the broader network.

In January 2023, a nationwide ground stop was ordered for a few hours, and domestic flights were delayed nationwide due to an FAA system outage. The FAA said at the time that its flight personnel alert system went down overnight.

Olivia Rinaldi, Pat Milton, Kris Van Cleave and Sarah N. Lynch contributed to this report.

ai_analysis.takeaway_zh: 此次事故暴露了关键性基础设施领域“打补丁式”升级的系统性风险，即在陈旧架构之上进行现代化升级极易产生兼容性灾难。这反映了美国在关键工业基础设施更新过程中，存在严重的性能与可靠性验证断层，必须从架构层面重构而非单纯依赖修补。
ai_analysis.takeaway_en: This accident exposes the systemic risk of 'patch-based' upgrades for critical infrastructure, where applying modern security patches to obsolete architectures often triggers compatibility failures. It highlights a critical disconnect between performance validation and industrial infrastructure management in the U.S., necessitating an architectural overhaul rather than ad-hoc remediation.

美国联邦航空管理局表示，周五持续数小时的所有美国出发航班在全国范围内罕见的地面停留已经取消，航班正在恢复。官员们表示，问题源于“电信中断”。

“东部时间今晚 8 点 15 分，我们开放了领空，”交通部长肖恩·达菲 (Sean Duffy) 在周五晚上的新闻发布会上表示。 “这是否意味着现在每个航班都会起飞？速度会很慢。所以，如果你在机场观看，请咨询你的航空公司。”

美国联邦航空局在简报后的社交媒体帖子中表示，“在批准航班恢复之前，我们彻底测试了我们的系统，以确认它们稳定且运行仍然可靠。”

由于“特殊情况和安全原因”，美国联邦航空局已对所有离港航班发出地面停止令。地面停留持续了大约五个小时。

达菲将这次地面停靠归咎于过时的空中交通管制技术和数据超载的路由器。

达菲在新闻发布会上说：“我们拥有的是非常古老的空中交通管制系统。” “..我们的路由器实际上数据过载..他们开始给我们带来来自这些路由器的数据不一致。因此，我们关闭了系统。”

“美国联邦航空局取消了地面停止，一些航班起飞正在恢复，”美国联邦航空局在简报后在社交媒体上发帖证实。 “在批准航班恢复之前，我们彻底测试了我们的系统，以确认它们稳定且运营仍然可靠。”

周五早些时候，多名消息人士告诉哥伦比亚广播公司新闻，连接美国空中交通管制系统的私人通信网络的更新导致系统重新启动，导致坠机和通信中断。该系统由 L3Harris 运营，该公司没有立即回应哥伦比亚广播公司新闻的置评请求。

国土安全部部长马克韦恩·穆林在周五的新闻发布会上表示，旧系统中引入的新安全补丁似乎“压垮”了其路由器。

达菲表示，美国联邦航空局将根据机组人员容量，在周五晚上尝试调动尽可能多的航班。

“如果没有，我们将于明天（周六）早上开始与我们的航空公司合作伙伴一起转移这些飞机。但我们需要一些时间来解决今天下午发生的事情，”达菲说。

根据航班跟踪网站 FlightAware 的数据，周五有超过 10,000 起延误和超过 4,000 起取消航班。

达菲表示，他认为本月晚些时候的感恩节假期期间，航班将“随着我们进入旅行热潮而恢复并投入运营”。

穆林周五在白宫外举行的早些时候的新闻发布会上告诉记者，“到目前为止，没有迹象表明这是针对我们的邪恶行为。到目前为止，这只是一次电信中断。”

title: Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data
title_en: Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Listing the details of everything for sale everywhere is meant to make Amazon more useful than Reddit for people and AI agents.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon has plans to build a vault of data on every product sold anywhere on the internet, even products Amazon doesn’t sell, and make the information available through its own site, according to Reuters. The project, called the “World Product Graph,” is meant to make it less likely that shoppers leave Amazon to do their product research on Reddit or Google, and make it more likely shoppers end up at Amazon even if they’re searching for a product sold elsewhere. The same goes for AI agents — if Amazon has the largest stockpile of shopping data, AI agents may rely on its index of products over others, so even people shopping with bots will end up on its pages.

Links to outside retailers’ products have already started popping up on Amazon through the “shop direct” feature it launched last year. The company also has its own AI shopping assistant, Alexa for Shopping, previously called Rufus. The World Product Graph project would also be aimed at fixing issues with the AI by providing it more data. According to Reuters, an internal Amazon document on the project says “Many Rufus answers are factually wrong or incomplete” and running users’ Amazon searches with the AI is expensive. Adding more data is reportedly supposed to make the system more accurate and able to use cheaper models.

Whether this actually ships is still up in the air. The internal document reportedly says the project “depends on discovering how brands organize their products on their own websites,” which could involve Amazon crawling other retailers’ sites. Reuters says it’s unclear “if or when this plan may be implemented,” but said the document on it included an October 1st, 2027 release date.

Amazon said in a statement to Reuters that “Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn’t necessarily reflect our current plans.”

该主题的帖子将添加到您的每日电子邮件摘要和主页源中。

列出各地待售商品的详细信息，旨在让亚马逊比 Reddit 对人们和人工智能代理更有用。

该作者的帖子将添加到您的每日电子邮件摘要和主页源中。

亚马逊计划为互联网上任何地方销售的每种产品（甚至亚马逊不销售的产品）建立一个数据库，并通过自己的网站提供这些信息。该项目名为“世界产品图谱”，旨在降低购物者离开亚马逊而在 Reddit 或 Google 上进行产品研究的可能性，并让购物者更有可能最终选择亚马逊，即使他们正在搜索其他地方销售的产品。人工智能代理也是如此——如果亚马逊拥有最大的购物数据库存，人工智能代理可能会比其他人更依赖其产品索引，因此即使是使用机器人购物的人最终也会访问其页面。

通过去年推出的“直接购买”功能，外部零售商产品的链接已经开始在亚马逊上出现。该公司还拥有自己的人工智能购物助手 Alexa for Shopping，以前称为 Rufus。世界产品图项目还旨在通过向人工智能提供更多数据来解决人工智能的问题。据路透社报道，亚马逊关于该项目的一份内部文件称，“许多 Rufus 的答案实际上是错误的或不完整的”，并且使用人工智能运行用户的亚马逊搜索成本高昂。据报道，添加更多数据应该会使系统更加准确并能够使用更便宜的模型。

这是否真的可以发货仍然悬而未决。据报道，内部文件称该项目“取决于发现品牌如何在自己的网站上组织产品”，这可能涉及亚马逊抓取其他零售商的网站。路透社表示，目前尚不清楚“该计划是否或何时实施”，但表示文件中包含了 2027 年 10 月 1 日的发布日期。

亚马逊在给路透社的一份声明中表示，“过时的草稿文件常常描绘出不完整的画面，像这样的集思广益文件的存在并不一定反映我们当前的计划。”

title: ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you
title_en: ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
After adding a card to the wallet, your Dots agents can use it to buy things in response to your prompts, but they’ll check in with you each time before checking out. OpenAI’s support page says every purchase with ChatGPT Wallet requires a security check with biometric verification like Face ID or a fingerprint scan.

[Image: Users have to approve every purchase from ChatGPT Wallet. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/openai-chatgpt-wallet-approval-pop-up.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all]

[Media: https://twitter.com/ChatGPT/status/2121283151729496235?a=Dzv0TkF6sRIc6NCqEso&s=20]

After you review the AI agent’s purchase and sign off on it, OpenAI says that, similar to using tap to pay, Apple Pay, or Google Wallet, it substitutes your credit card details with a payment token, so your actual card info isn’t shared with your Dots agent or the business you’re buying from. Eventually, OpenAI says it expects “users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases.”

ChatGPT Wallet might not work everywhere. Some retailers have restrictions on AI agents or block them altogether. Earlier this year, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agents. OpenAI says that in order for agents to use ChatGPT Wallet, “websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.”

title_en: Jensen Huang's ouster likely traces back to Nvidia's risky business practices more than his personal life
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
A WSJ report suggests Jensen Huang was pushed out more over his business practices than over his affairs.

Nvidia built a risky credit program under Huang, the Wall Street Journal reports. The company offered AI cloud providers and data center developers billions of dollars in financial guarantees so they could afford Nvidia chips. Huang's son-in-law Nico Caprez pushed the program and promised partners quick closings. In return, the cloud providers were supposed to give Nvidia a cut of their revenue.

The largest deal involved talks with OpenAI over a $250 billion guarantee for a data center in Ohio. Nvidia shares fell 5% after the deal became public. Interim CEO Colette Kress, who had been CFO, then cut Nvidia's commitment to OpenAI in half. The scaled-back deal was signed in August.Ad

According to the WSJ, Kress had already questioned internally how the guarantees were valued and what they would return and had tried to rein in Caprez. In an August meeting, Huang reportedly called her "a deer in the headlights" and dismissed her as a mere "reporting CFO" who didn't help him with strategy or decision-making. Circular AI deals by Nvidia and other cloud and chip companies have drawn criticism since at least last year for inflating a bubble.Ad

Nvidia's stock valuation also reportedly frustrated Huang. The company's average monthly stock multiple fell from 23 to 16 between May and October, and Nvidia responded with the largest share buyback in its history.

Major cloud providers were planning to adopt alternative chips and reduce their dependence on Nvidia. With Nvidia committed to buying large volumes of wafers and memory, Huang described the threat as an “avalanche” rolling toward the chipmaker.Ad

At the GTC conference in Berlin in October, Huang used a story about a soup vendor in Japan to put pressure on half a dozen cloud CEOs. He said he had stood in a long line and eaten one of the best soups of his life. When he asked for seconds, the vendor said no because too many people were waiting and he was running out of soup. "He's a better businessperson than all of you," Huang told the CEOs, according to the WSJ.

The reasoning behind the story was that the soup vendor didn't sell his whole inventory to one or two customers. He kept prices high and his customer base broad. Huang said the cloud providers weren't following that example and were selling too much compute to a handful of big customers instead of spreading it across many buyers. "You are not establishing the value of my products," Huang said.Ad

Whether Huang left voluntarily because the situation was slipping away from him, which seems unlikely, or whether the board saw an opportunity to use the affairs as leverage, hasn't been reported.Ad

Separately, the spy allegations involving Alice Huang rest on shaky ground, according to CNN. The intelligence gathered so far doesn't prove she actually worked as a spy for Beijing. Even within the US government, there's disagreement about the strength of the evidence.

article_content_zh:
《华尔街日报》的一篇报道表明，黄仁勋被驱逐的更多原因是他的商业行为，而不是他的事务。

据《华尔街日报》报道，英伟达在黄仁勋的领导下建立了一项高风险信贷计划。该公司为人工智能云提供商和数据中心开发商提供了数十亿美元的财务担保，以便他们能够买得起 Nvidia 芯片。黄的女婿尼科·卡普雷斯 (Nico Caprez) 推动了该计划，并向合作伙伴承诺快速关闭。作为回报，云提供商应该向英伟达提供一定的收入分成。

最大的一笔交易涉及与 OpenAI 就俄亥俄州数据中心 2500 亿美元的担保进行谈判。交易公开后，英伟达股价下跌 5%。随后，曾担任首席财务官的临时首席执行官科莱特·克雷斯 (Colette Kress) 将 Nvidia 对 OpenAI 的承诺削减了一半。缩减规模的协议于八月签署。

据《华尔街日报》报道，克雷斯已经在内部质疑这些担保的价值以及它们将返回什么，并试图控制卡普雷兹。据报道，在 8 月份的一次会议上，黄称她为“车灯下的鹿”，并斥责她只是一个“汇报的首席财务官”，无法帮助他制定战略或决策。至少从去年开始，英伟达和其他云和芯片公司的循环人工智能交易就因吹大泡沫而受到批评。

据报道，英伟达的股票估值也让黄仁勋感到沮丧。 5 月至 10 月期间，该公司的平均月度股票市盈率从 23 倍下降至 16 倍，英伟达采取了其历史上最大规模的股票回购作为回应。

主要云提供商计划采用替代芯片并减少对 Nvidia 的依赖。随着英伟达承诺购买大量晶圆和内存，黄仁勋将这一威胁描述为向芯片制造商滚滚而来的“雪崩”。

10 月份在柏林举行的 GTC 会议上，黄用一个关于日本汤供应商的故事向六位云首席执行官施加压力。他说他排了很长的队，吃了一生中最好的汤之一。当他要求再来一份时，摊贩拒绝了，因为太多人在等待，而他的汤已经用完了。据《华尔街日报》报道，黄告诉首席执行官们：“他是一个比你们所有人都更好的商人。”

这个故事背后的原因是，汤贩并没有把他的全部库存卖给一两个顾客。他保持高价格并扩大客户群。黄说，云提供商没有效仿这个例子，而是向少数大客户出售过多的计算，而不是将其分散给许多买家。黄说：“你没有确立我产品的价值。”

黄是否自愿离开是因为形势正在从他身边溜走（这似乎不太可能），或者董事会是否看到了利用这一事件作为杠杆的机会，目前尚未报道。

另外，据美国有线电视新闻网 (CNN) 报道，涉及爱丽丝·黄 (Alice Huang) 的间谍指控站不住脚。到目前为止收集到的情报并不能证明她实际上是北京的间谍。即使在美国政府内部，对于证据的强度也存在分歧。
