title: Silicon Valley Is Still Defending Jensen Huang
title_en: Silicon Valley Is Still Defending Jensen Huang
author: Wired AI
article_content:
News of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security was first met with a muted response in Silicon Valley—including inside Nvidia itself. Huang’s resignation, after news of two other alleged romantic relationships with Nvidia staffers, has left both the company and the broader AI industry stunned.

As revelations about Huang’s initial affair came out earlier this week, rank-and-file Nvidia employees at first pursued business as usual, according to two current and three former employees at the chipmaker, speaking anonymously to protect relationships at the company. They trusted the board to investigate and act accordingly, but few workers thought Huang would actually leave.

Nvidia’s roughly 60,000 employees are loyal to the point that its global turnover rate is reportedly among the lowest in tech. Workers say they have heard it called having “green in your blood” or being “green-pilled” or on “team green,” referring to the company’s signature color. Huang was the company’s soul and the founder who stuck with it through challenges for 33 years. Employees appreciated that he kept layoffs rare and red tape sparing.

“In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” one employee said. One former employee insisted in Huang’s defense that something “more sinister” must have been in play, and that affairs alone shouldn’t have led to his departure.

Huang’s peers in Silicon Valley echoed that sentiment, remaining vocal in their support of the embattled CEO even after his ouster. “One mistake does not erase a lifetime of leadership and contribution in building NVDA,” venture capitalist Antonio Gracias wrote on X earlier this week, using the company’s ticker symbol.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang has also had an extramarital affair with a vice president at Nvidia, and Reuters revealed on Thursday a second “intimate relationship” with an employee. Before those alleged affairs became public, multiple industry executives told WIRED that Huang is “irreplaceable” and that his biggest mistake, aside from his relationship with Alice Huang, was admitting the affair in writing to the whole company.

That appears to still be the prevailing sentiment. “A founder who has spent 30 years building such a unique company so capably has earned the presumption that he should keep leading it,” venture capitalist Sarah Guo wrote on X after Huang resigned, and a few hours before the Reuters report.

Authorities and Nvidia’s board have yet to formally accuse Huang of wrongdoing in his interactions with the businesswoman and suspected intelligence asset Alice Huang, and China has denied that she’s a spy. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the FBI “is looking into it.” Nvidia’s board has stated that it doesn’t believe Huang compromised any secrets, but it has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate.

Add to all that, some corners of Nvidia had already been whispering about the relationship with Alice Huang; one venture capitalist who declined to be named recalled a recent dinner where an Nvidia executive claimed there had been rumors about Jensen’s romantic relationship with a young Asian woman.

On Monday, the venture capitalist had estimated a “less than 10 percent” chance Huang would lose his job at the top of the world’s most valuable company. “The wind’s going to blow over on this,” they said. “People are going to hate him for three months, and forget this ever happened.”

The big anxiety in Silicon Valley remains the possibility that instability at Nvidia will burst an AI bubble, but analysts aren’t so sure.

The chief executive of one AI company, who spoke on condition of anonymity so as not to affect business relationships, says Nvidia’s recent bankrolling of AI startups and even buying companies such as model-hosting provider Hugging Face has helped prop up the need for chips. A “new professional CEO won’t do any of that,” meaning “systemic risk for the AI trade and AI bubble increases substantially,” the entrepreneur says.

Between bubble talk and Huang rumors, Nvidia shares in recent days have sunk to their lowest point in more than a year. Nvidia reports its latest quarterly earnings next week.

Inside Nvidia, meetings, projects, and the company’s aggressive culture are rapidly pressing ahead with what’s left of Huang’s vision.

Additional reporting by Will Knight and Zoë Schiffer.

article_content_zh:
黄仁勋与中国国家安全部一名涉嫌资产有染的消息首先在硅谷——包括英伟达内部——反应冷淡。在另外两名涉嫌与 Nvidia 员工发生恋情的消息传出后，黄仁勋的辞职让该公司和更广泛的人工智能行业都感到震惊。

据芯片制造商两名现任员工和三名前员工透露，随着本周早些时候黄仁勋最初的婚外情被曝光，英伟达的普通员工一开始还是照常营业。为了保护公司关系，英伟达员工匿名表示。他们相信董事会会进行调查并采取相应行动，但很少有员工认为黄真的会离开。

英伟达大约有 6 万名员工，其忠诚度据说是全球科技行业中最低的。工人们表示，他们听说过“血液里有绿色”、“绿色球”或“团队绿色”，指的是公司的标志性颜色。黄先生是公司的灵魂，也是公司创始人，他在挑战中坚持了33年。员工们对他极少裁员和减少繁文缛节表示赞赏。

“在短短三天内，我们从超级英雄斗篷变成了‘哎呀，我忘了穿裤子’，但没有人知道如何接受这一点，”一名员工说。一名前雇员坚称，黄的辩护中一定有“更险恶”的事情在起作用，单凭这件事不应该导致他离开。

黄在硅谷的同行也表达了同样的观点，即使在这位陷入困境的首席执行官被罢黜后，他们仍然直言不讳地支持他。本周早些时候，风险投资家安东尼奥·格拉西亚斯 (Antonio Gracias) 在 X 上使用该公司的股票代码写道：“一个错误并不能抹去一生对建立 NVDA 的领导力和贡献。”

《纽约时报》周三报道称，黄仁勋还与英伟达的一名副总裁有婚外情，而路透社周四则披露了与一名员工的第二次“亲密关系”。在这些所谓的风流韵事曝光之前，多位行业高管告诉《连线》杂志，黄是“不可替代的”，除了与爱丽丝·黄的关系之外，他最大的错误就是以书面形式向整个公司承认了这件事。

这似乎仍然是普遍的情绪。 “一位创始人花了 30 年的时间打造了一家如此出色的独特公司，他理所当然地认为他应该继续领导这家公司，”在黄仁勋辞职后、路透社报道前几个小时，风险投资家莎拉·郭 (SarahGuo) 在 X 上写道。

当局和英伟达董事会尚未正式指控黄在与女商人和可疑情报人员黄爱丽的交往中存在不当行为，中国也否认她是间谍。唐纳德·特朗普总统周二表示，联邦调查局“正在调查此事”。英伟达董事会表示，不相信黄仁勋泄露了任何机密，但已聘请 Wachtell Lipton 律师事务所进行调查。

除此之外，Nvidia 的一些角落已经开始窃窃私语与 Alice Huang 的关系；一位不愿透露姓名的风险投资家回忆起最近的一次晚宴，一位英伟达高管声称有传言称詹森与一位年轻的亚洲女性有恋情。

周一，这位风险投资家估计黄仁勋失去全球最有价值公司高层职位的可能性“不到 10%”。 “风会吹过来的，”他们说。 “人们会恨他三个月，然后忘记这件事曾经发生过。”

硅谷最大的担忧仍然是英伟达的不稳定可能会戳破人工智能泡沫，但分析师并不那么确定。

一家人工智能公司的首席执行官不愿透露姓名，以免影响业务关系，他表示，英伟达最近向人工智能初创公司提供资金，甚至收购了模型托管提供商 Hugging Face 等公司，这有助于支撑对芯片的需求。这位企业家表示，“新的职业首席执行官不会做任何事情”，这意味着“人工智能贸易和人工智能泡沫的系统性风险大幅增加”。

在泡沫言论和黄传言之间，英伟达股价最近几天跌至一年多来的最低点。英伟达下周将公布最新季度财报。

在英伟达内部，会议、项目和公司积极进取的文化正在迅速推进黄仁勋仅存的愿景。

title: Jensen Huang Is Out. Will Nvidia’s Rivals Cash In?
title_en: Jensen Huang Is Out. Will Nvidia’s Rivals Cash In?
author: Wired AI
article_content:
Meet Colette Kress, Nvidia’s New Interim CEO

Jensen Huang Basically Lit More Than $1 Trillion on Fire in Less Than a Month

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at uncannyvalley@wired.com.

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Zoë Schiffer: I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Brian Barrett: We're bringing you an extra episode this week because Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, has officially resigned. His resignation caps a swift, stunning fall for the man who spent more than three decades building a company into the engine of the AI boom. We're going to talk about how a board known for deferring to its celebrity CEO finally changed its tune and who's going to be running Nvidia, at least for now. Let's get started. Just for the room, we released a podcast this morning before this happened and then it happened. So now we're talking again.

Leah Feiger: I mean, who doesn't want multiple offerings from the Uncanny Valley crew, Brian?

Brian Barrett: It's true. Constant updates. We're going to do an hourly podcast from now on, just iterative, getting real in the weeds. No. How surprised is everybody that this happened? And I guess first, if you want some setup about what happened, you can listen to our previous episode, but I guess I'll first say really quickly, Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who was selling a lot of chips to—and then a report came out that he had another affair allegedly with someone who reported directly to him at Nvidia, and that feels like the final straw. So we're caught up. Are we surprised still?

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, the first thing to say is the company does have rules on the books saying that you're not supposed to have a relationship with a direct report. And so when we talked and it was the Chinese spy, although that is the obviously more scandalous thing that has happened, it also really felt to me like Jensen was going to weather that storm. But then when the second affair came out, that felt like it gave the board a really good excuse if they needed one to say, "OK, we have to stop." And I think it's fair to say here that while there is no current reporting on additional affairs, I think the concern is if two have already come out, what if more continued to become public and they need to stop the bleeding?

Leah Feiger: But he still fought pretty hard to retain his role, right?

Zoë Schiffer: I don't think the board wanted him to resign. I don't think Jensen wanted to resign. I think that their backs were completely against the wall on this one. The company has already been through an incredibly embarrassing scandal that will drag out for the next many months as Jensen is dragged before the Senate and has to answer to people who have serious concerns about his advocacy for China and where the Nvidia chips have been going and all of that. Now there's a second affair again with a direct report, and I think that the situation became very, very quickly untenable for everyone involved.

Leah Feiger: Absolutely. And now Nvidia has a new CEO in the name of CFO Colette Kress. Tell me about her.

Brian Barrett: Interim. So yeah, she'll be there for the time being, but she's been at Nvidia for a long time. She's been there since 2013, which means that she's worked closely with Jensen since before the company was the darling of the AI world back when it was a graphics processor for gaming laptops company. She was at Cisco and Microsoft before that. She's a real industry veteran. I think my understanding is she's really a classic CFO. I don't know if she's a long-term visionary leader of this company, but she knows Nvidia inside and out. And I think if you're looking for stability and you're looking for someone who's not going to create new drama and who's not going to have a scandal, that seems like she really fits that bill.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I think what they need right now is stability, like you said. They need someone to take the reins. They don't want anything else dramatic to happen to the company. And of course they're going to immediately kick off a search for a new visionary leader, which as we said in the last episode, there's not an obvious successor here. They've got to find someone who has incredible technical prowess, who has a real vision for where the AI industry is going and who will be able to learn Nvidia's business. I think it's doubtful that person.. Well, actually, I really should have learned from this experience that I shouldn't have hot takes. I was going to say, I don't think the person's going to come from—

Zoë Schiffer.. Nvidia internally, but what do we know at this point? It could be anything. So yeah, Colette will take the reins for the moment, and the company needs to weather this storm and come out the other side.

Brian Barrett: And I think she does, as you might have guessed she's going to be operating the business the way Jensen had, at least in terms of advocating for closer collaboration with China and the business lines that Nvidia has been going down, leaning more into CPUs recently, open source. I don't think you're going to expect anything other than business as usual. And when you have her in there, as we talked before, China is so important to Nvidia's future. Jensen Huang had lost all credibility on that point. So having someone in there who can make the case that, hey, we should have a better relationship with China, we should be able to sell more to China, who is not compromised in the way that Jensen has been, that's an upside. I mean, it's a lot of downside for Nvidia that Jensen's gone, but at least they can come into these conversations without that baggage. I think that's the main point here.

Leah Feiger: And perhaps even right the ship even slightly. I mean, with news of Jensen's departure, Nvidia's stock plunged, absolutely plunged, but one of Kress' big roles as CFO was communicating with Wall Street. So I'm assuming that there's a world where this could be slightly reassuring to investors, perhaps.

Brian Barrett: I think so. The thing about the market, I guess, is that everything's always baked in. The market has already accounted for so much. So it did take a big plunge. I think as we're recording this, it had been stabilizing a little bit. I shouldn't say that, because by the time this is out, it's going to go wildly in one direction or another.

Leah Feiger: It means it's a time for another emergency pod. We're just going to keep this going all day.

Brian Barrett: We're going to have to do another emergency pod. Exactly. All day. Get ready, folks.

Zoë Schiffer: We have been talking a lot though about how interconnected, not just the AI industry is, but the entire US economy, how tied up it is with just a few companies. And Nvidia really is, it's kind of Nvidia and Anthropic that so much of this is riding on. And so I think we have yet to see what the ramifications of this will be if Nvidia is able, like we said, to weather the storm, continue growing and leading the AI boom. It has been, perhaps it won't be dire, but so much of what has happened already has been completely unexpected for everyone involved so that I think there's a lot of uncertainty and instability that we still have yet to account for.

Leah Feiger: So from the politics side, I can see this very much impacting the White House's relationship with AI-related firms. I can just see this becoming a thing and we're going to continue reporting this out, but WIRED is keeping a very close eye on what this means for these relationships. Talk to me from the Silicon Valley side, what is going to get impacted here? Is it crazy to say that Anthropic's IPO could get tossed up in the storm? What are we really looking at?

Brian Barrett: No, so here's my thing. I'm not sure about the Anthropic IPO. I think, again, everything's priced in, and I think they're going to do just fine. It'll still be worth—whether it's $1.2 trillion or $1.4 trillion, whatever. It's going to be a huge IPO, one of the biggest in history regardless of this. What I'm interested in is right now, people don't have many alternatives. Even if you wanted to separate yourself from Nvidia because of this scandal for some reason, you're not going to find something better out there for the most part. Some other companies have had some gains lately. So in the short term, I don't know. I don't think that this maybe changes that much. This will be one of the takes, much like Zoë writes her takes, I'm going to regret saying this. I think short term it doesn't do that much. I think longer term though, we've already seen a lot of companies investing in making their own silicon and making their own chips and finding ways to optimize their own sort of hardware stack against their software. I think of it the way that after everyone saw Apple making its own processors and having huge efficiency gains on the iPhone, companies started doing that within smartphone world. Everyone has their own sort of processor in the smartphone world. I think that's happening increasingly in the AI world, and I think that's long-term a threat, not to the industry, but to Nvidia itself. It comes at a time when other companies are really trying to find a path to do this without relying so much on Nvidia, and this is only going to accelerate that process.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I mean, but that was true regardless. This isn't a software moment. I think when Elon Musk took over X and suddenly people were fleeing the platform, you saw Meta kind of seize its moment and launch Threads in a few short months. You can't really do that with GPUs. Other companies have been trying to compete with Nvidia for years, and that competition has only heated up as the AI industry has become more and more powerful and there's more and more money to be had. But this is some of the most complex technology on the planet, and so you cannot just see an opportunity and turn it around really, really fast. It takes years of research and manufacturing. And so I think there already was this opportunity for other companies to come in and try and grab some of Nvidia's market share, and I'm sure they will try and capitalize on the moment, but it's not going to be as easy as other examples we've seen in recent history.

Brian Barrett: Oh, for sure. But I think it's more like if you're OpenAI and you're like, "I've been dabbling with making my own chips." I think then you go from dabbling to saying, "Oh, maybe there's more urgency here, and I need to put more behind that." So I agree with you 100 percent. I just think it maybe accelerates and changes the way some people are thinking about how they go forward.

Leah Feiger: Yeah. And the people that are already doing it, I mean, is Lisa Su from AMD doing a victory lap right now? I assume that she's ordered balloons.

Zoë Schiffer: Isn't Jensen her cousin or something?

Brian Barrett: Great Thanksgiving coming up.

Leah Feiger: Has this happened before, you guys? I mean, I know that CEOs have stepped down over in some ways less. The spy of it all makes it extra fun here. Have we built the entire US economy around the very horny behavior of a very powerful man?

Brian Barrett: I don't know if we built it around.. Yes? We've built it. I would say—

Leah Feiger: I'm asking the questions our listeners want to know.

Brian Barrett: I would tweak the sentence, we've built the economy around the behavior of a horny man, not around the horny behavior of a man. Does that make sense?

Brian Barrett: Just trying to diagram that.

Leah Feiger: All right. Good editing. Good editing.

Brian Barrett: I'm just trying to diagram that sentence a little bit out. I want to hear what Zoë has to say about this too. I think we talked about this a little bit yesterday where yes, so much of the economy relies on too few companies right now, Nvidia being the main sort of bulwark there, but also so interesting, I think we wouldn't have seen this at other companies in that other tech companies are set up where their CEOs are untouchable and Jensen is not. So Jensen owns 3.5 percent or so of Nvidia. The board can do this. If Mark Zuckerberg could do anything short of getting arrested and still be in charge of Meta, there's just no recourse. Elon will be in charge of his companies for as long as he wants. So I think there's the fact that there was even an opportunity for accountability here is in and of itself interesting in a way that's sad. You know what I mean? There should be accountability everywhere, but that's not how these companies are set up.

Leah Feiger: And perhaps that's why it's so shocking. We never get to see accountability in this manner and speed.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. I feel like there are examples of really unexpected departures or departures that were expected, but still came as a real shock. Even Steve Jobs, which it was known that he was very ill for a long time, but he was so synonymous with Apple and Apple's success before his death, and yet he had this really solid bench of potential executives who could come in and take his place, maybe not completely, maybe not with the total vision, but Apple would and did continue to grow. I think the moment that I think of more right now is Sam Altman's very brief and dramatic ouster from OpenAI, because that one like this, no one really saw coming. It was such a shock. It was so unexpected. There were a lot of questions as to why, but of course that took place over the course of essentially a single weekend where the board pushed him out. There were all of these background negotiations, and then ultimately he was able to come back and resume his role as CEO.

Leah Feiger: How long did that take? How long did righting that ship take? Are the stakes similar or different here?

Zoë Schiffer: Oh my gosh. Is OpenAI's ship righted? I think is the..

Zoë Schiffer: Sam Altman was able to come back. Obviously, he was able to remake the board with friendlier people, but I think that Anthropic has really continued to be pretty ascendant and pretty focused in the wake of that, what employees call the blip when Sam Altman left. Whereas OpenAI, it felt like has continued to spin out, have drama after drama and be a little less focused in comparison. I think Nvidia overall is a much more disciplined company. It's not like the AI labs. It has a typical corporate structure. It has very defined goals. It's been around for a lot longer. And so I think these are different and very significant ways.

Brian Barrett: Although Zoë, what they didn't have was a succession plan, right? I think Jensen pointedly, as of he did interviews within the last few weeks or month where he was like, "I'm going to be here for decades. I don't really need to have.. " Well, sort of proudly not worried about a succession plan and a structure that's so flat. We've talked about this before too, but he had 60 direct reports all up to him. So I think it is a little irresponsible maybe. Here we go. I think he probably had a fiduciary responsibility to shareholders to think a little bit harder about what happens if I'm not here. I think that there is sort of this sense of, "I'm the only person who can do this. I'll be here forever." And I see how that you'd need to have that attitude to be the CEO of the biggest company in the world or one of the biggest companies in the world. But the backside of that is we're going to find out if that's true really soon.

Zoë Schiffer: No, for sure. I mean, I think he's been leading this company for 30 years, and it seems like while we are not sure what the board knew when, certainly within Nvidia, there were whispers about these things happening. And like we talked about in the last episode, Jensen had an affair with a woman, a former TV journalist who was running basically a smuggling operation that by all accounts he should have known about.

Zoë Schiffer: He should have known exactly what was going on there. And so I think if you have enough hubris that you can make those decisions and still feel completely untouchable, then it makes sense in that kind of twisted logic that you would also think like I don't need a successor because I'm untouchable. And in fact, that has proved to not be the case.

Brian Barrett: One thing we've been seeing in the lead up to this was Silicon Valley really vocally defending Jensen Huang and saying, "It's one mistake, it's no big deal." And then saying, "It's two mistakes. What's the problem?" And even this morning after the news happened, we're still seeing people say he's an irreplaceable icon. It's sort of like they're trying to take you have to separate the artist from the art kind of argument, but for CEOs, does that surprise anybody that they're still hanging onto this? And I guess I know how I feel. Is that a fair argument? Can you separate the artist from the art in a Silicon Valley big tech CEO context? Does that make any sense whatsoever?

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, this is an area that Silicon Valley is very sensitive about. It's such a founder oriented environment here, and I think that Jensen is the founder of this business. He built this company from the ground up. He started it at a Denny's 30 years ago. So yeah, I think there is a lot of loyalty, not just to him, but to the idea that a founder is a unique type of person and that they bring something to the table that no one else can replace. I had conversations with people that really made me laugh where they would say, "Well, Jensen's irreplaceable and his biggest mistake was admitting the affair in writing." I was like, "Well, I do feel like the biggest mistake was having a relationship with the Chinese spy perhaps, but yeah, I hear you."

Leah Feiger: I also wonder how much this is, I don't know, even slightly a little bit of lip service. On the DC side, Trump has been voraciously defending Jensen, and yet we also know that there's machinations behind the scenes to figure out some sort of accountability measure in some kind, whether that's congressional hearings or other things that could be coming down the pipeline. Two things can be true at once. It's like what Brian said earlier, everyone's saying like, "Oh no, Jensen." And yet they're all ready to start building their own chips or figuring out how to diversify that pool.

Zoë Schiffer: And the interesting thing about a lot of these relationships is they are very transactional. I don't know if we're going to continue to see the types of defenses that we have seen so far, but this is a moment. I mean, the China hawks, this is their time. I feel like it's not conspiratorial to say in some ways they orchestrated this moment in so far as they were instrumental in getting the information out there. And so I think they're going to, I would assume, be using this moment to try and turn Trump more toward their side, to be more anti-China, to not have as many trade loopholes or what have you.

Leah Feiger: And Jensen has been the voice against that, in many times the only voice against that in the room. So I'm really curious to see how this plays out.

Brian Barrett: And Zoë, you've got your kids guesting on the pod, which is adorable, and again, another thing that I think should become a fixture. Thank you for doing this when you've got your hands full.

Zoë Schiffer: Oh my gosh. They would love it. Yeah, they're in the laundry room right now watching Unicorn Academy. So this is honestly the best morning they've ever had in their lives, but..

Brian Barrett: Love that for them. Love it for us. All right. Well, good luck to Colette Kress. Good luck to your 401(k), everybody. Thank you all for jumping on this emergency podcast.

Zoë Schiffer: That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. It was fact checked by Matt Giles and Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

利亚·费格：我是政治和科学主任利亚·费格。

Brian Barrett：本周我们将为您带来一集额外节目，因为 Nvidia 首席执行官黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 已正式辞职。他的辞职标志着这位花了三十多年时间将一家公司打造成人工智能繁荣引擎的人迅速而惊人的陨落。我们将讨论一个以服从名人首席执行官而闻名的董事会如何最终改变态度，以及谁将负责管理英伟达，至少目前是这样。让我们开始吧。就为了这个房间，我们今天早上在这件事发生之前发布了一个播客，然后它就发生了。所以现在我们又开始说话了。

布莱恩·巴雷特：确实如此。不断更新。从现在开始，我们将制作一个每小时的播客，只是迭代，在杂草中变得真实。不。发生这样的事大家有多惊讶？我想首先，如果你想了解一下发生的事情，你可以听听我们的上一集，但我想我首先要说的是，黄仁勋承认与一名所谓的中国情报人员有染，这名情报人员向他出售大量芯片，然后有报道称他与英伟达直接向他汇报的人有另一起婚外情，这感觉就像是最后一根稻草。所以我们被追上了。我们还感到惊讶吗？

Zoë Schiffer：我的意思是，首先要说的是，公司确实有书面规定，规定你不应该与直接下属建立关系。因此，当我们交谈时，发现是中国间谍，尽管这显然是发生过的更可耻的事情，但我也确实感觉詹森将度过这场风暴。但当第二件事曝光时，感觉这给了董事会一个非常好的借口，如果他们需要一个人说，“好吧，我们必须停下来。”我认为可以公平地说，虽然目前没有关于其他事件的报道，但我认为令人担忧的是，如果两个事件已经曝光，如果更多事件继续公开并且他们需要止血怎么办？

title: Google’s new Gemini model is better at understanding complicated questions
title_en: Google’s new Gemini model is better at understanding complicated questions
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google’s Robby Stein says Gemini 4 Hydrogen is ‘the biggest model upgrade to Search yet.’﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google says Gemini 4 Hydrogen also gives users a wider range of links in its responses by “conducting simultaneous queries across all the relevant subtopics.” Its responses have more visuals, too, like images, comparison tables, graphs, and maps. One of Stein’s examples shows the AI generating an interactive animated driving simulation in response to a user’s question about how phones locate which lane of a highway a car is on in areas without cell service. Google says the new model also has improved language understanding “across all supported AI Mode languages.”

Users have more thinking level options with Gemini 4 Hydrogen, as well, including low, medium, high, and a new “xhigh” mode. According to Google, the new model “delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence” compared to Gemini Flash 3.8, and it “matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class,” like Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Terra.

title: Jensen Huang Didn’t Name His Own Replacement as One of Tech’s Most Powerful Women
title_en: Jensen Huang Didn’t Name His Own Replacement as One of Tech’s Most Powerful Women
author: Wired AI
article_content:
The most powerful woman in tech at this very moment is Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia—but her predecessor, Jensen Huang, failed to mention her in a recent back-and-forth about the topic.

Earlier this fall, WIRED published a feature story exploring the complex topic of power for women working in an industry traditionally dominated by men. We questioned why Silicon Valley doesn't have an Elon-esque or Jensen-like female hero (or villain) and determined that the rubric of power still looks different for women, whether they manage to hold significant financial capital, flex their political prowess, dictate cultural norms, or run intellectual circles around the industry.

We also determined there wasn’t just one singular impressive woman in tech, but a whole lot of them: Lisa Su, Gwynne Shotwell, Laurene Powell Jobs, and dozens more. Kress, then-CFO of Nvidia, was also given a nod.

As part of the reporting process, WIRED wanted to include the insights of a few established men in Silicon Valley. So we emailed Huang directly to ask for his thoughts.

He responded that “[Meta’s] Dina Powell, [Google’s] Ruth Porat” came to mind, because he “see[s] them when I’m in DC.” After some prompting, Huang also agreed that Shotwell, the president and COO of SpaceX, was impressive.

Notably, Huang didn’t mention the highest-ranking woman executive in his own company, someone who joins him on nearly every quarterly earnings call and has deeper knowledge of Nvidia’s finances than probably anyone else in the world. As CFO, Kress was an integral part of one of the most valuable companies in the world—one of the most powerful women in tech by any measure.

As interim CEO, Kress now sits atop the bedrock of the entire AI industry at its most precarious moment. The choices she makes while in this role will reverberate across tech, geopolitics, and the broader economy.

Regardless of whether that promotion becomes permanent, we now know just how powerful Kress is in the tech industry—and that her omission from Huang’s list was just one in a long line of bad calls.

article_content_zh:
目前科技界最有权势的女性是英伟达新任临时首席执行官科莱特·克雷斯 (Colette Kress)，但她的前任黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 在最近的一次有关该话题的讨论中没有提及她。

今年秋天早些时候，《连线》杂志发表了一篇专题报道，探讨了在传统上由男性主导的行业中工作的女性权力的复杂话题。我们质疑为什么硅谷没有埃隆式或詹森式的女性英雄（或恶棍），并确定女性的权力标准仍然不同，无论她们是否设法持有大量金融资本、展示政治实力、规定文化规范，或在行业内管理知识圈。

我们还确定，科技行业中不仅有一位令人印象深刻的女性，而且还有很多这样的女性：苏丽莎 (Lisa Su)、格温·肖特韦尔 (Gwynne Shotwell)、劳伦·鲍威尔·乔布斯 (Laurene Powell Jobs) 等等。时任英伟达首席财务官克雷斯也获得了认可。

作为报道过程的一部分，《连线》希望纳入硅谷一些知名人士的见解。所以我们直接给黄发了邮件询问他的想法。

他回答说，“我想到了（Meta 的）迪娜·鲍威尔（Dina Powell）和（谷歌的）露丝·波拉特（Ruth Porat）”，因为他“在华盛顿时看到了他们”。经过一番提示，黄也同意 SpaceX 的总裁兼首席运营官肖特韦尔令人印象深刻。

值得注意的是，黄仁勋并没有提到他自己公司中级别最高的女性高管，她几乎每个季度的财报电话会议都会与他一起参加，并且对英伟达的财务状况的了解可能比世界上任何人都更深入。作为首席财务官，克雷斯是世界上最有价值的公司之一不可或缺的一部分——无论以何种标准衡量，她都是科技界最有权势的女性之一。

作为临时首席执行官，克雷斯现在在整个人工智能行业最不稳定的时刻占据了基石。她在担任这一职位期间做出的选择将在科技、地缘政治和更广泛的经济领域产生反响。

不管这种晋升是否成为永久性的，我们现在都知道克雷斯在科技行业有多么强大——而她从黄的名单中被遗漏只是一长串糟糕的电话中的一个。

title: Claude Meetings lets Anthropic's AI join your video calls
title_en: Claude Meetings lets Anthropic's AI join your video calls
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Anthropic has launched Claude Meetings, a feature that puts Claude into video calls as a visible participant. During a call, Claude can answer questions, generate documents and whiteboards, and log notes and action items, responding in text by default and accessing connected tools when granted permission.

All notes, transcripts, and documents Claude produced are available on a dedicated page in claude.ai once the meeting ends. Privacy controls prevent Claude from joining calls with external participants by default.

The feature is in beta for Team and Enterprise plans, with Google Meet as the only supported platform so far. Anthropic says more platforms will follow. Organizations running HIPAA or customer-managed encryption configurations can't use Meetings yet.Ad

Claude Meetings extends recently announced capabilities like whiteboards and data dashboards that are gradually reshaping the Claude app into an all-in-one office tool.Ad

title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
title_en: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
author: MIT Tech Review
article_content:
Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”

But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them.

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.

Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.

Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”

The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.

Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

福斯特周四在接受《麻省理工科技评论》采访时表示，英伟达的代表告诉伊利诺伊州代表比尔·福斯特，实施《芯片安全法》中所要求的反走私措施在技术上是可能的，尽管一个行业组织声称这些措施“可能不可行”。

福斯特是科学、空间和技术委员会的民主党人，也是该法案的共同发起人之一，该法案将引入地理跟踪要求来验证先进人工智能芯片的位置，以防止其走私到中国。这是正在考虑纳入参议院国防授权法案的三项芯片安全法案之一，在英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋辞职并被报道与一名所谓的中国间谍有染后，每一项法案都重新引起了人们的关注。

2025 年 5 月，《芯片安全法案》出台时，立法者表示实现该法案的技术已经存在，但 Nvidia 尚未公开证实这一点。 2026 年 3 月，英伟达所属的半导体行业协会明确反对该法案，并写道，其对芯片跟踪的规定是“新的、未经测试的，而且可能不可行”。

但私下里，与福斯特合作的英伟达代表告诉这位立法者，该公司可以实施这些计划。

福斯特说：“他们从来没有写过任何东西。”但在关于此类保障措施的可能性的技术讨论中，他们的反应是“是的，我们当然可以做到这一点。”这份对福斯特的私下致谢比英伟达此前公开的任何内容都要深入。

英伟达为其客户开发的其他技术表明，该公司确实可以提供对其芯片位置的准确跟踪。例如，2025 年 12 月，它发布了一款名为 Fleet Intelligence 的新工具，允许客户监控其先进芯片在不同数据中心位置的性能。英伟达向路透社证实，通过这样做，该工具可以显示芯片来自哪个国家，但该公司没有详细说明这项技术是否可以用于防止走私。

英伟达没有回应置评或确认福斯特描述的请求。

10 月初，据报道，立法者越来越担心 Nvidia 在走私中所扮演的角色，《麻省理工科技评论》询问该公司是否可以利用舰队情报来阻止这种行为。该公司拒绝直接回应，而是发表声明：“政府和媒体发现美国受控产品的转移情况微不足道，与中国已经拥有的国内计算海洋相比，只是九牛一毛。”

英伟达最近的事件涉及一些涉嫌参与芯片走私的个人和公司。据报道，黄仁勋与爱丽丝·黄有染，她经营着一家新加坡公司 Megaspeed，目前因向中国走私先进 GPU 而受到调查。据报道，美国商务部对该公司的调查因英伟达的发明而停止。据报道，Megaspeed 从 Supermicro 购买了芯片，该公司将 Nvidia 的芯片封装到服务器上。

起草的《芯片安全法》将需要一种机制来跟踪芯片的位置，可以通过设施检查、公司证明或基于 ping 的定位机制。基于 ping 的技术是最难规避的选项，它要求 GPU 在上线时发送其位置信号。九月，安全与新兴技术中心发现这将是最具成本效益的选择。

福斯特表示，他没有询问英伟达的代表，如果技术上可以的话，他们为什么不自愿采用这种芯片跟踪工具。

但如果该法案的要求作为参议院国防授权法案的一部分获得通过，新的跟踪机制只会告诉调查人员芯片在哪里，而不会在发现芯片被走私时提供断开连接的方法。福斯特告诉《麻省理工科技评论》，他打算在新的一年推出新的、更严格的立法，以提供解决办法。新规则要求获得操作高级 GPU 的许可证，并且在 GPU 连接之前，需要验证其有效许可证。

福斯特表示，与此同时，英伟达的争议加剧了他的同事们对该法案中规则的支持：“在发生这一切之后，公司将面临很大的政治压力，要求他们切实做好芯片实际位置的地理验证工作。”

AlphaGo 与围棋冠军李世石的比赛已经过去十年了，今天的人工智能仍然没有利用让这场胜利成为可能的机制。

title: How Amplitude ships product improvements in 1–2 days with OpenAI
title_en: How Amplitude ships product improvements in 1–2 days with OpenAI
author: OpenAI 官方动态
article_content:
Built primarily on OpenAI models, Amplitude’s proactive product agent, Wave, identifies what to build, helps teams ship changes with coding agents, and measures the impact.

Lift in agent engagement vs. control after one day

Lower mean model cost per dispatch for GPT‑6.1 Sol in Amplitude’s Data Science Agent evaluation.

Model cost for GPT‑6.1 Sol in Amplitude’s Opportunity Investigator evaluation.

Amplitude has always helped teams see how people actually use their products. Its proactive product agent Wave⁠(opens in a new window) helps teams turn those insights into shipped improvements. Amplitude describes Wave as roughly 80% powered by OpenAI models, including GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Luna, and GPT‑Image‑2.5 Flare. Wave turns product insights into implementation plans teams can ship to coding agents, including Codex, then measures the impact.

Amplitude estimates that Wave can help teams ship product improvements in 1–2 days, down from roughly a month. On Amplitude’s own homepage, Wave helped personalize suggestion cards, driving a 160% lift in card-driven sends.

Wave is Amplitude’s proactive product agent. Teams give it a product area and the goals and metrics they want to improve. Wave brings together Amplitude data, session replays, customer feedback, and code to identify and prioritize opportunities, develop solutions, and coordinate implementation with people and coding agents. It then tracks outcomes and uses those learnings to inform the next round of improvements.

Behind that workflow, Amplitude uses different OpenAI models for different tasks. GPT‑6.1 Sol supports the opportunity manager and deep investigations into code and data. GPT‑6 Luna handles frequent, lower-cost tasks such as scanning code and running small evaluation checks. GPT‑Image‑2.5 Flare generates product mockups using screenshots from session replays as visual references.

When an opportunity is ready to build, teams can send it directly from Wave to coding agents, including Codex, with a technical plan and acceptance criteria to guide implementation.

“The idea with Wave is you have a unified platform with agents that comb through massive amounts of session replays, analytics, and code to find opportunities to improve products,” explains Jacob Newman, Principal AI Product Manager at Amplitude.

Amplitude tested Wave on its own homepage, where generic suggestion cards were meant to help users start a conversation with an AI agent. Wave discovered that people often bypassed them: in a sample of 100 session replays, 80 users typed their own questions and only 12 selected a suggestion.

Wave proposed personalizing the cards using recent charts, dashboards, or the page a user had come from. It illustrated the change and produced a technical plan, including preserving free typing and showing generic suggestions when personalization context was unavailable. After a brief review, the team handed the work to a coding agent and A/B tested the change.

In the experiment readout Amplitude shared, messages sent through homepage suggestion cards increased 160% relative to control after one day. “It is a great example of how non-groundbreaking things that just get ignored can increase the adoption of features in unexpected ways.” explains Eric Carlson, Senior Principal AI Engineer at Amplitude.

Wave’s tasks place different demands on its models. A deep investigation needs strong reasoning and well-supported conclusions. A small check repeated hundreds of times needs to be fast and inexpensive. Amplitude evaluates quality, latency, and cost for each task, then assigns models accordingly.

For Wave’s Opportunity Investigator, Amplitude evaluated whether models corroborated findings, avoided false positives, incorporated evaluator feedback, recovered from tool failures, and kept claims aligned with evidence. GPT‑6.1 Sol scored 4.06 out of 5 overall, compared with 3.62, 3.52, and 2.94 for three alternative models. It led on all five investigation criteria and had the fastest median investigation time, at 54 minutes.

In a separate evaluation of Wave’s Data Science Agent, GPT‑6.1 Sol scored 67.5 out of 100, compared with 69.3 for another leading model, at a mean model cost of $1.28 versus $2.63 per dispatch. GPT‑6.1 Sol also scored higher on tool-contract compliance, estimation and uncertainty, and evidence grounding.

For high-volume work such as scanning code and running small evaluation checks, Amplitude uses GPT‑6 Luna to keep latency and cost low. Splitting work across specialist agents lets the team reserve more expensive reasoning for the tasks that need it the most.

For generating wireframes and mockups, OpenAI’s image generation model scored 80.3 out of 100 for solution wireframes, compared with 63.9 for another image generation model. Amplitude’s evaluation covered communication quality, product fidelity, instruction adherence, text and UI legibility, and visual coherence across 15 opportunities.

Customers across industries are already using Wave in beta to identify and ship product improvements. Wave analyzes session and analytics data, then develops recommendations with a proposed fix, technical plan, and acceptance criteria.

From there, teams can control the level of automation. Most teams send bug fixes straight to coding agents, while new features and bigger bets get a human review.

For changes that reach launch, the path from discovery to execution can be short: among customer-launched experiments, flags, and guides, one in four went live the same day Wave surfaced the opportunity, half in under four days, and two in three within a week.

Interpolated from supplied milestones; the curve is illustrative, not individual observations.

“Our ambition with OpenAI is to make self-improving products the way companies build software,” says Skates. As OpenAI’s models get better at reasoning and coding, teams will be able to delegate more investigation and implementation work to agents, ultimately resulting in better products reaching users faster. Amplitude is already seeing it, as agents find and help deliver improvements in its own product while the team works on other priorities: “I think teams will be surprised by how much they can accomplish when their software is working alongside them to make the product better.”

Product updates, practical guides, upcoming events, and more.

article_content_zh:
Amplitude 的主动产品代理 Wave 主要基于 OpenAI 模型构建，可确定要构建的内容、帮助团队通过编码代理交付变更并衡量影响。

一天后座席参与度与控制力的提升

在 Amplitude 的数据科学代理评估中，GPT-6.1 Sol 的每次调度平均模型成本较低。

Amplitude Opportunity Investigator 评估中 GPT‑6.1 Sol 的模型成本。

Amplitude 始终帮助团队了解人们实际如何使用他们的产品。其主动产品代理 Wave⁠（在新窗口中打开）帮助团队将这些见解转化为已交付的改进。 Amplitude 描述 Wave 大约 80% 由 OpenAI 模型提供支持，包括 GPT-6.1 Sol、GPT-6 Luna 和 GPT-Image-2.5 Flare。 Wave 将产品见解转化为实施计划，团队可以将其发送给编码代理（包括 Codex），然后衡量影响。

Amplitude 估计 Wave 可以帮助团队在 1-2 天内完成产品改进，而不是大约一个月。在 Amplitude 自己的主页上，Wave 帮助个性化建议卡，使卡片驱动的发送量增加了 160%。

Wave 是 Amplitude 的主动产品代理商。团队为其提供一个产品领域以及他们想要改进的目标和指标。 Wave 汇集了 Amplitude 数据、会话重播、客户反馈和代码，以识别机会并确定优先级、开发解决方案并与人员和编码代理协调实施。然后，它会跟踪结果并利用这些经验教训为下一轮改进提供信息。

在该工作流程背后，Amplitude 使用不同的 OpenAI 模型来执行不同的任务。 GPT-6.1 Sol 支持机会管理器以及对代码和数据的深入调查。 GPT-6 Luna 可以处理频繁的、低成本的任务，例如扫描代码和运行小型评估检查。 GPT‑Image‑2.5 Flare 使用会话回放的屏幕截图作为视觉参考来生成产品模型。

当机会准备好构建时，团队可以将其直接从 Wave 发送给编码代理（包括 Codex），并附上技术计划和验收标准来指导实施。

Amplitude 首席人工智能产品经理 Jacob Newman 解释道：“Wave 的想法是，你拥有一个统一的平台，其中的代理可以梳理大量的会话重播、分析和代码，以寻找改进产品的机会。”

Amplitude 在自己的主页上测试了 Wave，其中通用建议卡旨在帮助用户与人工智能代理开始对话。 Wave 发现人们经常绕过它们：在 100 个会话重播的样本中，80 个用户输入了自己的问题，只有 12 个用户选择了建议。

Wave 建议使用最新的图表、仪表板或用户来自的页面来个性化卡片。它说明了这一变化并制定了技术计划，包括保留自由打字并在个性化上下文不可用时显示通用建议。经过简短的审查后，团队将工作交给编码代理并对变更进行 A/B 测试。

在 Amplitude 共享的实验读数中，一天后通过主页建议卡发送的消息相对于对照组增加了 160%。 “这是一个很好的例子，说明那些被忽视的非突破性事物如何以意想不到的方式增加功能的采用。” Amplitude 高级首席人工智能工程师 Eric Carlson 解释道。

Wave 的任务对其模型提出了不同的要求。深入的调查需要强有力的推理和有充分支持的结论。重复数百次的小检查需要快速且便宜。 Amplitude 评估每项任务的质量、延迟和成本，然后相应地分配模型。

title: No, AI agents did not discover a previously unknown Maya site
title_en: No, AI agents did not discover a previously unknown Maya site
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Scientists are getting tired of amateurs parachuting into their fields and making ‘discoveries’ with AI.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Armed with a team of AI agents, Google researcher Pietro Miotti claimed earlier this week to have discovered a potentially unmapped Maya site in Mexico. There was just one problem: The site had already been discovered and was published in an academic journal last year. The incident, which sparked criticism among archeologists online, underscores a growing tension in science as amateurs wielding increasingly powerful AI tools parachute into specialist fields, often without the expertise needed to understand what they are looking at.

Local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area.

Miotti said the idea to use AI to search for archeological sites came to him while traveling in Peru, when he began wondering what historic explorers might do with access to modern technology. He settled on lidar, a laser-based mapping technology that can produce detailed three-dimensional images of the environment, and set a team of 48 AI agents to comb through NASA lidar data for signs of undocumented sites. As “Peru isn’t well covered” by public lidar data, Miotti wrote, he shifted his focus to the Maya region.

The agents flagged numerous promising locations, including “one major village [that] doesn’t seem to have been registered” in existing records. Miotti, who described the research to The Verge as a personal side project done without any Google compute or resources, said he then reached out to Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to check whether the apparent discovery was already known, including through unpublished research. Using the agents to translate his correspondence into Spanish, Miotti said INAH told him it had no record of a registered site at that location.

“It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive,” Miotti wrote on his blog.

Miotti stressed that he is not an archeologist and emphasized that the finding would need to be verified with fieldwork. Nevertheless, he hailed it as proof that “we’re on the brink of a revolution across every science” and called for the “entire planet” to be mapped with lidar so AI agents could “help us find the rest.” Had he been an archaeologist familiar with the region, however, Miotti might have spotted a problem: The site was already known, and had been documented in an academic journal more than a year earlier.

“I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.”

Archeologists were quick to point out the oversight on social media. In a series of posts on Bluesky, Sarah Parcak, an archeology professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, stressed the importance of carefully checking findings against existing research. “This is why we have peer review,” Parcak wrote, adding that just because the Mexican government doesn’t have something in its database doesn’t mean it is unknown or unmapped. Other archeologists echoed her criticism, slamming the project for spreading misinformation and taking credit away from archeologists, who have been using advanced digital tools in their work for decades.

“This was a personal project that I was excited to share,” Miotti told The Verge. “I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.” He added that as a non-archaeologist, he had not realized a site not being registered wasn’t the same as it not having been mapped, adding that expert knowledge “is needed to verify what the agents find.” He also addressed the limits of his AI tools: “My agents and I missed it. Archaeologists rightly don’t publish the coordinates of sites, so checking whether a site is already known means comparing images against figures in papers, not searching a database. That’s much harder for agents, and it’s something these tools need to get better at. When people pointed it out, I updated the post and the blog as soon as I could to credit their work.”

Nevertheless, Miotti said this was an example of how agents could be used to help experts sort through large amounts of data. He said he has been encouraged by the archaeologists and PhD students that he said were reaching out to him “excited about the workflow and wanting to know how it works and whether it could help with their own survey data.”

“Our ‘problem’ is not discovering new sites,” Elizabeth Graham, a professor of Mesoamerican archaeology at University College London, told The Verge. “Most of us working in the Maya area know about tons of sites not explored or excavated or mapped, most of these found on foot,” she said. Graham also critiqued the use of the word “discover,” noting that local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area.

While she credited Miotti with doing a decent job of using AI to map the mounds from lidar data — “the interpretation of lidar data can be tricky” — Graham argued the bigger obstacle is funding for research. “The fact is, there just isn’t the funding to excavate or map sites as there was in the past, so in a way it doesn’t matter how many more are ‘discovered.’”

“Just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.”

The controversy reflects a broader problem with AI in science, perhaps most visible with OpenAI’s recent advances in mathematics. While AI tools are increasingly capable of producing genuinely impressive results, they don’t always engage with the existing research those findings build upon. The result can be claimed breakthroughs that have, as is the case here, already been made by someone else, or a general failure to credit earlier work. Even when the findings are actually new, they can lack context a specialist would bring. Ultimately, amateur use of AI tools often ends up shifting the burden of establishing what has actually been found and why it matters to actual experts, work that would ordinarily be part of making a scientific discovery in the first place.

Ivan Šprajc, a professor of archaeology at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts in Ljubljana and a coauthor of the paper documenting the site, told The Verge he wasn’t particularly impressed by the agents’ work. Archeologists have been using lidar and “other sophisticated remote sensing tools for quite some time,” he said, adding that “just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.” He told The Verge that while it is commendable that Miotti checked in with INAH, doing so is “not sufficient” as the institution does not have access to all possible information. “The fact that INAH has no official knowledge of a particular cluster of archaeological features does not necessarily mean that it has not been spotted or even explored by archaeologists.”

Šprajc said that he worries the growing use of AI tools by amateurs could overwhelm archeologists with claims of new discoveries. “Just today I have received an email from another AI ‘discoverer,’ so I am a little bit concerned about being flooded by this kind of message,” he said. He also raised another potential risk of amateurs publicizing the locations of archeological sites: attracting looters. “But as long as these findings do not lead to looting, I don’t see a major problem,” he added.

该主题的帖子将添加到您的每日电子邮件摘要和主页源中。

科学家们已经厌倦了业余爱好者跳入他们的领域并利用人工智能做出“发现”。

该作者的帖子将添加到您的每日电子邮件摘要和主页源中。

谷歌研究员 Pietro Miotti 本周早些时候声称，在人工智能代理团队的帮助下，他们在墨西哥发现了一个可能未绘制地图的玛雅遗址。只有一个问题：该网站已于去年被发现并发表在一份学术期刊上。这一事件在网上引发了考古学家的批评，突显了科学界日益紧张的局势，因为业余爱好者使用日益强大的人工智能工具空降到专业领域，而他们往往缺乏理解他们所看到的东西所需的专业知识。

当地社区通常已经非常了解其所在地区的遗址。

米奥蒂说，使用人工智能搜索考古遗址的想法是他在秘鲁旅行时产生的，当时他开始想知道历史上的探险家可以利用现代技术做什么。他选择了激光雷达，这是一种基于激光的测绘技术，可以生成环境的详细三维图像，并组建了一个由 48 名人工智能代理组成的团队，梳理 NASA 激光雷达数据，寻找未记录地点的迹象。米奥蒂写道，由于公共激光雷达数据“没有很好地覆盖秘鲁”，他将注意力转向了玛雅地区。

特工们标记了许多有希望的地点，包括现有记录中“似乎没有登记的一个主要村庄”。米奥蒂向 The Verge 表示，这项研究是一项个人业余项目，没有任何谷歌计算或资源，他随后联系了墨西哥国家人类学和历史研究所 (INAH)，以核实这一明显的发现是否已经为人所知，包括通过未发表的研究。米奥蒂说，通过特工将他的信件翻译成西班牙语，INAH 告诉他，该地点没有注册站点的记录。

“从旅途中的一个随意想法到墨西哥政府的正式答复，只用了不到72小时。这是迄今为止活着的最好时光，”米奥蒂在博客中写道。

米奥蒂强调，他不是考古学家，并强调这一发现需要通过实地考察来验证。尽管如此，他还是称赞这证明“我们正处于每门科学革命的边缘”，并呼吁用激光雷达绘制“整个星球”的地图，以便人工智能代理可以“帮助我们找到其余的部分”。然而，如果米奥蒂是一位熟悉该地区的考古学家，他可能会发现一个问题：该地点已经为人所知，并且一年多前就已在学术期刊上记录下来。

“我没想到它会受到如此多的关注。”

考古学家很快指出了社交媒体上的疏忽。伯明翰阿拉巴马大学考古学教授莎拉·帕卡克 (Sarah Parcak) 在 Bluesky 上发表的一系列帖子中强调了根据现有研究仔细检查发现的重要性。 “这就是我们进行同行评审的原因，”帕卡克写道，并补充说，仅仅因为墨西哥政府的数据库中没有某些内容，并不意味着它是未知的或未映射的。其他考古学家回应了她的批评，猛烈抨击该项目散布错误信息，并剥夺了考古学家的信誉，几十年来，考古学家一直在工作中使用先进的数字工具。

“这是一个我很高兴能分享的个人项目，”米奥蒂告诉 The Verge。 “我没想到它会受到如此多的关注。”他补充说，作为一名非考古学家，他没有意识到未注册的地点与未绘制地图的地点不同，并补充说“需要专业知识来验证特工的发现”。他还谈到了他的人工智能工具的局限性：“我和我的特工错过了这一点。考古学家理所当然地不发布遗址的坐标，因此检查某个遗址是否已知意味着将图像与论文中的数据进行比较，而不是搜索数据库。这对特工来说要困难得多，这是这些工具需要改进的地方。当人们指出这一点时，我会尽快更新帖子和博客以表彰他们的工作。”

尽管如此，米奥蒂表示，这是一个如何使用代理帮助专家整理大量数据的例子。他说，考古学家和博士生给他带来了鼓励，他们向他伸出援手，“对工作流程感到兴奋，想知道它是如何工作的，以及它是否对他们自己的调查数据有帮助。”

“我们的‘问题’不是发现新遗址，”伦敦大学学院中美洲考古学教授伊丽莎白·格雷厄姆告诉 The Verge。她说：“我们大多数在玛雅地区工作的人都知道，还有大量未经勘探、挖掘或绘制的遗址，其中大部分是步行发现的。”格雷厄姆还批评了“发现”一词的使用，指出当地社区通常已经非常了解其所在地区的遗址。

title: Jensen Huang’s $470 Billion Affair
title_en: Jensen Huang’s $470 Billion Affair
author: Wired AI
article_content:
Jensen Huang Hired a PR Firm Known for Handling Sex Scandals Last Year

Jensen Huang’s Troubles Leave the AI Industry Reeling

‘We Have to Take Over’: Far-Right Extremists Want to Seize Control of the GOP

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at uncannyvalley@wired.com.

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Zoë Schiffer: I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Zoë Schiffer: This week, we're getting into the scandal that has had everyone talking. On Sunday, Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a businesswoman who US intelligence says is also a Chinese spy.

Brian Barrett: The affair has brought up all kinds of questions from what information might have been linked to China to why the White House was previously warned about the relationship but didn't do much about it seemingly. We're taking a step back and discussing what this whole mess means for the AI industry at large and for the future of the chip export controls that Jensen Huang has pushed back against for so long.

Leah Feiger: And after last week's democratic sweep in the midterms, you would think that the far-right would be hiding in the corner, licking their wounds. And they did for about a week, but that's all. Instead, now white nationalists, Christian nationalists, and the Proud Boys have declared that the MAGA movement is dead and the Republican Party is theirs for the taking. We're going to get into what these groups are saying and why they see the election results as an opportunity.

Zoë Schiffer: OK. So this past weekend, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sent a message to his employees that no CEO ever wants to write. He admitted basically that he has been having an affair with this woman, Alice Huang. Same last name, no relation. I keep laughing at that. I'm like, the only way this scandal could be more insane is if they were second cousins or something, but in fact, no.

Brian Barrett: And this is not something people care about necessarily, but it does make writing these stories a little bit trickier because you have to sort of switch back to first names for a while. Anyway, yes, but not the point.

Zoë Schiffer: I feel like it's fairly obvious that they're not related. However, yeah, I guess you do need to say it out loud. The New York Times has been reporting for weeks that US intelligence identified she was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, basically they're like CIA, to gather information on him. Nvidia's board has now opened an investigation into this incident and Huang is absolutely staying in charge, at least for now while this all plays out. But this whole saga has been both a very embarrassing PR nightmare with potential national security consequences, and it has the company on track to lose more than $470 billion in market value over just two days.

Leah Feiger: It's an unbelievable amount of money for an also unbelievable story. Honeypotting in this day and age, incredible stuff. Zoë, I'm sorry to be this person, but can you take us through year by year what we knew, when we knew it? Because this whole scandal didn't just break in the last couple of days.

Zoë Schiffer: Let me go back to 2023. This is when Megaspeed, the company that Alice Huang is in charge of, was created and it splits off from a Chinese gaming company just a few months after the US began restricting advanced chip exports to China. And the reason that this is important is a couple things. Number one, Malaysia where this company is operating out of, almost immediately when the export controls become a thing is identified as a very obvious loophole. Malaysia doesn't have a big AI industry, so if you see big data centers cropping up and they're full of Nvidia chips, you can be sure that those chips are actually on their way to China. And in fact, it looks like most people in Silicon Valley and in the Trump administration were aware of this and it just wasn't a huge deal. The other thing that's worth saying is that Alice Huang was a former TV journalist. This is not someone with a computer science background. It's not the person you would expect to be in charge of a company that becomes a very big part, a very important part of Nvidia's business. So in 2024, Jensen begins appearing in public with Alice Huang. Around this time, they're photographed together multiple times. Their body language is a little bit funny. So there are whispers starting at least inside the company. And again, Megaspeed begins multi-billion dollar purchases of advanced Nvidia chips, which looks a little suss. And I think it's very, very, very difficult, some might say impossible to imagine that Jensen isn't fully aware of where the chips are headed.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. Well, and he also has been very vocal about saying, "I think China should have chips." He doesn't feel any.. Yeah.

Leah Feiger: Few AI executives have had as much sway over Trump's approach to AI and China as Huang, and he's made his position incredibly clear multiple times.

Jensen Huang, archival audio: I did my best to inform the policymakers in the United States of the importance of engaging the Chinese market and making sure that we serve that market for as long as we can. I've been very clear that even though although we compete against China, they're not our enemies. If we care deeply about the safety of the world with respect to artificial intelligence, then of course we must open dialogues. We must work with them in every possible way.

Zoë Schiffer: He was vocal about this before he and Alice knew each other.

Zoë Schiffer: This is a core part of his belief system. The two theories are either you sell advanced chips to China and thus China becomes reliant on US chips and maybe they don't build their own industry or you don't and you hope that you kneecap them in the short term and your AI industry is able to stay far enough ahead that it's not a huge problem. But Jensen had a very legitimate, I think, argument here. Obviously now he's never allowed to talk about export controls ever again because he's going to look-

Brian Barrett: I bet he will though. I bet he will.

Zoë Schiffer: I mean, maybe. Yeah. But it's like China does do this. They make competitive hardware all the time and then underprice it, and so it harms US industry. And I think that in addition to this being a very good business play, Nvidia could have doubled its business because China is going through the same data center build out that the US is. He also had a national security argument that wasn't totally farfetched.

Brian Barrett: I think too, and I think he also, I've heard him argue, it's a related point, but I think if China builds their own competitive chips, then they'll build their own whole tech stack and you'll have this entire world of AI that is largely open source, open weight, broadly accessible that the US is totally shut out of because it's not just Nvidia chips, it's everything around them. Setting the merits of it aside, the point is it's not like Alice Huang said, "Hey Jensen, have you heard about China?" That's not what this is.

Zoë Schiffer: Certainly not. And I think there's a lot of different facets of these arguments, but one that you hear with the open source angle a lot is China will be able to spread its Chinese AI around the world and gain influence by making a bunch of other countries dependent on their technology instead of US technology. And that in and of itself would be a big threat.

Brian Barrett: I think you really can't overstate the importance of Jensen Huang with the China conversation in the US. He is not only the leading voice, I think he's one of the only prominent voices among Silicon Valley CEOs who has taken this stance of, "We should work closely with them." Everybody else is running the other direction as fast as they can. Between that and the Democrats coming in, I really do wonder what this is going to mean for our relationship with China. I assume nothing great. I assume when you lose a voice like that.. Trump is still swayable probably, but who's there to sway him?

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. And to be clear, China has already come out and said that Alice is not a Chinese spy, and how dare anyone suggest otherwise.

Leah Feiger: Can we talk about the Marco Rubio thing of it all?

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, so this is the question. So during Trump's latest return to the White House, he and Jensen become quite close. And this is a switch for Jensen who previously wasn't political. You had other CEOs, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman, who were known liberals, Democrats, and then made a big switch with Trump's return to the White House. Jensen wasn't like that. He was apolitical and then decided to go all in on Trump and they seemingly became quite close. And behind the scenes, Jensen is advocating for his point of view. He wants special exemptions so that he can sell chips to China. He certainly doesn't want Trump cracking down on the Malaysia of it all, this obvious loophole in the export controls. And this makes people like Marco Rubio and other China hawks not so happy with Jensen, to say the very least. And so at some point the government becomes aware that there is this affair going on and Marco Rubio drafts a memo that starts circulating around the White House basically saying, "Hey, this is happening and we think that it's a problem." We don't know who, but someone takes that opportunity to leak the memo to the press and make Jensen look really bad. And the timing of this is crucial because Jensen is more vulnerable in this moment, I think, than he has been in recent past because Democrats just took the House. And so while previously Elizabeth Warren asked him to come testify before the Senate Banking Committee and he essentially said, "No, thank you." I think it's fair to imagine that he's not going to have that option again.

Brian Barrett: And in fact, he's been invited to a closed door briefing by three Republican house committee chairs on November 18th, so that may be coming sooner than later.

Leah Feiger: Let's talk next CEO. Have there been any rumors or conversations about who would take over?

Zoë Schiffer: No, I don't think there's an obvious name. I mean, I've been talking to a lot of people in Silicon Valley about this this week, and I have yet to find a CEO who's like, "They should get rid of Jensen." But, almost everyone has been like, "It is such a red flag that he didn't see the obvious red flags of this random TV journalist who's in charge of this seemingly shell company that is obviously selling chips to China." The whole thing is just incredibly irresponsible at the very, very least. And I think that that's going to continue to come up.

Brian Barrett: I think one thing I keep going back to, which is maybe slightly related, is that Nvidia, it is such a different company than it was five years ago, four years ago. For almost 30 of the years he's talking about, he was building a really great GPUs for gaming laptops business. And it's only in the last three years that he has ascended to the top of the mountain because those chips happen to also be very good for AI.

Zoë Schiffer: Well, yes. And he did make a bet that that was going to be a really important business and that bet enormously paid off.

Zoë Schiffer: But when you talk to people in Silicon Valley who worked at Nvidia 10 years ago, they will be like, "I worked for lame Nvidia. I worked for Nvidia when the stock was like.. " They always differentiate the people who work for this phase of the company, which is explosive growth, leading.. It's worth what? $4 trillion. It's leading the AI industry. Jensen, until this moment, could do absolutely no wrong. And the company before that was, like Brian said, making gaming chips and was like, "What? Who?"

Brian Barrett: Yeah. Not taking away anything from him. He proactively made that bet and is responsible for Nvidia's success. It is just, I remember lame Nvidia, and to see all of this happening to new Nvidia boggles the mind.

Leah Feiger: We have to talk about.. I know that last week, again, shout out to the politics team. Everyone came on over. We wrenched the episode away from you two and discussed all sorts of midterms results, including how the country has really apparently turned away from Silicon Valley. It's been sort of amazing over the last week to watch everyone fully feel their reactions to all of this. Shout out to Palantir CEO Alex Karp, who is now a Democrat once more. Everyone's feeling things is all I have to say. But I would have to add that one of my favorite storylines that WIRED is staying on top of is white nationalists and extremists seeing this as a massive opportunity. So on election day last week, white nationalist Nick Fuentes, can't believe we're still saying his name in this day and age, he urged his supporters on X to quote, "Get out and vote Democrat." The post racked up over 12 million views and hours later when the Democrats performed so well, Fuentes took credit for the victory writing, "We did it again," on Telegram. And he later called it the groyper effect in reference to the nickname given to his followers. He sees the Democratic Party winning as part of a larger strategy for the far right to take over. He's not the only one that felt this way. David Gilbert, senior politics at WIRED, reviewed a number of comments from white supremacists, Christian nationalists, other far-right groups in the wake of the midterm results that shows much of the same. These groups basically said that Donald Trump did not go far enough. That's why they didn't win. But now that they didn't win, this is a way for them to get back in the saddle. I know that this logic is a little bit weird here, but stay with me. There is part of it that I look at and I go, "Yeah, of course there's an opportunity for them." In the last year and a half of Donald Trump being in office, you didn't really need the Proud Boys terrorizing immigrants on the street. You had ICE. You did not need a variety of rights being taken away from trans people. That was happening in the DOJ. So many different platforms that these groups espouse were being taken over by the Trump administration themselves, which they had promised these groups in effect. So all of these folks have been sort of sitting idly by, hanging out, talking to each other online with not a whole lot to do, which in theory sounds nice except for the fact that all a white supremacist really wants is to be needed, it turns out. And now the call to action is here.

Brian Barrett: My first question is you mentioned opportunity and they see this as an opportunity for whatever. These people are also.. How much of it is Nick Fuentes and his ilk seeing an opportunity for their movement versus an opportunity to draw attention to themselves, which is what so often this is about? You know what I mean? How do we separate that out?

Leah Feiger: For sure. I mean, look, I don't think we're going to be able to for a while, but you're absolutely right because there, again, has been no need to call attention to their play. The Proud Boys are like, "Guys, immigrants suck." And the entire Trump administration is like, "We're with you. This is not new info." So the idea of drawing attention, perhaps getting more supporters from people who are so devastated from this democratic sweep is part and parcel of the plan here.

Zoë Schiffer: But wait, just so I understand the "plan," their theory is that they're going to help?? Democrats get elected, then Democrats will screw up their experience of being in power and thus people will be more disillusioned. And in the meantime, they'll be taking over the void that was left by the MAGA movement. And so then when they go to the right again, they'll be going to the Proud Boys. Is that..

Leah Feiger: That's basically it, minus the part at the beginning about them "helping Democrats take over." I'm not giving them any sort of credit for that. This is just Nick Fuentes speaking.

Zoë Schiffer: Right. I'm just trying to understand their logic.

Brian Barrett: It's either tremendous cope or 5D chess, and I think I know what side I'm coming down on. Yeah, obviously.

Leah Feiger: Yeah. 5D chess. It's 5D chess. And that's 100 percent true, but I do want to talk about this other stat that I'm going to spend a little bit of time thinking about in the coming weeks. And I think that we're all going to have to contend with it a little bit, which is that many extremist candidates still won their seats. While some of the Republican parties, extremist candidates were rejected, the Institute for Research and Education on Human Rights was tracking 535 candidates in statewide races who are members of at least one far right Facebook group. So I'm not even just talking about tweeted something one time. No, no, no. They are members of these various groups.

Brian Barrett: And still using Facebook.

Brian Barrett: Which should be disqualifying in some way.

Zoë Schiffer: The biggest red flag of all.

Leah Feiger: Of the 476 races that were called by last Friday, we now have more that have been called. It's just been taking everyone a while to kind of pull everything together. 338 of those candidates won, which is a 71 percent win rate. To be clear, the vast majority of these races saw GOP incumbents keep their seats. These were GOP-heavy arenas, which is all just to say though that extremism didn't necessarily go anywhere, even if part of this is perhaps going to be taking a little bit of a winding direction. The reason I think this is interesting, and we have to discuss it at all, even if it is cope or 5D chess, is 2028 is around the corner. And if any of these groups are able to mobilize in any sort of way, link up with election denial folks and actually get re-inspired by MAGA in general, if, big if, 2028 could look a little bit different than Democrats want it to.

Zoë Schiffer: OK. I'm just going to say before we end this segment that, boy, was I wrong about what was going to happen during the election. Every time I have a hot take as a journalist, it turns out poorly for me. I'm so happy I'm not that kind of journalist, but I just.. Credit where credit is due. That was not my moment.

Leah Feiger: I don't think it was anyone's moment, and that's the wild part. We all said Dems are going to do pretty well, but I don't think that.. There's very few who had any idea about the majorities that we were looking at.

Brian Barrett: All right. Coming up after the break, we have a special edition of WIRED/TIRED this week. Stay with us.

Leah Feiger: OK. It is time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. Whatever is new and cool is WIRED. Whatever is old is TIRED, but we're doing it a little bit differently this week. Instead of sharing our personal picks for what's new and exciting this week, we're actually going to take a look at what seems to be in and what is out in this new post-election landscape. Who wants to go first?

Brian Barrett: I'll do one. OK. Well, I'm going to say in is seasteading, but for data centers. In addition to wanting to send data centers to outer space, there's a push led by a big Peter Thiel investment in a company called Panthalassa that wants to put data centers in the ocean and power them by waves. The reason there's an acceleration for this, of course, is that Democrats are now in charge of Texas, which is a data center hot spot, and also all of Congress. They're going to be passing all kinds of data center bills, probably. There's going to be a big pullback, or at least people are worried about that, for domestic data center build-out. So look to the oceans where no one can stop you. That's in.

Zoë Schiffer: Incredible. OK. Mine is Woke 1 versus Woke 2. Does this mean anything to you? Is that what you were going to say? OK. Well, we can talk about it. I feel like last election kind of.. No, no. The one before.. Wait, where was peak Woke 1? OK. So previously, I feel like Woke 1 was not the most humorous. It felt like the right had the "We're speaking truth to power, we're going to make fun of everything" thing handled, and the left liberals were more sanctimonious, I think we can say. One thing that I saw immediately after the election was, I'm calling it Woke 2 humor. I think other people are saying that now, this rise of, like, "We're in on the joke. We're going to make jokes about how we love pronouns and inclusivity and DEI and own that storyline in a way." I don't know, X that night, Bluesky that night, I was laughing, were some good ones.

Leah Feiger: So good. Libbing out is in. Millennial optimism is back.

Zoë Schiffer: Wow. The gift that keeps on giving.

Leah Feiger: So what's in is this is a bit more predictive. I think this is more a to come than we're experiencing so far. What's in is blaming your lame-duck president. Donald Trump is officially a lame-duck president, entirely shielded from all of his decisions by members of his own party, by members of the content creator community that rallied behind him and helped get him elected. He is now a lame duck. We already reported that people in the same content creator community, that other politicians are starting to throw him under the bus, as they should. They need to for 2028. What happened here has tanked so many people's careers, and everyone just needs to claw right out of it. So he has spent the last few years not experiencing the blame game, but it's here for him, and I can't wait to see where this goes.

Brian Barrett: I'll say what's out, I'm going to add out, is whatever technolibertarian political views you had as a CEO before the election are by and large out, manifestos are out..

Leah Feiger: Manifestos are out. I don't want to read another 20,000-word manifesto from a technolibertarian 22-year-old that's telling me that Peter Thiel actually is the person who should be in charge of my Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. Out.

Brian Barrett: They're out. And instead we have a delightful tweet from Sam Altman just after the election saying, "People should always be in control of the future." And we have Palantir CEO Alex Karp saying that he's always been.. He thinks of Palantir as progressive technology.

Leah Feiger: I think of anyone that works with ICE as progressive. That's always been the case, right?

Brian Barrett: Yeah. They're progressing toward something. Yeah.
